docs.title: New in DualSPHysics v5.4
docs.text:
Novelties in pre-processing tools

  • Advanced particle generation for simulations using variable resolution.
  • Significant performance improvements on automatic normal calculation.
  • Supports output files larger than 4 GB to generate hundreds of millions of particles.

Novelties in DualSPHysics solver

  • Variable resolution model.
  • New mDBC modes: no-slip and free-slip.
  • Inlet-outlet using mesh data.
  • New shifting model with accurate free-surface detection.

Novelties in post-processing tools

  • Variable resolution output is automatically supported.
  • New options to compute several water elevations in the same water column (MeasureTool).

Other improvements in DualSPHysics solver

  • Precompiled library dependencies removed (MoorDynPlus, JVtkLib, JNumexLib).
  • mDBC can be applied to FlexStruct.
  • Filters for output particle data (space saving).

docs.title: New in DualSPHysics v5.2
docs.text:
Novelties in pre-processing tools

  • Advanced method to fill external geometries especially useful for mDBC (filling depth configurable by depthmin and depthmax)
  • Improved management of data for normal vectors (simpler, faster and less space required)
  • Automatic bathymetry from elevation points
  • Initial distribution with degree of randomness for non-deterministic simulations
  • Improved initial density gradient for complex simulations
  • Creates help VTK files with domains of main drawing operations

Novelties in DualSPHysics solver

  • mDBC can be applied now to floating bodies
  • New options to configure mDBC normal vectors in DualSPHysics
  • Lagrangian formulation for flexible-structure interaction (FSI)
  • DualSPHysics updated for latest compilers (Visual Studio 2022 (v143), gcc 11.2, CUDA 11.7)
  • DualSPHysics compiled for AMD GPUs as well
  • Focused waves generation (1st and 2nd order theory)
  • Advanced refilling rate to increase performance of inlet/outlet

Novelties in post-processing tools

  • New post-processing tool for particle trajectories (TracerParts)
  • New options to calculate fluid elevation and depth
  • Calculation of fluid energy with PartVTK
  • Simple definition of measurement positions by execution parameters
  • Calculation of intrinsic and extrinsic moment forces
  • Automatic viscosity setting from XML or BI4 files
  • ViscoBoundFactor is supported by post-processing tools
  • Supports single and double precision mixing of PARTs

Other improvements in DualSPHysics solver

  • CFL number configuration by execution parameters
  • New options to configure an initial ramp for DDT
  • BoundCorr feature was replaced with mDBC
  • Execution parameter for saving VTK with mDBC normals during simulation
  • Chrono features can be used with different RigidAlgorithm options
  • Updates mooring library with MoorDynPlus v2.041
  • GainStroke is applied to stroke calculation for focused waves
  • Add timers for gauge tasks

docs.title: New in DualSPHysics v5.0
docs.text:
Novelties in pre-processing tools

  • New mode to create particles at free positions instead of following the cartesian grid
  • Definition of variables in the XML file that makes easier the particle generation of complex cases with GenCase and the configuration of DualSPHysics
  • Computation of normal vectors for boundary particles (to be used with new boundary conditions)
  • Option to create several layers of particles (to be used with new boundary conditions)

Novelties simulating fluid-driven objects

  • Problems dealing with objects with density very different from water are solved
  • Floating objects can be combined with imposed linear and angular velocity

New SPH formulations

  • Density Diffusion Term (DDT) [Fourtakas et al. 2019]
  • Modified Dynamic Boundary Conditions (mDBC) [English et al. 2019]

Improvements in performance

  • Both CPU and GPU implementations use now double precision for arrays of position and for updating magnitudes
  • GPU executions are more efficient using relative position of the particles instead of absolute position
  • Greater robustness, usability and efficiency of the inlet/outlet implementation

New coupling with MoorDyn++ library

  • Mooring lines can be simulated modelling axial elasticity and bottom friction
  • Several mooring lines can be connected to a floating device and a mooring line can be connected to different floating devices
  • Numerical tensions are solved at fairleads and anchor points
  • Maximum breaking tension can be also defined by the user

New functionalities in the coupling with Project Chrono

  • Collisions can be solved using non-smooth contacts or smooth contacts
  • Multicore implementation is now available for collisions
  • Springs can be simulated as linear dampers or using Coulomb friction
  • New constraints such as “pulleys” are now possible

New rheology models, non-Newtonian formulations and multiphase flows

  • Velocity gradients calculated by a finite differences method (FDM) or an SPH gradient
  • Explicit calculation of shear rates and apparent viscosity for non-Newtonian fluids
  • Viscous forces modelled by the [Morris et al. 1997] operator or the SPH deviatoric stress tensor
  • Combination of Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids (Newtonian, dilatant and pseudo-plastic) using the generalised Herschel–Bulkley-Papanastasiou model
  • Capable of modelling Power law, Bingham and any other non-linear fluid
  • Platform for implementation of any non-Newtonian formulation
  • Up to nine different phases per simulation

Improved documentation

  • New structure of the online Documentation
  • XML_GUIDE for Open boundaries, Chrono, MoorDyn, mDBC and multi-phase

docs.title: New in DualSPHysics v4.4
docs.text:
Coupling with Project Chrono library

  • Collisions between solids (using restitution and friction coefficient)
  • Realistic frictional behavior with a full Coulomb sliding/sticking/rolling model
  • Large variety of mechanical constraints (joints, hinges and springs)
  • Examples can be found in the subfolder examples/chrono

Coupling with wave propagation models

  • Employing the multi-layered piston wavemaker (with SWASH)
  • Relaxation zone technique for wave and current generation
  • Examples can be found in the subfolder examples/wavecoupling

Open boundary conditions: inlet & outlet

  • A time- and/or space-dependent velocity field can be assigned at an open boundary
  • The density at an open boundary can be either predefined (fixed and hydrostatic options available) or varied according to information retrieved from the adjacent fluid
  • The water elevation at an open boundary can be either predefined (fixed and time-dependent options available) or varied according to information retrieved from the adjacent fluid
  • The buffer areas are built to allow dual inlet/outlet behaviour
  • Examples can be found in the subfolder examples/inletoutlet

Wave generation

  • Automatic generation of single and multiple solitary waves
  • Example can be found in examples/main/16_SolitaryWaves

Novelties on post-processing tools

  • The moment about an axis can be now computed using ComputeForces.exe

More help to produce XML input file

  • Several templates are now available in doc/xml_format
  • New and more complete "XML_v4.4_GUIDE.pdf"

Other changes

  • New definition of domain limits (simulationdomain)
  • Numerical gauge during simulation (gauges)
  • Easy way to restrain the motion (DOF) of floating bodies (examples/others/FtRestrictions)

docs.title: New in DualSPHysics v4.2
docs.text:
New structure of package (now linux and windows in only one package)

Multiphase code: LiquidGas

  • Source code and examples

New capacity to simulate up to 65,000 floating or moving bodies

  • Pre-processing and post-processing tools are adapted to this
  • Compiling option for this functionality

Wave generation and absorption

  • 2nd Order Stokes: piston and flap
  • Passive absorption using sponge layers
  • Active absorption: AWAS for piston

New test cases (all can be visualised in Youtube)

  • Poiseuille flow
  • Many floating objects
  • Dike with AWAS where overtopping is computed

New post-processing tools

  • FlowTool.exe; to compute inflow, outflow… overtopping!
  • IsoSurface.exe; now also creates slices

Graphical User Interface using FreeCAD

  • DesignSPHysics: http://design.sphysics.org/

Advanced visualisation using Blender

  • VisualSPHysics: http://visual.sphysics.org/

Other changes

  • Several bugs are solved: shifting correction and others reported by users
  • CUDA 9.2
  • Visual Studio Community 2015 (free)
  • Improvements in the code documentation (WIKI)
  • Improved implementation of floating objects to facilitate coupling with other models
  • New functionalities in the XML of GenCase to create more complex cases
  • New output VTK file 1000 times less heavy to easily visualise huge cases

New license of the code: LGPL v2.1- GNU Lesser General Public License (LGPL)

  • Developers and companies can integrate LGPL software into their software without being required to release the source code of their own software-parts

docs.title: Dambreak 2D
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a 2-D dam break simulation with gauge measurements for validation. A rectangular water column is initially held at rest, then suddenly released at time \(t=0\). The water collapses under gravity and propagates along a horizontal tank. The simulation includes numerical gauges to measure water surface elevation and wave front propagation, allowing comparison with experimental data from Koshizuka and Oka, 1996.

What's Covered in This Tutorial

This case demonstrates the following DualSPHysics capabilities:

  • 2-D simulation setup with appropriate boundary configuration
  • Numerical gauge implementation for quantitative measurements
  • Multiple gauge types (vertical and horizontal SWL gauges)
  • Validation workflow comparing with experimental data
  • VTK output generation for both particles and gauges
Video 1: 2-D dam break simulation with particle visualization (left) and free surface (right).

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a simplified 2-D dam break with:

  • Water column: 1.00 m × 2.00 m (length × height)
  • Tank: 4 m length × 3 m height
  • Particle spacing: dp = 0.01 m

For this case, we use: - Fluid mkfluid=0 for water particles - Boundary mkbound=0 for tank walls

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.01" units_comment="metres (m)">
    <pointref x="0.00" y="0.00" z="0.00" />
    <pointmin x="-1.00" y="0.00" z="-1.00" />
    <pointmax x="4.50" y="0.00" z="3.50" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.01 m (10 mm).

Domain boundaries: The computational domain extends from -1.00 to 4.50 m in x-direction and -1.00 to 3.50 m in \(z\)-direction, providing sufficient space for the wave splash. Remember, this domain setups sets the canvas within which you can draw particles and what is used by GenCase to place your geometries. Practically, it should be slightly bigger than the space required to host all the geometry you have in mind.

docs.title: Fluid Block (Water Column)
docs.text:
<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0.00" y="-1.00" z="0.00" />
    <size x="1.00" y="2.00" z="2.00" />
</drawbox>

Marker assignment: setmkfluid mk="0" designates all particles as fluid with marker 0. Solid fill: The geometry of the water column is completely filled with particles arranged in a regular lattice at spacing \(dp\).

Position and size: The water column starts at the origin and extends:

  • 1.00 m in the \(x\)-direction (length)
  • 2.00 m in the \(y\)-direction (width for 3-D representation)
  • 2.00 m in the \(z\)-direction (height)

Drawing in 3D for 2-D cases

In general, it is convenient to set your geometry in 3D even if you are going to use it in 2D.

docs.title: Tank Boundaries
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>bottom | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
    <point x="0.00" y="-1.00" z="0.00" />
    <size x="4.00" y="2.00" z="3.00" />
</drawbox>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="0" designates these as boundary (solid wall) particles with boundary marker 0.

Selective filling: When boxfill uses the edges to create surfaces over which particles are created. The sequnece generates the following surfaces:

  • bottom: Floor of the tank (\(z\)=0 plane)
  • left/right: Side walls for 2-D confinement (\(y\)=-1.00 and \(y\)=1.00)
  • front/back: Not used in this 2-D case

Tank dimensions: The tank extends 4.00 m in length, which is consistent with experimental tank, in this case.

Overlapping Geometry: Last Wins

Critical concept: When geometry regions overlap, particles from the last drawn command supersede earlier ones. This happens in this example as you can see the fluid and the bounday have two edges in common intersecting at the origin.

docs.title: Numerical Gauges
docs.text: This case demonstrates the use of numerical gauges to measure flow properties during simulation (at runtime), creating output files as the computation evolves. Two types of surface water level (SWL) gauges are configured:

docs.title: Default Settings
docs.text:
<special>
    <gauges>
        <default>
            <savevtkpart value="true" comment="Creates VTK files for each PART" />
            <output value="true" comment="Creates CSV files of measurements" />
        </default>
        <swl name="">
        </swl>
    </gauges>
</special>

These settings ensure that:

  • VTK files are created for visualization of gauge locations
  • CSV files contain the measured time series data

docs.title: Vertical Water Column Gauge (Swl_x02)
docs.text:
Measures the water column height evolution at \(x\) = 0.20 m (within the initial water column region). This gauge allows validation of the collapse phase by comparing the decreasing water height with experimental measurements.

<swl name="Swl_x02">
    <pointdp coefdp="0.5" comment="Distance between check points (value=coefdp*Dp)" />
    <point0 x="0.2" y="0" z="-0.05" comment="Initial point" units_comment="m" />
    <point2 x="0.2" y="0" z="2.1" comment="Final point" units_comment="m" />
</swl>
Configuration:

  • Location: Vertical line from \(z\) = -0.05 m to \(z\) = 2.10 m at \(x\) = 0.20 m
  • Point spacing: 0.5 \(\times dp\) = 0.005 m between measurement points
  • Output: Water surface elevation versus time

docs.title: Horizontal Wave Front Gauge (Swl_z003)
docs.text:
This gauge enables direct comparison with the experimental data from Koshizuka and Oka, 1996, which provides the X-position of the dam tip before wall impact.

<swl name="Swl_z003">
    <computedt value="0.005" comment="Time between measurements" units_comment="s" />
    <outputdt value="0.005" comment="Time between output measurements" units_comment="s" />
    <pointdp coefdp="0.5" comment="Distance between check points" />
    <point0 x="-0.05" y="0" z="0.03" comment="Initial point" units_comment="m" />
    <point2 x="4.05" y="0" z="0.03" comment="Final point" units_comment="m" />
</swl>

Purpose: Tracks the \(x\)-position of the wave front (tip of the dam) as it propagates along the tank bottom.

Configuration:

  • Location: Horizontal line from \(x = -0.05\) m to \(x = 4.05\) m at \(z = 0.03\) m (near bottom)
  • Point spacing: \(0.5 \times dp = 0.005\) m between measurement points
  • Temporal resolution: Measurements every 0.005 seconds (only for this output file)
  • Output: Wave front position versus time

Figure 1: Location of numerical gauges in the 2D dam break case

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="2" comment="Interaction Kernel 1:Cubic Spline, 2:Wendland" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.02" comment="Viscosity value" />
  • Wendland kernel for particle interactions
  • Artificial viscosity with α = 0.02

docs.title: Density Diffusion
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="2" comment="Density Diffusion Term 0:None, 1:Molteni, 2:Fourtakas, 3:Fourtakas(full)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value" />

Uses Fourtakas formulation with δ = 0.1 for density correction.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseDambreakVal2D_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseDambreakVal2D_Def CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseDambreakVal2D_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseDambreakVal2D_Def CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Gauge Output Files
docs.text:
The simulation generates several output files in the gauge directories:

For Swl_x02 (vertical gauge): - Swl_x02.csv: Water surface elevation time series - Swl_x02_Points.vtk: VTK file showing gauge point locations

For Swl_z003 (horizontal gauge): - Swl_z003.csv: Wave front position time series - Swl_z003_Points.vtk: VTK file showing gauge point locations

docs.title: Comparison with Experimental Data
docs.text:
The file EXP_X-DamTipPosition_Koshizuka&Oka1996.txt includes experimental measurements of the wave front position before impact with the right wall.

Figure 3: Comparison of numerical results (blue) with experimental data from Koshizuka and Oka (1996) (red circles) for wave front position

The numerical results from the Swl_z003 gauge show excellent agreement with the experimental measurements, demonstrating the capability of DualSPHysics to accurately capture the dam break dynamics.

docs.title: Water Column Height Evolution
docs.text:
The Swl_x02 gauge provides the time history of water surface elevation at x = 0.2 m:

Figure 4: Water column height evolution at x = 0.2 m measured by vertical gauge

The rapid decrease in water height during the initial collapse phase (t < 0.5 s) is clearly captured, followed by oscillations as the reflected wave returns.

docs.title: References
docs.text: ◆ Koshizuka, S., & Oka, Y. (1996). Moving-particle semi-implicit method for fragmentation of incompressible fluid. Nuclear Science and Engineering, 123(3), 421-434.

docs.title: Dambreak 3D
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a 3-D dambreak simulation with an obstacle. A rectangular water column is initially held at rest, then suddenly released at time \(t=0\). The water collapses under gravity, flows through a rectangular tank, and impacts a building structure positioned downstream. The simulation captures the complex fluid dynamics including wave breaking, splashing, and fluid-structure interaction. you can find this case at DualSPHysics_v6\exxamples\main\01_DamBreak

Video 1: 3-D dam break simulation with particle visualization.

For this dam break case, we use:

  • Fluid mk=0 for water particles
  • Boundary mk=0 for tank walls
  • Boundary mk=1 for building structure
  • Boundary mk=10 for a specific building wall (left side)

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.0085" units_comment="metres (m)"> 
    <pointmin x="-0.05" y="-0.05" z="-0.05" />
    <pointmax x="2.00" y="1.00" z="1.00" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.0085 m (8.5 mm). This is the fundamental resolution of the simulation. Smaller spacing provides better resolution but dramatically increases particle count and computational cost.

Domain boundaries: The computational domain extends slightly beyond the physical geometry (from -0.05 to 2.00 m in \(x\), -0.05 to 1.00 m in \(y\) and \(z\)). This buffer zone allows for proper boundary particle placement.

docs.title: Shape Mode
docs.text:
<setshapemode>dp | bound</setshapemode>
<setdrawmode mode="full" />

Draw mode: full mode creates complete solid or hollow objects with particles filling the entire volume or surface as specified.

docs.title: Fluid Block (Water Column)
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0.00" y="0.00" z="0.00" />
    <size x="0.40" y="0.67" z="0.30" />
</drawbox>

Marker assignment: setmkfluid mk="0" designates all subsequent particles as fluid with marker 0.

Solid fill: The water column is completely filled with particles arranged in a regular lattice at spacing \(dp\).

Position and size: The water column starts at the origin \((0,0,0)\) and extends:

  • 0.40 m in the \(x\)-direction (length/downstream direction)
  • 0.67 m in the \(y\)-direction (width)
  • 0.30 m in the \(z\)-direction (height)

Aspect ratio: The water column is relatively wide (0.67 m) compared to its length (0.40 m), creating a 3-D dam break scenario rather than a 2-D one.

docs.title: Tank Boundaries
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>bottom | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
    <point x="0.0" y="0.0" z="0.0" />
    <size x="1.60" y="0.67" z="0.40" />
</drawbox>
<shapeout file="Box"/>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="0" designates these as boundary (solid wall) particles with marker 0.

Selective filling: The boxfill parameter specifies which faces to create:

  • bottom: Floor of the tank (\(z=0\) plane)
  • left/right: Side walls parallel to \(x-z\) plane (\(y=0.0\) and \(y=0.67\))
  • front/back: Side walls parallel to \(y-z\) plane (\(x=0.0\) and \(x=1.60\))

Tank dimensions: The tank extends 1.60 m in length, providing sufficient space for the water to propagate and interact with the obstacle. The width matches the water column (0.67 m), creating a channel-like flow.

Shape export: shapeout file="Box" saves this geometry to a separate file for visualization and verification before running the simulation.

docs.title: Obstacle (Building)
docs.text: The building is created in three steps: void creation, external walls, and marker assignment for specific surfaces.

docs.title: Step 1: Create Void
docs.text:
<setmkvoid />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0.9" y="0.24" z="0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>

Void marker: setmkvoid removes any particles in this region. This creates the hollow interior of the building, ensuring no fluid or boundary particles exist inside.

Position: The building is placed at \(x=0.90\) m, which is centered in the \(y\)-direction: \(y=0.24\) m.

Building size:$ 0.12 m \times 0.12 m \times 0.45 m$

docs.title: Step 2: External Walls
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="1" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>top | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
    <point x="0.90" y="0.24" z="0.0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>

Building marker: mk="1" distinguishes the building from the tank walls (mk="0"), allowing separate force calculations and analysis of building loads.

Wall surfaces: Creates boundary particles on five faces: - top: Roof of the building (\(z=0.45\) plane) - left/right: Side walls parallel to \(x-z\) plane - front/back: Side walls parallel to \(y-z\) plane - No bottom: The building sits directly on the tank floor (which already has boundary particles from the tank definition)

docs.title: Step 3: Special Marker for Impact Surface
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="10" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>left</boxfill>
    <point x="0.9" y="0.24" z="0.0" />
    <size x="0.12" y="0.12" z="0.45" />
</drawbox>
<shapeout file="Building"/>

Impact surface marker: The left face (facing upstream, where water first impacts) is reassigned marker mk="10". This allows our post-processing tools to more expeditiouly calculate impact forces, pressure distribution.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseDambreakVal2D_Def CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseDambreak_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseDambreakVal2D_Def CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseDambreakVal2D_out/CaseDambreakVal2D/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Fluid velocity
docs.text: Using MeasureTool code, numerical velocities have been computed in the list of points described in the file CaseDambreak_PointsVelocity.txt, which are (0.754, 0.31, 0.02), (0.754, 0.31, 0.04) and (0.754, 0.31, 0.06) using information of fluid particles within the kernel interaction. Numerical values of Vx-velocity in the x-direction are shown in Figure 7-4 for these three points.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat
%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -points CaseDambreak_PointsVelocity.txt/
-onlytype:-all,+fluid/
-vars:-all,+vel.x,+vel.m/
-savevtk %dirout2%/PointsVelocity/
-savecsv %dirout2%/_PointsVelocity

Figure 7-4. Numerical velocity computed at three different locations.

docs.title: Pressure
docs.text:
Pressure values are also computed using MeasureTool in the list of points described in the file CaseDambreak_PointsPressure.txt, which corresponds to locations in the front wall of the structure (Figure 2) using information of fluid particles within the kernel interaction. Due to the use of the dynamic boundaries, probes used for measuring quantities should not be placed at the exact position of boundary particles. The forces exerted by the boundary particles create a small gap between them and fluid particles (\(1.5 \times h\)); as a result, probes placed inside the gap will have a reduced fluid particle population and will produce either an incorrect or no result. To avoid this issue, it is proposed that probes are placed at a distance \(1.5h\) from the boundary positions.

In this example, the PointsPressure_Incorrect probes are placed at the exact position as the boundary particles at the building, while the PointsPressure_Correct probes are placed at a distance of \(1.5h\) (for the default conditions and parameters of the case) from the boundaries. The first probes produce no pressure results as the number of fluid particles for the interpolation is too small, while the second shows the pressure impact by the water flow.

Figure 2: Position of incorrect (red) and correct (green) pressure probes in CaseDambreak.

Boundary Gap

Note that the probes are not automatically associated with the smoothing length \(h\) and their position has to be changed manually if the resolution changes. Also, by increasing resolution (i.e., using a smaller \(dp\)) the gap is reduced.

Figure 7-6 shows the pressure computed at the correct numerical probes.

Figure 7-6. Pressure values computed at different locations in CaseDambreak.

This case also shows how to compute forces exerted against a structure. In this way the force is computed using ComputeForces as the summation of the acceleration values of the boundary particles that form the front wall of the structure (mk=21) multiplied by mass. Figure 7-7 shows the time series of the numerical force.

Figure 7-7. Force (X-component) exerted on the front wall of the structure in CaseDambreak.

In fact, the methodology outlined here was used in for the validation of DualSPHysics presented in [Crespo et al. (2011)].

Finally, an example to use FlowTool is also available in CaseDambreak. Two different domains are defined in the text file CaseDambreak_FileBoxes.txt. Figure 7-8 shows the red domain (RESERVOIR) where the water reservoir was initially created and the green box (TANK) to compute the flow rate in front of the obstacle. The output VTK files named Boxes_xxxx.vtk are also depicted in Figure 7-8 and the colour corresponds to the domain to which they belong.

Figure 7-8. Domains to compute flow in CaseDambreak; RESERVOIR (red) and TANK (green).

FlowTool also creates a CSV file, named ResultFlow.csv. Hence, figure 7-9 represents the outflow of the red domain and the inflow into the green one.

Figure 7-9. Outflow in the domain RESERVOIR and inflow in the domain TANK.

Video 1: 3D dam break simulation

docs.title: Flexible gate (with FEA)
docs.text:
This example reproduces a classic hydroelastic benchmark: a shallow water column is held back by a thin elastic gate, clamped at its top edge and free at the bottom, which bends under the hydrostatic and hydrodynamic loading of the water. This configuration follows the well-known flexible-gate dam-break experiments used to validate fluid-structure interaction solvers, such as those of Antoci, Gallati & Sibilla (2007).

What's covered in this tutorial:

  • Parametric case definition, with the particle spacing itself derived from the beam thickness and a target resolution
  • An open outlet boundary on an initially dry downstream channel
  • Material properties assigned to boundary markers from an external property file (propertyfile/links)
  • Mixed use of norplane (for flat rigid walls) and norparts (for the flexible plate) to compute mDBC normals
  • Coupling with Project Chrono's FEA module, with the beam clamped at the top and free at the bottom
  • Multiple free-surface (SWL) gauges to monitor the reservoir water level over time

docs.title: Physical setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a small 2-D–like tank with:

  • Reservoir: 0.10 m long × 0.14 m deep water column
  • Gate: a thin elastic plate, 0.079 m tall, clamped at the top and free at the bottom, standing at the downstream end of the reservoir

For this case, we use:

  • Fluid mkfluid=0 for the reservoir water, mkfluid=2 for the downstream outlet zone
  • Boundary mkbound=1 for the upstream (back) wall, mkbound=2 for the rigid wall above the gate, mkbound=3 for the tank floor, and mkbound=50 for the flexible gate.

docs.title: Parametric Geometry Definition
docs.text:
<predefinition>                
    <newvarcte beamLength="0.079" />
    <newvarcte N="4" />
    <newvarcte waterH="0.140" />
    <newvarcte tbeam="0.005" />  
    <newvarcte tdp="0.004" />
    <newvarcte res="#tdp/N" />  
    <newvarcte baseOffset="#res" />
</predefinition>

Beam-driven resolution: the particle spacing (res) is computed as tdp/N = 0.004/4 = 0.001 m, ensuring an even number of particles (N=4) will always resolve a reference thickness (tdp).

Base offset: baseOffset, equal to one particle spacing, is used to lift the base of the flexible beam slightly above the tank floor, avoiding particle overlap between the two independently drawn geometries.

docs.title: Domain setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="#res">
    <pointmin x="-1.000000" y="0.000000" z="-1.000000" />
    <pointmax x="1.000000" y="0.000000" z="0.500000" />
</definition>

Particle spacing: dp = 0.001 m, fine enough to resolve the thin (5 mm) elastic gate with several particles across its thickness.

docs.title: Outlet buffer (downstream channel)
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="2" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>right</boxfill>
    <point x="0" y="-0.5" z="0" />
    <size x="0.3" y="1" z="0.02" />
</drawbox>

Outlet positioning: boxfill="right" creates a thin strip of fluid particles only at the right-hand edge of this 0.30 m box, marked as mkfluid=2. This thin strip acts as the seed for the outlet buffer zone (defined later in the inout block); the rest of the downstream channel starts empty, i.e., dry, until the reservoir water reaches it.

docs.title: Reservoir fluid
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
  <point x="0.00000" y="-0.500000" z="0.0" />
  <size x="0.100000" y="1.000000" z="#waterH" />
</drawbox>

The reservoir is drawn as a solid block of fluid (mkfluid=0), 0.10 m long and waterH = 0.14 m deep, occupying the upstream end of the domain.

docs.title: Rigid boundaries
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="1" />
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
  <point x="#-tbeam" y="-0.500000" z="0.000000" />
  <size x="#tbeam" y="1.000000" z="0.170000" />
</drawbox>
<setmkbound mk="2" />
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
  <point x="0.10000" y="-0.500000" z="#beamLength" />
  <size x="#tbeam" y="1.000000" z="0.087000" />
</drawbox>
<setmkbound mk="3" />
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
  <point x="#-tbeam" y="-0.500000" z="#-tbeam" />
  <size x="0.31" y="1.000000" z="#tbeam" />
</drawbox>

Back wall (mkbound=1): a rigid wall, one beam-thickness wide, forming the closed upstream end of the reservoir.

Upper wall above the gate (mkbound=2): a rigid wall segment starting exactly where the flexible gate ends (z = beamLength) and continuing up to 0.166 m, so the full-height barrier between the reservoir and the downstream channel is rigid above the gate and flexible below it.

Floor (mkbound=3): a thin rigid slab spanning the whole domain length (0.31 m), forming the tank bed beneath both the reservoir and the downstream channel.

docs.title: Flexible gate
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="50" />
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
  <point x="0.100" y="-0.5" z="#baseOffset" />
  <size x="0.005" y="1.0" z="#beamLength" />
</drawbox>
<shapeout file="beam"/>

The gate (mkbound=50) occupies the same plane as the rigid wall above it, but only up to beamLength = 0.079 m in height, starting from baseOffset just above the floor.

docs.title: Material properties
docs.text:
<properties>
  <propertyfile file="Floating_Materials.xml" path="materials" />
  <links>
    <link mkbound="0" property="steel" comment="Property for the wall" />
    <link mkbound="50" property="steel" comment="Property for the beam" />
  </links>
</properties>

Try to see if we can remove this material if it is not needed for the simulation.

docs.title: Boundary normals
docs.text:
For the definition of the mirroring surfaces, this case utilizes automatic features from Gencase.

<normals active="true">     
    <norplane mkbound="1">
        <point auto="true" />
        <normal x="1" y="0" z="0" />
        <maxdisth v="3" />
    </norplane>         
    <norplane mkbound="2">
        <point auto="true" />
        <normal x="-1" y="0" z="0" />
        <maxdisth v="3" />
    </norplane>             
    <norplane mkbound="3">
        <point auto="true" />
        <normal x="0" y="0" z="1" />
        <maxdisth v="3" />
    </norplane> 
    <norparts mkbound="50">
        <maxdisth v="3" />
    </norparts>         
</normals>

Flat walls (norplane): since the back wall, the upper wall and the floor are all flat, their mDBC normals are given directly as constant vectors — pointing into the reservoir (+\(x\)) for the back wall, back towards the reservoir (−\(x\)) for the upper wall, and upward (+\(z\)) for the floor.

Flexible plate (norparts): because the gate deforms during the simulation, its normals cannot be fixed in advance and are instead computed directly from the particle distribution (as in the earlier flexible-beam case), up to a distance of 3\(H\).

docs.title: Open boundary (outlet zone)
docs.text:
<inout active="true">
    <memoryresize size0="2" size="4" />
    <determlimit value="1e-3" />
    <inoutzone>
        <refilling value="2" comment="Advanced for reverse flows" />
        <inputtreatment value="1" comment="Convert fluid (necessary for outlet)" />
        <layers value="4" />
        <zone2d>
           <particles mkfluid="2" direction="left" />
        </zone2d>
        <imposevelocity mode="2" comment="Extrapolated value" />
        <imposerhop mode="1" comment="Hydrostatic" />
        <imposezsurf mode="2" comment="Calculated from fluid domain">
            <zsurf0 value="0" comment="Initial Z-surface value" />
        </imposezsurf>
    </inoutzone>
</inout>

Reverse-flow-capable refilling: refilling="2" (the advanced mode) is used because the flow direction near the gate can reverse as it oscillates, which the simpler refilling modes are not designed to handle robustly.

Hydrostatic outlet density, dynamic surface: outlet density is imposed hydrostatically, while the outlet's z-surface is calculated directly from the evolving fluid domain rather than fixed, starting from an initial value of 0 m.

docs.title: Chrono FEA Coupling
docs.text:
<chrono>
    <schemescale value="1" />
    <configfea>             
        <savedata value="0.0001">
            <start value="0" />
            <finish value="10" />
            <precision value="16" />
        </savedata>
        <savevtk value="true" />
        <floating mkbound="50"/>
    </configfea>        
    <collision activate="false" />          
    <nodes>
        <node ref="0" mass="0" fixed="false" x="0.1025" y="0.0" z="#baseOffset" comment="Start of beam"/>
        <node ref="1" mass="0" fixed="true" x="0.1025" y="0.0" z="#beamLength+baseOffset" comment="End of beam"/>
    </nodes>                
    <feafloating id="cylinder1" mkbound="50" massbody="0" type="1" modelfile="AutoActual">
        <beamEuler segments="40">
            <pointA noderef="0"/>
            <pointB noderef="1"/>
            <section shape="1">
              <_size x="#tbeam" y="1" z="#beamLength" />
              <width value="1" />
              <thickness value="#tbeam" />                      
              <density value="1100" />
              <poisson value="0.5" />
              <youngmodulus value="6.5e6" />
              <rgdamping value="0.02" />
            </section>          
        </beamEuler>
    </feafloating>  
</chrono>

Clamped at the top, free at the bottom: node 1, at the top of the gate (z = beamLength + baseOffset), is fixed="true", anchoring the gate to the rigid wall above it, while node 0, near the floor, is free — the opposite arrangement to a standard cantilever, matching the way the physical gate hinges open at the bottom under load rather than at the top.

High-precision node output: savedata writes node positions and forces to CSV every 0.0001 s, with 16 digits of precision, between t = 0 s and t = 10 s (beyond the actual simulated time, so effectively covering the whole run), which supports extracting a detailed gate-deflection time history for validation.

Material properties: the gate has a density of 1100 kg/m³, Poisson ratio 0.5, Young's modulus 6.5 MPa and a Rayleigh damping ratio of 0.02 — parameters typical of a soft rubber-like gate material used in these hydroelastic benchmarks.

docs.title: Numerical Gauges
docs.text:
<gauges>
    <default>                    
        <computedt value="0.001" />
        <output value="true" />
        <outputdt value="0.002" />                    
    </default>
    <swl name="S0">                    
        <pointdp coefdp="0.25" />
        <point0 x="0.092" y="0" z="0.0" />
        <point2 x="0.092" y="0" z="0.16" />
    </swl>
    <swl name="S1">                    
        <pointdp coefdp="0.25" />
        <point0 x="0.05" y="0" z="0.0" />
        <point2 x="0.05" y="0" z="0.16" />
    </swl>
    <swl name="S2">                    
        <pointdp coefdp="0.25" />
        <point0 x="0.08" y="0" z="0.0" />
        <point2 x="0.08" y="0" z="0.16" />
    </swl>
</gauges>

Three vertical SWL gauges (S0, S1, S2), all inside the reservoir at \(x\) = 0.092, 0.05 and 0.08 m respectively, track the free-surface elevation from the tank floor up to 0.16 m as the water level responds to the gate's deflection. Measurements are computed every 0.001 s and written out every 0.002 s, matching typical probe locations used to validate this kind of hydroelastic gate experiment against physical measurements.

docs.title: Boundary Method
docs.text:
<parameter key="Boundary" value="2" comment="mDBC" />
<parameter key="SlipMode" value="2" comment="No-slip" />
<parameter key="NoPenetration" value="0" comment="Off" />

mDBC with no-slip is used at all rigid and flexible boundaries.

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="2" comment="Wendland" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="3" comment="Laminar" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="1e-06" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" />

A purely laminar viscosity treatment is used with the physical kinematic viscosity of water, and the full boundary viscosity contribution is retained (ViscoBoundFactor="1"), unlike some of the other flexible-structure cases seen previously.

docs.title: Density Diffusion and Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="3" comment="Fourtakas(full)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" />

The full Fourtakas density diffusion term is active.

docs.title: Rigid Algorithm
docs.text:
<parameter key="RigidAlgorithm" value="0" comment="Collision-free" />
<parameter key="FtPause" value="0.0" />

RigidAlgorithm is set to 0 (collision-free) here, since the only floating body in the case (the gate) is defined entirely as a flexible FEA beam through the chrono/feafloating block rather than as a classic rigid floating.

docs.title: Simulation Time
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="0.40" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.002" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />

The case runs for only 0.40 s, since the gate's deflection and the resulting water release happen very quickly once the simulation starts, with output written every 0.002 s.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script. As with other Chrono-coupled cases, this requires a Chrono-enabled build of DualSPHysics.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseFlexibleGate_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseFlexibleGate_Def CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU (Chrono-enabled build)
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseFlexibleGate_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseFlexibleGate_Def CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU (Chrono-enabled build)
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseFlexibleGate_out/CaseFlexibleGate/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

Required input file: Floating_Materials.xml must be present alongside the case definition, since the boundary material properties are read from it via the propertyfile link.

docs.title: Results and Validation
docs.text: As the simulation starts, the hydrostatic and hydrodynamic pressure of the 0.14 m water column deflects the flexible gate, which is clamped at the top and free at the bottom, so its lower edge swings downstream, opening a gap through which water escapes into the initially dry downstream channel and out through the open outlet boundary. The three SWL gauges (S0, S1, S2) record the resulting drop and oscillation of the free surface at three positions within the reservoir, while the Chrono savedata output provides the gate's node positions and internal forces over time. Together, these outputs allow both the free-surface response and the gate's own deflection history to be compared against reference data from flexible-gate dam-break experiments, such as those of Antoci, Gallati & Sibilla (2007), which this case configuration closely follows.

docs.title: References
docs.text: ◆ Antoci, C., Gallati, M., & Sibilla, S. (2007). Numerical simulation of fluid-structure interaction by SPH. Computers & Structures, 85(11-14), 879-890.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: 3D Dam Break Fluid Sloshing Wave Runup Wave Generation Dam Break with Debris       Flow interaction with moving debris.      Floating Box       Floating body motion in waves.      Moored Box       Wave interaction with a moored body.      Heave Decay       Free oscillations of a floating body.

docs.title: Wave Run-up
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a 3-D wave flume in which regular waves, generated by a piston-type wavemaker, propagate down a channel and shoal onto a sloped breakwater protected by a layer of armour blocks. The case reproduces a physical wave-flume test, with the piston motion prescribed from an external file and the resulting free-surface evolution monitored by a bank of gauges positioned across the width of the slope. This setup allows the numerical wave run-up to be compared directly against experimental measurements of surface elevation and run-up.

What's Covered in This Tutorial

This case demonstrates the following DualSPHysics capabilities:

  • Piston-type wavemaker driven by a prescribed motion file (mvpredef)
  • Import of complex boundary geometry from STL files (slope and armour layer), positioned and oriented with drawmove/drawrotate
  • Combination of parametric primitives (drawbox) and STL geometry in a single case
  • Multiple spanwise numerical gauges to reconstruct wave run-up along a slope
  • Validation workflow comparing with experimental wave-flume data
Video 1: Regular waves interacting with a layered armour breakwater at t = 7.50 s, coloured by pressure/velocity, with wave run-up visible climbing the armoured slope.

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a 3-D wave flume with:

  • Flume: approximately 7.5 m long × 0.39 m wide, with a piston wavemaker at the inlet
  • Breakwater: a sloped structure (imported from STL) located roughly 6 m from the piston, protected by a single layer of armour blocks (also imported from STL)
  • Particle spacing: dp = 0.008 m

For this case, we use:

  • Fluid mkfluid=0 for water particles
  • Boundary mkbound=10 for the piston paddle
  • Boundary mkbound=0 for the flume bottom
  • Boundary mkbound=40 for the breakwater slope
  • Boundary mkbound=50 for the armour layer

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.008">
    <pointref x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <pointmin x="-1" y="0" z="-0.2" />
    <pointmax x="12" y="0.37" z="0.7" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.008 m (8 mm).

Domain boundaries: The placement domain extends from -1.00 to 12.00 m in \(x\), 0.00 to 0.37 m in \(y\) (flume width), and -0.20 to 0.70 m in \(z\), providing enough headroom above the still water level for wave crests and run-up on the slope, and enough length downstream to host the breakwater.

docs.title: Piston Wavemaker
docs.text:
<setshapemode>dp | actual | bound</setshapemode>
<setdrawmode mode="solid" />
<setmkbound mk="10" />
<drawbox cmt="piston">
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.02" y="-0.01" z="0" />
    <size x="0.02" y="0.39" z="0.55" />
</drawbox>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="10" assigns a dedicated marker to the piston paddle so that motion can later be applied to it independently of the rest of the flume.

Thin solid paddle: The box is only 0.02 m thick in \(x\), filled solid (boxfill="solid") to create a rigid paddle spanning the full width (0.39 m) and height (0.55 m) of the flume.

docs.title: Flume Bottom
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>bottom</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.5" y="-0.01" z="0" />
    <size x="7.5" y="0.39" z="0.55" />
</drawbox>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="0" designates the flume bed as boundary marker 0.

Selective filling: boxfill="bottom" creates particles only on the floor of the flume, since the side walls and free surface are not needed as solid boundaries away from the paddle and breakwater region.

docs.title: Breakwater Slope and Armour Layer
docs.text:
<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkbound mk="40" />                  
<drawfilestl file="Slope.stl">
    <drawmove x="5.95" y="0.37" z="0.0" />
    <drawrotate angx="0" angy="0" angz="-90" />
</drawfilestl>

<setmkbound mk="50" />                  
<drawfilestl file="Blocks_3D_scaled.stl">
    <drawmove x="5.95" y="0.37" z="0.0" />
    <drawrotate angx="0" angy="0" angz="-90" />
</drawfilestl>

STL import: Both the underlying slope and the armour layer are imported as pre-meshed STL surfaces rather than built with primitives, since their geometry (a sloped ramp and an irregular rock/block layer) is impractical to describe parametrically.

Positioning: drawmove translates each STL to \(x\) = 5.95 m, \(y\) = 0.37 m, placing the structure downstream of the piston and aligned with the flume, while drawrotate applies a -90° rotation about \(z\) to orient the imported mesh correctly within the case coordinate system.

Layered markers: The slope is assigned mkbound=40 and the armour blocks mkbound=50, keeping the two components distinguishable in post-processing even though they occupy the same region of space.

docs.title: Fluid Body
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />                   
<fillbox x="2" y="0.18" z="0.1">
    <modefill>void</modefill>
    <point x="-1" y="-0.01" z="-0.5" />
    <size x="11" y="0.39" z="0.75" />
</fillbox>

Void fill mode: modefill="void" fills the water body into the space enclosed by the piston, flume bottom and breakwater, stopping automatically at each of these boundaries without needing to hand-tailor the fluid box to the flume bathymetry.

Seed point: The x="2" y="0.18" z="0.1" attributes give a point known to lie inside the water body (mid-flume, mid-width, just above the bed), which the flood-fill algorithm uses to identify the fluid region.

docs.title: Wave Generation (Piston Motion)
docs.text:
<motion>
    <objreal ref="10">
        <begin mov="1" start="0.00" finish="100" />
        <mvpredef id="1" duration="15">
            <file name="Mov_piston.dat" fields="2" fieldtime="0" fieldx="1" />
        </mvpredef>
    </objreal>
</motion>

Reference object: objreal ref="10" applies the prescribed motion to the boundary particles with mkbound=10, i.e. the piston paddle only.

Predefined motion: mvpredef reads the paddle's horizontal position directly from Mov_piston.dat (fields="2", with column 0 as time and column 1 as the \(x\)-position), generating regular waves whose characteristics are set entirely by the content of this file rather than by an analytical stroke function.

Duration: the motion is read for up to 15 s, sufficient to establish and sustain regular wave trains for the length of the run.

docs.title: Numerical Gauges
docs.text: Seven vertical-line SWL gauges are placed across the width of the breakwater to reconstruct the spanwise distribution of wave run-up on the slope.

docs.title: Default Settings
docs.text:
<gauges>
    <default>
        <savevtkpart value="true" comment="Creates VTK files for each PART" />
        <output value="true" comment="Creates CSV files of measurements" />
    </default>
    ...
</gauges>

VTK files are created for visualizing gauge locations, and CSV files record the measured time series.

docs.title: Run-up Gauges
docs.text:
<swl name="Run-up1">
    <pointdp coefdp="0.2" comment="Distance between check points (value=coefdp*Dp)" />
    <point0 x="5.72" y="0.03" z="0.04" comment="Initial point" units_comment="m" />
    <point2 x="6.81" y="0.03" z="0.62" comment="Final point" units_comment="m" />
</swl>

Configuration: Each gauge is defined by a line running from (5.72, \(y\), 0.04) to (6.81, \(y\), 0.62), i.e. following the slope of the breakwater rather than a purely vertical line, so that the detected surface elevation directly corresponds to the run-up position along the incline.

Point spacing: 0.2 × dp = 0.0016 m between measurement points, giving fine resolution of the water surface along the slope.

Spanwise distribution: Seven identical gauges (Run-up1 to Run-up7) are placed at \(y\) = 0.03, 0.08, 0.12, 0.18, 0.23, 0.28 and 0.33 m, spanning the 0.39 m width of the flume, so that both the mean run-up and its variability across the breakwater crest can be assessed.

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="2" comment="Interaction Kernel 1:Cubic Spline, 2:Wendland" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.01" comment="Viscosity value" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="0" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary" />
  • Wendland kernel for particle interactions
  • Artificial viscosity with α = 0.01
  • Zero boundary viscosity contribution, avoiding unwanted damping at the flume bed, piston, slope and armour layer

docs.title: Density Diffusion and Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="2" comment="Density Diffusion Term 0:None, 1:Molteni, 2:Fourtakas, 3:Fourtakas(full)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value" />
<parameter key="Shifting" value="0" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full" />

Uses the Fourtakas formulation with δ = 0.1 for density correction. Particle shifting is disabled for this case.

docs.title: Simulation Domain
docs.text:
<simulationdomain comment="Defines domain of simulation">
    <posmin x="default" y="default" z="default" />
    <posmax x="default" y="default" z="default + 50%" />
</simulationdomain>

The simulation domain defaults to the extent of the generated particles in \(x\) and \(y\), but is extended by an extra 50% in \(z\) above the default maximum, leaving room for wave crests, spray and run-up on the breakwater without particles leaving the computational domain.

docs.title: Simulation Time
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="20" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.02" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />

The case is run for 20 s of physical time, long enough to establish several regular wave periods incident on the breakwater, with particle data written every 0.02 s.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseWaveRunup_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseWaveRunup_Def CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseWaveRunup_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseWaveRunup_Def CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseWaveRunup_out/CaseWaveRunup/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

Required input files

Both Mov_piston.dat (piston motion history) and the STL meshes Slope.stl and Blocks_3D_scaled.stl must be present in the case folder before running GenCase, since the wavemaker stroke and the breakwater geometry are read from these files rather than defined analytically in the XML.

docs.title: Qualitative Behaviour
docs.text: The figure above shows the free surface at t = 7.50 s, coloured by pressure/velocity. The regular wave train generated at the piston propagates down the flume, shoals as it approaches the breakwater, and runs up through the armour layer, with the individual blocks of the armour clearly resolved by the particle discretisation.

docs.title: Run-up Validation
docs.text: The seven Run-up gauges reconstruct the position of the free surface along the slope at seven locations across the flume width, allowing the numerical run-up (maximum vertical excursion of the water surface on the slope) to be extracted as a function of time and compared with experimental measurements. Validation data were obtained from the CIEMito wave flume facility, comprising both wave surface elevation time series upstream of the structure and run-up measurements on the slope itself. The numerical gauges reproduce the timing and magnitude of the incident wave crests and the resulting run-up excursions, demonstrating the capability of DualSPHysics to model wave-structure interaction with complex, STL-defined armoured breakwaters.

docs.title: References
docs.text: ◆ Experimental validation data provided by the CIEMito wave flume facility.

docs.title: Sloshing Tank
docs.text:
This example demonstrates a 2-D sloshing tank in which a partially filled rectangular container is forced into motion by a prescribed rigid-body rotation. Unlike cases where the motion is defined analytically inside the XML, here the rotation angle is read at every time step from an external data file, allowing arbitrary (e.g. experimentally recorded) motion histories to be reproduced in the simulation. As the tank rotates, the internal water body sloshes from side to side, generating impact loads on the walls that are of practical interest in ship, tank-truck, and LNG-carrier design.

What's Covered in This Tutorial

This case demonstrates the following DualSPHysics capabilities:

  • 2-D partially-filled tank setup using drawbox and fillbox
  • Prescribed rigid motion driven by an external file (mvrotfile)
  • Rotation about an arbitrary axis defined by two points
  • Definition of a custom simulation domain independent of the initial particle bounding box
  • Qualitative and quantitative (pressure) validation against a SPHERIC benchmark
Video 1: 2-D sloshing tank driven by a prescribed rotation read from file (top row) and by an external acceleration read from file (bottom row), shown at t = 0.00, 1.80, 2.40 and 3.30 s.

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a 2-D sloshing tank with:

  • Tank: 0.90 m length × 0.508 m height (0.20 m thick in the out-of-plane direction to give 2-D behaviour)
  • Water column: 0.90 m length × 0.093 m still water depth
  • Particle spacing: dp = 0.002 m

For this case, we use:

  • Fluid mkfluid=0 for water particles
  • Boundary mkbound=0 for tank walls

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.002" units_comment="metres (m)">
    <pointref x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <pointmin x="-1" y="0" z="-1" />
    <pointmax x="1" y="0" z="1" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.002 m (2 mm), fine enough to resolve the free-surface impacts against the tank walls during sloshing.

Domain boundaries: The bounding box used by GenCase to place particles extends from -1.00 to 1.00 m in both the \(x\)- and \(z\)-directions. This is intentionally generous: because the tank rotates during the simulation, the actual region swept by particles is much smaller than this placement domain, which only needs to contain the geometry at the moment it is drawn.

docs.title: Tank Boundaries
docs.text:
<setshapemode>dp | bound</setshapemode>
<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>all</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.45" y="-0.1" z="0" />
    <size x="0.9" y="0.2" z="0.508" />
</drawbox>

Boundary marker: setmkbound mk="0" designates these as boundary (solid wall) particles with boundary marker 0.

Full filling: boxfill="all" creates particles over every face of the box, closing the tank completely on the bottom, sides, front and back.

Tank dimensions: The box is centred on the \(x\)-axis, spanning -0.45 m to 0.45 m in length, -0.10 m to 0.10 m in the out-of-plane \(y\)-direction, and 0 m to 0.508 m in height.

docs.title: Water Column
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<fillbox x="0" y="0" z="0.02">
    <modefill>void</modefill>
    <point x="-0.45" y="-0.1" z="0" />
    <size x="0.9" y="0.2" z="0.093" />
</fillbox>

Marker assignment: setmkfluid mk="0" designates all particles created here as fluid with marker 0.

Void fill mode: modefill="void" fills only the empty space enclosed by previously drawn boundary geometry, rather than solidly filling the whole box. This is what lets the fluid stop exactly at the inner face of the tank walls without having to hand-tune the fluid box to the wall thickness.

Seed point: The x="0" y="0" z="0.02" attributes on fillbox provide a seed point, offset 0.02 m above the base of the box, used internally by the flood-fill algorithm to identify which enclosed region should be treated as fluid.

Still water depth: The fluid box height of 0.093 m sets the initial still water level inside the tank.

Drawing in 3D for 2-D cases

As in the dam break example, the geometry is drawn with a finite thickness in \(y\) even though the case is run in 2-D, since GenCase always builds particles in three dimensions.

docs.title: Prescribed Motion
docs.text:
The tank is driven by a rigid rotation whose time history is supplied externally rather than defined analytically in the XML:

<motion>
    <objreal ref="0">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" finish="100" />
        <mvrotfile id="1" duration="100" anglesunits="degrees">
            <file name="CaseSloshingMotionData.dat" />
            <axisp1 x="0" y="-1" z="0" />
            <axisp2 x="0" y="1" z="0" />
        </mvrotfile>
    </objreal>
</motion>

Reference object: objreal ref="0" applies the motion to the boundary particles with mkbound=0, i.e. the whole tank.

Rotation axis: axisp1 and axisp2 define the rotation axis as the line joining (0, -1, 0) and (0, 1, 0), i.e. the \(y\)-axis passing through the origin, so the tank rotates about its centreline out of the plane of motion.

Motion source: mvrotfile reads the instantaneous rotation angle (in degrees, as set by anglesunits) at each time step from CaseSloshingMotionData.dat, which is expected in the case folder alongside the case definition file.

Duration vs. simulated time: the motion block is declared valid for up to 100 s (duration="100"), well beyond the 8.35 s actually simulated (see TimeMax below); only the portion of the file covering the simulated time is used.

docs.title: Time Integration
docs.text:
<parameter key="StepAlgorithm" value="2" comment="Step Algorithm 1:Verlet, 2:Symplectic" />
<parameter key="VerletSteps" value="40" comment="Verlet only: steps to apply Euler timestepping" />
<parameter key="CoefDtMin" value="0.05" comment="Coefficient to calculate minimum time step" />
  • Symplectic time-stepping scheme is used.

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="2" comment="Interaction Kernel 1:Cubic Spline, 2:Wendland" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.05" comment="Viscosity value" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="0" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary" />
  • Wendland kernel for particle interactions
  • Artificial viscosity with α = 0.05
  • Zero boundary viscosity contribution, since ViscoBoundFactor="0" switches off the extra viscous damping normally applied at solid boundaries

docs.title: Density Diffusion and Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="3" comment="Density Diffusion Term 0:None, 1:Molteni, 2:Fourtakas, 3:Fourtakas(full)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value" />
<parameter key="Shifting" value="0" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full" />

Uses the full Fourtakas formulation with δ = 0.1 for density correction, which is particularly important here to keep pressure fields clean during the violent free-surface impacts against the walls. No particle shifting is applied.

docs.title: Simulation Domain
docs.text:
<simulationdomain comment="Defines domain of simulation">
    <posmin x="-0.5" y="0" z="-0.05" comment="e.g.: x=0.5, y=default-1, z=default-10%" />
    <posmax x="0.5" y="0" z="0.56" />
</simulationdomain>

Because the tank rotates during the simulation, the region occupied by particles at run time can extend beyond the box used to draw the initial geometry. The simulationdomain block explicitly fixes the computational domain to \(x \in [-0.5, 0.5]\) m and \(z \in [-0.05, 0.56]\) m, large enough to accommodate the rotating tank throughout the run without particles leaving the simulated region.

docs.title: Simulation Time
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="8.35" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.01" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />

The case is run for 8.35 s of physical time, with particle data written every 0.01 s.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseSloshingTank_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseSloshingTank_Def CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseSloshingTank_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseSloshingTank_Def CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseSloshingTank_out/CaseSloshingTank/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

Motion data file

CaseSloshingMotionData.dat must be present in the same folder as the case definition file before running GenCase, since the rotation angle history is read from it at run time rather than computed from the XML.

docs.title: Qualitative Comparison
docs.text:
The figure above shows the free surface at four instants (t = 0.00, 1.80, 2.40 and 3.30 s), coloured by pressure (blue: low, red: high). As the tank rotates, the water climbs progressively towards the leading wall, and by t = 3.30 s a clear pressure concentration (red) develops in the corner where the water impacts the tank, consistent with the expected sloshing behaviour.

Two related setups are provided in this folder:

  • Rotation from file (top row of the figure): the case described above, where the rigid-body rotation of the tank is read directly from CaseSloshingMotionData.dat via mvrotfile. A reference Video of this run is available.
  • External acceleration from file: a variant in which the tank motion is instead driven by an externally supplied acceleration time history. This variant is validated against SPHERIC Benchmark #10, for which pressure at a probe location is directly compared with the benchmark data, and the density diffusion term is likewise applied to control pressure noise.

docs.title: Pressure Validation
docs.text: For the external-acceleration variant, the computed pressure time history at the benchmark probe location is compared against the reference SPHERIC Benchmark #10 data. The density diffusion term (Fourtakas, δ = 0.1) is essential in this comparison, as it suppresses the high-frequency pressure oscillations that would otherwise contaminate the impact peaks and mask the agreement with the reference signal.

docs.title: References
docs.text: ◆ SPHERIC Benchmark Test Case #10: Sloshing in a tank with an external, prescribed motion. SPH European Research Interest Community (SPHERIC).

docs.title: Turek-Hron FSI Benchmark
docs.text:
This example reproduces the well-known Turek-Hron fluid-structure interaction (FSI) benchmark, using a flexible structures module. The flap, clamped on to the rigid cylider, deforms and oscillates under the hydrodynamic loading of the incoming flow. This case is built parametrically, and inlet/outlet open-boundary formulation is used with a time-varying parabolic velocity profile. Modified Dynamic Boundary Conditions (mDBC) are used for the whole set of solid boundaries.

What's Covered in This Tutorial

This case demonstrates the following DualSPHysics capabilities:

  • Parametric case definition using reusable variables (newvarcte) for geometry and physical quantities
  • Open boundary conditions (inlet/outlet) with a time-varying, parabolic velocity profile
  • Modified Dynamic Boundary Conditions (mDBC) with precomputed boundary normals
  • Free-draw geometry generation for a smooth circular boundary
  • Fluid-structure interaction via the flexstrucs (flexible structures) module

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a 2-D channel flow with:

  • Channel: 2.50 m long × 0.41 m high
  • Cylinder: 0.10 m diameter, centred at (0.20, 0.20) m
  • Elastic flap: clamped to the cylinder, extending downstream to \(x\) = 0.60 m, 0.02 m thick, centred on the channel mid-height
  • Particle spacing: dp = 0.0025 m

For this case, we use:

  • Fluid mkfluid=0 for the bulk of the channel, mkfluid=1 for the inlet zone and mkfluid=2 for the outlet zone
  • Boundary mkbound=0 for the channel walls, mkbound=1 for the cylinder and mkbound=2 for the elastic flap

docs.title: Parametric Geometry Definition
docs.text:
<predefinition>
    <newvarcte cyl_freedraw="true" mdbc="true" />
    <newvarcte dom_padding="0.1" inout_layers="8" />
    <newvarcte fluid_min_x="0.0" fluid_max_x="2.5" fluid_min_z="0.0" fluid_max_z="0.41" />
    <newvarcte cyl_cen_x="0.2" cyl_cen_z="0.2" cyl_radius="0.05" />
    <newvarcte struc_min_x="#cyl_cen_x" struc_max_x="0.6" struc_min_z="0.19" struc_max_z="0.21" />
</predefinition>

Reusable variables: newvarcte defines named constants (#cyl_radius, #fluid_max_x, etc.) that are referenced throughout the rest of the geometry and execution blocks. This keeps the channel size, cylinder position, flap dimensions and switches such as mdbc and cyl_freedraw centralised in one place, so the whole case can be resized or reconfigured by editing only these few lines.

Switches: mdbc="true" and cyl_freedraw="true" are boolean-style flags used later in the file (via #eval(...) and setfrdrawmode) to toggle the boundary method and the cylinder drawing mode without duplicating geometry commands.

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.0025" units_comment="metres (m)">
    <pointref x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <pointmin x="#fluid_min_x-(inout_layers+4)*Dp-dom_padding" y="0.0" z="#fluid_min_z-dom_padding" />
    <pointmax x="#fluid_max_x+(inout_layers+4)*Dp+dom_padding" y="0.0" z="#fluid_max_z+dom_padding" />
</definition>

Particle spacing (dp): The inter-particle distance is 0.0025 m, which fine enough to resolve the boundary layer around the cylinder and the bending of the thin flap. However, a particle size of about 1mm is required to compare against literature results.

Domain sized from variables: the placement domain is computed directly from the fluid extents, the number of inlet/outlet particle layers (inout_layers) and a general dom_padding, guaranteeing enough space for the open-boundary buffer zones on both sides of the channel.

docs.title: Geometry for mDBC Normals
docs.text:
<list name="GeometryForNormals">
    <setactive drawpoints="0" drawshapes="1"/>
    <setshapemode>actual | bound</setshapemode>
    <setnormalinvert invert="true" />
    <setmkbound mk="0" />
    <drawbox>
        <boxfill>top | bottom</boxfill>
        <point x="#tank_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#tank_min_z+Dp/2" />
        <size x="#tank_max_x-tank_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#tank_max_z-tank_min_z-Dp" />
    </drawbox>
    <setnormalinvert invert="false" />
    <setmkbound mk="1" />
    <drawcylinder radius="#cyl_radius+Dp/2">
        <point x="#cyl_cen_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#cyl_cen_z" />
        <point x="#cyl_cen_x" y="#dom_padding" z="#cyl_cen_z" />
    </drawcylinder>
    <setmkbound mk="2" />
    <drawbox>
        <boxfill>top | bottom | right</boxfill>
        <point x="#struc_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#struc_min_z-Dp/2" />
        <size x="#struc_max_x-struc_min_x+Dp/2" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#struc_max_z-struc_min_z+Dp" />
    </drawbox>
    <shapeout file="hdp" />
    <resetdraw />
</list>

Purpose: this reusable command list does not generate the final simulation particles; it draws a slightly offset version of the walls, cylinder and flap (note the +Dp/2 offsets) purely to produce the hdp shape file used afterwards to compute accurate boundary normals for mDBC.

Normal orientation: setnormalinvert flips the normal direction for the channel walls (which face inward) relative to the cylinder and flap (which face outward), ensuring all boundary normals point consistently into the fluid domain.

Isolated execution: because this geometry is only needed for the normals calculation, it is defined as a named list and executed with runlist from the main command sequence, then reset with resetdraw so it does not persist as part of the actual case geometry.

docs.title: Main Geometry
docs.text:
<newvarcte tank_min_x="#fluid_min_x-(inout_layers+4)*Dp" tank_min_z="#fluid_min_z" />
<newvarcte tank_max_x="#fluid_max_x+(inout_layers+4)*Dp" tank_max_z="#fluid_max_z" />
<runlist name="GeometryForNormals" />
<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="#fluid_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#fluid_min_z" />
    <size x="#fluid_max_x-fluid_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#fluid_max_z-fluid_min_z" />
</drawbox>
<setmkfluid mk="1" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>left</boxfill>
    <point x="#fluid_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#fluid_min_z" />
    <size x="#fluid_max_x-fluid_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#fluid_max_z-fluid_min_z" />
</drawbox>
<setmkfluid mk="2" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>right</boxfill>
    <point x="#fluid_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#fluid_min_z" />
    <size x="#fluid_max_x-fluid_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#fluid_max_z-fluid_min_z" />
</drawbox>
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>top | bottom</boxfill>
    <point x="#tank_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#tank_min_z" />
    <size x="#tank_max_x-tank_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#tank_max_z-tank_min_z" />
    <layers vdp="0,1,2,3,4" />
</drawbox>
<setfrdrawmode auto="#cyl_freedraw" />
<setmkbound mk="1" />
<drawcylinder radius="#cyl_radius">
    <point x="#cyl_cen_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#cyl_cen_z" />
    <point x="#cyl_cen_x" y="#dom_padding" z="#cyl_cen_z" />
</drawcylinder>
<setfrdrawmode auto="false" />
<setmkbound mk="2" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="#struc_min_x" y="#-dom_padding" z="#struc_min_z" />
    <size x="#struc_max_x-struc_min_x" y="#2*dom_padding" z="#struc_max_z-struc_min_z" />
</drawbox>

Bulk fluid: setmkfluid mk="0" fills the whole channel cross-section solidly with fluid particles.

Inlet and outlet marking: two thin slices at the left and right edges of the fluid domain are re-marked as mkfluid=1 (inlet) and mkfluid=2 (outlet). These particles are not geometrically distinct from the rest of the fluid; the separate marker is what lets the inout configuration (below) recognise and treat them as open-boundary zones.

Layered walls for mDBC: the channel walls (mkbound=0) are drawn with layers vdp="0,1,2,3,4", generating five stacked layers of boundary particles at increasing depth, which is the layer arrangement mDBC needs to correctly extrapolate pressure and velocity from the fluid to the wall.

Free-draw cylinder: setfrdrawmode auto="#cyl_freedraw" switches on automatic free-draw placement for the cylinder, giving a smoother particle distribution around the curved boundary than a fixed-lattice projection would; it is switched back off immediately afterwards so it does not affect the flap.

Elastic flap boundary: the flap is drawn as a solid box (mkbound=2) directly attached to the cylinder at \(x\) = 0.20 m, forming the structural body that will later be coupled to the flexible-structure solver.

docs.title: Boundary Normals
docs.text:
<normals active="true">
    <norgeometry comment="Define initial configuration of normals before applying other configurations">
        <geometryfile file="[CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk" comment="File with boundary geometry (VTK format)" />
        <distanceh v="2" comment="Maximum orthogonal distance (H*value) to compute normals data" />
        <maxsizeh v="0" comment="Maximum allowed normal size (H*value) (disabled=0)" />
        <svshapes v="true" comment="Saves VTK with geometry in triangles and quads with its normals for debug" />
    </norgeometry>
</normals>

This block feeds the hdp geometry file produced earlier into GenCase's normals calculator, computing a boundary normal for every mDBC particle up to a distance of 2\(H\), which is what allows mDBC to correctly extrapolate fluid quantities onto the walls, cylinder and flap.

docs.title: Flap Boundary Motion
docs.text:
<motion>
    <objreal ref="2">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvnull id="1" />
    </objreal>
</motion>

The flap (mkbound=2) is assigned a null motion (mvnull). This is not an oversight: the flap is not meant to move as a rigid body under a prescribed law, but to deform under the fluid loading according to the elastic material model defined in flexstrucs below. The mvnull entry simply confirms that no external kinematic motion is imposed, leaving the structural solver in full control of its displacement.

docs.title: Open Boundaries (Inlet/Outlet)
docs.text:
<inout>
    <memoryresize size0="2" size="4" comment="Initial memory resize and following resizes" />
    <determlimit value="1e-3" comment="Use 1e-3 for first_order or 1e+3 for zeroth_order" />
    <extrapolatemode value="3" comment="Calculation mode for rhop/velocity extrapolation from ghost nodes: 3:double" />
    ...
</inout>

Extrapolation settings: determlimit="1e-3" selects first-order extrapolation from ghost nodes, and extrapolatemode="3" uses the more accurate double-precision extrapolation for reconstructing pressure and velocity at the open boundaries.

docs.title: Inlet Zone (mkfluid=1)
docs.text:
<inoutzone>
    <refilling value="0" comment="Simple full refilling" />
    <inputtreatment value="2" comment="Remove fluid entering the zone (recommended for inlet)" />
    <layers value="#inout_layers" comment="Number of inlet/outlet particle layers" />
    <zone2d>
        <particles mkfluid="1" direction="right" />
    </zone2d>
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Variable value">
        <velocitytimes3 comment="Parabolic inlet velocity in time">
            <timevalue time="0.0" v2="0.0" z="0.0" z2="0.205" z3="0.41" />
            <timevalue time="1.0" v2="0.75" z="0.0" z2="0.205" z3="0.41" />
            <timevalue time="2.0" v2="1.5" z="0.0" z2="0.205" z3="0.41" />
        </velocitytimes3>
    </imposevelocity>
    <imposerhop mode="2" comment="Extrapolated from ghost nodes" />
    <imposezsurf mode="0">
        <zsurf value="#fluid_max_z" />
        <remove value="false" />
    </imposezsurf>
</inoutzone>

Direction and treatment: the inlet zone corresponds to the mkfluid=1 particles, with flow entering in the right (+\(x\)) direction; inputtreatment="2" removes any fluid that would otherwise cross back into the inlet buffer, which is the recommended setting for a well-posed inlet.
