Time-varying parabolic profile: velocitytimes3 imposes a parabolic velocity profile across the channel height, defined by three reference heights (\(z\)=0, \(z_2\)=0.205, \(z_3\)=0.41 — bottom, mid-height and top) at each time-value entry. The mid-height velocity \(v_2\) is ramped smoothly from 0 to 1.5 m/s over the first 2 s of the simulation, giving a gentle, numerically well-behaved start-up rather than an impulsive inflow — a standard feature of the Turek-Hron benchmark protocol.

Density and free surface: rhop is extrapolated from the interior flow, and the characteristic inlet water surface is fixed at \(z\) = 0.41 m (the full channel height), since the channel runs completely full.

docs.title: Outlet Zone (mkfluid=2)
docs.text:
<inoutzone>
    <refilling value="2" comment="Advanced refilling for reverse flows" />
    <inputtreatment value="1" comment="Convert fluid (necessary for outlet)" />
    <layers value="#inout_layers" />
    <zone2d>
        <particles mkfluid="2" direction="left" />
    </zone2d>
    <imposevelocity mode="2" comment="Extrapolated value" />
    <imposerhop mode="0" comment="Imposed fixed value" />
    <imposezsurf mode="0">
        <zsurf value="#fluid_max_z" />
        <remove value="false" />
    </imposezsurf>
</inoutzone>

Outlet behaviour: the outlet zone (mkfluid=2, direction left, i.e. facing back into the domain) extrapolates its velocity from the interior flow rather than imposing a fixed value, and uses the more expensive but more robust "advanced" refilling mode, which is recommended whenever reverse flow through the outlet (caused by the wake behind the cylinder and flap) is expected.

docs.title: Flexible Structure (FSI Coupling)
docs.text:
<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="2" mkclamp="1">
        <density value="10000.0" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="1.4e6" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.4" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="1" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.1" comment="Hourglass correction factor" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

Coupling definition: flexstrucbody designates the boundary particles with mkbound=2 (the flap) as a deformable elastic body, clamped at mkclamp="1" — the cylinder — so that the flap is rigidly attached to the cylinder at its root and free to bend along its length.

Material properties: the flap is given a density of 10,000 kg/m³, a Young's modulus of 1.4 × 10⁶ Pa and a Poisson ratio of 0.4, matching the classical Turek-Hron benchmark parameters that produce a large, low-frequency bending oscillation under the incoming flow.

Constitutive model and stabilisation: a plane-strain formulation is used, appropriate for this 2-D case, and a small hourglass correction factor (0.1) is applied to suppress spurious zero-energy deformation modes in the structural discretisation.

docs.title: Boundary Method
docs.text:
<parameter key="Boundary" value="#eval(mdbc,2,1)" comment="Boundary method 1:DBC, 2:mDBC" />
<parameter key="SlipMode" value="2" comment="Slip mode for mDBC 2:No-slip" />
<parameter key="NoPenetration" value="0" comment="Prevent particle penetration in mDBC: Off" />

Since the mdbc variable is set to true, #eval(mdbc,2,1) evaluates to 2, selecting mDBC with a no-slip condition at all solid boundaries (walls, cylinder and flap).

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="StepAlgorithm" value="2" comment="Symplectic" />
<parameter key="Kernel" value="2" comment="Wendland" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="2" comment="Laminar+SPS" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.001" comment="Viscosity value" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary" />

A Laminar+SPS viscosity formulation is used with a low viscosity value of 0.001, appropriate for the moderate-Reynolds-number laminar flow of the benchmark, with full viscous coupling at the boundary (ViscoBoundFactor="1").

docs.title: Density Diffusion and Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="1" comment="Molteni" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value" />
<parameter key="Shifting" value="3" comment="Full" />
<parameter key="ShiftCoef" value="-20" comment="Coefficient for standard shifting computation" />
<parameter key="ShiftTFS" value="0.0" comment="Free-surface detection threshold" />

The Molteni density diffusion term is used with δ = 0.1, and full particle shifting is enabled with a strong coefficient (-20) to maintain a regular particle distribution around the cylinder and along the oscillating flap, where large local deformations would otherwise degrade particle quality.

docs.title: Time Step and Stopping Criteria
docs.text:
<parameter key="CoefDtMin" value="0.001" comment="Coefficient to calculate minimum time step" />
<parameter key="DtAllParticles" value="1" comment="Velocity of all particles used to calculate DT" />
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="15.0" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.05" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="MinFluidStop" value="0.5" comment="Minimum proportion of initial fluid particles to continue" />

All-particle time-step control: DtAllParticles="1" includes boundary and flexible-structure particles (not just fluid) in the time-step calculation, which is important here since the flap's own motion can otherwise become the limiting factor for stability.

Simulation length: the case runs for 15 s, long enough for the inflow ramp-up (2 s) followed by several periods of the flap's self-sustained oscillation.

Mass conservation safeguard: MinFluidStop="0.5" automatically stops the simulation if the number of fluid particles falls below 50% of the initial count, guarding against runaway mass loss through the open boundaries.

docs.title: Simulation Domain
docs.text:
<simulationdomain comment="Defines domain of simulation">
    <posmin x="default - 5%" y="default" z="default - 5%" />
    <posmax x="default + 5%" y="default" z="default + 5%" />
</simulationdomain>

The computational domain is extended by 5% beyond the generated particle bounding box in both \(x\) and \(z\), giving the open boundaries and the deforming flap a small additional margin.

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseTurekFSI_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseTurekFSI_Def CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseTurekFSI_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseTurekFSI_Def CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseTurekFSI_out/CaseTurekFSI/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

Parametric case

Because this case is built almost entirely from #variables, most changes — channel size, cylinder position, flap length, material properties — can be made by editing the predefinition block and the flexstrucbody material entries, without touching the drawing commands themselves.

docs.title: Results and Validation
docs.text: As the parabolic inflow ramps up, vortices begin to shed from the cylinder and impinge on the elastic flap, which starts to oscillate. Once the inflow reaches its steady value, the flap settles into a large-amplitude, self-sustained bending oscillation driven by the periodic vortex shedding, characteristic of the Turek-Hron benchmark. The typical quantities of interest for validation are the time history of the flap tip displacement in the streamwise and transverse directions, and the drag and lift forces on the cylinder-flap assembly, both of which can be compared against the reference values reported in the original Turek-Hron benchmark study and against other FSI solvers that have reproduced it.

docs.title: References
docs.text: ◆ Turek, S., & Hron, J. (2006). Proposal for numerical benchmarking of fluid-structure interaction between an elastic object and laminar incompressible flow. In Fluid-Structure Interaction (pp. 371–385). Springer.

docs.title: Wave Generation
docs.text:
This example demonstrates wave generation using a piston-type wavemaker with second-order correction. Regular waves are generated in a numerical wave flume with a damping zone at the far end to absorb reflected waves. This case illustrates the implementation of the Biesel transfer function and Madsen's second-order wave theory.

What's Covered in This Tutorial

This case demonstrates the following DualSPHysics capabilities:

  • Second-order piston-type wave generation
  • Moving boundary implementation for wavemaker motion
  • Passive wave absorption using damping zones
  • VTK output for wave visualization

Video 1: Regular wave generation with piston wavemaker showing wave propagation and damping

docs.title: Physical Setup
docs.text:
The simulation represents a 2-D wave flume with:

  • Water depth: \(d\) = 0.66 m
  • Wave height: \(H\) = 0.15 m
  • Wave period: \(T\) = 2.00 s
  • Flume length: 15.5 m (with 4.50 m damping zone)
  • Particle spacing: \(dp\) = 0.02 m

For this case, we use:

  • Boundary mkbound=10 for piston wavemaker (moving)
  • Boundary mkbound=0 for tank bottom
  • Boundary mkbound=1 for right wall
  • Fluid mkfluid=0 for water

docs.title: Domain Setup
docs.text:
<definition dp="0.02">
    <pointref x="0.0" y="0.0" z="0.0" />
    <pointmin x="-1.00" y="0.0" z="-1.00" />
    <pointmax x="20.0" y="0.0" z="2.00" />
</definition>

Domain boundaries: Extends from -1.0 to 20.0 m in \(x\)-direction and -1.0 to 2.0 m in \(z\)-direction, accommodating the wave flume and allowing space for particle motion. Having \(y\)-direction set to 0.0 indicates that a 2-D simulation will be created.

docs.title: Piston Wavemaker
docs.text:
<setshapemode>real | bound</setshapemode>
<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkbound mk="10" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.05" y="-1.0" z="0.0" />
    <size x="0.05" y="2.00" z="1.00" />
</drawbox>

Shape mode: real | bound indicates real (moving) boundary particles.

Wavemaker configuration: - Position: x = -0.05 to 0.00 m (5.0 cm thick piston) - Height: 1.00 m (extends above water depth of 0.66 m) - Marker: mkbound=10 for identification in motion definition

Wavemaker Thickness

The piston thickness should be at least 2-3 particle spacings (here 0.05 m \(\approx 2.5\times dp\)) to ensure structural integrity during motion.

docs.title: Tank Bottom and Walls
docs.text:
<setmkbound mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>bottom</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.50" y="-1.0" z="0.0" />
    <size x="16.0" y="2.0" z="1.00" />
</drawbox>

<setmkbound mk="1" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>right</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.50" y="-1.0" z="0.0" />
    <size x="16.0" y="2.0" z="1.00" />
</drawbox>

Tank configuration:

  • Bottom wall (mkbound=0): Extends 16 m from piston
  • Right wall (mkbound=1): Far end of flume

docs.title: Water Volume
docs.text:
<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<fillbox x="1.00" y="0.0" z="0.05">
    <modefill>void</modefill>
    <point x="-1.00" y="-1.0" z="-1.00" />
    <size x="20.0" y="2.0" z="1.66" />
</fillbox>

Fluid filling: fillbox can automatically generate particles in complex shapes with modefill="void" by filling the domain within which the seed point (fillbox x="1.00" y="0.0" z="0.05") is located.

Fillbox Method

The fluid fills all available space not occupied by boundaries or voids.

docs.title: Wavemaker Motion Definition
docs.text:
<motion>
    <objreal ref="10">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvnull id="1" />
    </objreal>
</motion>

Motion setup:

  • objreal ref="10": References boundary particles with mkbound=10 (piston)
  • begin mov="1" start="0": Activates motion ID 1 at \(t=0.0\)
  • mvnull id="1": Placeholder motion (actual motion controlled by wavepaddles)

Motion Control

The mvnull serves as a placeholder. The actual piston motion is computed dynamically by the wavepaddles functionality based on wave parameters.

docs.title: Wave Generation Parameters
docs.text:
Wave generation in DualSPHysics follows the Biesel transfer function for piston-type wavemakers. This case implements second-order wave generation following Madsen's theory, which prevents the generation of spurious secondary waves.

Wave Generation Theory

For detailed mathematical derivations of the Biesel transfer function, first-order and second-order wave generation theories, and validity conditions, see the Wave Generation documentation.

docs.title: Piston Wavemaker Configuration
docs.text:
<special>
        <wavepaddles>
            <piston>
                <mkbound value="10" comment="Mk-Bound of selected particles" />
                <waveorder value="2" comment="Order wave generation 1:1st order, 2:2nd order (def=1)" />
                <start value="0" comment="Start time (def=0)" />
                <duration value="0" comment="Movement duration, Zero is the end of simulation (def=0)" />
                <depth value="0.66" comment="Fluid depth (def=0)" />
                <pistondir x="1" y="0" z="0" comment="Movement direction (def=(1,0,0))" />
                <waveheight value="0.15" comment="Wave height" />
                <waveperiod value="2" comment="Wave period" />
                <phase value="0" comment="Initial wave phase in function of PI (def=0)" />
                <ramp value="1" comment="Periods of ramp (def=0)" />
                <savemotion periods="20" periodsteps="20" xpos="6.0" zpos="-0.26" 
                            comment="Saves motion data. xpos and zpos are optional. zpos=-depth of the measuring point" />
            </piston>
        </wavepaddles>
    </special>

Key parameters explained:

Wave characteristics:

  • waveheight="0.15": Wave height \(H\) = 0.15 m
  • waveperiod="2.00": Wave period \(T\) = 2.0 s
  • depth="0.66": Water depth \(d\) = 0.66 m

Generation control:

  • waveorder="2": Second-order wave theory (includes correction for spurious waves)
  • start="0": Wave generation begins at simulation start
  • duration="0": Continues until simulation end
  • phase="0": Initial phase \(\delta = 0\) (wave starts at equilibrium)
  • ramp="1": Smooth ramp-up over 1 wave period to avoid initial transients (2 or more should be used)

Motion direction:

  • pistondir x="1" y="0" z="0": Horizontal motion in positive \(x\)-direction

Output:

  • savemotion periods="20" periodsteps="20": Records piston motion for 20 wave periods with 20 time steps per period
  • xpos="6.0" zpos="-0.26": Saves theoretical wave elevation and velocity at \(x=6.00\) m, \(z=-0.26\) m (within water depth)

Wave Order Selection

Second-order generation (waveorder="2") is strongly recommended for physical accuracy. It prevents the generation of parasitic long waves that would contaminate the wave field.

docs.title: Damping Zone Configuration
docs.text:
<damping>
    <dampingzone>
        <limitmin x="11" y="0" z="0" />
        <limitmax x="15.5" y="0" z="0" />
        <overlimit value="1" />
        <redumax value="10" />
    </dampingzone>
</damping>
  • Location: \(x\) = 11.0 to 15.5 m (4.50 m length, approximately 3 wavelengths)
  • Overlap: overlimit="1" extends damping 1.00 m beyond specified limits for smooth transition
  • Damping coefficient: redumax="10" controls dissipation strength

Function: Gradually reduces particle velocities to absorb wave energy and minimize reflection from the far boundary.

Damping Zone Length

A damping zone of 1-2 wavelengths is typically sufficient. For this case with wavelength L ≈ 1.5 m, the 4.5 m zone provides effective absorption.

docs.title: Smoothing Length
docs.text:
<constantsdef>
    <coefh value="1.2" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)" />
</constantsdef>

Smoothing length: \(h = 1.2 \times \sqrt{(2×dp²)}\)

Slightly larger than default (coefh=1.0) for improved stability in wave simulations.

docs.title: Kernel and Viscosity
docs.text:
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.01" comment="Viscosity value" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="0" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
  • Artificial viscosity \(\alpha = 0.01\)
  • No boundary viscosity (ViscoBoundFactor="0") to reduce boundary drag forces

docs.title: Simulation Duration
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="30" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.05" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />
  • Total time: 30 seconds (15 wave periods)
  • Output interval: 0.05 seconds (40 outputs per wave period)

docs.title: Running the Simulation
docs.text: Execute the case using the provided batch/shell script:

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
wCaseWavemaker_win64_GPU.bat
REM Generate case geometry
gencase.exe CaseWavemaker_Def CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker -save:all

REM Run simulation on GPU
dualsphysicsgpu.exe -gpu CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker/data

REM Convert to VTK format
partvtk.exe -dirdata CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
xCaseWavemaker_linux64_GPU.sh
# Generate case geometry
./gencase CaseWavemaker_Def CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker -save:all

# Run simulation on GPU
./dualsphysicsgpu -gpu CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker/data

# Convert to VTK format
./partvtk -dirdata CaseWavemaker_out/CaseWavemaker/data -savevtk post/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

docs.title: Visual Results
docs.text:
Video 1 shows the wave generation and propagation.

Figure 1: Snapshots of wave propagation at different time instants

Video 1: Regular wave generation with piston wavemaker showing wave propagation and damping

docs.title: Wavemaker Motion
docs.text:
The piston motion is saved in the output files and can be compared with theoretical predictions:

Figure 2: Piston displacement showing first-order (dashed) and second-order corrected (solid) motion

The second-order correction modifies the piston stroke to eliminate parasitic long waves, as described in Madsen's theory.

docs.title: Wave Profile Analysis
docs.text:
Free surface elevation measured at \(x = 6.00\) m:

Figure 3: Free surface elevation at x = 6 m showing regular wave pattern with H ≈ 0.15 m and T ≈ 2 s

The wave maintains constant amplitude and period, demonstrating successful second-order wave generation without spurious components.

docs.title: Damping Zone Effectiveness
docs.text:
Wave amplitude decay in the damping zone:

Figure 4: Wave amplitude reduction through the damping zone (x = 11-15.5 m)

The damping zone effectively absorbs >95% of wave energy, minimizing reflection.

docs.title: Irregular Wave Generation
docs.text:
To generate irregular waves, replace <piston> with: 

<piston_spectrum>

</piston_spectrum>

docs.title: Active Wave Absorption
docs.text:
Add active absorption to prevent reflection: 

<piston>
    ...
    <awas value="1" comment="Enables AWAS (default=0)" />
    <awas_elevation value="0.02" comment="Distance to measure elevation" />
</piston>

docs.title: References
docs.text:
◆ Madsen, O. S. (1971). On the generation of long waves. Journal of Geophysical Research, 76(36), 8672-8683. https://doi.org/10.1029/JC076i036p08672

◆ Schäffer, H. A., & Klopman, G. (2000). Review of multidirectional active wave absorption methods. Journal of Waterway, Port, Coastal, and Ocean Engineering, 126(2), 88-97.

docs.title: MkDocs Documentation Setup Guide
docs.text: This guide sets up a local copy of the DualSPHysics documentation, so that you can preview it in your browser and work on it.

docs.title: Windows Setup
docs.text:
After cloning the repository from git clone https://github.com/btagliafierro/DualSPHDocs, open PowerShell in its folder and paste this block:

# Create and activate the virtual environment
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Install the dependencies (exact versions from requirements.txt)
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt

# Verify the installation and start the preview server
mkdocs --version
mkdocs serve

If PowerShell refuses to run Activate.ps1

Allow scripts for your user once with Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, then run the block again. In the classic Command Prompt, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate.bat instead.

docs.title: macOS/Linux Setup
docs.text:
After cloning the repository from git clone https://github.com/btagliafierro/DualSPHDocs, open a terminal in its folder and paste this block:

# Create and activate the virtual environment
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install the dependencies (exact versions from requirements.txt)
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt

# Verify the installation and start the preview server
mkdocs --version
mkdocs serve

Done!

Open your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8000/. The page reloads by itself every time you save a file.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 (3.10 and 3.11 also work; 3.13 is not supported yet by the pinned packages). Check with python --version or python3 --version.
  • Git, to clone the repository.

If Python is not installed, download it from python.org.

docs.text:

├── docs/                    # Documentation source, one folder per menu section

docs.title: Starting Work
docs.text:
Windows (PowerShell): 

cd path\to\DualSPHDocs; .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1; mkdocs serve

macOS/Linux: 

cd path/to/DualSPHDocs && source .venv/bin/activate && mkdocs serve

docs.title: Stopping Work
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+C to stop the server, then: 

deactivate

docs.title: Before Pushing Changes
docs.text:
Build the whole site once and read the output. Lines starting with WARNING point to broken links or missing images.

mkdocs build
python tools/fix_absolute_paths.py --check

The second command checks that no path starts with / (such as /assets/images/...). Those work locally but break on the published site. Without --check, the script fixes them.

docs.title: Updating Dependencies
docs.text: Only needed when a package is added or upgraded. requirements.txt is then regenerated and committed, so that everyone installs the same versions.

docs.title: Add New Dependency
docs.text:
1. Add it to requirements/requirements.in: 

       new-package

  2. Regenerate and install: 

    pip install pip-tools
pip-compile requirements/requirements.in -o requirements/requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt

docs.title: Update All Dependencies
docs.text:
pip install pip-tools
pip-compile --upgrade requirements/requirements.in -o requirements/requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt

docs.title: Build Static Site
docs.text:
mkdocs build

The result is written to site/, which is ignored by Git.

docs.title: Deploy to GitHub Pages (maintainers only)
docs.text:
The published site lives in a subfolder of the GitHub Pages address, which must be given in SITE_URL.

Windows (PowerShell): 

$env:SITE_URL = "https://USER.github.io/REPOSITORY/"
python tools/fix_absolute_paths.py --check
mkdocs gh-deploy

macOS/Linux: 

python tools/fix_absolute_paths.py --check
SITE_URL="https://USER.github.io/REPOSITORY/" mkdocs gh-deploy

mkdocs gh-deploy publishes your local folder as it is, uncommitted changes included, so deploy from an up-to-date main.

docs.title: Complete Reinstall (Fresh Start)
docs.text:
If something goes wrong, delete the virtual environment and run the setup again.

Windows (PowerShell): 

Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .venv
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

macOS/Linux: 

rm -rf .venv
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Couplings
docs.text: UNDER CONSTRUCTION

docs.title: General implementation and capabilities
docs.text:
Devices composed of rigid bodies interacting through frictional contacts and several nonlinear constraints are extensively used in many engineering fields, either featuring a small number of unilateral contacts or including thousands of contacts between a large number of parts. Mechanisms involving contacts and impacts between parts can be modeled in terms of multi-body systems with unilateral constraints. The simulation of rigid contacts entails the solution of non-smooth equations of motion: the dynamics are non-smooth since the non-interpenetration, collision, and adhesion constraints are discontinuous. Considering the success of SPH for fluid descriptions and non-smooth multibody solvers for mechanical systems, attempting to couple both under a generalized framework should provide new simulation possibilities, by leveraging the strengths in both methods.

The multi-body solver used is Project Chrono, an open-source high-performance library and set of applications enabling many applications such as wheeled and tracked vehicles operating on deformable terrains, robots, mechatronic systems, compliant mechanisms, and fluid solid interaction phenomena (Tasora et al. 2016). Systems can be made of rigid and flexible/compliant parts with constraints, motors and contacts; parts can have three-dimensional shapes for collision detection.

DualSPHysics at the moment uses the rigid body, constraints and collision detection parts of the library. This allows a user to use a set of bodies described in meshes, specify restrictions applied to the bodies (from the implemented list of joints, hinges and springs) and compute interactions between bodies, in a similar fashion to the DEM implementation, but in a more stable manner. Realistic frictional behavior is also now possible, since a full Coulomb sliding/sticking/rolling model is used.

The implementation strategy is to couple both models with a message passing interface, as structured in Figure ?. Once quantities from the rigid bodies are computed by DualSPHysics, the time step, along with the linear and angular accelerations from each body, computed solely from fluid- body interaction, are sent to our Project Chrono module. For that time step, Chrono returns the linear and angular velocities, as well as CC position, computed by integrating the fluid contributions with the dynamic or kinematic restrictions of the system, including collisions.

Flow chart of the coupling between DualSPHysics and Project Chrono.

docs.title: Multibody representation for rigid bodies - System representation
docs.text:
Section 3.8 lays the fundamental ideas behind the modelling of the fluid phase and the modelling of otherwise unconstrained floating rigid bodies. Mechanisms to cope with interactions between rigid bodies and other constraints need to be explored. The ideas laid by (Potapov et al. 2001) and later adapted by (Canelas et al. 2016) represent traditional regularization strategies, which model contacts and other restrictions by means of spring-dashpot systems (DEM class methods). From a SPH implementation perspective, this approach requires small code adaptations and allows the adoption of already used integrators. The high stiffness affecting the explicit integration, however, typically imposes prohibitively small time steps to ensure stability and guarantees the need to tune parameters (Elskamp et al. 2017). These issues motivate the search for methods that can deal with multiple frictional restrictions, even in cases with thousands or millions of moving bodies. To that end, much attention was drawn by time-stepping approaches that produce weak solutions of the DVI that describes the continuous time motion of rigid bodies with collision, contact, and friction, as those applied in Project Chrono. The DVI as a problem formulation was recently introduced in full generality and classified by differential index (Pang and Stewart 2008), though earlier numerical approaches based on DVI formulations do exist. On the following subsections, a DVI description is built by defining the notation space, writing constraints that represent physical characteristics of the system and finally writing the full equation system.

At a time \(t\), the position of the system is described by generalized coordinates \(\mathbf{q}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m\) (which may include rotational coordinates that cannot be defined over a subspace homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^n\), for some \(n\)), and generalized velocities \(\mathbf{v}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^m\). In classical mechanics, \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) is continuous, and we can write:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{1} \label{mechanics_velocity} \frac{d\mathbf{q}}{dt} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathbf{q}),\mathbf{v}, \end{equation}\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathbf{q})\) is used to transform the generalized velocities into derivatives of the generalized positions. For instance, when dealing with rotations, \(\boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\mathbf{q})\) can be a linear mapping from three-dimensional angular speeds into four-dimensional time derivatives of unit quaternions.

Four-dimensional unit quaternions are adopted, \(\boldsymbol{\eta}(t) \in S^3 \subset \mathbb{H}\), although this space is not homeomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}^3\). This allows the position vector to be written as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{2} \label{pos} \mathbf{q} = \left\{ \mathbf{x}_1^T, \boldsymbol{\eta}_1^T, \mathbf{x}_2^T, \boldsymbol{\eta}_2^T, \ldots \right\}, \end{equation}\]

and the velocity vector as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{3} \label{vel} \mathbf{v} = \left\{ \dot{\mathbf{x}}_1^T, \boldsymbol{\omega}_1^T, \dot{\mathbf{x}}_2^T, \boldsymbol{\omega}_2^T, \ldots \right\}. \end{equation}\]

Therefore, a system with \(n\) bodies in three dimensions is represented by \(m_p = 8n\) position coordinates and \(m_s = 6n\) velocity coordinates.

docs.title: Non-penetration constraints
docs.text:
Two rigid bodies should not penetrate and, if they are in contact, friction should act at the interface. To enforce the non-penetration constraint, we assume that there exists a function \(\Phi(\mathbf{q})\), called the gap function, that satisfies

\[\begin{equation} \tag{4} \label{constraints} \Phi(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{cases} > 0, & \text{if the bodies have no intersection}, \\ = 0, & \text{if the bodies are in contact}, \\ < 0, & \text{if the bodies intersect}. \end{cases} \end{equation}\]

For such a function, the non-penetration constraint becomes \(\Phi(\mathbf{q}) \ge 0\). An example of such a mapping is the signed distance function, which is differentiable when the bodies are smooth and convex, at least up to some value of the interpenetration. In many cases, even simple ones involving the relative position of two spheres, a differentiable signed distance function cannot be defined for all values of \(\mathbf{q}\).

The fact that \(\Phi(\mathbf{q})\) can be differentiably defined only on a neighborhood of the set \({ \Phi(\mathbf{q}) \ge 0}\) can be accommodated at the cost of substantially more involved analysis. This motivates the following assumption: any contact is described by a gap function \(\Phi(\mathbf{q})\) that is everywhere twice continuously differentiable.

docs.title: Frictional constraints - The Coulomb friction model
docs.text:
The model we represent and approximate is the Coulomb friction model. If a position \(\mathbf{q}\) is feasible and the contact is active, that is, \(\Phi(\mathbf{q}) \ge 0\), then at the contact we have a normal force and a tangential force. Let \(\mathbf{n}\) be the normal at the contact, pointing toward the exterior of the body, and let \(\mathbf{t}_1\) and \(\mathbf{t}_2\) be the tangents at the contact such that \(\mathbf{n}\), \(\mathbf{t}_1\), and \(\mathbf{t}_2\) are mutually orthogonal unit vectors and are functions of the position \(\mathbf{q}\).

Let \(\mathbf{v}\) denote velocities, and let the subscripts \(1\) and \(2\) refer to quantities associated with the two linearly independent tangential directions at a given contact. The reaction force is applied to the system through the multipliers \(\gamma_n\), \(\gamma_{v_1}\), and \(\gamma_{v_2}\). The normal component of the contact force is given by \(\mathbf{F}_n = \gamma_n \mathbf{n}\), and the tangential component of the contact force is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{5} \label{contact} \mathbf{F}_t = \gamma_{v_1} \mathbf{t}_1 + \gamma_{v_2} \mathbf{t}_2. \end{equation}\]

The Coulomb friction model then consists of the following constraints:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{6} \label{coulomb} \begin{aligned} \gamma_n &\ge 0, \\ \Phi(\mathbf{q}) &\ge 0, \\ \Phi(\mathbf{q}),\gamma_n &= 0, \\ \mu \gamma_n & \ge \sqrt{\gamma_{v_1}^2 + \gamma_{v_2}^2}, \\ |\mathbf{V}*t| \left( \mu \gamma_n - \sqrt{\gamma*{v_1}^2 + \gamma_{v_2}^2} \right) &= 0, \\ \langle \mathbf{F}_t, \mathbf{V}_t \rangle &= - |\mathbf{F}_t|,|\mathbf{V}_t|. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbf{V}_t\) is the relative tangential velocity at contact. The first part of the constraint can be restated as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{7} \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}_n + \mathbf{F}_t = \gamma_n \mathbf{n} + \gamma_{v_1} \mathbf{t}_1 + \gamma_{v_2} \mathbf{t}_2 \in \mathbb{K}, \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathbb{K}\) is a cone in three dimensions, whose slope is \(\arctan(\mu)\). The constraint

\[\begin{equation} \tag{8} \langle \mathbf{F}_t, \mathbf{V}_t \rangle = - \|\mathbf{F}_t\| \, \|\mathbf{V}_t\| \end{equation}\]

requires that the tangential force be opposite to the tangential velocity. This results in the reaction force being dissipative. In fact, an equivalent convenient way of expressing this constraint is by using the maximum dissipation principle

\[\begin{equation} \tag{9} (\gamma_{v_1}, \gamma_{v_2}) = \mathrm{argmin}_{\sqrt{\gamma_{v_1}^2 + \gamma_{v_2}^2} \le \mu \gamma_n} (\gamma_{v_1} \mathbf{t}_1 + \gamma_{v_2} \mathbf{t}_2)^T \mathbf{V}_t \end{equation}\]

These constraints are represented by mapping vectors \(\mathbf{n}\), \(\mathbf{t}_1\), and \(\mathbf{t}_2\) from contact coordinates to generalized coordinates. For example, if we have a two-body system, then the generalized coordinates in the three-dimensional space are embedded in a twelve-dimensional space by using the coordinates \([ x_1,\, y_1,\, z_1,\, \phi_1,\, \Theta_1,\, \zeta_1,\, x_2,\, y_2,\, z_2,\, \phi_2,\, \Theta_2,\, \zeta_2 ]\). For a three-dimensional vector \(\mathbf{v}\), the mapping to generalized coordinates is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{10} \mathbf{v} \to \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ r_1 \times \mathbf{v} \\ -\mathbf{v} \\ -r_2 \times \mathbf{v} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}\]

where \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are the relative positions of the contact point with respect to the centers of mass of the two bodies. Using this mapping, we denote the generalized vector version of \(\mathbf{n}\), \(\mathbf{t}_1\), and \(\mathbf{t}_2\) by \(D_n\), \(D_1\), and \(D_2\). One unfortunate side effect of generalized coordinates mapping is that, in the new coordinates, \(D_n\), \(D_1\), and \(D_2\) cease to be mutually orthogonal.

If \(u\) is the generalized velocity, the tangential velocity satisfies the following:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{11} \mathbf{t}_1^T \mathbf{V}_t = u^T D_1, \quad \mathbf{t}_2^T \mathbf{V}_t = u^T D_2 \end{equation}\]

In generalized coordinates, the Coulomb model can now be written as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{12} \begin{aligned} F_n &= \gamma_n D_n, \\ F_t &= \gamma_{v_1} D_1 + \gamma_{v_2} D_2, \\ \gamma_n &\ge 0, \quad \Phi(\mathbf{q}) \ge 0, \quad \Phi(\mathbf{q}) \gamma_n = 0, \\ \mu \gamma_n &\ge \sqrt{\gamma_{v_1}^2 + \gamma_{v_2}^2}, \\ (\gamma_{v_1}, \gamma_{v_2}) &= \mathrm{argmin}_{\sqrt{\gamma_{v_1}^2 + \gamma_{v_2}^2} \le \mu \gamma_n} (\gamma_{v_1} D_1 + \gamma_{v_2} D_2)^T u \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

docs.title: Complete multi-body model
docs.text:
The other dynamical data needed for the model are the mass matrix \(\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\) and the external force \(\mathbf{f}_e(t,\mathbf{q},\mathbf{v})\). The mass matrix \(\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}\) is positive definite and constant.

Assuming now that we have \(p\) potential contact constraints, these are enforced by the non-penetration conditions

\[\begin{equation} \tag{13} \Phi^i(\mathbf{q}) \ge 0, \qquad i = 1,2,\ldots,p. \end{equation}\]

The superscript \(i\) denotes the data associated with the potential contact \(i\). The continuous model is given by the following differential variational inequality.

\[\begin{equation} \tag{14} \label{dvi} \begin{aligned} \frac{d\boldsymbol{q}}{dt} &= \boldsymbol{\Gamma}(\boldsymbol{q}) \boldsymbol{v}, \\ M \frac{d\boldsymbol{v}}{dt} &= \sum_{i=1}^p \big(\gamma_n^i D_n^i + \gamma_{v_1}^i D_1^i + \gamma_{v_2}^i D_2^i \big) + \boldsymbol{f_e}(t, \boldsymbol{q}, \boldsymbol{v}), \\ \gamma_n^i &\ge 0 \;\;\bot\;\; \Phi^i(\boldsymbol{q}) \ge 0, \quad i = 1, 2, ..., p, \\ (\gamma_{v_1}^i, \gamma_{v_2}^i) &= \mathrm{argmin}_{\sqrt{(\gamma_{v_1}^i)^2 + (\gamma_{v_2}^i)^2} \le \mu^i \gamma_n^i} (\gamma_{v_1}^i D_1^i + \gamma_{v_2}^i D_2^i)^T u, \quad i = 1, 2, ..., p. \end{aligned} \end{equation}\]

System \(\eqref{dvi}\) must be discretized for use in a numerical model. Casting the system in Cone Complementary Problem (CCP) form and solving it with a fixed point iterative method allows for the expected performance levels, while taking advantage of the DVI capabilities in describing generalized restrictions. The full discretization can be seen in Project Chrono’s reference papers, (Monaghan, J.J. 2005) Anitescu (2010) and (Tasora and Anitescu 2011).

docs.title: Discrete Element Method
docs.text:
The discrete element method (DEM) allows for the computation of rigid particle dynamics, by considering contact laws to account for interaction forces. The coupled numerical solution, based on SPH and DEM discretisations, resolves solid-solid and solid-fluid interactions over a broad range of scales.

Forces arise whenever a particle of a solid object interacts with another. In the particular case of a solid-solid collision, the contact force is decomposed into Fn and Ft, normal and tangential components respectively. Both of these forces include viscous dissipation effects. This is because two colliding bodies undergo a deformation which will be somewhere between perfectly inelastic and perfectly elastic, usually quantified by the normal restitution coefficient

\[\begin{equation} \tag{73} \label{eq:dem_restitution} e_n = \frac{\left|v_n'\right|}{\left|v_n\right|} \end{equation}\]

The total forces are decomposed into a repulsion force, Fr, arising from the elastic deformation of the material, and a damping force, Fd, for the viscous dissipation of energy during the deformation.

Figure ? illustrates the proposed viscoelastic DEM mechanism between two interacting particles.

Schematic interaction between particles with viscoelastic DEM mechanism.

The normal force is given by

\[\begin{equation} \tag{74} \label{eq:dem_normal} \mathbf{F}_n = \mathbf{F}_r + \mathbf{F}_d = k_{n,ij}\,\delta_{ij}^{3/2}\,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{ij} - \gamma_{n,ij}\,\delta_{ij}^{1/2}\,\dot{\delta}_{ij}\,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{ij} \end{equation}\]

where the stiffness is given by

\[\begin{equation} \tag{75} \label{eq:dem_kn} k_{n,ij} = \frac{4}{3}\,E^*\sqrt{R^*} \end{equation}\]

and the damping coefficient is

\[\begin{equation} \tag{76} \label{eq:dem_gamma} \gamma_{n,ij} = -\frac{\log e_{ij}}{\sqrt{\pi^2+\log^2 e_{ij}}} \end{equation}\]

where \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{ij}\) is the unit vector between the centers of particles i and j.

The restitution coefficient ij e is taken as the average of the two materials coefficients, in what is the only calibration parameter of the model. It is not a physical parameter, but since the current method does not account for internal deformations and other energy losses during contact, the user is given a choice to change this parameter freely in order to control the dissipation of each contact. The reduced radius and reduced elasticity are given by

\[\begin{equation} \tag{77} \label{eq:dem_reduced} R^* = \left(\frac{1}{R_i}+\frac{1}{R_j}\right)^{-1}, \qquad E^* = \left(\frac{1-\nu_{p_i}^2}{E_i}+\frac{1-\nu_{p_j}^2}{E_j}\right)^{-1} \end{equation}\]

where Ri is simply the particle radius, Ei is the Young modulus and νp is the Poisson coefficient of material i, as specified in the Floating_Materials.xml.

This results in another restriction to the time-step, adding

\[\begin{equation} \tag{78} \label{eq:dem_dt} \Delta t_{c,ij} = 3.21\left(\frac{M^*}{k_{n,ij}}\right)^{2/5} v_n^{-1/5} \end{equation}\]

to the existing CFL restrictions (Eq. (35) in Governing equations), where vn is the normal relative velocity and M* is the reduced mass of the system where there is a contact.

Regarding tangential contacts, friction is modelled using the same model:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{79} \label{eq:dem_tangential} \mathbf{F}_t = \mathbf{F}_r + \mathbf{F}_d = -k_{t,ij}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}^t_{ij} - \gamma_{t,ij}\,\dot{\boldsymbol{\delta}}^t_{ij} \end{equation}\]

where the stiffness and damping constants are derived to be

\[\begin{equation} \tag{80} \label{eq:dem_kt} k_{t,ij} = \frac{2}{7}\,k_{n,ij}, \qquad \gamma_{t,ij} = \frac{2}{7}\,\gamma_{n,ij} \end{equation}\]

as to insure internal consistency of the time scales between normal and tangential components. This mechanism models the static and dynamic friction mechanisms by a penalty method. The body does not statically stick at the point of contact, but is constrained by the spring-damper system. This force must be bounded above by the Coulomb friction law, modified with a sigmoidal function in order to make it continuous around the origin regarding the tangential velocity:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{81} \label{eq:dem_coulomb} F_t = \min\left(\mu_{IJ}\,F_n\tanh\left(8\,\dot{\delta}^t_{ij}\right),\; F_t\right) \end{equation}\]

where \(μIJ\) is the friction coefficient at the contact of object I and object J and is simply taken as the average of the two friction coefficients of the distinct materials, indicated in the Floating_Materials.xml.

More information about DEM implementation can be found in [Canelas, 2015; Canelas et al., 2016].

docs.title: The MoorDyn library
docs.text:
MoorDyn is an open-source dynamic mooring line model that has been designed for coupling with other numerical models (http://www.matt-hall.ca/moordyn.html). MoorDyn discretizes mooring lines as point masses (nodes \(i\)) connected by linear spring-damper segments to provide elasticity in the axial direction. If ri and ri+1 represent the absolute position vectors of two adjacent nodes, the strain in the segment connecting them (\(i\)+1/2) is calculated as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{93} \label{eq:md_strain} \varepsilon_{i+1/2} = \frac{\left\|\mathbf{r}_{i+1}-\mathbf{r}_i\right\| - l}{l} \end{equation}\]

where \(l\) is the segment unstretched length.

The tension forces acting within each segment due to material stiffness and internal damping are then calculated, respectively, as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{94} \label{eq:md_tension} \mathbf{T}_{i+1/2} = E\,\frac{\pi}{4}\,\mathit{diam}^2\,\varepsilon_{i+1/2}\,\frac{\mathbf{r}_{i+1}-\mathbf{r}_i}{\left\|\mathbf{r}_{i+1}-\mathbf{r}_i\right\|} \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{95} \label{eq:md_damping} \mathbf{C}_{i+1/2} = C_{int}\,\frac{\pi}{4}\,\mathit{diam}^2\,\dot{\varepsilon}_{i+1/2}\,\frac{\mathbf{r}_{i+1}-\mathbf{r}_i}{\left\|\mathbf{r}_{i+1}-\mathbf{r}_i\right\|} \end{equation}\]

where \(diam\) is line diameter, \(E\) is elasticity modulus and \(C_{int}\) is the internal damping coefficient. For chains, which have very small internal structural damping, a small amount of structural damping is still included in the model to critically damp non-physical resonances that can occur at the individual segment natural frequencies due to the model discretization. Bending and torsional stiffnesses are neglected. Hydrodynamic damping and added mass are represented using the Morison equation applied to each node. The tangent direction at a node \(i\) is approximated as a unit vector aligned between the nodes on either side:

(96)

From the Morison equation, the drag force in the transverse (Dn) and tangential (Dt) directions applied to node \(i\) are:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{97.1} \label{eq:md_drag_n} \mathbf{D}_{n,i} = -\frac{1}{2}\,\rho_w\,C_{dn}\,\mathit{diam}\,l\,\left\|\mathbf{v}_{n,i}\right\|\,\mathbf{v}_{n,i} \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{97.2} \label{eq:md_drag_t} \mathbf{D}_{t,i} = -\frac{1}{2}\,\rho_w\,C_{dt}\,\pi\,\mathit{diam}\,l\,\left\|\mathbf{v}_{t,i}\right\|\,\mathbf{v}_{t,i} \end{equation}\]

where \(C_{dn}\) and \(C_{dt}\) are transverse and tangential drag coefficients, respectively. These forces are calculated assuming quiescent water; wave kinematics are neglected in MoorDyn’s calculation of hydrodynamic loads.

Added mass on each node (ai) is calculated as a matrix

\[\begin{equation} \tag{98} \label{eq:md_added_mass} \mathbf{a}_i = \rho_w\,\frac{\pi}{4}\,\mathit{diam}^2\,l\left[C_{an}\left(\mathbf{I}_m-\hat{\mathbf{q}}_i\hat{\mathbf{q}}_i^T\right) + C_{at}\,\hat{\mathbf{q}}_i\hat{\mathbf{q}}_i^T\right] \end{equation}\]

where \(C_{an}\) and \(C_{at}\) are transverse and tangential added mass coefficients, respectively, and Im is the identity matrix.

Vertical seabed contact forces (Bi) are modelled by a spring-damper approach using a stiffness coefficient kb and damping coefficient \(c_{b}\) with magnitude (Hall, 2017):

\[\begin{equation} \tag{99} \label{eq:md_seabed} B_i = \mathit{diam}\,l\left[\left(z_b-z_i\right)k_b - \dot{z}_i\,c_b\right] \end{equation}\]

that is activated whenever the elevation of a node, \(z_{i}\), passes below the defined seabed depth, \(z_{b}\). The model is only active when a node contacts the seabed (i.e. when \(z_{i}\) ≤ \(z_{b}\)).

The total equation of motion for each node along a mooring line, accounting for the terms already mentioned along with node mass (matrix mnode,i), and submerged weight (Wsub,i), is then

\[\begin{equation} \tag{100} \label{eq:md_motion} \left(\mathbf{m}_{node,i}+\mathbf{a}_i\right)\ddot{\mathbf{r}}_i = \mathbf{T}_{i+1/2}-\mathbf{T}_{i-1/2}+\mathbf{C}_{i+1/2}-\mathbf{C}_{i-1/2}+\mathbf{W}_{sub,i}+\mathbf{B}_i+\mathbf{D}_{n,i}+\mathbf{D}_{t,i} \end{equation}\]

This three-by-three matrix equation is solved for each node within a constant-time-step second-order Runge–Kutta integrator.

With its simple formulation, MoorDyn has shown to be computationally efficient and reliable for common offshore renewable energy mooring scenarios, typically giving accurate results with discretizations in the order of 20 segments per mooring line (Hall and Goupee, 2015; Vissio et al., 2015; Sirnivas et al., 2016). Finer discretizations are usually only necessary when transients emerge in the seabed contact forces due to individual nodes touching down abruptly.

Information on using MoorDyn is available in the MoorDyn Users Guide.

docs.title: Two-way coupling DualSPHysics-MoorDyn
docs.text:
Fundamentally, coupling MoorDyn with other codes is based on a loose coupling approach in which fairlead kinematics are passed to MoorDyn, the mooring system dynamics are calculated for one or more time steps, and then the resulting fairlead tension vectors are transferred back to the other simulation code used for the coupling.

The coupling between DualSPHysics and the MoorDyn library can split into three steps:

1st) the motions and rotations initially solved in DualSPHysics (V, Ω, R0) are passed to MoorDyn and used as input for the mooring line fairlead kinematics;

2nd) MoorDyn solves the mooring line behaviour during the time step used in the DualSPHysics model, namely MoorDyn updates the position of the segments of the mooring line and computes the forces at the fairlead connections (dV/\(dt\), dΩ/\(dt\)), which are transferred back to DualSPHysics;

3rd) the extra forces calculated in the second step are added in DualSPHysics to obtain the final resulting force acting onto the floating structure that is used to compute the final motions and rotations of the floating structure.

The computational cost of MoorDyn at each time step is negligible compared to the execution time needed to solve one time step in the SPH model.

Flow chart of the coupling between DualSPHysics and MoorDyn.

The work of Domínguez et al., 2019 included more details about this coupling and a complete validation comparing numerical values with experimental data. Overall, the results demonstrate the accuracy of the coupling between DualSPHysics and MoorDyn to simulate the motion of a moored floating structure under the action of regular waves in terms of free-surface elevation, motions of the floater and mooring tensions.

Going forward, this modelling approach can be employed to simulate more complex floating structures such as floating wind turbines, buoys, WECs, offshore platforms, etc.

docs.title: Coupling with wave propagation models
docs.text:
Multi-scaled complex simulations, often characterised by three-dimensional domains and long duration, require huge computational resources, if only one stand-alone model is employed. Despite the significant improvements in computational time of SPH-based solvers by using GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) and multi-GPU techniques (Domínguez et al., 2013), the computational cost is still high to model realistic engineering problems. In coastal engineering, in particular, it is required modelling properly all processes from wave generation to wave-structure/beach interaction. SPH-based solvers provide a detailed modelling of local phenomena, such as interaction between sea waves and coastal defenses, e.g. Altomare et al. (2015a) and St-Germain et al. (2014). The mesh-free nature of SPH allows mimicking the wave generation system of experimental facilities, employing moving boundaries as piston- or flap-type wavemakers. But, using this schemes, waves need to be generated and to propagate over relative long domains in order to simulate properly wave transformation and to guarantee the correct wave sea state at the toe of the structure, similarly to what happens in physical model tests. To reduce the computational cost of such simulations, less computationally demanding wave propagation models (e.g. Boussinesq models, Non-Linear Shallow Water equation models) can be coupled with SPH-based solvers. Here two coupling schemes between DualSPHysics model and SWASH model are briefly described (Figure ?): multi-layered piston wavemaker (Altomare et al., 2015b) and relaxation zone technique (Altomare et al., 2018). Both techniques are 1-way offline coupling schemes. The SWASH model is an open-source non-hydrostatic wave-flow model (available at swash.sourceforge.net). A full description of the numerical model, boundary conditions and numerical scheme and applications are given in (Zijlema et al., 2011). The differences are following described: * In (Altomare et al., 2015b) the real time displacement of the multi-layered piston wavemaker (consisting of boundary particles) is reconstructed on the basis of the velocity time series calculated by SWASH model in a specific point of the fluid domain. There is no reflection compensation, therefore the use of this technique is recommended for low-reflective cases or very short time series. * In the relaxation zone technique implemented by (Altomare et al., 2018), the coupling zone is extended from one single location to an area. The orbital velocity calculated by the wave propagation model is imposed to the fluid particles in the SPH model. The particle velocity is controlled by analytical solution with a weighting \(C\) function: in this way, the reflected waves are compensated inside the relaxation zone.

Representation of the coupling techniques between DualSPHysics and SWASH.

docs.title: Multi-layered piston wavemaker
docs.text:
A scheme of the multi-layered approach is depicted in Figure ?. For sake of simplicity, the geometry of the wave flume at Flanders Hydraulics Research (Belgium) is resembled as example. The top picture represents the whole flume domain and indicates the points where the coupling is set. The middle picture represents the DualSPHysics domain and multi-layered piston wavemaker consisting of SPH boundary particles. The bottom picture is the SWASH domain: the real flume geometry is replaced after the coupling point by horizontal bottom and absorbing boundary conditions. In this way, only incident wave characteristics will be measured at the coupling location. In the small box on the left-hand side of Figure ?, a scheme of the multi-layered boundary is depicted: the different layers indicate the number of layers used in SWASH simulation (8 is recommended). The velocities provided by SWASH at the coupling point for each layer are then translated in the boundary particle displacement and are passed to DualSPHysics. The final displacement for each of the boundary particles in SPH is calculated based on the interpolated and velocity between neighbor layers. The method, validated for 2DV or quasi-3D applications, has been implemented to work fully in 3D, by reading the velocity in x- and y- directions and integrated them over time to obtain the three-dimensional displacement of the moving boundaries.

Scheme of the multi-layered approach.

docs.title: Relaxation Zone (RZ)
docs.text:
Relaxation zone technique is a general framework to generate waves and currents in DualSPHysics, which can be employed as stand-alone wave generation and wave absorption method, as alternative moving boundaries, or as a proper coupling scheme between DualSPHysics and a wave propagation model. The basics of the method remain the same in both cases. We refer here to implementation in 2DV or quasi-3D. Horizontal and, if necessary, vertical velocities are imposed to SPH fluid particles within a specific generation. The particle velocity distribution between the center of the relaxation zone and its extremes is controlled by with a weighting \(C\) function, the use of which prevents potential particle disorder due to the discontinuity of particle velocities at the interface between the RZ and main computational region. The velocities in the RZ can be expressed as follows:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{90.1} \label{eq:rz_u} u = C\,u_0 + (1-C)\,u_1 \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{90.2} \label{eq:rz_w} w = C\,w_0 + (1-C)\,w_1 \end{equation}\]

where \(u\) and \(w\) are the controlled horizontal and vertical velocities, \(u_0\) and \(w_0\) are the imposed horizontal and vertical velocities, \(u_1\) and \(w_1\) are the actual horizontal and vertical velocities measured in the numerical model. DualSPHysics gives the option to the user to use either the horizontal velocity only or both horizontal and vertical velocities to correct the particle kinematics. In DualSPHysics as stand-alone model, the imposed velocity consists of the analytical orbital velocities of target waves or uniform horizontal velocity profiles (for current generation). For the coupling, the time series of the velocity per layer as calculated by SWASH is used. To reconstruct the velocity profile in the RZ, several measurements along the direction of wave propagation are needed in SWASH to cover the whole generation area. Spatial interpolation and interpolation in time (time step in DualSPHysics is smaller than in SWASH) are performed before imposing the velocities to the SPH fluid particles. The weighting function is implemented in the form of a hyperbolic function (Figure ?). For a specific width of the relaxation zone, \(W_{RZ}\), the \(C\) function can be expressed as follows:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{91} \label{eq:rz_C} C(x,\psi,\beta) = \frac{\tanh\left(\beta\left(\frac{2x}{W_{RZ}}+\psi\right)\right) - \tanh\left(\beta\left(\frac{2x}{W_{RZ}}-\psi\right)\right) - \tanh\left(\beta(1+\psi)\right) + \tanh\left(\beta(1-\psi)\right)}{\tanh(\beta\psi) - \tanh(-\beta\psi) - \tanh\left(\beta(1+\psi)\right) + \tanh\left(\beta(1-\psi)\right)}, \qquad -1 \le \frac{2x}{W_{RZ}} \le 1 \end{equation}\] Shape of the weighting function C for different values of ψ and β.

The value assumed by the function depends on the set of values chosen for the 𝜓 and β parameters and on the distance from the center of the RZ, being zero at both extremes. The variation of the two parameters allows exploring the performance of the RZ depending on the shape of \(C\). The basic scheme of RZ is depicted in Figure ?, where the RZ is defined by the area bounded by the red dotted line. At the right side of the RZ it is located the main fluid domain. Since the generated waves will freely propagate in both directions along the x-axis, a damping area is placed at the left side of the RZ (bounded by a blue dotted line). It has been verified that a damping area 0.25 times the characteristic wavelength is already quite effective.

Generic scheme of relaxation zone in DualSPHysics model.

For wave generation, non-linear effects might induce a drift in the particle displacement that can be identified actually by the mass transport predicted by Stokes at second-order solution for monochromatic waves. The drift velocity can be expressed by the following equation:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{92} \label{eq:rz_stokes_drift} U_S(z) = \frac{\omega k H^2}{8}\,\frac{\cosh\left(2k(z+d)\right)}{\sinh^2(kd)} \end{equation}\]

This mass transport leads to water level increase in the main fluid domain and consequent water level drop in the RZ. In order to avoid unrealistic increase of water level outside the generation zone, a correction to prevent this drift has been implemented. This correction is proportional to the velocity as predicted by Stokes. The performance of the relaxation zone technique to generate waves and to compensate wave reflection is is described in detailed in Altomare et al. (2018), where a step-by-step procedure to design properly the RZ is detailed.

docs.title: Wave Generation
docs.text: Wave generation is included in this version of DualSPHysics, which includes piston- and flap-type long-crested wave generation. In this way, the numerical model can be used to simulate a physical wave flume. Both monochromatic (regular) and random waves can be generated. Second-order correction for bound long waves (sub-harmonics) is implemented for random waves with piston-type wave maker only. For regular waves, second-order correction (super-harmonics) is implemented for both piston- and flap-type wavemaker. The following sections refer only to the piston-type wavemaker.

docs.title: First order wave generation
docs.text:
The Biesel transfer functions express the relation between wave amplitude and wavemaker displacement [Biesel and Suquet, 1951], under the assumption of irrotational and incompressible fluid and constant pressure at the free surface. The transfer function links the displacement of the piston-type wavemaker to the water surface elevation, under the hypothesis of monochromatic sinusoidal waves in one dimension in the x-direction:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{1} in original \label{wave_fisrtOrder} \eta(x,t)=\frac{H}{2}\cos(\omega t -kx+\delta) \end{equation}\]

where \(H\) is the wave height, d the water depth, \(x\) is distance and \(\delta\) is the initial phase. The quantity \(\omega=2\pi/T\) is the angular frequency and \(k=2\pi/L\) is the wave number with \(T\) equal to the wave period and \(L\) the wave length. The initial phase \(\delta\) is given by a random number between 0 and \(2\pi\).

Equation \(\eqref{wave_fisrtOrder}\) expresses the surface elevation at infinity that Biesel defined as the far-field solution. The Biesel function can be derived for the far-field solution and for a pistontype wavemaker as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{2} \label{eq_piston_tranfer} \frac{H}{S_0} = 2\frac{\sinh^2(kd)}{\sinh(kd)\cosh(kd)+kd}, \end{equation}\]

where \(S_0\) is the piston stroke. Once the piston stroke is defined, the time series of the piston movement is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{3} \label{eq_piston_motion} e_1(t) = \frac{S_0}{2} \sin(\omega t+\delta), \end{equation}\]

docs.title: Second-order wave generation of regular waves
docs.text:
The implementation of a second order wavemaker theory will prevent the generation of spurious secondary waves. The second order wave generation theory implemented in DualSPHysics is based on (Madsen 1971) who developed a simple second-order wavemaker theory to generate long second order Stokes waves that would not change shape as they propagated. The theory proposed by (Madsen 1971) is straightforward, controllable, computationally inexpensive with efficient results, and is accurate for waves of first and second order.

The piston stroke \(S_0\) can be redefined from Equation \(\eqref{eq_piston_tranfer}\) as \(S_0=H/m_1\) where:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{4} m_1(t) = \frac{2\sinh^2(kd)}{\sinh(kd)\cosh(kd)+kd}, \end{equation}\]

Following (Madsen 1971), to generate a wave of second order, an extra term must be added to Equation \(\eqref{eq_piston_motion}\). This term, for piston-type wavemaker, is equal to:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{5} \label{eq_piston_motion2nd} e_2(t) = \bigg(\frac{H^2}{32d} \bigg(\frac{3\cosh(kd)}{\sinh^3(kd)}-\frac{2}{m_1}\bigg)\bigg) \sin(2\omega t+2\delta), \end{equation}\]

Therefore, the piston displacement, for regular waves, is the summation of Equations \(\eqref{eq_piston_motion}\) and \(\eqref{eq_piston_motion2nd}\):

\[\begin{equation} \tag{6} \label{eq_piston_motion_tot} e(t) = \frac{S_0}{2}\sin(\omega t+\delta)+\frac{H^2}{32d} \bigg(\frac{3\cosh(kd)}{\sinh^3(kd)}-\frac{2}{m_1}\bigg) \sin(2\omega t+2\delta), \end{equation}\]

Madsen limited the application of this approximate second order wavemaker theory to waves that complied with the condition given by \(HL^2/d^3 < (8\pi^2)/3\). A specific warning is implemented in DualSPHysics to inform the user whether or not this condition is fulfilled.

docs.title: First order wave generation of irregular waves
docs.text:
Monochromatic waves are not representative of sea states that characterise real wave storm conditions. Sea waves are mostly random or irregular in nature. Irregular wave generation is performed in DualSPHysics based on [Liu and Frigaard, 2001]. Starting from an assigned wave spectra, the Biesel transfer function (Equation \(\eqref{eq_piston_tranfer}\)) is applied to each component in which the spectrum is discretised. The procedure for the generation of irregular waves is summarised as follows:

* 1 Defining the wave spectrum through its characteristic parameters (peak frequency, spectrum shape, etc.). * 2 Dividing the spectrum into \(N\) parts (\(N>50\)) in the interval (\(f_{start}, f_{stop}\)), where generally the values assumed by the spectrum (\(S_η\)) at the extremes of this interval are smaller than the value assumed for the peak frequency, \(f_p: S_η(f_{start})≤0.01·S_η(f_p)\) and \(S_\eta(f_{stop}) ≤ 0.01 \cdot S_\eta(f_p)\). * 3 The frequency band width is so-defined as \(Δf=(fstop-fstart)/N\). The irregular wave is decomposed into \(N\) linear waves. * 4 Determining the angular frequency \(\omega_i\), amplitude \(a_i\) and initial phase \(\delta_i\) (random real number between 0 and \(2\pi\)) of each \(i\)-th linear wave. The angular frequency \(\omega_i\) and amplitude ai can therefore be expressed as follows:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{7} \label{irreg_wave_frequency} \omega_i=2\pi f_i; a_i=\sqrt{2S_\eta(f_i)\Delta f}=\frac{H_i}{2}. \end{equation}\]

* 5 Converting the time series of surface elevation into the time series of piston movement with the help of Biesel transfer function:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{8} \label{irreg_wave_transfer_function} \frac{H_i}{S_{0,i}} = \frac{2\sinh^2(k_id)}{\sinh(k_id)\cosh(k_id)+k_id}; \end{equation}\]

* 6 Composing all the \(i\)-th components derived from the previous equation into the time series of the piston displacement as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{9} \label{irreg_wave_piston_displacement} e(t) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{S_{0,i}}{2}\sin(\omega_it+\delta_i). \end{equation}\]

In DualSPHysics two standard wave spectra have been implemented and used to generate irregular waves: JONSWAP and Pierson-Moskowitz spectra. The characteristic parameters of each spectrum can be assigned by the user together with the value of \(N\) (number of parts in which the spectrum is divided).

The user can choose among four different ways to define the angular frequency. It can be determined assuming an equidistant discretization of the wave spectrum (\(f_i=f_{start}+iΔf-Δf/2\)), or chosen as unevenly distributed between \((i-0.5)\Delta f\) and \((i+0.5)\Delta f\). An unevenly distributed band width should be preferred: in fact, depending on N, an equidistant splitting can lead to the repetition of the same wave group in the time series that can be easily avoided using an unevenly distributed band width. The last two ways to determine the angular frequency of each component and its band width consist of the application of a stretched or cosine stretched function. The use of a stretched or cosine stretched function has been proven to lead the most accurate results in terms of wave height distribution and groupiness, even when the number of spectrum components \(N\), is relatively low. If there is a certain wave group that is repeating, finally the full range of wave heights and wave periods is not reproduced and statistically the wave train is not representing a real sea state of random waves.

A phase seed is also used and can be changed in DualSPHysics to obtain different random series of \(\delta_i\). Changing the phase seed allows generating different irregular wave time series both with the same significant wave height (\(H_{m0}\)) and peak period (\(T_p\)).

docs.title: Second-order bound long waves
docs.text:
When natural waves are reproduced in a laboratory or in a numerical model the wave generator is normally controlled by a first-order signal. The wave set-down (bound long waves) generates drift velocities directed landwards under the crests and seawards under the troughs [Ottesen-Hansen et al., 1980]. However, at the wavemaker, there is no flow through the paddle, therefore the natural drift velocities are compensated by identical ones with opposite signs. The latter velocities create a progressive long wave that is not bound anymore but free. This phenomenon is called parasitic long waves and it results in an exaggeration of the long wave effects. Second-order wave generation is required in order to cancel out this parasitic long wave to achieve the drift velocities that characterise the set-down. Another long wave, called displacement long wave, is caused by finite wavemaker displacements away from the mean position.

The correction of the first-order wave generation at the wavemaker must be capable of compensating both parasitic long waves and displacement long waves. The method implemented in DualSPHysics is based on the solution for the control signal of the wavemaker that is described in [Barthel et al., 1993].

docs.title: Solitary waves
docs.text: Generation of solitary waves in DualSPHysics is achieved by means moving boundaries. In particular, a piston-type wavemaker is employed to generate single and multiple solitary waves [Dominguez et al., 2019].

docs.title: Single solitary wave
docs.text:
Goring [1978] laid the groundwork for the generation of solitary waves by means of a piston-type wavemaker.His method was based on one fundamental hypothesis: the horizontal velocity of the water particles under the wave crest, u (depth-integrated velocity), is equal to the velocity of the wavemaker.

Equation \(\eqref{ss_1}\) defines the aforementioned assumption, where \(xs\) refers to the piston displacement.

\[\begin{equation} \tag{10} \label{ss_1} u(x_s,t) = \frac{dx_s}{dt}. \end{equation}\]

The depth-average velocity can be expressed by Equation \(\eqref{ss_2}\), where \(c\) is the wave celerity, \(h\) is the still water depth and \(η\) is the free surface elevation.

\[\begin{equation} \tag{11} \label{ss_2} u(x_s,t) = \frac{c_\eta(x_s,t)}{h+\eta(x_s,t)}. \end{equation}\]

Combining and integrating Equations \(\eqref{ss_1}\) and \(\eqref{ss_2}\), the piston displacement in time can be expressed as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{12} \label{solitary_piston_displacement} x_s(t) = \frac{2H}{kh}\tanh\big(k(ct-x_s(t))\big). \end{equation}\]

where the parameter \(k\) is the outskirt coefficient, which describes the way the free surface elevation tends towards the mean level at infinity. The solitary wave profile is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{13} \label{ss_wave} \eta(x_s,t) = H {sech}^2(k(ct-x_s)). \end{equation}\]

Equation \(\eqref{ss_wave}\) is an implicit equation that needs to be solved by numerical methods.

In order to give the possibility to the user to generate the solitary wave profile that would be the most appropriate for his problem and the closest the the real studied phenomenon (e.g., tsunami wave), three different theories for solitary wave generation have been implemented in DualSPHysics. For all cases, a piston-type wavemaker is employed. The three different approaches result in different wave propagation properties (i.e. different loss of amplitude and differences in generated trailing waves) [Dominguez et al., 2019]. One solution is derived from the Rayleigh solitary wave solution; the second one uses a wavemaker law-of-motion derived from the KdV solution; the third one consists of solving Equation \(\eqref{ss_wave}\) iteratively using the Newton\(--\)Raphson method. The following subsections described the three different theories.

docs.title: Rayleigh approximation to a solitary wave
docs.text:
Following Serre (1953), the theoretical free-surface elevation expressed by Equation \(\eqref{ss_wave}\) can be re-written as follows:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{14} \label{ss_wave_rayleigh} \eta(x_s,t) = H \, \operatorname{sech}^{2}\!\left( k (x - c t) \right), \qquad k = \sqrt{\frac{3H}{4h^{3}}}. \end{equation}\]

The quantity \(\sqrt{4H(H+h)/3}\) corresponds to half wavemaker stroke (SR) and takes into account that in DualSPHysics the origin of the wavemaker movement is set as \(x=0\). The quantity defined as \(c\) is the wave celerity; \(Tf\) is the generation time used to form the solitary wave, \(x_s\) is the wavemaker displacement and \(k\) is the outskirt coefficient. All these parameters are defined as follows (\(H\) and h refer to the wave height and to the water depth, respectively):

\[\begin{equation} \tag{15} \label{solitary_wave_celerity} c = \sqrt{g(H+h)}. \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{16} \label{solitary_generation_time} T_f = \frac{2}{kc}(3.8+\frac{H}{h}); \end{equation}\] \[\begin{equation} \tag{17} \label{solitary_piston_motion} x_s(t) = \frac{H}{k}\frac{gh(k_c(t-T_f))t}{h+H(1-gh^2(kc(t-T_f)t))}, \end{equation}\]

where:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{18} \label{solitary_k_coefficient} k = \sqrt{\frac{3H}{4h^2(H+h)}}. \end{equation}\]

docs.text:

docs.title: Goring solution (Boussinesq)
docs.text: Equations \(\eqref{solitary_piston_displacement}\) and \(\eqref{ss_wave}\) correspond, respectively, to the equation of the piston displacement and the theoretical water elevation using the solution proposed by Goring which requires an iterative procedure to solve Equation \(\eqref{solitary_piston_displacement}\).

docs.title: Multiple solitary waves
docs.text:
To generate a series of multiple solitary waves, the law of motion of the wavemaker is calculated for each i-th solitary wave. Any of the three theories indicated in the previous sections can be used. Then, the time lag between the \(i+1\)-th and the \(i\)-th solitary wave has to be specified as a fraction or multiple of the generation time used for the \(i\)-th solitary wave. The time lag-between the generation of the two solitary waves will be expressed by \(\lambda T_f\), being \(T_f\) the generation time used to generated the first solitary wave. The coefficient \(λ\) is a positive real number that multiplies \(T_f\). If \(\lambda<1\), the generation of the second solitary wave starts when the displacement of the piston has not reached yet the maximum stroke that is needed to generate the first solitary wave.

The generation of multiple solitary waves is a simple but efficient way to model a wave train of several tsunamis which might have been triggered by the same tectonic event.

docs.title: Focused waves
docs.text:
NewWave theory [Whittaker et al., 2017] is employed to create the time series of focused wave groups. The NewWave theory describes the most probable shape of a large wave in a given sea state. Theoretically, the focus wave group energy reaches the structure in a compact, maximized form if the focus location is close enough to the focus location. A NewWave-type focused wave group comprising N infinitesimal wave components is given by:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{21} \label{eq:newwave} \eta(x,t) = \frac{A}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} S_{\eta\eta}(\omega_i)\,\Delta\omega\,\cos\left(k_i(x-x_f)-\omega_i(t-t_f)\right) \end{equation}\]

where \(S_{ηη}\) is the power spectral density, \(ω\) is the angular frequency, \(t\) is time, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the sea state (with an associated variance \(\sigma^2=\sum S_{ηη} (\omega_i )\Delta_\omega\) in this discretised form) and \(k_i\) is the wavenumber of the \(i\)-th wave component with angular frequency ωi and related to it by the familiar linear dispersion relation \(\omega^2=gk\tanh⁡(kh)\) (where \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity and \(h\) is the water depth), and \(x\) is the horizontal distance. All wave components come into phase at the focus location \(x_f\) and focus time \(t_f\) to form a large wave with a linear focus amplitude equal to \(A\).

A full range of focusing behaviours can be allowed by introducing the the phase angle \(\phi\) of the group at focus (e.g. crest, trough, otherwise), while the energy concentration within the group is independent of the value of \(\phi\). However, the wave shape can affect its breaking patterns and therefore the impacts exerted on the structure.

docs.title: Passive and active wave absorption
docs.text: The use of wave absorption allows generating long time series of sea waves in relatively short domains with negligible wave reflection. Wave absorption techniques can be categorized as passive and active, respectively. Passive wave absorbers are usually required to damp the wave energy and to reduce reflection exerted by the boundary of the model domain. In active absorption systems, the wavemaker real-time displacement is corrected to cancel out the reflected waves and to damp the re-reflection phenomenon. Active wave absorption is implemented in DualSPHysics for a piston-type wavemaker only.

docs.title: Passive wave absorption
docs.text:
A damping zone is implemented in DualSPHysics as passive absorption system. The implemented damping system consists in gradually reducing the velocity of the particles at each time step according to their location, but using quadratic decay rather than exponential. In this way, the velocity is modified following

\[\begin{equation} \tag{22} \label{eq:damping_velocity} v = v_0\,f(x,\Delta t) \end{equation}\]

where \(v_0\) is the initial velocity of the particle \(i\), \(v\) is the final velocity and \(f(x,\Delta t)\) is the reduction function defined as

\[\begin{equation} \tag{23} \label{eq:damping_function} f(x,\Delta t) = 1 - \Delta t\,\beta\left(\frac{x-x_0}{x_1-x_0}\right)^2 \end{equation}\]

where \(Δt\) is the duration of the last time step, \(x\) is position of the particles, \(x0\) and \(x1\) are the initial and final position of the damping zone, respectively. It is recommended to use one wavelength, L, as the length of the damping zone. The coefficient \(β\) modifies the reduction function that is applied to the velocity.

docs.title: Active wave absorption
docs.text:
The active wave absorption system implemented in DualSPHysics is based on the time-domain filtering technique that uses the free-surface elevation at the wavemaker position as feedback for the control of the wavemaker displacement. The target wavemaker position e(t) is corrected in real time in order to avoid reflection at the wavemaker. It is necessary to estimate the free-surface elevation of the reflected waves, \(ηR\), to be absorbed, by comparing the target incident free-surface elevation, \(ηI\), with the measured one in front of the wavemaker, \(ηSPH\). This is measured at 4-10·hSPH from the wavemaker. The reflected free-surface elevation can be expressed as

\[\begin{equation} \tag{24} \label{eq:awas_etaR} \eta_R(t) = \eta_{SPH}(t) - \eta_I(t) \end{equation}\]

The wavemaker velocity is then modified to match the velocity induced by the wave that will be absorbed. For a piston-type wavemaker the wave absorption is performed using linear long wave theory [Schaffer and Klopman, 2000; Dean and Dalrymple, 1991]. The velocity correction to absorb the reflected waves, UR, is expressed as

\[\begin{equation} \tag{25} \label{eq:awas_UR} U_R(t) = \eta_R(t)\,\sqrt{g/d} \end{equation}\]

where \(ηR\) is the free-surface elevation of the reflected waves and g is the gravitational acceleration. The corrected wavemaker velocity \(U_C\) is the subtraction of \(U_R\) from the theoretical wave maker velocity UI. This \(U_I\) is the derivative in time of the wavemaker displacement \(e(t)\). Here the implementation details are expressed for the regular wave case. The theoretical velocity at time t, \(_UI(t)\), can be computed as:

\[\begin{equation} \tag{26} \label{eq:awas_UI} U_I(t) = \frac{de(t)}{dt} = \frac{\omega S_0}{2}\cos(\omega t+\delta) \end{equation}\]

The free-surface elevation in front of the wavemaker is measured, the target incident free-surface elevation is calculated and therefore the velocity correction UR is estimated. The corrected wavemaker velocity at the instant \(t+dt\) can be expressed as

\[\begin{equation} \tag{27} \label{eq:awas_UC} U_C(t+dt) = U_I(t+dt) - U_R(t) \end{equation}\]

The wavemaker position at \(t+dt\) is then corrected using the following expression

\[\begin{equation} \tag{28} \label{eq:awas_position} e(t+dt) = e(t) + \left(U_C(t+dt)+U_C(t)\right)\frac{dt}{2} \end{equation}\]

Small deviations of the mean water level from the zero can imply accumulations in time leading to a drift of the wavemaker from its initial position that will grow indefinitely. In order to prevent this drift, the wavemaker should be forced back to its zero position. Hence, a drift correction algorithm is implemented in the code. The algorithm checks when the 80
