docs.title: 03_ROLLINGTANK
docs.text:
• A 2-D reproduction of the rolling tank experiment from Idelsohn et al. (2008), with an elastic beam attached to the bottom of the tank.

  • The case consists of a standing beam in a deep oil solution so that the tip of the beam is flush with the top of the fluid level.

  • The real tank motion from the experiment is imposed and the rolling frequency is set to match the critical sloshing frequency of the tank.

  • The natural frequency of the flexible is beam is also matched with the rolling frequency, leading to simple dynamics in the coupled fluid-structure interactions.

Watch on YouTube

  • A 2-D reproduction of the rolling tank experiment from Idelsohn et al. (2008), with an elastic beam attached to the top of the tank.

  • The case consists of a hanging beam in a shallow water solution so that the tip of the beam is flush with the top of the fluid level.

  • The real tank motion from the experiment is imposed and the rolling frequency is set to match the critical sloshing frequency of the tank.

  • The natural frequency of the flexible is beam is different from the rolling frequency, leading to chaotic dynamics in the motion of the beam as it is impacted by the sloshing waves generated by the tank motion.

Watch on YouTube

Figure 3: Selected instant(s) of flow in the rolling tank.

docs.text:
• A 2-D still water tank encloses a trigonal wedge in the bottom centre of the tank with. A low value of artificial viscosity is used to observe better the effects and noise generated by the different boundary conditions (DBC and mDBC).

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, and mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip

Watch on YouTube

Figure 1: Selected instant(s) of still-water simulations with DBC and mDBC.

docs.title: 02_Poiseuille
docs.text:
• Poiseuille flow is simulated with the boundary walls located at z=±0.5m, the maximum velocity is U= 1m/s and the viscosity is ν=0.1m^2/s resulting in a Reynolds number of Re=10.

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip, and mDBC SlipMode3: FreeSlip Watch on YouTube

  • Run Down flow is with boundary walls at z=±0.5m and initial velocity U=1m/s with no body forces to drive the flow, the flow is then slowed down by the chosen slip condition. Includes execution with mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip, and mDBC SlipMode3: FreeSlip

Figure 2: Selected instant(s) of Poiseuille flow at two particle resolutions.

docs.title: 03_Sloshing
docs.text:
• The case will reproduce a sloshing experiment that includes moving boundaries: SPHERIC Benchmark Test Case #10

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip and SlipMode2: No-Slip with No-Penetration activated

Watch on YouTube

Figure 3: Selected instant(s) of sloshing simulations with DBC and mDBC.

docs.title: 04_Dambreak
docs.text:
• 3-D dam break experiment that includes moving boundaries proposed as SPHERIC Benchmark Test Case #2.

  • Includes execution with mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0 and mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip with no-Penetration activated. Watch on YouTube

  • 3-D dam break with high resolution (12M) for multi-GPU execution.

Figure 4: Dam-break flow and boundary discretisation.

docs.title: 05_FlowCylinder
docs.text:
• 2-D flow passing a cylinder of diameter D=0.2m, which is surrounded by a viscous fluid. Dimensions of the fluid domain are chosen to minimise boundary effects. The fluid is initialized with a constant velocity of U=1m/s and with Re=200.

  • The circle is created using the Free Draw Mode instead of the Cartesian grid.

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip

Watch on YouTube

Figure 5: Selected instant(s) of flow past a cylinder.

docs.title: 06_WaveTank
docs.text:
• 2-D regular waves are generated and propagated in a numerical wave flume using DBC and the new mDBC.

  • The beach is created using the Free Draw Mode instead of the Cartesian grid.

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip and SlipMode2: No-Slip with No-Penetration activated

Watch on YouTube

Figure 6: Selected instant(s) of wave-tank simulations with DBC and mDBC.

docs.title: 07_WavesCylinder
docs.text:
• 3-D regular waves (H=0.1m, T=1.2s, d=0.5m) passing a cylinder of diameter D=0.2m and 0.7m high located in the middle of a wave flume.

  • The cylinder is created using the Free Draw Mode instead of the Cartesian grid.

  • Includes execution with mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip Watch on YouTube

  • 3-D dam break with high resolution (12M) for multi-GPU execution.

Figure 7: Selected instant(s) of wave interaction with the cylinder.

docs.title: 08_FloatingWaves
docs.text:
• 2-D floating box under the action of regular waves with piston.

  • The beach is created using the Free Draw Mode instead of the Cartesian grid.

  • mDBC is applied not only to the tank and piston, but also to the floating box.

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0, mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip Watch on YouTube

  • 2-D floating box under the action of regular waves with piston with validation data (motions of the box) from Ren et al., 2015.

  • Includes execution with mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0 and mDBC SlipMode2: No-Slip

Figure 8: Selected instant(s) of floating-box simulations with DBC and mDBC.

docs.title: 09_FloatingDuck
docs.text:
• 3-D floating external STL (duck) in a square tank using DBC and mDBC.

  • mDBC is applied to an external STL using advanced tools during pre-processing in order to create normal vectors and to fill the geometry with floating particles.

  • Includes execution with DBC, mDBC SlipMode1: Vel0 applied to duck only, and SlipMode2: No-Slip with No-Penetration activated applied to all boundaries

Watch on YouTube

Figure 9: Selected instant(s) of floating-duck simulations with DBC and mDBC.

docs.title: 10_InitializeFlow
docs.text:
Source directory: examples/mdbc/10_InitializeFlow.

  • Flow initialisation from previous particle data, illustrated by flow past a cylinder and two- and three-dimensional bridge cases. The initialised cases interpolate velocity and pressure; the initialised bridge cases also reconstruct the free surface.

docs.title: 11_MixBC
docs.text:
Source directory: examples/mdbc/11_MixBC.

  • Examples of assigning different boundary conditions to boundary marker sets, covering flow past a cylinder, a three-dimensional dam break and waves on a beach with a cylinder. The mixed cases combine no-slip and free-slip boundaries; the wave case also uses a zero tangential velocity condition for the piston.

docs.title: How-To Guides
docs.text:
Edited by Alejandro Crespo

This page indexes the step-by-step guides for setting up (pre-processing) and analysing (post-processing) DualSPHysics cases.

docs.title: Pre-Processing
docs.text:
How to:

  • Change the geometry
  • Change the resolution/particle size
  • Change the viscosity formulation
  • Change the time duration
  • Change the still-water level (pending)
  • Add a new structure (scope still to be defined)
  • Add an inlet/outlet — define the geometry of the open-boundary zone, then set the parameters that control the inlet (velocity, density, water surface, refilling, etc.)
  • Add a floating object — generate the object's particles and define its floating properties (mass, centre of gravity, motion constraints)
  • Add two coupled objects — first define both bodies individually, then define the mechanical constraint linking them
  • Select a multi-phase formulation
  • Select flexible structures — for example, converting the rigid geometry of the Turek-Hron case into a flexible one
  • Use Variable Resolution
  • Use DesignSPHysics
  • How is the simulation domain determined in DualSPHysics?
  • How are MK labels assigned to particle groups?

docs.text:
How to:

  • Measure the velocity in the fluid domain
  • Measure the pressure exerted by the fluid

docs.title: How-To: Change the Resolution/Particle Size
docs.text: Change the initial particle spacing, dp, in the case-definition XML, then regenerate the particles with GenCase. A smaller spacing resolves the geometry with more particles and typically increases memory use and computational cost; it does not by itself establish convergence or accuracy.

docs.title: 1. Locate the spacing definition
docs.text:
In examples/benchmarks/00_GettingStarted/Dambreak2D_Def.xml, the following fragment belongs to case/casedef/geometry:

<definition dp="0.01" units_comment="metres (m)">
    <pointref x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <pointmin x="-1" y="0" z="-1" />
    <pointmax x="4.5" y="0" z="3.5" />
</definition>

Here the initial spacing is 0.01 m. That is this benchmark's setting, not a recommended spacing for every case. Equal minimum and maximum y coordinates define this example's 2-D x–z generation plane.

Some cases use an expression instead of a literal value. For example, examples/benchmarks/01_DamBreak/Dambreak_Def.xml defines Dp="BoxLength/20" and uses dp="#Dp". Follow the expression back to its definition before editing; changing an unrelated literal does not change the spacing used by GenCase. Keep any grid-alignment expressions consistent with the intended resolution.

docs.title: 2. Choose and apply the intended spacing
docs.text:
1. Identify the physical features, boundary representation and fluid regions that the particles must resolve.
  2. Replace the dp value, or its defining expression, with the spacing chosen for that case. Keep length units consistent with the geometry.
  3. Review geometry coordinates or layer definitions expressed in multiples of Dp: they can change when the spacing changes. Do not rescale the physical geometry simply to change resolution.
  4. Preserve unrelated physical and numerical settings. Review any coefficients explicitly dependent on Dp, including expressions used for viscosity.

There is no universal dp suitable for every geometry or flow. Compare appropriate resolutions for the quantities of interest rather than treating one particle count as proof of adequate resolution.

docs.title: 3. Regenerate and inspect the particles
docs.text:
Run GenCase through the case-generation workflow so that the edited definition produces new initial particle data. Editing dp does not alter existing BI4 results or rebuild an already generated particle configuration.

Inspect the generated particle count, fluid fill, boundaries, gaps and floating bodies. Check that small features and intended boundary layers are represented without unwanted overlaps. Keep results from different resolutions identifiable when comparing them.

docs.title: 4. Distinguish spacing from related settings
docs.text:
Setting Meaning Particle spacing dp Initial distance used for the particle-generation lattice. Smoothing length h Numerical length scale configured through the case's smoothing-length settings, such as coefh or hdp. It is not the same quantity as dp. Kernel support Neighbourhood over which the selected kernel interacts; it depends on the kernel and smoothing length. Physical geometry The tank, fluid volume and objects being represented. Generation bounds pointmin and pointmax, limiting where GenCase may create particles. Simulation domain Solver bounds derived from generated particles or customised using simulationdomain.

When smoothing length depends on dp, changing spacing also changes that numerical scale. More particles increase the work per saved state, and the solver's timestep calculation can also change. Assess memory, run cost and output size for the new configuration without assuming a fixed runtime multiplier.

See resolution and physical scales, smoothing length and generation bounds for related XML settings.

docs.title: How-To: Change the Still-Water Level
docs.text: This guide is being prepared.

docs.title: How-To: Change the Simulation Time Duration
docs.text: Set the maximum simulation time with TimeMax in case/execution/parameters. Keep it distinct from the interval between saved outputs and from the numerical integration timestep.

docs.title: 1. Locate TimeMax and TimeOut
docs.text:
examples/benchmarks/00_GettingStarted/Dambreak2D_Def.xml contains:

<parameter key="TimeMax" value="1.0" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.01" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />
Setting Meaning in this example TimeMax Maximum simulation time: 1.0 s. TimeOut Regular output interval: 0.01 s. Integration timestep Individual numerical advance of the solution; neither of the two values above specifies it.

These are benchmark settings, not default durations for another case. Increasing TimeMax extends the requested simulated time; reducing TimeOut requests more frequent saved states. Changing the output interval does not select the numerical integration timestep.

docs.title: 2. Change the intended duration in XML
docs.text:
1. Choose the maximum simulation time needed for the physical event being studied.
  2. Edit the existing TimeMax value, keeping seconds as its units. Do not add a second entry with the same key.
  3. Keep TimeOut unchanged unless a different output schedule is also intended. More frequent output increases stored data; it does not recover events already absent from existing results.
  4. Follow the case-preparation and execution workflow so that the edited definition reaches the execution XML used by the solver. Check the script for an existing maximum-time override.

Other benchmarks use expressions. For example, 01_DamBreak/Dambreak_Def.xml defines timeMax="7.40" and supplies value="#timeMax" to TimeMax. Follow such references to the defining variable before editing; leave the expression consistent with the intended case.

Changing the input file does not extend already saved results or automatically resume a previous simulation.

docs.title: 3. Use the command-line override when appropriate
docs.text:
The v6 solver option -tmax:<float> overrides the maximum simulation time for that execution. In the existing wDambreak2D_win64_GPU.bat variable context, an explicit override using the same 1.0 s as the XML is:

%dualsphysicsgpu% -gpu %dirout%/%name% %dirout% -tmax:1.0

This is an execution-command fragment: %dualsphysicsgpu%, %dirout% and %name% must already be defined by the script. Replace only the time value with the intended stop time when using an override, retaining the case's other execution arguments. The option does not modify the XML or resume a previous simulation. It is a maximum simulation time, not an additional duration to append to an existing run.

-tout:<float> separately controls the regular output interval. Keep duration and output scheduling independent when inspecting the final execution configuration.

See simulation duration and saving for the XML settings and related output controls.

docs.title: How-To: Change the Viscosity Formulation
docs.text: Configure viscosity in case/execution/parameters. Select the formulation and its coefficient together: artificial viscosity and physical kinematic viscosity have different meanings and are not interchangeable numerical settings.

docs.title: 1. Select the formulation
docs.text:
For the core single-phase fluid configuration, v6 uses these textual selections:

Formulation ViscoTreatment Turbulence Meaning of Visco Artificial viscosity ART NO Artificial-viscosity coefficient. Laminar viscosity LAM NO Kinematic viscosity, in m²/s. Laminar + SPS LAM SPS Kinematic viscosity, with the sub-particle-scale turbulence model enabled separately.

Use the current textual keys rather than copying old numeric selectors. SPS requires LAM; do not combine it with ART. SPS adds a turbulence treatment to laminar viscosity; it does not turn an artificial coefficient into a physical fluid property.

docs.title: 2. Read the benchmark examples
docs.text: The following fragments belong to execution/parameters; they are alternatives from different cases, not blocks to paste together.

docs.title: Artificial viscosity
docs.text:
examples/benchmarks/00_GettingStarted/Dambreak2D_Def.xml uses:

<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="ART" comment="Viscosity formulation: LAM:Laminar, ART:Artificial (default=LAM)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="#alpha" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Turbulence" value="NO" comment="Turbulence model: NO:None, SPS:Sub-particle scale (default=NO)" />

#alpha evaluates the case's existing alpha expression. Keep its definition and dependencies available; do not replace the expression with a guessed coefficient. Artificial viscosity supplies numerical dissipation, so its coefficient should be assessed for the intended method and resolution.

docs.title: Laminar viscosity
docs.text:
examples/benchmarks/08_HeaveDecay/HeaveDecay_Def.xml uses:

<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="LAM" comment="Viscosity formulation: LAM:Laminar, ART:Artificial (default=LAM)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="1e-06" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Turbulence" value="NO" comment="Turbulence model: NO:None, SPS:Sub-particle scale (default=NO)" />

Here Visco is kinematic viscosity, in m²/s. Use the value for the intended fluid and conditions; the benchmark's value is not a universal material property.

docs.title: Laminar + SPS
docs.text:
examples/benchmarks/03_WaveGeneration/WaveGeneration_Def.xml uses:

<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="LAM" comment="Viscosity formulation: LAM:Laminar, ART:Artificial (default=LAM)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="1e-6" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Turbulence" value="SPS" comment="Turbulence model: NO:None, SPS:Sub-particle scale (default=NO)" />

This selects LAM and enables SPS separately. It is a different model choice from the laminar-only example, even when the kinematic-viscosity values agree.

docs.title: 3. Apply the change consistently
docs.text:
1. Locate the existing ViscoTreatment, Visco and Turbulence entries. Edit those entries rather than adding duplicates.
  2. Select a compatible pair from the table and set Visco with the meaning and units required by that formulation. Do not carry an artificial coefficient unchanged into a laminar configuration.
  3. Review ViscoBoundFactor, which multiplies the viscosity value for boundary interaction. Preserve its case-specific value unless the intended change also requires revising it.
  4. If the case already uses ViscoTime, review that external viscosity file as well; changing one constant does not replace an active time-dependent definition. Do not add this conditional setting to cases that do not use it.
  5. Check the execution script for viscosity or turbulence command-line overrides, then prepare the case through the existing workflow. Inspect the resolved execution settings before comparing results.

Changing the formulation can change dissipation and flow predictions; it is a modelling decision, not a syntax-only substitution. Specialised multiphase or non-Newtonian material selectors require their own configuration guides.

See viscosity and turbulence for the related parameters and model explanations.

docs.title: How-To: Compute the Motion of a Floating Body
docs.text: Use FloatingInfo to extract floating-body time series from recorded DualSPHysics simulation information. It post-processes the motion already calculated by the simulation; it does not change that motion or perform another fluid–structure interaction calculation.

docs.title: 1. Locate the floating-body data
docs.text:
Start with existing results from examples/benchmarks/06_FloatingBox/. FloatingInfo reads PartFloatInfo.ibi4, which contains floating-body information, rather than interpolating particle velocities at measurement points. Keep the simulation's associated data together in FloatingBox_out/data/.

The normal v6 input option is -dirdata <dir>. For variable-resolution simulations it takes the main output directory instead. The separate -dirdatax <dir> reads the extra-frequency floating data, PartFloatInfo2.ibi4, when that output exists. An ordinary particle VTK series alone is not a substitute for these floating records.

docs.title: 2. Identify the floating marker
docs.text:
Use the generated case information and simulation log to identify the MK of the floating body. -onlymk selects floating bodies by that marker, not by a particle ID or a body's ordinal number.

The FloatingBox XML defines the body with local boundary identifier mkbound="50". The generated global MK also includes the boundary-marker offset; do not assume that mkbound and MK are interchangeable. Check the mapping for the actual output before selecting a different body.

The benchmark command uses -onlymk:10-120: the hyphen defines an inclusive range of MK values, 10 through 120. Floating bodies whose markers fall in that range are selected; this does not create 111 bodies or select fixed/moving walls as floatings. The range is specific to this example. Choose markers belonging to the floating bodies of interest in another simulation.

docs.title: 3. Extract the motion
docs.text:
Work in a Windows Command Prompt in examples/benchmarks/06_FloatingBox/. The following post-processing fragment uses the variables from wFloatingBox_win64_GPU.bat, after its simulation results exist:

set name=FloatingBox
set dirout=%name%_out
set diroutdata=%dirout%\data
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set floatinginfo="%dirbin%/FloatingInfo_win64.exe"
set dirout2=%dirout%\post

Define these variables in the same command session or BAT before using:

%floatinginfo% -dirdata %diroutdata% -savemotion -onlymk:10-120 -savedata %dirout2%/

The fragment does not run GenCase or the solver. %floatinginfo% includes the quoted executable path; %diroutdata% points to the simulation data and %dirout2% to the CSV output directory. Adapt paths for another installation, quoting directory arguments if they contain spaces.

Option Meaning -dirdata %diroutdata% Read the saved floating-body data. -savemotion Include motion data in the floating CSV output. The explicit control is -savemotion:0/1, enabled by default. -onlymk:10-120 Select floating bodies with MK in the indicated range. -savedata %dirout2%/ Generate floating-data CSV files under FloatingBox_out/post/.

docs.title: 4. Read the time series
docs.text:
The floating CSV naming pattern is _mk<marker>.csv; for example, _mk60.csv identifies MK 60. Open the files for the selected floatings in FloatingBox_out/post/. The accompanying postFloater.m illustrates reading the _mk60.csv series, including surge, heave and pitch. Use your actual output directory rather than copying another case's directory name from a plotting script.

Read the CSV header before plotting: the available fields and motion columns depend on the saved data, dimensionality and output options. Typical header labels include part, time [s], fvel.x [m/s], fomega.x [rad/s] and center.x [m], with corresponding Cartesian components where present. The motion columns use labels such as surge [m], heave [m] and pitch [deg]. Do not assume a fixed column index or that every file contains every quantity below.

Quantity Meaning and units center Position of the centre of mass, in m; distinguish position from displacement. surge, sway, heave Displacement of the centre of mass along X, Y and Z respectively, in m. roll, pitch, yaw Rotation about X, Y and Z respectively, in degrees. fvel Linear velocity of the floating body, in m/s. fomega Angular velocity, in rad/s. face, faceomega Linear and angular accelerations calculated from changes in the respective velocities, in m/s² and rad/s².

For this 2-D x–z FloatingBox case, surge describes horizontal X displacement, heave vertical Z displacement, and pitch rotation about Y, normal to the simulation plane. Plot each quantity against time [s], retaining its units. Do not interpret center.x as surge or confuse pitch in degrees with angular velocity in rad/s. The pitch sign convention changed since v5.0.204; check conventions before comparing with older files or experimental axes.

Other documented quantities, when present, include external linear/angular forces, fluid linear/angular forces, and acceleration before constraints. Use their own headers and units rather than treating these as additional displacement or rotation columns. For a separate particle-based force calculation, see Measure the force on an object.

docs.title: Limitations and checks
docs.text:
• FloatingInfo requires the floating records for the selected simulation and bodies. If a series is missing, check the input directory, available PartFloatInfo.ibi4, generated MK mapping and selected range.
  • -savemotion:0 omits motion data; retain motion output when surge, heave or pitch are needed.
  • Extra-frequency data require PartFloatInfo2.ibi4 and the corresponding input option; they cannot be recovered from missing output by changing plotting settings.
  • Time-series resolution is limited by the recorded data. Inspect time values when selecting records with -first, -last or -files.
  • CSV separators are configurable with -csvsep; choose the matching separator when importing a file.
  • Particle or body geometry animation in ParaView provides spatial context; it is a different output from these body-level CSV time series.

docs.title: How-To: Measure the Force on an Object
docs.text: Use ComputeForces to calculate the documented fluid-force quantities for selected boundary particles from saved DualSPHysics v6 data. This differs from sampling pressure at a point.

docs.title: 1. Identify the object and marker
docs.text:
Keep the existing particle BI4 files and associated case metadata. Inspect generated case information and the simulation log to identify the object's particle marker MK and boundary type.

-onlymk selects the generated particles' MK. A local XML mkbound label (MKBound), or a fluid mkfluid label (MKFluid), is not interchangeable with this selector. Verify the generated mapping rather than assuming equal numbers. Marker fields can also be inspected in ParaView when exported; see the visualisation guide.

The command below uses -onlymk:20 from examples/main/01_DamBreak/wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat. Marker 20 is case-specific, not a universal object identifier. Do not change a case's marker configuration to match this example.

docs.title: 2. Define the command context
docs.text:
For a Windows Command Prompt in examples/main/01_DamBreak/, with existing CaseDambreak results:

set "name=CaseDambreak"
set "dirbin=../../../bin/windows"
set computeforces="%dirbin%/ComputeForces_win64.exe"
set "dirout=%name%_out"
set "diroutdata=%dirout%\data"
set "dirout2=%dirout%\forces"

%computeforces% contains the quoted executable, %diroutdata% the saved particle directory, and %dirout2% the force-output directory. Adapt the context and marker for your own case. This is a post-processing fragment, not a complete execution script. Quote directory arguments if paths contain spaces.

docs.title: 3. Use the saved viscosity configuration
docs.text:
%computeforces% -dirdata %diroutdata% -onlymk:20 -viscoauto -savecsv %dirout2%/_ForceBuilding
Option Meaning -dirdata Read the directory containing saved particle data. -onlymk:20 Select boundary particles with this example's MK 20. -viscoauto Load viscosity configuration from BI4 files; also the current v6 default. -savecsv Request a CSV time history using _ForceBuilding as output name/prefix.

Automatic viscosity uses the saved simulation metadata. It does not choose a new viscosity model or retune the case. If input metadata are unavailable, inspect the tool's log rather than supplying an arbitrary viscosity.

docs.title: 4. Interpret the time history
docs.text:
Documented quantity Meaning ForceFluid [N] Linear force from the fluid; inspect Cartesian components in the CSV headers. Weight [N] Gravity multiplied by floating-body mass; for floating bodies. ForceTotal [N] Sum of ForceFluid and Weight; for floating bodies.

Plot the required component against time. Interpret signs using the case's global axes and distinguish fluid force from a total including weight. Do not assume all boundary categories provide floating-body columns. The v6 help reports force in N; check a 2-D case's represented extent separately before comparing with a 3-D load.

Moments require separately specified axes/options and are outside this command. The help warns that Cartesian moment signs changed since v5.0.205; do not transfer an older moment convention without checking.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
• The documented CSV/ASCII selection cannot mix one floating body's particles with another floating body or another boundary-particle type. Process the intended body separately.
  • Fixed, prescribed-moving and floating objects require their own appropriate selection and saved data.
  • A fluid-force CSV alone is not a complete external-load balance for a Chrono- or mooring-coupled body. Review coupling-specific outputs separately.
  • Saved-time spacing limits the load history; unsaved peaks cannot be recovered. The procedure does not validate the model.

docs.title: How-To: Measure the Free-Surface Elevation
docs.text: Use MeasureTool as a virtual wave gauge: define vertical columns at selected horizontal locations and obtain elevation time histories from saved fluid-particle results. This is a location-based measurement, rather than reconstruction of the full free-surface geometry.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the data and gauge columns
docs.text:
Keep the existing Part_XXXX.bi4 files and associated simulation metadata together in the case's output data/ directory. Work in the corresponding benchmark folder so that relative executable and input-file paths resolve correctly.

There are two ways to define the sampling positions:

Method Benchmark Convenient when -points elevation.txt examples/benchmarks/01_DamBreak Several named columns are easier to maintain and reuse in a file. -pointsdef:ptls[...] examples/benchmarks/03_WaveGeneration A regular column can be defined directly in the command.

Coordinates use the case's Cartesian frame and units: metres in these benchmarks. Columns must span the intended surface excursion. Their coordinates and spacing are case-specific. In 2-D, y must match the simulation plane; in 3-D, each column has a chosen (x, y).

docs.title: 2. Choose the dimensional example
docs.text:
-elevation calculates fluid elevation from the kernel sum for each (x, y) column. Its optional number is the detection threshold. The defaults are 0.4 in 2-D and 0.5 in 3-D; these are numerical detection settings, not physical constants or universal accuracy guarantees.

DamBreak below is 3-D and uses -elevation:0.5. WaveGeneration below is 2-D and uses -elevation:0.4. Keep the input data, dimensionality and point definition consistent.

The following are post-processing fragments, used after simulation results exist. They do not run GenCase or the solver. Their variables follow the corresponding benchmark BAT scripts. Define the variables and run the relevant fragment in the same Windows Command Prompt or BAT; do not treat a line containing %measuretool% as a self-contained command. The commands assume paths without spaces; quote directory arguments if needed.

docs.title: 3-D DamBreak: points in elevation.txt
docs.text:
Work in examples/benchmarks/01_DamBreak/. Its wDambreak_win64_GPU.bat defines the following context for the Dambreak results:

set name=Dambreak
set dirout=%name%_out
set diroutdata=%dirout%\data
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set measuretool="%dirbin%/MeasureTool_win64.exe"
set dirout2=%dirout%\post

The existing elevation.txt defines four vertical columns, labelled H4 to H1:

POINTSLIST #H4
0.582000 0.000000 0.010733
0 0 0.002
1 1 495
POINTSLIST #H3
1.732000 0.000000 0.010733
0 0 0.002
1 1 495
POINTSLIST #H2
2.228000 0.000000 0.010733
0 0 0.002
1 1 495
POINTSLIST #H1
2.724000 0.000000 0.010733
0 0 0.002
1 1 240

After each POINTSLIST, the three rows give the starting x y z, coordinate increments dx dy dz, and counts nx ny nz. Here each column has one x and one y; z increases by 0.002 m. H4–H2 contain 495 positions each, while H1 contains 240. The #H... comments identify the gauges; they do not change their coordinates.

Use:

%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -points elevation.txt -onlytype:-all,+fluid -elevation:0.5 -savecsv %dirout2%/

docs.title: 2-D WaveGeneration: points in the command
docs.text:
Work in examples/benchmarks/03_WaveGeneration/. The variable context from wWaveGeneration_win64_GPU.bat is:

set name=WaveGeneration
set dirout=%name%_out
set diroutdata=%dirout%\data
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set measuretool="%dirbin%/MeasureTool_win64.exe"
set dirout2=%dirout%\post

Define the column directly, without a TXT file:

%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -pointsdef:ptls[x=0.0:0:1,y=0:0:1,z=-6.00:0.01:1200] -onlytype:-all,+fluid -elevation:0.4 -savecsv %dirout2%/

ptls is the inline equivalent of POINTSLIST. Each axis uses start:step:count:

Specification Meaning x=0.0:0:1 One position at x = 0.0 m. y=0:0:1 One position at y = 0, the simulation plane. z=-6.00:0.01:1200 1200 positions, starting at z = -6.00 m with spacing 0.01 m, ending at 5.99 m.

The final number is a count, not an end coordinate. This defines one vertical column at (x, y) = (0, 0). The inline definition and the TXT format describe sampling positions for the same tool; neither changes the simulation geometry.

docs.title: 3. Read the outputs
docs.text:
Both commands use these options:

Option Meaning -dirdata %diroutdata% Read the saved particle data. -onlytype:-all,+fluid Clear the particle-type selection and include non-excluded fluid particles. -elevation:0.5 or -elevation:0.4 Select elevation calculation with the threshold appropriate to the example's dimensionality. -savecsv %dirout2%/ Write CSV time histories under the benchmark's post/ directory.

Open the elevation CSV in Dambreak_out/post/ or WaveGeneration_out/post/. Elevation output is organised by time by default (-elevationoutput:time); the elevation file uses the _Elevation.csv suffix. Read its headers to identify time and the column locations, then plot each gauge's elevation against simulation time. For SI results, elevations are in metres and time is in seconds. Use the input-column positions to associate DamBreak's results with H4, H3, H2 and H1, rather than assuming a different gauge order.

The usual elevation is the maximum elevation for each column (eta in the height variables). It uses the case coordinates; the separate -elevationrel option references the bottom point and is not enabled here. Distinguish elevation, relative elevation and water depth when comparing data. DamBreak's separate BAT command with -hvars:+depthfirst requests an additional depth quantity; that is not the same as the elevation command above.

These fragments request CSV output only. To inspect existing VTK data and gauge surroundings, use the ParaView guide.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Columns must span the intended surface. Gauge spacing and selected-fluid support limit what can be resolved; the example spacing is not mandatory.
  • Disconnected fluid or splashes can make the maximum elevation differ from the interface of interest. Inspect the geometry and the additional -hvars quantities where needed.
  • Saved states do not resolve events between output times.
  • Full-surface VTK reconstruction, such as existing IsoSurface output, is a separate operation from these virtual gauges.

docs.title: How-To: Measure the Pressure Exerted by the Fluid
docs.text: Use MeasureTool to sample fluid pressure at specified positions in saved DualSPHysics v6 results. A point on the fluid side of a wall can describe local fluid pressure near that wall. It is not a direct measurement of solid stress or the integrated force on the object; use ComputeForces for the latter.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the inputs
docs.text:
Keep the existing Part_XXXX.bi4 files and associated simulation metadata together. Define measurement positions in the case coordinates and units. Place them in the intended fluid region; a point inside a solid does not provide a reliable fluid-side pressure sample.

Position definition Benchmark Use TXT file: -points PressurePoints.txt examples/benchmarks/01_DamBreak Store and reuse several pressure-sensor positions. Inline point: -pointsdef:pt=-0.450:0:0.093 examples/benchmarks/02_Sloshing Specify a single position directly in the command.

docs.title: 2. Define the command context
docs.text: The commands below are post-processing fragments, used after simulation results exist. Their variables are defined in the corresponding benchmark BAT scripts. Work in the indicated benchmark folder, and define the context in the same Windows Command Prompt or BAT before using its command. They do not run GenCase or the solver. Paths in these fragments assume no spaces; quote directory arguments if needed.

docs.title: DamBreak: positions in PressurePoints.txt
docs.text:
Work in examples/benchmarks/01_DamBreak/. The context from wDambreak_win64_GPU.bat is:

set name=Dambreak
set dirout=%name%_out
set diroutdata=%dirout%\data
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set measuretool="%dirbin%/MeasureTool_win64.exe"
set dirout2=%dirout%\post

The existing PressurePoints.txt contains:

POINTS
2.395500 -0.025500 0.026367 #P1:(2.395500,-0.025500,0.026367)
2.395500 -0.025500 0.066367 #P2:(2.395500,-0.025500,0.066367)
2.395500 -0.025500 0.106367 #P3:(2.395500,-0.025500,0.106367)
2.395500 -0.025500 0.146367 #P4:(2.395500,-0.025500,0.146367)
2.416500 -0.025500 0.166367 #P5:(2.416500,-0.025500,0.166367)
2.456500 -0.025500 0.166367 #P6:(2.456500,-0.025500,0.166367)
2.496500 -0.025500 0.166367 #P7:(2.496500,-0.025500,0.166367)
2.536500 -0.025500 0.166367 #P8:(2.536500,-0.025500,0.166367)

POINTS is followed by Cartesian x y z triples in metres for this SI case. The #P1–#P8 comments identify the sensors. These eight positions belong to this dam-break geometry; do not transfer them unchanged to another case.

docs.title: Sloshing: position in the command
docs.text:
Work in examples/benchmarks/02_Sloshing/. The context from wSloshingAcc_win64_GPU.bat is:

set name=SloshingAcc
set dirout=%name%_out
set diroutdata=%dirout%\data
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set measuretool="%dirbin%/MeasureTool_win64.exe"
set dirout2=%dirout%\post

Here -pointsdef:pt=-0.450:0:0.093 is the inline equivalent of a POINTS entry: one point at (x, y, z) = (-0.450, 0, 0.093) m. No external measurement TXT file is needed.

docs.title: 3. Select pressure and inspect support
docs.text:
For DamBreak, use:

%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -points PressurePoints.txt -onlytype:-all,+fluid -vars:-all,+press -kcusedummy:0 -kclimit:0.01 -savecsv %dirout2%/

For Sloshing, use its benchmark fragment:

%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -pointsdef:pt=-0.450:0:0.093 -onlytype:-all,+fluid -vars:-all,+press -kcusedummy:0 -kclimit:0.01 -savecsv %dirout2%/
Option Purpose -onlytype:-all,+fluid Clear the particle-type selection and include non-excluded fluid particles. -vars:-all,+press Clear the variable selection and request pressure. -kcusedummy:0 Do not use the dummy value for an interpolated quantity when kernel correction is not applied. -kclimit:0.01 Set the minimum sum_wab_vol required to apply kernel correction to 0.01. -savecsv %dirout2%/ Write CSV time histories in the benchmark's post/ directory.

The two kc settings are benchmark-specific. The default minimum kernel sum is 0.5; the default dummy value is 0 (-kcdummy), with dummy output enabled (-kcusedummy:1). These fragments instead disable dummy use and lower the correction threshold to 0.01. They do not change sensor coordinates or guarantee adequate fluid support. Inspect the local fluid and tool output before interpreting zero or poorly supported samples. The separate kcorr variable can be requested to inspect the kernel sum; the two commands above select pressure only.

docs.title: 4. Interpret the results
docs.text:
Open _Press.csv in Dambreak_out/post/ or SloshingAcc_out/post/. Read the CSV headers to identify saved time, positions and pressure fields. Associate DamBreak's eight traces with the input positions P1–P8; Sloshing has one measurement position. Use the appropriate CSV separator when importing the file. The fragments request CSV output only, not a VTK export.

Pressure is in Pa (N/m²) for SI results. Its reference is that of the saved simulation and pressure calculation; do not relabel it as absolute pressure or add an atmospheric offset without a separate physical justification.

Use existing ParaView data to inspect the measurement positions and surrounding flow. A point-pressure history, a near-boundary pressure distribution and a total object force are different quantities. Do not convert one point pressure to a total load using an arbitrary area.

Saved-time spacing and incomplete fluid support can limit the interpretation of short pressure peaks.

docs.title: How-To: Measure the Velocity in the Fluid Domain
docs.text: Use MeasureTool to sample velocity at specified positions in saved DualSPHysics v6 results. Samples use the selected neighbouring fluid particles; they are not the trajectory of an individual particle.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the data and positions
docs.text:
Retain the existing Part_XXXX.bi4 files and associated simulation metadata together. Create velocity.txt in the case folder. For one position:

POINTS
6 0 0.4

POINTS is followed by Cartesian x y z coordinates, in metres for an SI case. Multiple points can follow this keyword; regular grids can use POINTSLIST. The position above comes from examples/main/09_WavesPiston/velocity.txt. Choose coordinates suitable for your flow, and use the actual simulation plane for y in a 2-D case.

docs.title: 2. Define the command context
docs.text:
The following is a post-processing fragment for a Windows Command Prompt in examples/main/09_WavesPiston/, after CasePistonBeach_REG results exist. It does not run GenCase or the solver. The variable structure follows the existing BAT; adapt the name and paths for another case.

set "name=CasePistonBeach_REG"
set "dirbin=../../../bin/windows"
set measuretool="%dirbin%/MeasureTool_win64.exe"
set "dirout=%name%_out"
set "diroutdata=%dirout%\data"
set "dirout2=%dirout%\measuretool"

%measuretool% includes the quoted executable path, %diroutdata% is the saved-particle directory, and %dirout2% is the measurement-output directory. Define these in the same command session or BAT. The command below assumes paths without spaces; quote directory arguments if needed.

docs.title: 3. Sample velocity
docs.text:
%measuretool% -dirdata %diroutdata% -points velocity.txt -onlytype:-all,+fluid -vars:-all,+vel -savecsv %dirout2%/_velocity -savevtk %dirout2%/velocity
Option Meaning -dirdata Read the saved particle data. -points velocity.txt Load the sampling positions. -onlytype:-all,+fluid Clear the particle-type selection and include non-excluded fluid particles. -vars:-all,+vel Clear the variable selection and request velocity. -savecsv Request time-history CSV output with the supplied prefix. -savevtk Request VTK data at the interpolation points for spatial inspection.

docs.title: 4. Interpret the output
docs.text:
Open the CSV outputs beginning with _velocity. Inspect their headers for time, positions and velocity components. Velocity is in m/s for SI results, with components along the simulation's global Cartesian axes. A component is not the same quantity as speed. The training example produces a velocity file ending in _Vel.csv; inspect the actual names generated by your tool.

Open the velocity VTK output in ParaView to verify the sampling locations.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The time history contains saved states only; unsaved transients cannot be recovered.
  • Positions outside the fluid, inside solids or near a free surface may lack adequate selected-fluid support.
  • Current help documents a kernel-correction threshold through -kclimit (default 0.5). When correction is not applied, default dummy output is 0 (-kcdummy) with dummy output enabled (-kcusedummy:1). A zero sample therefore needs interpretation and does not automatically prove still water.
  • Inspect the local flow and sampling support before interpreting results. This procedure does not establish numerical accuracy.

docs.title: How are MK labels assigned to particle groups?
docs.text:
MK labels identify fluid and boundary particle groups for features such as prescribed motion, floating bodies, boundary treatment, material properties and post-processing. Distinguish the local fluid label mkfluid, the local boundary label mkbound, and the final MK written by GenCase.

Within casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist, commands such as these select the local label for subsequent fluid or boundary drawing operations; they do not create particles by themselves:

<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<setmkbound mk="0" />

casedef/mkconfig reserves the fluid and boundary label ranges through fluidcount and boundcount. GenCase writes final MK values and their offsets in execution/particles of the generated case XML. For example, the XML Guide's generated Case.xml contains these particle blocks:

<particles np="8079" nb="1795" nbf="1659" mkboundfirst="10" mkfluidfirst="1">
    <fixed mkbound="0" mk="10" begin="0" count="1659" />
    <moving mkbound="10" mk="20" begin="1659" count="136" refmotion="0" />
    <fluid mkfluid="0" mk="1" begin="1795" count="6284" />
</particles>
Figure 1: Example mapping from local fluid and boundary labels to final MK values. The offsets depend on the case configuration.

Here boundary labels 0 and 10 become MK 10 and 20, while fluid label 0 becomes MK 1. The offsets 10 and 1 belong to this example's configured ranges; they are not universal values. Use local labels where an XML feature requests mkbound or mkfluid, and inspect your own generated case before selecting a final MK.

Post-processing -onlymk:20, for example, selects final MK 20; it does not identify the same object in every case. When generated, Case_All.vtk, Case_Bound.vtk and Case_Fluid.vtk help inspect all particles, boundary particles and fluid particles respectively; Case is the case's actual filename prefix. See markers and generated particle information.

For an introduction, see Particle types and the mk number.

docs.title: Add a floating object
docs.text: Add a fluid-driven rigid body to a compatible 3-D fluid case, using CaseFloating_Def.xml as the reference. The excerpts below are additions to a case definition, not a complete XML file.

docs.title: Starting example
docs.text:
Use examples/main/11_Floating/CaseFloating_Def.xml from your v6 package. Its boundary particles with mkbound="50" form a freely moving rigid box; the piston has prescribed motion under marker 10 and the tank is fixed under marker 20. No Chrono or MoorDynPlus coupling is required. See the 11_Floating catalogue entry.

Start with a working 3-D DBC fluid case using Symplectic integration. Its fluid-generation step must select fluid marker 0 and use fillbox with modefill set to void, as in the reference. Marker 50 must be unused and within the range allocated by its mkconfig. The reference allocates 230 boundary markers and 9 fluid markers; those allocations do not need replacing when they already accommodate the selected identifiers.

The literal geometry below assumes room for a box from (10, 2, 3) to (12, 4, 5) m. In the reference, the tank is 16 × 6 m in plan, the initial water level is 4 m, particle spacing is 0.1 m, and generation bounds run from (-1, -1, -1) to (17, 7, 6) m. These are case-specific assumptions, not settings to insert into an arbitrary case. Check your geometry, water level, resolution and expected body excursion before using the excerpts; adapt body dimensions, position and mass consistently if your case differs.

The reference file already contains this body. Use it to identify the additions to your existing case; do not paste a second copy into the reference itself.

docs.title: 1. Draw the body before filling the fluid
docs.text:
Location: case/casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist, before the existing fluid-marker selection and fillbox.

Action: add the following commands.

<setdrawmode mode="full" />
<setmkbound mk="50" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="10" y="2" z="3" />
    <size x="2" y="2" z="2" />
</drawbox>

This draws the source box as boundary particles under marker 50. Keep it separate from the tank and other bodies. The existing void fill must follow these commands so that it fills only unoccupied nodes. Check fluid exclusion around the body; other fluid-generation methods require a separate ordering check.

docs.title: 2. Identify the floating body and set its mass
docs.text:
Location: case/casedef, after the existing motion section in the reference and before the closing casedef tag.

Action: add this block. If floatings already exists, insert only the floating child into it.

<floatings>
    <floating mkbound="50">
        <massbody value="10000" />
    </floating>
</floatings>

The matching mkbound="50" classifies the drawn particles as one floating rigid body. Its total mass is 10,000 kg in this example; it is not a default for other bodies or a guarantee of buoyant equilibrium. The source leaves the centre of gravity and inertia for GenCase to calculate. Inspect the generated values for your particle distribution rather than adding guessed properties.

Keep the box out of prescribed motion/objreal definitions. In the reference, only marker 10 appears there; marker 20 remains fixed. Use the local boundary identifier mkbound consistently, rather than substituting a generated global mk value from post-processing.

docs.title: 3. Check the rigid-body interaction setting
docs.text:
Location: case/execution/parameters.

Action: retain an existing matching entry. Otherwise, add or modify the single RigidAlgorithm entry to use the source SPH interaction treatment:

<parameter key="RigidAlgorithm" value="SPH" comment="Rigid Algorithm: FREE:collision-free, SPH, DEM, CHR:Chrono collision (default=SPH)" />

This adopts the reference's solid-interaction model. A case using another contact or coupling model needs a separate compatibility check before changing it. Do not copy the remaining parameter block: preserve the working case's physical and numerical settings. The reference uses FtPause=0.0; an intentional warm-up interval in another case delays floating-body motion.

docs.title: Check your configuration
docs.text:
These checks are for your edited case:

  1. Confirm that marker 50 is available and matches both the geometry commands and the floating definition. It must not also be assigned prescribed motion.
  2. Regenerate the case with compatible v6 GenCase. Inspect the particles: the box must be complete, inside the generation bounds, clear of existing solids and free of overlapping fluid particles.
  3. Inspect the generated floating-body classification, total mass, centre of gravity and inertia. Confirm that the piston and tank retain their intended moving/fixed classifications.
  4. Check the DBC/Symplectic setup, the SPH rigid-body entry, any warm-up interval and sufficient solver-domain clearance for the expected motion. Mass, immersion and fluid density must describe the intended physical configuration.
  5. Run and inspect your case using the existing execution workflow. Correct source XML and regenerate the particle data if the geometry is wrong; editing generated execution XML does not rebuild the particles.

docs.title: Reference and further details
docs.text:
• Source XML: examples/main/11_Floating/CaseFloating_Def.xml in the v6 package. The corresponding Windows script is wCaseFloating_win64_GPU.bat; it calls GenCase and the v6 GPU solver. Use your package's compatible tools and retain the existing workflow.
  • 11_Floating example description.
  • Floating bodies and material properties in the Main Configuration XML Guide.
  • Rigid-body interaction parameters.
  • Official examples and full-package information. The public repository contains only some examples; locate this source file in your v6 package rather than assuming a public GitHub copy is identical.

docs.title: How is the simulation domain determined in DualSPHysics?
docs.text:
The particle-generation domain is defined by pointmin and pointmax in casedef/geometry/definition. These limits specify where GenCase may create particles; they are not automatically the solver's simulation boundaries.

Figure 1: Particle-generation bounds and the simulation domain. The relationship shown is schematic; the simulation-domain limits depend on the generated particles and any explicit domain settings.

By default, the simulation domain is calculated from the minimum and maximum positions of the particles generated by GenCase. It can therefore differ from the generation bounds. To customise it, use simulationdomain inside execution/parameters, with posmin and posmax:

<simulationdomain>
    <posmin x="0.5" y="default - 2" z="default - 20%" />
    <posmax x="default" y="default + 1" z="default + 10%" />
</simulationdomain>

In this example, default retains the automatically calculated limit, default - 2 subtracts two metres from that limit, and default + 10% adds 10% of the domain extent along that coordinate. A number such as 0.5 sets an absolute coordinate. These example values are not required settings for other cases.

Allow enough space for the expected fluid and moving-object motion. If particles leave the computational domain, the consequences depend on the simulation configuration. See generation bounds and simulation-domain settings.

docs.title: How-To: Use ParaView to Visualise Normal Vectors for mDBC
docs.text:
Inspect existing DualSPHysics v6 boundary-normal data using ParaView's Glyph filter. ParaView displays these data; it does not generate the normals used by DualSPHysics, activate mDBC or modify its numerical configuration.

See the mDBC XML Guide for the separate preparation/configuration workflow.

docs.title: 1. Locate the existing normals file
docs.text:
For a fresh initialisation using normals, the v6 solver writes CfgInit_Normals.vtk in its main output directory, for example CaseName_out/CfgInit_Normals.vtk. It is not a particle time series in data/. Initial GenCase geometry export alone does not create this diagnostic.

Availability depends on the configured case and completed initialisation, so not every simulation produces it. Restart diagnostics can append _Restart to the filename.

Use existing output. If unavailable, inspect the run log, actual output root and mDBC preparation separately; do not modify XML or regenerate normals merely to obtain a plot.

Documented point array Meaning Normal Three-component vector from boundary particle towards the physical boundary interface; not necessarily a unit vector. NormalSize Scalar magnitude of that vector. Idp, Mk Particle identifier and generated marker information.

Other boundary VTKs need not contain these arrays. CfgInit_NormalsGhost.vtk represents vectors towards ghost nodes, a different diagnostic; do not substitute it without checking its meaning.

docs.title: 2. Open the dataset
docs.text:
1. In ParaView, select File → Open and choose the existing CfgInit_Normals.vtk.
  2. Select the loaded dataset in the Pipeline Browser and click Apply in Properties.
  3. Confirm boundary-particle points are displayed and inspect the point arrays for Normal and NormalSize.
  4. Where available, load initial boundary particles and actual boundary-surface geometry for context. Keep the normals dataset selected for Glyph.

docs.title: 3. Display arrows with Glyph
docs.text:
Choose Glyph from Filters or its toolbar shortcut. Use these settings:

Control Setting Glyph Type Arrow Orientation Array Normal Scale Array NormalSize Scale Factor 1 Glyph Mode, under Masking All Points

Click Apply and show the Glyph output. Labels/grouping may differ between ParaView versions; select the same direction array, scalar scaling array and complete point set.

Normal supplies direction and NormalSize supplies size. Do not select “No orientation array” or substitute another vector. The official Glyph documentation confirms that vector scale modes apply when the scale array itself is a vector. Here it is scalar NormalSize; a vector-component scaling mode is not a substitute for that selection.

Factor 1 is a display setting, not an mDBC parameter. Display scaling does not change the stored vectors or those used by the solver.

docs.title: 4. Inspect directions and coverage
docs.text:
1. Orient the camera towards a flat region, then zoom to corners, sloping surfaces and marker transitions.
  2. Compare arrows with the actual fluid-facing physical interface, not only the outer particle layers.
  3. Inspect directions, lengths and spatial coverage relative to the particle positions and surface.
  4. Examine suspicious directions or gaps with points and contextual geometry visible.

The training wave example creates five particle layers but only three near-interface layers carry normals. Those counts reflect its support distance and geometry; they are not universal requirements. A zero vector produces no finite arrow even with All Points.

A plausible plot helps inspection but does not prove physical correctness or validate an mDBC simulation. Review suspicious regions separately. Do not automatically alter normals, maxdisth, particle layers or mDBC parameters to improve display.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Observation Check File unavailable Existing run log, output root, initialisation status, restart suffix and whether the configured case uses normals. Expected arrays absent Confirm this is the normals diagnostic, rather than a generic geometry/particle VTK. Do not invent a substitute array. Arrows missing or difficult to see Glyph visibility, Arrow type, selected arrays, factor 1, camera/zoom and zero NormalSize values. Only some points have arrows Non-zero normal coverage and All Points. Not all particle layers necessarily carry normals. Arrows too large/small Recheck NormalSize and factor 1; distinguish display scaling from stored data.

For conversion and animation, use the separate general ParaView guide.

docs.title: How-To: Use ParaView to Visualise DualSPHysics Results
docs.text: Use PartVTK to export saved DualSPHysics v6 particle results, then ParaView to inspect VTK data and time series. Existing initial GenCase VTK files can be opened directly.

docs.title: 1. Open the initial particle configuration
docs.text:
1. Start ParaView and choose File → Open.
  2. Select the case's existing initial boundary and fluid files, for example CaseName_Bound.vtk and CaseName_Fluid.vtk.
  3. Select each loaded item in the Pipeline Browser and click Apply in Properties.
  4. Use the visibility controls to show fluid and boundary together.
  5. Reset/orient the camera and inspect particle distribution and geometry.
  6. Choose an array actually present in Coloring, such as Rhop when available.

Availability depends on the case and GenCase's save selections, including vtkbound and vtkfluid among the -save options. Do not assume every case has both files. This guide starts from existing output rather than requiring regeneration.

docs.title: 2. Convert saved particle results
docs.text:
Simulation particle data are stored in BI4 files such as Part_XXXX.bi4; use PartVTK to convert them, rather than opening BI4 as VTK. Keep associated metadata together with the raw data.

For existing CasePistonBeach_REG results, use the following post-processing fragment. Open a Windows Command Prompt in examples/main/09_WavesPiston/:

set "name=CasePistonBeach_REG"
set "dirbin=../../../bin/windows"
set partvtk="%dirbin%/PartVTK_win64.exe"
set "dirout=%name%_out"
set "diroutdata=%dirout%\data"
set "dirout2=%dirout%\particles"

Adapt the case and executable paths as needed. The commands assume paths without spaces; quote directory arguments when necessary.

Export fluid particles:

%partvtk% -dirdata %diroutdata% -savevtk %dirout2%/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid -vars:+mk

Export boundary particles separately:

%partvtk% -dirdata %diroutdata% -savevtk %dirout2%/PartBound -onlytype:-all,+bound -vars:+mk
Option Purpose -dirdata Read particle data. For variable-resolution simulations, current help specifies the main output directory instead; follow that case's workflow. -savevtk Write VTK files with the supplied prefix. -onlytype:-all,+fluid Select non-excluded fluid particles. -onlytype:-all,+bound Select boundary particles, including fixed, moving and floating types. -vars:+mk Add the marker field to defaults including particle ID, velocity, density, pressure and type.

docs.title: 3. Load and animate the VTK series
docs.text:
1. Choose File → Open and browse to the particle-output directory.
  2. Select the grouped PartFluid_*.vtk series, rather than only one frame. Use file-series grouping where offered.
  3. Click Apply, then load/apply the corresponding PartBound_*.vtk series.
  4. Keep both datasets visible and select the fluid item before changing its colour field.
  5. Select an available array such as Rhop (density). In the colour-map editor, choose a preset and show the colour bar.
  6. Rescale to the data range or choose a custom range appropriate to the quantity and comparison. Training-case density limits are not universal fluid settings.
  7. Use Play, pause and time-step controls. Inspect time values/series metadata rather than interpreting a file number as physical time.

If an expected field is absent, inspect the exported arrays and PartVTK variable selection. Changing the colour map does not calculate missing simulation quantities.

docs.title: Basic viewing operations
docs.text: Toggle dataset visibility to compare fluid and boundaries. Reset the camera when data are out of view, and choose an axis view suited to the geometry; a view along y is useful for an x-z 2-D case. Select the intended dataset/array before editing its colour map or range. The colour bar identifies the displayed range; consistent ranges help comparisons across time or cases.

docs.title: Other existing outputs
docs.text:
Result Suitable existing data Floating or prescribed-moving body Its boundary/particle series or case-specific body export. Moorings Existing mooring VTK series, with particle data; the training example uses MooringsVtk. Flexible structure Structure/boundary particle series; the training example also extracts a case-specific tip-particle series. Free surface Existing surface VTK, such as IsoSurface output; a gauge CSV is not a complete surface mesh.

Names and temporal sampling are case-specific. This page does not prescribe extra coupling or surface-generation commands.

To inspect boundary normal vectors used by mDBC, see the separate How-To on visualising mDBC normals in ParaView.
