docs.title: DualSPHysics Workflow and Advanced Configuration
docs.text:
Contents

  1. Overview of the DualSPHysics Workflow
  2. Pre-Processing
  3. Advanced SPH Configurations
  4. Post-Processing

docs.title: Overview of the DualSPHysics Workflow
docs.text:
The following diagram shows the workflow with representative example input and output files of the executable files. This figure will be used later to explain in detail each of the codes and the main tools.

Pre-processing 📄 Case_Def.xml object.vtk • object.stl • object.ply GENCASE mov.datforces.csv Case.xml Case.bi4 Case_All.vtk • Case_Bound.vtk Case_Fluid.vtk • Case__Dp.vtk Processing Part_Head.ibi4 • PartFloat.fbi4 Part_xxxx.bi4 • PartOut.obi4 Run.out Post-processing PointsPos.csv • Points.txt PARTVTK PartFluid.vtk PartBound.vtk PartMoving.vtk BOUNDARYVTK Fixed.vtk Moving_xxxx.vtk Floating_xxxx.vtk ISOSURFACE Surface_xxxx.vtk MEASURETOOL Pressure.csv Velocity.csv Height_xxxx.vtk

Summary: GENCASE is the pre-processor which generates the initial particle distribution and additional input files needed to run the SPH simulation. DUALSPHYSICS is the SPH simulation engine, which calculates all the 3 mains steps of (i) Neighbour List (NL) creation, (ii) Particle Interaction (PI), (iii) System Update (SU). PARTVTK, BOUNDARYVTK, ISOSURFACE, MEASURETOOL are the post-processing routines for visualisation of results.

docs.title: Pre-Processing
docs.text: A program named GENCASE is included to define the initial configuration of the simulation, movement description of moving objects and the parameters of the execution in DualSPHysics. All this information is contained in a definition input file in XML format; CaseName_Def.xml. (where CaseName represents the name of a given case). GenCase is very fast and able to generate millions of particles in seconds on the CPU.

docs.title: Particle Generation:
docs.text:
GENCASE employs a 3-D Cartesian lattice to position particles. The idea is to build any object using particles. These particles are created at the nodes of the 3-D Cartesian mesh. Firstly, the mesh nodes around the object are defined and then particles are created only in the nodes needed to draw the desired geometry. Figure 5-7 illustrates how this mesh is used; in this case a triangle is generated in 2D. First the nodes of a mesh are defined starting from the maximum dimensions of the desired triangle, then the edges of the triangle are defined and finally particles are created at the nodes of the Cartesian mesh which are inside the triangle.

Step 1 Geometry Definition 1. Geometry Definition The user inputs the boundary geometric definition (XML surface description, STL mesh, or PLY CAD model) establishing the continuous shape volume. 2. Lattice Creation GenCase overlays a uniform background 2D/3D grid (lattice) of candidate points spaced at inter-particle distance dp across the domain. 3. Point-in-Polygon Testing A ray-casting / point-in-polyhedron algorithm evaluates each candidate point to test whether its coordinates lie strictly inside the defined shape. 4. Particle Selection & Pruning All points outside the boundary are discarded. The surviving internal points are assigned SPH properties and exported as initial simulation particles.

All particles are placed over a regular Cartesian grid. The geometry of the case is defined independently to the inter-particle distance. This allows the discretization of each test case with a different number of particles simply by varying the resolution (or particle size) dp.

Complex Geometry Generation

Complex geometries can be easily created using a wide variety of dedicated XML labels to define distinct physical shapes and primitives. You can quickly generate basic elements using <drawpoint />, <drawpoints />, <drawline />, and <drawlines />, or build multi-dimensional planar surfaces with <drawtriangle />, <drawquadri />, <drawtrianglesstrip />, <drawtrianglesfan />, <drawpolygon>, and <drawtriangles />. For three-dimensional objects, specialized commands include <drawpyramid />, <drawprism />, <drawbox />, <drawbeach />, <drawsphere />, <drawellipsoid />, <drawcylinder />, and <drawwave />.

Once the mesh nodes that represent the desired object are selected, these points are stored as a matrix of nodes. The shape of the object can be transformed using a translation (<move />), a scaling (<scale />), or a rotation (<rotate />, <rotateline />).

With the generation process creating particles at the nodes, different types of particles can be created: a fluid particle (<setmkfluid />), a boundary particle (<setmkbound />), or none (<setmkvoid />). Hence, mk is the marker value used to mark a set of particles with a common feature in the simulation. Note that values of the final mk are different from mkfluid, mkbound, and mkvoid following these rules:

Source Container: mkfluid & mkbound Arrays Void ... mk=0 mk=1 mk=2 mk=3..8 mk=9 mk=10 mk=11 mk=12 Target Container: mk Array (fluidcount = 9) mkfluid=0 Fluid 0 mkfluid=1 Fluid 1 mkbound=0 Bound 0 mkbound=1 Bound 1 mkbound=2 Bound 2
  • mk for boundaries = mkbound + 1 + fluidcount (usually fluidcount = 9)
  • mk for fluid particles = mkfluid + 1

Particles can be created only at the object surface (<setdrawmode mode="face" />), only inside the bounds of the objects (<setdrawmode mode="solid" />), or both (<setdrawmode mode="full" />).

The set of fluid particles can be labelled with features or special behaviours (<initials />). For example, initial velocity (<velocity />) can be imposed for fluid particles, or a solitary wave can be defined (<velwave />). Furthermore, particles can be defined as part of a floating object (<floatings />).

Once boundaries are defined, filling a region with fluid particles can be easily obtained using the following commands: <fillpoint />, <fillbox />, <fillfigure />, and <fillprism />. This works also in the presence of arbitrarily complex geometries.

In cases with more complex geometries, external objects can be imported from 3DS files (Figure 5-8) or CAD files (Figure 5-9). This enables the use of realistic geometries generated by 3D designing applications with the drawing commands of GenCase to be combined.

These files (3DS or CAD) must be converted to STL format (<drawfilestl />), PLY format (<drawfileply />), or VTK format (<drawfilevtk />), formats that are easily loaded by GenCase.

Any object in STL, PLY, or VTK (object.vtk, object.stl, or object.ply in Figure 9-1) can be split in different triangles and any triangle can be converted into particles using the GenCase code.

docs.title: Input XML file structure
docs.text:
The XML input file is organized into two main sections:

  • <casedef>: Defines the physical setup including fluid properties, domain geometry, and initial particle configuration
    • <geometry>: Describes the geometrical layout of numerical environment for the simulation
    • <floatings>: Includes the parameters for the defition of fluid-driven bodies
    • <normals>: Manages the defintion and properties of normals used for boundary sets
    • <motion>: Includes the
  • <execution>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings
    • <special>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings
    • <parameters>: Specifies numerical methods, time integration parameters, and output settings
<constantsdef>                      
    <gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2" />
    <rhop0 value="1000" comment="Reference density of the fluid" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
    <rhopgradient value="2" comment="Initial density gradient 1:Rhop0, 2:Water column, 3:Max. water height (default=2)" />
    <hswl value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum still water level to calculate speedofsound using coefsound" units_comment="metres (m)" />
    <gamma value="7" comment="Polytropic constant for water used in the state equation" />
    <speedsystem value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum system speed (by default the dam-break propagation is used)" />
    <coefsound value="20" comment="Coefficient to multiply speedsystem" />
    <speedsound value="0" auto="true" comment="Speed of sound to use in the simulation (by default speedofsound=coefsound*speedsystem)" />
    <coefh value="1.0" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)" />      
    <_hdp value="2" comment="Alternative option to calculate the smoothing length (h=hdp*dp)" />
    <cflnumber value="0.2" comment="Coefficient to multiply dt" />          
</constantsdef>

docs.title: Constants Definition
docs.text: The <constantsdef> section establishes the fundamental physical properties and numerical coefficients that govern the simulation behavior.

docs.title: Fluid Properties
docs.text:
<gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2" />
<rhop0 value="1000" comment="Reference density of the fluid" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
<gamma value="7" comment="Polytropic constant for water used in the state equation" />

Gravity: Generally, it is used to simulate gravity's pull, and in this case it is set to -9.81 m/s² in the negative \(z\)-direction (Earth's gravitational acceleration) in SI. The \(x\) and \(y\) components are zero since gravity acts only vertically.

Reference density (rhop0): The reference density of the fluid being simulated. This value is used in the equation of state to relate pressure and density. All density calculations reference this baseline value.

Gamma: The polytropic constant (\(\gamma\)=7) used in the weakly compressible equation of state for water. This value provides a good balance between computational efficiency and physical accuracy for liquid flows.

docs.title: Density Initialization
docs.text:
<rhopgradient value="2" comment="Initial density gradient 1:Rhop0, 2:Water column, 3:Max. water height (default=2)" />

Density gradient mode: This parameter is used for the initialization of the density field for the fluid particles. Option 1 assigns \(\rho_0\) to all particles; Option 2 means the initial density distribution accounts for the hydrostatic pressure gradient in the water column, following the gravity direction, creating a physically realistic initial condition. This may help reduce initial transients when the simulation starts. Option 3 uses the max value of pressure according to the whole domain and the follows a global gradient rather than a local one. This option can be useful for floting body initialization.

docs.title: Speed of Sound Configuration
docs.text:
<hswl value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum still water level to calculate speedofsound using coefsound" units_comment="metres (m)" />
<speedsystem value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum system speed (by default the dam-break propagation is used)" />
<coefsound value="20" comment="Coefficient to multiply speedsystem" />
<speedsound value="0" auto="true" comment="Speed of sound to use in the simulation (by default speedofsound=coefsound*speedsystem)" />

Automatic speed of sound calculation: The speed of sound is automatically computed based on the maximum expected flow velocity. The auto="true" flag enables this automatic calculation.

Speed system: Represents the characteristic velocity scale of the problem. For dam breaks, this is typically estimated from Torricelli's formula: \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\), where \(h\) is the initial water height, taken as max position minus the min position of fluid particles.

Sound speed coefficient: The artificial speed of sound is usually set to 20 times the maximum system speed. This ensures that density fluctuations remain small (typically \(\leq\) 1%) while maintaining numerical stability. However, this definition may be case dependent. A higher coefficient makes the fluid less compressible but requires smaller time steps.

Note

Why artificial speed of sound?: Real water has a speed of sound around 1500 m/s, which would require mush smaller time steps. By using an artificially reduced speed of sound (typically 10-50 m/s for these flows), this approach allows maintaining weakly compressible behavior while making the simulation computationally feasible. However, this reduction applies only to scaled systems.

docs.title: Smoothing Length
docs.text:
<coefh value="1.0" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)" />      
<_hdp value="2" comment="Alternative option to calculate the smoothing length (h=hdp*dp)" />

Smoothing length coefficient: The smoothing length \(h\) determines the size of the interaction region between particles. With coefh=1.0, the smoothing length is calculated as \(h = \text{coefh} \times \sqrt{3dp^2}\) in 3D, which equals approximately \(1.73\cdot dp\).

Alternative formula: The commented _hdp parameter shows an alternative approach where \(h = 2\cdot dp\). The underscore prefix disables this option, so in this case the coefh formula is used instead.

Note

The smoothing length defines the "reach" of each particle's influence. Particles within a distance of \(2h\) from each other can interact. Larger \(h\) values create smoother fields but may over-diffuse sharp features.

docs.title: Time Step Control
docs.text:
<cflnumber value="0.2" comment="Coefficient to multiply dt" />

CFL number: The Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) number of 0.20 scales the adaptive time step. The expression \(dt = 0.2 \cdot h/c\), where \(c\) is the speed of sound, is an acoustic estimate, not the complete time-step selection rule. The solver also considers acceleration and viscous constraints, with additional limits when divergence cleaning or flexible structures are active. Prescribed time-step settings can also affect the selected value. A smaller CFL coefficient is not, by itself, a guarantee of stability.

docs.title: Marker Configuration
docs.text:
<mkconfig boundcount="230" fluidcount="9">
        <mkorientfluid mk="0" orient="Xyz" />
    </mkconfig>

Boundary markers: Up to 240 different boundary types can be defined (mk=0 to mk=239). This allows for tracking different wall sections, obstacles, or boundary conditions separately.

Fluid markers: Up to 9 different fluid types can be defined (mk=0 to mk=8). This is useful for multi-phase flows or tracking different fluid regions.

docs.title: Execution Parameters
docs.text: The <execution> section controls the numerical methods and simulation settings.

docs.title: Output Precision
docs.text:
<parameter key="SavePosDouble" value="0" comment="Saves particle position using double precision (default=0)" />

Single precision output: With value="0", particle positions are saved in single-precision (32-bit) format, reducing file sizes by ~50% compared to double precision. Internal calculations still use double precision for accuracy; this only affects output files.

When to use double precision: Use value="1" for cases requiring very precise particle tracking over long times or when post-processing requires high precision (e.g., computing derivatives).

docs.title: Time Integration
docs.text:
<parameter key="StepAlgorithm" value="1" comment="Step Algorithm 1:Verlet, 2:Symplectic (default=1)" />
<parameter key="VerletSteps" value="40" comment="Verlet only: Number of steps to apply Euler timestepping (default=40)" />

Verlet algorithm: option 1 uses the velocity-Verlet scheme, which is second-order accurate in time and preserves energy well. It has been employed as a standard choice for SPH simulations.

Symplectic alternative: option 2 is a symplectic integrator that provides better long-term energy conservation.

docs.title: Kernel Function
docs.text:
<parameter key="Kernel" value="1" comment="Interaction Kernel 1:Cubic Spline, 2:Wendland (default=2)" />

Cubic Spline kernel: option 1 uses the standard cubic spline (M4 cubic) kernel function. This kernel has compact support (particles interact only within distance \(2h\)) and provides good balance between smoothness and computational efficiency.

Wendland alternative: option 2 provides a \(C²\) continuous kernel with better tensile stability properties but is slightly more computationally expensive.

Physical role: The kernel function \(W(r,h)\) acts as a weighting function, determining how much influence nearby particles have on each other. The cubic spline has a peak at \(r=0\) and smoothly decreases to zero at \(r=2h\).

docs.title: Viscosity Model
docs.text:
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="1" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Laminar (default=1)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.01" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />

Artificial viscosity: option 1 uses an artificial viscosity term with dimensionless coefficient \(\alpha=0.01\). This approach:

  • Provides numerical stability by damping high-frequency oscillations
  • Is computationally efficient
  • Does not directly represent physical viscosity (water's kinematic viscosity is \(10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)/s)

Alternative formulations:

  • option 2: It includes viscosity and the Sub-Particle Scale (SPS) turbulence model for more physical representation;
  • option 3: Pure viscosity.

Viscosity at boundaries: ViscoBoundFactor="1" means boundary particles use the same viscosity coefficient as fluid particles. Setting this \(>1\) allows imitating surface roughness or other preferred behavior.

Typical values: For artificial viscosity in dam breaks, \(α\) ranges from 0.01 (less dissipative) to 0.1 (more dissipative). Its definition may be problem dependent and require tuning. However, there is consolidated literature to which the reader is deferred.

docs.title: Density Diffusion Term
docs.text:
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="2" comment="Density Diffusion Term 0:None, 1:Molteni, 2:Fourtakas, 3:Fourtakas(full) (default=0)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value (default=0.1)" />

Fourtakas formulation: option 2 implements the density diffusion term proposed by Fourtakas et al., which: - Reduces long-term density drift and accumulation errors - Smooths density fields without excessive dissipation - Improves pressure field quality, especially near boundaries

Diffusion coefficient: \(\delta=0.1\) controls the strength of density diffusion. Higher values provide more aggressive density correction but may over-smooth the solution.

Why density diffusion is needed: SPH simulations can accumulate density errors over time due to particle disorder and boundary interactions. The density diffusion term acts as a corrective mechanism, smoothing particle densities back toward more locally omogeneous values.

Alternative options:

  • option 0: No density diffusion (may lead to density fluctuations)
  • option 1: Molteni formulation (older approach)
  • option 3: Full Fourtakas formulation (more accurate but slower)

docs.title: Particle Shifting
docs.text:
<parameter key="Shifting" value="0" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full (default=0)" />
<parameter key="ShiftCoef" value="-2" comment="Coefficient for shifting computation (default=-2)" />
<parameter key="ShiftTFS" value="0" comment="Threshold to detect free surface. Typically 1.5 for 2D and 2.75 for 3D (default=0)" />

No shifting: With value="0", particles maintain their Lagrangian positions without artificial displacement. This is appropriate for violent flows like dam breaks where natural particle disorder is physical.

Shifting alternatives: - options 1-3 activate particle shifting techniques that improve particle distribution and reduce void formation - Useful for low-Reynolds number flows or long-duration simulations - Can introduce non-physical effects in highly dynamic flows

Shift coefficient: The value -2 would be used if shifting were activated. Negative values indicate the shifting direction opposes concentration gradients.

Free surface detection: Would determine which particles are shifted if shifting were active.

docs.title: Rigid Body Algorithm
docs.text:
<parameter key="RigidAlgorithm" value="1" comment="Rigid Algorithm 0:collision-free, 1:SPH, 2:DEM, 3:Chrono (default=1)" />
<parameter key="FtPause" value="0.0" comment="Time to freeze the floatings at simulation start (warmup) (default=0)" units_comment="seconds" />

SPH rigid body forces: Option 1 computes forces on rigid bodies (like the building) using standard SPH pressure and viscous force calculations. The building is treated as a fixed rigid body.

Alternative methods:

  • option 0: No interaction (rigid bodies do not interact)
  • option 2: Discrete Element Method for contact mechanics
  • option 3: Chrono physics engine for complex multi-body dynamics

No floating bodies: FtPause="0.0" is irrelevant here since the building is fixed, not floating. For floating objects, this parameter allows them to remain stationary during an initial warm-up period before dynamics begin.

docs.title: Time Step Calculation
docs.text:
<parameter key="CoefDtMin" value="0.05" comment="Coefficient to calculate minimum time step dtmin=coefdtmin*h/speedsound (default=0.05)" />
<parameter key="DtIni" value="0" comment="Initial time step. Use 0 to default use (default=h/speedsound)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtMin" value="0" comment="Minimum time step. Use 0 to default use (default=coefdtmin*h/speedsound)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtFixed" value="0" comment="Fixed Dt value. Use 0 to disable (default=disabled)" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="DtAllParticles" value="0" comment="Velocity of particles used to calculate DT. 1:All, 0:Only fluid/floating (default=0)" />

Minimum time step coefficient: The minimum allowed time step is \(dt_{min} = 0.05 × h/c\). This prevents the simulation from taking unreasonably small steps that would make it impractically slow.

Automatic initial time step: DtIni="0" requests automatic initialisation. The expression \(dt = CFL × h/c\) is an acoustic estimate, not the complete initialisation rule. Initial and subsequent time steps also depend on the solver configuration and its other time-step controls.

Automatic minimum time step: DtMin="0" uses the formula \(dt_{min} = 0.05 × h/c\) automatically.

Variable time stepping: DtFixed="0" enables adaptive time stepping. The code automatically adjusts dt each step based on:

  • Maximum particle velocity
  • Speed of sound
  • CFL condition
  • Force magnitudes

Time step based on fluid only: DtAllParticles="0" means the time step is determined by fluid particle velocities only, not boundary particles.

docs.title: Simulation Duration and Output
docs.text:
<parameter key="TimeMax" value="1.6" comment="Time of simulation" units_comment="seconds" />
<parameter key="TimeOut" value="0.01" comment="Time out data" units_comment="seconds" />

Output frequency: Data is saved every 0.01 seconds, producing 1.6/0.01 = 160 output files. This provides sufficient temporal resolution for accurate visualization and analysis without creating excessive file sizes.

docs.title: Particle Validity Checks
docs.text:
<parameter key="PartsOutMax" value="1" comment="%/100 of fluid particles allowed to be excluded from domain (default=1)" units_comment="decimal" />
<parameter key="RhopOutMin" value="700" comment="Minimum rhop valid (default=700)" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
<parameter key="RhopOutMax" value="1300" comment="Maximum rhop valid (default=1300)" units_comment="kg/m^3" />

Maximum particle loss: Up to \(1%\) of fluid particles (value="1" means 100×1%=1% as a decimal fraction) can exit the domain or become invalid before the simulation terminates with an error.

Density validity range: Particles with density outside 700-1300 kg/m³ are considered invalid and removed. This represents:

  • Lower limit: 70% of reference density
  • Upper limit: 130% of reference density (indicates excessive compression)

Why these limits?: In weakly compressible SPH, density variations should remain small (<1-2% ideally). The \(±30%\) range provides tolerance for numerical oscillations while catching catastrophic errors like particle penetration.

What happens to invalid particles: They are removed from the simulation and counted toward the PartsOutMax limit. If this limit is exceeded, the simulation terminates early, indicating numerical instability or poor parameter choices.

docs.title: Simulation Domain
docs.text:
<simulationdomain comment="Defines domain of simulation">
    <posmin x="default" y="default" z="default" comment="e.g.: x=0.5, y=default-1, z=default-10%" />
    <posmax x="default" y="default" z="default + 50%" />
</simulationdomain>

Automatic domain sizing: x="default", y="default", z="default" means the simulation domain is automatically determined from the initial minimum and maximum particle positions. These limits are determined by GenCase once all the particles are placed to define the initial conditions. GenCase tends to default values to narrow the domain as much as possible for numerical and computational efficience.

Unexpected behavior

While for fluid particles going beyond this limit are excluded from the simulation, boundary particles cause its immediate failure.

Extended upper boundary: z="default + 50%" extends the upper boundary by \(50%\) in the \(z\)-direction. If the initial maximum \(z\)-position, providing space for:

  • Water splashing above boundary particles (example Dambreak 2D)
  • Moving or floating particles

Alternative specifications: You could manually set boundaries like x="0", y="0", z="-0.1" for posmin and x="2", y="1", z="1" for posmax to have full control over the computational domain.

docs.title: CPU, GPU and Multi-GPU Execution
docs.text:
DualSPHysics v6 supports CPU execution with OpenMP, single-GPU execution with CUDA, and a separate Multi-GPU solver. This guide explains executable selection, command-line options, execution requirements and feature compatibility. The numerical features available depend on the selected executable and execution mode.

For the basic preparation, solver and post-processing sequence, see The DualSPHysics Workflow.

docs.title: Execution modes at a glance
docs.text:
Feature CPU / OpenMP Single GPU / CUDA Multi-GPU Main parallel work OpenMP threads on the host CPU CUDA computation on one NVIDIA GPU CUDA computation on several GPUs in one workstation or node Host coordination OpenMP CPU execution Host code manages one GPU Workshop implementation: standard C++ threads and CUDA streams Windows executable used here DualSPHysics6.0CPU_win64.exe DualSPHysics6.0_win64.exe DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_win64.exe Linux executable used here DualSPHysics6.0CPU_linux64 DualSPHysics6.0_linux64 DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_linux64 Selection -cpu, -ompthreads:N -gpu or -gpu:N -gpus:N, optionally -gpusid:id0,id1,... Main resource considerations Host memory and CPU resources available to the process Device memory, compatible CUDA software and driver Memory on each device, host resources, data exchange and synchronisation Compatibility Depends on the selected CPU build Depends on the selected GPU build Distinguish mode restrictions from features absent from the MGPU executable; see the compatibility table below

The standard solver help also documents CPU execution. The dedicated CPU executable provides an explicit CPU path in the examples below. The Windows MGPU executable also supports CPU and single-GPU modes, with the feature limits described below; this does not make the executables interchangeable. The presence of OpenMP among the Multi-GPU build's available features does not mean that OpenMP coordinates its GPUs.

docs.title: CPU execution with OpenMP
docs.text:
OpenMP distributes CPU work among threads within a process. A physical core is a hardware processing core; logical processors are the execution contexts exposed to the operating system, which may include simultaneous multithreading. An OpenMP thread is a software thread. These quantities should not be treated as interchangeable measures of useful parallel performance.

The documented options are:

Option Meaning -cpu Select CPU execution; CPU is the default execution option in the documented interface. -ompthreads:N Set the number of host threads for CPU execution. -ompthreads:0 Use the documented default, described as the number of cores of the device.

The help does not specify whether its default core count denotes physical cores or logical processors, or how process affinity affects that count. Select an explicit positive thread count when a controlled allocation is required, and measure its effect on the actual case. Increasing the thread count does not guarantee a shorter runtime: memory access, scheduling and the work available for parallel execution also matter.

Use a CPU build and its compatible runtime libraries for the operating system. Ensure that the case and its outputs fit in host memory. No universal minimum CPU model or optimal thread count is established here.

docs.title: Single-GPU execution with CUDA
docs.text:
The single-GPU solver performs GPU computation using NVIDIA CUDA. The host CPU still performs management and other work; selecting a GPU does not eliminate CPU or host-memory requirements.

The syntax -gpu[:id] means that -gpu selects GPU execution and that an optional identifier can be supplied, for example -gpu:0. The help does not define the automatic selection rule when the identifier is omitted. Confirm the CUDA devices reported by the actual solver and use an identifier available to that execution environment. Do not infer device identifiers from the order of cards in a system utility or assume that a Multi-GPU identifier list has identical numbering semantics.

The particle data and working arrays must fit the selected device's usable memory. The number of particles alone does not determine the required memory: numerical features and associated arrays also contribute. A CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPU, a compatible driver and the runtime libraries required by the particular build are necessary. The available v6 sources do not establish universal minimum driver, CUDA toolkit or compute-capability versions; use the requirements accompanying the distributed build rather than requirements from an older release.

Choosing one device with -gpu:0 does not distribute a case over several GPUs. Multi-GPU execution uses its separate executable and options.

docs.title: Single-node architecture and domain decomposition
docs.text:
The January 2026 workshop describes a single process using several GPUs within one workstation or computing node. The physical domain is partitioned into subdomains, with each GPU computing the particles assigned to its part. Dynamic load balancing can move the partition boundaries as the workload evolves.

Figure 1: Domain decomposition over four GPUs in the implementation presented by Domínguez at the 8th DualSPHysics Workshop. The original diagram labels the parts GPU 1–4; these labels do not specify command-line device identifiers.

This implementation differs from the earlier MPI-based distributed implementation discussed in the same presentation. It uses shared host execution data within one process rather than separate MPI processes exchanging their own copies. Historical MPI supercomputer results should therefore not be treated as measurements of the present single-node execution method.

The workshop describes a main CPU thread and one CPU thread per GPU. Standard C++ threads and CUDA streams provide host and device coordination. Host synchronisation uses std::mutex and std::atomic; CUDA streams and events support device synchronisation and overlap of computation with asynchronous transfers. Synchronisation may involve the main thread and all GPU threads, the GPU threads, or two particular threads.

Figure 2: Main thread and per-GPU host threads in the workshop architecture. The arrows depict coordination of work and transfers; they do not represent OpenMP teams or MPI processes.

The supplied Multi-GPU executable documents a separate execution mode and its configuration interface. The detailed threading account above describes the published workshop architecture; changes to those internals in later builds require corresponding implementation documentation.

docs.title: Particle exchange, synchronisation and numerical work
docs.text:
Neighbour interactions cross subdomain boundaries. A GPU therefore needs neighbouring particle and cell information from adjacent subdomains, including halo data. Particles that move across a partition must migrate with their associated arrays. Rebalancing also redistributes data when a new partition is selected.

These operations introduce work beyond the corresponding single-GPU computation: identifying exchanged particles, updating cell information, transferring arrays, assessing imbalance and synchronising dependent tasks. Asynchronous transfers can overlap useful calculation, but they do not remove all communication or synchronisation costs.

Global operations also require coordination. The workshop identifies a global time-step decision, motions of bodies spanning GPUs, wave-gauge results and couplings such as Chrono and MoorDynPlus. The published design reuses SPH CUDA calculation code while introducing a different neighbour-list and Multi-GPU management path. Shared kernels alone do not establish numerical equivalence between execution modes. Validate the relevant physical quantities, conservation behaviour and numerical tolerances for the intended case.

The workshop describes particle exchange between GPUs. This does not mean that every transfer necessarily uses a direct hardware peer-to-peer route. The current -mgp2p option is disabled by default, and the actual transfer path depends on the build, configuration and device interconnect.

docs.title: Multi-GPU command-line controls
docs.text:
Use DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_win64.exe on Windows or DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_linux64 on Linux. Do not assume that the standard single-GPU executable accepts these options.

Option Documented interpretation -gpus:N Number of GPUs to use; documented default is 0. This is a count, not a device identifier. -gpusid:id0,id1,... Optional list of selected GPU identifiers. Verify identifiers for the Multi-GPU executable. -mgdiv:MODE Partition axis: x, y, z, plong for the longest particle axis, or dlong for the longest domain axis. Default: dlong. -mgbal:MODE[:weights] Balancing mode and optional list of domain weights. Help prints the default as Npf; the documented dynamic fluid-and-floating-particle mode is npf. -mgbalrun:LIMIT:FREQUENCY:TMEAN Dynamic balancing settings: expected improvement limit from 0–100, assessment frequency in time steps, and averaging interval in time steps. Defaults: 1:100:30. -mgp2p:0 / -mgp2p:1 Disable or enable peer-to-peer use between GPUs. Default: disabled. -svdomainvtk Save the domain in VTK form; retained in the supplied four-GPU example.

Balancing modes are fixed (initial domain size), fixednp (initial particle count), fixednpf (initial fluid and floating particle count), np (dynamic particle count), npf (dynamic fluid and floating particle count), and time (dynamic execution time). Particle-count balancing and execution-time balancing measure different aspects of the workload. The default is not a claim of optimal performance for every case.

The help also contains cell-domain and interaction controls, including -cellfit, -cellrgauto and -cellxrange. Preserve the supplied case configuration unless a documented reason requires changing it; these controls are not additional mandatory settings in the example below.

The available help does not establish precedence or mutual-exclusion behaviour when CPU, single-GPU and Multi-GPU selectors are combined. Each example selects one mode. Do not construct mixed-selector commands by assuming an undocumented precedence rule.

docs.title: Feature compatibility and development-stage limitations
docs.text:
The following table concerns DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_win64.exe, including its CPU and single-GPU modes. It reflects the feature support confirmed by José M. Domínguez Alonso on 2 November 2026.

Feature Multi-GPU mode CPU/single-GPU modes in this executable All mDBC modes, with or without NoPenetration Supported Supported DivCleanKp Supported Supported Periodic boundary conditions Not supported Supported Inlet/outlet Not supported Supported ChronoFEA Not supported Supported Flexible structures Not included Not included Advanced Shifting Not included Not included Variable Resolution Not included Not included

Not supported denotes a restriction of Multi-GPU mode: the executable reports a Multi-GPU limitation if that feature is requested with several GPUs, but allows it in CPU and single-GPU modes. Not included means the feature is absent from this executable in every mode, and the solver reports that the requested functionality is not included. These limits do not apply automatically to the standard CPU/GPU executables or to DualSPHysics v6 as a whole.

ChronoFEA is distinct from other Project Chrono functionality. The supplied Multi-GPU help lists Project Chrono and MoorDynPlus couplings, and the distributed mooring example below uses two GPUs; neither establishes support or numerical validation for every coupled configuration. Other specialised formulations require their own executable-specific compatibility information.

The Linux MGPU binary exposes CPU, single-GPU and Multi-GPU command-line selectors, but the Windows confirmation above does not establish identical Linux feature support. Use the support information for the particular Linux build before transferring specialised configurations.

The workshop's suggested workstation sizes and test GPU counts are development and measurement context, not a verified current minimum or maximum device count. Likewise, a failure caused by too few detected GPUs does not establish an incompatibility of the physical or boundary formulation.

docs.title: Windows BAT and Linux shell examples
docs.text:
The paths below are relative to examples/main/01_DamBreak in a distribution with bin/windows and bin/linux three directory levels above the case folder. Run commands from that case directory. The solver's first positional argument is the generated case prefix; the second is the output directory. A _Def.xml geometry definition is not a substitute for the initial files produced by GenCase.

These are documented command examples, not benchmark results or a guarantee that a particular local installation is ready to run. Use a v6-compatible case definition, the libraries supplied for the build and a separate working copy. Check existing output directories before launching an example.

docs.title: Multi-GPU examples supplied with DualSPHysics v6
docs.text:
The following Windows BAT scripts use DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_win64.exe. Paths are relative to the package root:

  • examples/main/01_DamBreak/:
    • wCaseDambreak_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs.
    • wCaseDambreak_win64_4GPU.bat — four GPUs.
  • examples/main/18_Bathymetry/:
    • wCaseBathymetryWalls_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs.
  • examples/mdbc/04_Dambreak/:
    • wCaseDamBreak3D_mDBC_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs, mDBC-M22 selected by -mdbc22.
    • wCaseDamBreak3D_NS_mDBC_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs, mDBC-NS with NoPenetration=Y set in CaseDamBreak3D_NS_Def.xml.
  • examples/mdbc/07_WavesCylinder/:
    • wCaseWavesFrCylinder_mDBC_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs, mDBC-M22 selected by -mdbc22.
    • wCaseWavesFrCylinder_mDBC_NS_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs, mDBC-NS selected by -mdbc_ns.
  • examples/moordynplus/03_WavesMoorings3D/:
    • wCaseMoorings3D_win64_2GPU.bat — two GPUs with MoorDynPlus.

These scripts demonstrate supplied configurations, not numerical validation or universal performance. Keep their case-specific options: the four-GPU example below includes its own particle-spacing override. The Linux commands below are direct solver invocations; no matching Multi-GPU shell scripts were found in these five example directories.

docs.title: CPU on Windows
docs.text:
For initial files already prepared under CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak, this command uses the verified CPU executable name and the documented default thread selection:

"../../../bin/windows/DualSPHysics6.0CPU_win64.exe" -cpu -ompthreads:0 CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

This command is assembled from the supplied executable path and current help syntax; it is not presented as an unmodified CPU BAT file.

docs.title: One GPU on Windows
docs.text:
The supplied wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat uses the standard solver with -gpu. Its expanded solver call is:

"../../../bin/windows/DualSPHysics6.0_win64.exe" -gpu CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

To request identifier 0, where that identifier is available to the solver, use the documented optional device argument:

"../../../bin/windows/DualSPHysics6.0_win64.exe" -gpu:0 CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

docs.title: CPU and one GPU on Linux
docs.text:
The following shell commands use the corresponding distributed Linux binaries and their documented options. They are direct solver invocations, not names of supplied case-specific SH scripts. The initial files must already exist, the binaries must have executable permission, and their runtime libraries must be available. Use one command for the selected mode:

../../../bin/linux/DualSPHysics6.0CPU_linux64 -cpu -ompthreads:0 CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

../../../bin/linux/DualSPHysics6.0_linux64 -gpu:0 CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

docs.title: Four GPUs on Windows
docs.text:
The workshop's wCaseDambreak_win64_4GPU.bat has a corresponding supplied example. The following preparation and solver excerpt retains its case name, output suffix, particle spacing, four-GPU count and domain-output option. It omits the script's interactive menu and post-processing, and does not delete existing directories.

set name=CaseDambreak
set dirout=%name%_20M_g4_out
set dirbin=../../../bin/windows
set gencase="%dirbin%/GenCase_win64.exe"
set dualsphysicsmgpu="%dirbin%/DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_win64.exe"
%gencase% %name%_Def %dirout%/%name% -save:all -dp:0.0016
if not "%ERRORLEVEL%" == "0" exit /b %ERRORLEVEL%
%dualsphysicsmgpu% -gpus:4 %dirout%/%name% %dirout% -svdomainvtk

The -dp:0.0016 override is part of this particular example. Selecting a backend does not itself require changing particle spacing. This four-GPU input is therefore not automatically the same numerical problem as the standard GPU example. The _20M_g4_out suffix is the supplied directory name, not an independently verified particle count.

docs.title: Four GPUs on Linux
docs.text:
The Linux Multi-GPU binary contains the same documented -gpus interface. For the already prepared four-GPU case prefix, the corresponding direct solver command is:

../../../bin/linux/DualSPHysics6.0MGPU_linux64 -gpus:4 CaseDambreak_20M_g4_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_20M_g4_out -svdomainvtk

Four usable GPUs must be available to that execution environment. This is a translation of the verified solver invocation using the distributed Linux executable, rather than a claim that a matching four-GPU SH script is supplied. Successful execution depends on case compatibility and the runtime environment.

docs.title: Resources and communication
docs.text:
For CPU execution, provide sufficient host memory and compatible OpenMP runtime libraries. GPU execution additionally requires compatible NVIDIA CUDA devices, drivers and the libraries required by the solver build. Multi-GPU execution requires enough usable devices for the requested count and sufficient memory on each device for its assigned particles, neighbouring data and working arrays. Memory across several cards should not be treated as a single unrestricted allocation.

Interconnect bandwidth, transfer overlap, domain shape and load imbalance affect Multi-GPU performance. Peer-to-peer capability must be checked for the actual device topology. NVLink is not established as a universal requirement: the workshop measurements used PCIe-connected L40S GPUs without NVLink. This observation does not guarantee that every PCIe arrangement performs similarly.

docs.title: Workshop scaling measurements
docs.text:
The following results belong to the January 2026 workshop implementation. The hardware comprised two AMD EPYC 7282 CPUs at 2.8 GHz, listed with 16 cores, and eight NVIDIA L40S GPUs, each with 48 GB GDDR6 ECC, 864 GB/s memory bandwidth and a PCIe 4.0 ×16 interface, without NVLink. The L40S specifications quoted in the presentation include Ada Lovelace, 18,176 CUDA cores, 142 multiprocessors and 91.6 TFLOPS FP32. These are the measurement platform's specifications, not minimum v6 requirements.

The dam-break tests covered 4 million to 256 million particles. Four formulations were compared:

Test Time integration Viscosity DDT Boundaries Floating bodies Basic Verlet Artificial None DBC None Advanced Symplectic Laminar + SPS Fourtakas Full mDBC no-slip + no penetration None Advanced + 1 body Symplectic Laminar + SPS Fourtakas Full mDBC no-slip + no penetration One large body Advanced + 8 bodies Symplectic Laminar + SPS Fourtakas Full mDBC no-slip + no penetration Eight bodies

Weak scaling increases the total problem size with the GPU count while keeping the nominal particles per GPU fixed. The presentation reports these weak efficiencies, with the single-GPU baseline equal to 100% in each column:

Test GPUs 4M/GPU 8M/GPU 16M/GPU 32M/GPU Basic 2 96.0% 99.1% 100.6% 103.3% Basic 4 88.9% 94.8% 97.9% 101.3% Basic 8 75.8% 86.3% 92.7% 97.4% Advanced 2 98.6% 100.8% 103.5% 104.6% Advanced 4 93.5% 98.3% 101.9% 102.9% Advanced 8 82.0% 92.6% 98.1% 100.1% Advanced + 1 body 2 97.8% 99.3% 102.4% 103.2% Advanced + 1 body 4 91.9% 94.8% 98.3% 99.7% Advanced + 1 body 8 80.4% 86.5% 91.2% 93.0% Advanced + 8 bodies 2 98.2% 99.7% 103.4% 104.3% Advanced + 8 bodies 4 93.9% 97.2% 101.0% 102.4% Advanced + 8 bodies 8 84.2% 85.4% 96.3% 97.9%

Values above 100% are reproduced as reported; they are measurements relative to the workshop baseline, not a general speed guarantee. For the 16M-particle single-GPU runs, the presentation gives normalised step costs of 2.19, 6.47, 7.83 and 7.65 ms/(steps×M) for these four tests respectively, where M denotes a million particles. These values are normalised costs, not the unnormalised wall time of a complete 16M-particle step.

Strong scaling keeps the total problem size fixed. For the 32M-particle SPHERIC Benchmark Test Case #2, using Symplectic integration, Laminar + SPS viscosity, Fourtakas Full DDT and mDBC no-slip with no penetration, the presentation reports:

GPUs Reported runtime Reported speedup over one GPU 1 13.3 h Baseline 4 3.5 h 3.8× 8 2.5 h 5.3×

These are elapsed runtimes for the reported benchmark, not per-step timings. Eight GPUs did not provide an eightfold speedup in this test. Weak-scaling efficiency and fixed-problem speedup answer different questions and should not be compared as interchangeable metrics.

Figure 3: GPU ownership of particles during the workshop's SPHERIC benchmark at physical times of 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 s. The original GPU colour scales and time labels are retained. Changing particle distributions explain why workload balance can evolve during a simulation.

docs.title: Selecting and checking an execution mode
docs.text:
Choose an executable that supports the numerical features used by the case. CPU execution provides a route when an appropriate CPU build and sufficient host resources are available. Single-GPU execution requires one compatible device with enough memory. Multi-GPU execution can distribute a larger workload across supported devices, but introduces exchange and synchronisation costs and requires its own compatibility checks.

Keep the physical case, particle spacing, numerical methods and requested outputs controlled when comparing backends. Record the solver version, CPU thread count or device identifiers, GPU count, memory use and elapsed time. Separate case generation and post-processing time from solver time when assessing a solver measurement. Compare scientifically relevant outputs with appropriate tolerances; neither the reuse of CUDA kernels nor a reproducibility option proves bitwise agreement between different backends.

Use the compatibility table for the supplied Windows MGPU executable, and the help and release documentation for the actual build when selecting a mode. Check both whether a feature is included in that executable and whether it is supported in the requested mode. Historical scaling results do not guarantee current performance; confirm specialised combinations not covered by the available support information with the developers.
