docs.title: Run Your First Simulation
docs.text:
This page takes you from the downloaded package to your first simulation on screen. You will run the Dam Break example: a column of water collapses inside a tank and hits an obstacle. It is small enough to finish in a few minutes on a GPU, yet shows the full DualSPHysics workflow.

INPUT XML STL OUTPUT BATCH FILES (.bat / .sh) Executes full SPH simulation pipeline

DualSPHysics is an open-source solver for free-surface flows based on Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH). It runs on NVIDIA graphics cards (GPUs) or on ordinary multi-core processors (CPUs), hence the "Dual" in its name. The package contains pre-compiled programs for Windows and Linux, so no compilation is needed.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • a Windows or Linux computer: desktop, laptop or cluster;
  • for GPU runs, an NVIDIA CUDA-capable graphics card. Without one, every case can still run with the CPU version, only more slowly;
  • ParaView to look at the results, free from paraview.org.

A little SPH background helps

You can run the examples without knowing SPH. To set up your own cases, however, it helps to understand a few basic ideas, such as the particle spacing, the smoothing length and how walls are represented. The Theory section, now in preparation, will introduce them from scratch.

docs.title: Install DualSPHysics
docs.text:
Download the package from the DualSPHysics website and extract it wherever you like. Inside you will find:

DualSPHysics_v6.0/
├── bin/
├── doc/
├── examples/
├── src/
├── src_extra/
├── src_geomech/
├── src_mphase/
├── CHANGES.txt
├── chpermissions.sh
├── Files_DualSPHysics_v6.0.pdf
└── LICENSE

The programs in bin/windows and bin/linux are ready to use. You never call them directly: each example has batch files that run them in the right order.

Linux: set the file permissions once

On Linux, extracted files may lose their permission to be executed. Run the script chpermissions.sh, in the root of the package, once after extracting.

Installing on a cluster

DualSPHysics runs on cluster machines, which are usually Linux-based, with no compilation needed.

  • Local security policies may require an administrator to allow the programs and batch files to be executed. Ask your system administrator if a program refuses to start.
  • Clusters usually start jobs through a submission script (for example for Slurm). Copy the commands of the case's .sh batch file into that script. The batch files explains each of those commands.

docs.title: Go to the example folder
docs.text:
Open examples/benchmarks/00_GettingStarted/ in the extracted package.

The case inputs are:

00_GettingStarted/
├── Dambreak2D_Def.xml
├── EXP_DamTipPosition.txt
└── wDambreak2D_win64_GPU.bat

The inspected working copy also contains Command Prompt.lnk and generated results under Dambreak2D_out/. These are not required input files, and their presence in the working copy does not establish that they are included in the release ZIP.

docs.title: What is in the folder
docs.text:
File or folder Purpose Dambreak2D_Def.xml Case definition for a 2-D water column collapsing under gravity in a tank. wDambreak2D_win64_GPU.bat Windows script for particle generation, GPU simulation and post-processing. EXP_DamTipPosition.txt Experimental dam-front position data for reference. Keep the filename exactly as supplied. Dambreak2D_out/ Generated results; created when the case is run. Command Prompt.lnk Optional Windows shortcut to cmd.exe. Its working-directory field is empty; check the current directory before running the BAT. Windows may hide the .lnk extension.

The XML defines a 1 m × 2 m initial water column in a 4 m long, 3 m high tank, with 0.01 m particle spacing and no-slip mDBC walls. It specifies 1 s of simulated time and an output interval of 0.01 s. These are the supplied case settings; no XML edits are needed for this tutorial.

docs.title: Start the simulation
docs.text:
This procedure uses Windows and an NVIDIA CUDA-capable GPU. The supplied case has a Windows GPU BAT; no CPU or Linux launch script is supplied in the inspected folder.

In File Explorer, open examples/benchmarks/00_GettingStarted/. Type cmd in the address bar and press Enter to open a console there. Check that the prompt shows this folder, then run:

wDambreak2D_win64_GPU.bat

The BAT finds its executables through ../../../bin/windows, so keep the case in its package directory structure. It uses GenCase_win64.exe, DualSPHysics6.0_win64.exe, PartVTK_win64.exe, PartVTKOut_win64.exe and IsoSurface_win64.exe.

Double-clicking the BAT is also possible. Using an existing console makes it easier to inspect messages; the script pauses before closing.

Running the same case again

If Dambreak2D_out/ already exists, the BAT offers three choices: delete it and run again, execute post-processing only, or abort. Choose deliberately: the first option removes the existing results. See The batch files.

docs.title: CPU and Linux launch scripts
docs.text:
The final package is intended to provide four launch variants for this case:

Platform Target Script Current status Windows GPU wDambreak2D_win64_GPU.bat Available in the inspected working copy. Windows CPU wDambreak2D_win64_CPU.bat Planned. Linux GPU xDambreak2D_linux64_GPU.sh Planned. Linux CPU xDambreak2D_linux64_CPU.sh Planned.

Use a variant only when its script and compatible executables are present in your package. Run the Windows CPU BAT from the same case directory. On Linux, open a terminal in that directory and use the matching command once the scripts are supplied:

./xDambreak2D_linux64_GPU.sh

For the CPU variant:

./xDambreak2D_linux64_CPU.sh

The GPU variant requires a supported NVIDIA GPU; the CPU variant uses the CPU solver. Retain the package directory structure so each script can find the appropriate executables. See the Linux permissions instructions above before launching a .sh file.

docs.title: What happens while it runs
docs.text:
1. GenCase reads Dambreak2D_Def.xml and creates the initial particle files under Dambreak2D_out/.
  2. DualSPHysics runs the GPU simulation and writes raw results to Dambreak2D_out/data/. The XML also configures a horizontal water-front gauge at a height of 0.03 m.
  3. PartVTK exports fluid and boundary particle VTK files. PartVTKOut exports excluded-particle information, and IsoSurface writes free-surface slices with the Slices filename prefix.

The script checks the return code after each tool. It prints All done when all stages finish without a reported error, or Execution aborted. after a failed stage. Reaching All done confirms script completion, not physical validation.

docs.title: Look at the results
docs.text:
The generated output includes:

Dambreak2D_out/
├── data/
├── gaugesvtks/
├── particles/
└── surface/

The result subdirectories are:

Folder Contents data/ Raw simulation results (Part_####.bi4). gaugesvtks/ VTK files showing the position calculated by the Swl_z003 gauge at each saved output (GaugesSWL_Swl_z003_####.vtk). particles/ Particle data for ParaView (PartFluid_####.vtk). surface/ Free-surface data in VTK format (.vtk).

The inspected output also contains PartBound_####.vtk in particles/ and Slices_####.vtk in surface/, matching the BAT's export commands. The solver writes the gauge VTK files because the XML enables savevtkpart. Each VTK contains the calculated gauge point, which can be displayed in ParaView; it is not the complete free-surface geometry. The time-series measurements are stored separately in GaugesSWL_Swl_z003.csv in the output root.

To view the results in ParaView:

  1. Choose File → Open, go to Dambreak2D_out/particles/ and select the PartFluid_####.vtk file series. Click Apply.
  2. Select the velocity field Vel for colouring and press Play to animate the saved states.
  3. Open the PartBound_####.vtk series from the same folder to display the tank particles.
  4. Open the Slices_####.vtk series from Dambreak2D_out/surface/ to inspect the exported free surface.

The files listed here were inspected in the provided output. Their presence does not by itself establish that a complete run has finished or that the simulation agrees with experiment.

docs.title: Experimental reference
docs.text:
EXP_DamTipPosition.txt contains a citation to Koshizuka and Oka (1996), followed by tab-separated time and Xmax(tip_dam) columns. It supplies experimental reference values for the advancing dam front; the BAT does not read this file or perform a comparison automatically.

The generated GaugesSWL_Swl_z003.csv records the numerical gauge position over time, with units in its header. Comparing that measurement with the experimental data requires attention to the definitions of the measured quantities. No numerical agreement or completed validation is claimed here; detailed comparisons belong in the benchmark documentation.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• The DualSPHysics Workflow explains each stage in detail: how GenCase builds a case, what the batch files do, and how to run the post-processing tools yourself.
  • Case Definition (XML) is the reference for the case definition file.
  • The Examples Catalogue shows what else the examples in examples/main/ can do.
  • DesignSPHysics lets you set up cases with a graphical interface instead of editing XML.

docs.title: The DualSPHysics Workflow
docs.text:
Every DualSPHysics simulation goes through the same three stages:

  1. Pre-processing. GenCase reads your case definition (an XML file) and creates the initial particles.
  2. Running the case. The DualSPHysics solver advances the particles in time and writes the results.
  3. Post-processing. A set of small tools turn those results into files you can visualise (in ParaView) or plot (in Python, Excel, MATLAB, …).

The three stages are separate programs that communicate only through files. A batch file in each case folder runs them in the right order, so a simulation normally starts with a single command. This page follows the 01_DamBreak example through all three stages.

Pre-processing 📄 Case_Def.xml object.vtk • object.stl • object.ply GENCASE mov.datforces.csv Case.xml Case.bi4 Case_All.vtk • Case_Bound.vtk Case_Fluid.vtk • Case__Dp.vtk Processing Part_Head.ibi4 • PartFloat.fbi4 Part_xxxx.bi4 • PartOut.obi4 Run.out Post-processing PointsPos.csv • Points.txt PARTVTK PartFluid.vtk PartBound.vtk PartMoving.vtk BOUNDARYVTK Fixed.vtk Moving_xxxx.vtk Floating_xxxx.vtk ISOSURFACE Surface_xxxx.vtk MEASURETOOL Pressure.csv Velocity.csv Height_xxxx.vtk Stage Program Reads Writes Pre-processing GenCase CaseName_Def.xml CaseName.xml, CaseName.bi4, geometry files (.vtk) Running DualSPHysics (CPU or GPU) CaseName.xml, CaseName.bi4 data/Part_####.bi4, Run.out, Run.csv Post-processing PartVTK, MeasureTool, ComputeForces, IsoSurface, … data/Part_####.bi4 .vtk for ParaView, .csv for plots

About the file names

CaseName stands for the name of your case, e.g. CaseDambreak. The .bi4 files are DualSPHysics' own binary format: compact and fast to write, but not readable by other programs. That is why the post-processing stage exists.

docs.title: Pre-processing: defining the case with GenCase
docs.text:
GenCase builds the initial state of the simulation from a definition file, CaseName_Def.xml. This file contains everything about the case:

  • the geometry: tanks, walls, obstacles, wavemakers, floating objects;
  • the fluid: where it is initially and with which properties;
  • the motion of moving objects, e.g. a piston wavemaker;
  • the simulation parameters: particle spacing, physical constants, formulation options, simulated time.

GenCase is very fast: it creates millions of particles in seconds on an ordinary CPU.

docs.title: How particles are created
docs.text:
GenCase places all particles on a regular Cartesian lattice. The spacing between lattice nodes is the particle spacing dp, the single most important parameter of a simulation: halving dp doubles the resolution, but multiplies the number of particles by 4 in 2-D and by 8 in 3-D.

Objects are drawn onto the lattice. For each object, GenCase selects the lattice nodes that fall inside it, or on its surface, and creates particles only there. The diagram below shows this for a triangle in 2-D: the lattice is laid over the triangle's bounding box, the triangle's edges are traced, and particles are created at the nodes inside.

Step 1 Geometry Definition 1. Geometry Definition The user inputs the boundary geometric definition (XML surface description, STL mesh, or PLY CAD model) establishing the continuous shape volume. 2. Lattice Creation GenCase overlays a uniform background 2D/3D grid (lattice) of candidate points spaced at inter-particle distance dp across the domain. 3. Point-in-Polygon Testing A ray-casting / point-in-polyhedron algorithm evaluates each candidate point to test whether its coordinates lie strictly inside the defined shape. 4. Particle Selection & Pruning All points outside the boundary are discarded. The surviving internal points are assigned SPH properties and exported as initial simulation particles.

Because the geometry is described independently of the lattice, the same case can be run at any resolution just by changing dp. Nothing else in the definition file needs to change.

docs.title: Drawing geometry
docs.text:
The definition file offers a set of drawing commands:

Kind Commands Points and lines <drawpoint />, <drawpoints />, <drawline />, <drawlines /> Surfaces <drawtriangle />, <drawquadri />, <drawtrianglesstrip />, <drawtrianglesfan />, <drawpolygon>, <drawtriangles /> Volumes <drawpyramid />, <drawprism />, <drawbox />, <drawbeach />, <drawsphere />, <drawellipsoid />, <drawcylinder />, <drawwave /> Imported geometry <drawfilestl />, <drawfileply />, <drawfilevtk /> Transformations <move />, <scale />, <rotate />, <rotateline /> Filling with fluid <fillpoint />, <fillbox />, <fillfigure />, <fillprism />

For complex, real-world geometry, draw the object in any CAD tool, export it as STL, PLY or VTK, and load it with the matching <drawfile... /> command. Imported and drawn objects can be combined freely in the same case.

The draw mode decides which lattice nodes of an object receive particles:

  • <setdrawmode mode="face" />: only the surface of the object;
  • <setdrawmode mode="solid" />: only the inside;
  • <setdrawmode mode="full" />: both.

Once the walls exist, the fill commands flood a region with fluid up to those walls, which works even for very complex containers.

docs.title: Particle types and the mk number
docs.text:
Each particle created is of one of three types, set before drawing:

  • fluid: <setmkfluid mk="..." />
  • boundary: <setmkbound mk="..." />
  • none (the nodes are left empty): <setmkvoid />

The mk value is a marker that labels a group of particles sharing the same role, for example "the tank walls" or "the moving gate". Later you use it to give that group a motion, to make it a floating body, or to compute the force acting on it.

The marker you write in the XML is not the final mk stored with the particles. GenCase shifts the numbers so that fluid and boundary markers never overlap:

  • mk of fluid particles = mkfluid + 1
  • mk of boundary particles = mkbound + 1 + fluidcount (usually fluidcount = 9)
Source Container: mkfluid & mkbound Arrays Void ... mk=0 mk=1 mk=2 mk=3..8 mk=9 mk=10 mk=11 mk=12 Target Container: mk Array (fluidcount = 9) mkfluid=0 Fluid 0 mkfluid=1 Fluid 1 mkbound=0 Bound 0 mkbound=1 Bound 1 mkbound=2 Bound 2

Check the final mk values

GenCase writes the final mk of every particle group to CaseName.out. When a post-processing command needs an mk (for example -onlymk: in ComputeForces), take the value from that file.

Fluid particles can also receive initial conditions with <initials />, for example an initial velocity (<velocity />) or a solitary wave (<velwave />), and groups of boundary particles can be declared as floating bodies with <floatings />.

docs.title: Running GenCase
docs.text:
GenCase takes the definition file (without the _Def.xml ending) and the output name:

WindowsLinux 
GenCase_win64.exe CaseDambreak_Def CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak -save:all

./GenCase_linux64 CaseDambreak_Def CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak -save:all

-save:all asks GenCase to also write the geometry as VTK files. Inside CaseDambreak_out/ you then find:

File What it is CaseDambreak.xml the full case configuration, as read by the solver CaseDambreak.bi4 the initial particles (binary) CaseDambreak.out GenCase's log: number of particles, final mk values, warnings CaseDambreak_All.vtk, _Bound.vtk, _Fluid.vtk the initial particles (all, boundary only, fluid only) for ParaView other .vtk files additional diagnostic geometry

Look before you run

Open CaseDambreak_Bound.vtk and CaseDambreak_Fluid.vtk in ParaView before starting a long simulation. A misplaced wall or a tank filled to the wrong level is much cheaper to spot here than after hours of computation.

docs.title: Running the case
docs.text:
GenCase prepares the initial particles and case files; the DualSPHysics solver then runs the numerical simulation. CPU execution uses the host processor, while GPU execution uses a compatible NVIDIA GPU with CUDA. Executables are available for Windows and Linux. Windows examples typically use BAT scripts; Linux examples use shell scripts or equivalent commands. These scripts show the complete preparation, simulation and post-processing sequence.

For executable selection, command-line options, hardware requirements and Multi-GPU execution, see CPU, GPU and Multi-GPU Execution.

docs.title: The solver
docs.text:
The DualSPHysics executable reads the files written by GenCase and simulates the flow. It comes in two versions:

Version Windows Linux GPU (NVIDIA, CUDA) DualSPHysics5.4_win64.exe DualSPHysics5.4_linux64 CPU (multi-core, OpenMP) DualSPHysics5.4CPU_win64.exe DualSPHysics5.4CPU_linux64

The version number in the name (5.4 here) changes between releases; check the bin/windows or bin/linux folder of your installation for the exact names. CPU and GPU availability does not establish identical numerical results or a fixed speedup. Check feature compatibility and assess numerical agreement and runtime for the intended case, software build and hardware.

The solver takes the case name (as written by GenCase, without extension) and the output folder:

WindowsLinux 
DualSPHysics5.4_win64.exe -gpu CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

./DualSPHysics5.4_linux64 -gpu CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak CaseDambreak_out

-gpu selects the graphics card; use -cpu to run on the processor instead. While it runs, the solver prints its progress in the terminal: the simulated time reached, the number of particles, and an estimate of the remaining run time.

The results are written to CaseDambreak_out/:

File What it is data/Part_0000.bi4, Part_0001.bi4, … the state of all particles at each output time (one file per saved instant) data/PartOut_000.obi4 particles that left the domain during the simulation Run.out the solver's log: configuration, progress, warnings, total run time Run.csv, RunPARTs.csv run statistics, per output step, in table form

Command-line options

Run the solver with -h to list every option it accepts. Many parameters of the XML file (for example the simulated time or the formulation options) can be overridden from the command line. This is handy for quick tests without editing the case.

docs.title: The batch files
docs.text:
Typing these commands by hand every time would be tedious, and the post-processing steps add many more. Each example therefore comes with batch files that run the whole chain. Their names tell you the system (w…_win64 for Windows, x…_linux64 for Linux) and the processor they use:

File System Runs on wCaseDambreak_win64_GPU.bat Windows GPU wCaseDambreak_win64_CPU.bat Windows CPU xCaseDambreak_linux64_GPU.sh Linux GPU xCaseDambreak_linux64_CPU.sh Linux CPU

A batch file is a plain text file: open it in any text editor to read or change it. All DualSPHysics batch files follow the same structure, in five blocks. The excerpts below are from xCaseDambreak_linux64_GPU.sh; the Windows .bat files contain the same steps in Windows syntax (set name=... instead of export name=..., and %name% instead of ${name}).

docs.title: 1. Case name and output folders
docs.text:
export name=CaseDambreak
export dirout=${name}_out
export diroutdata=${dirout}/data

name must match the definition file (CaseDambreak_Def.xml). All results go to CaseDambreak_out/, with the particle data in its data/ subfolder.

docs.title: 2. Where the executables are
docs.text:
export dirbin=../../../bin/linux
export gencase="${dirbin}/GenCase_linux64"
export dualsphysicsgpu="${dirbin}/DualSPHysics5.4_linux64"
export partvtk="${dirbin}/PartVTK_linux64"
export measuretool="${dirbin}/MeasureTool_linux64"
# ... one line for each post-processing tool

dirbin points to the folder with the programs, relative to the case folder. If you copy a case to another location, this is the line to update.

docs.title: 3. What to do if results already exist
docs.text:
If CaseDambreak_out/ already exists, the batch file stops and asks:

The folder "CaseDambreak_out" already exists. Choose an option.
  [1]- Delete it and continue.
  [2]- Execute post-processing.
  [3]- Abort and exit.

Option 2 is worth remembering: it keeps the simulation results and only reruns the post-processing, for example after you have changed which variables PartVTK writes.

docs.title: 4. Pre-processing and simulation
docs.text:
${gencase} ${name}_Def ${dirout}/${name} -save:all
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then fail; fi

${dualsphysicsgpu} -gpu ${dirout}/${name} ${dirout}
if [ $? -ne 0 ] ; then fail; fi

These are exactly the two commands of the previous sections. The line after each one checks whether the program finished successfully, and stops the whole chain if it did not. That way a GenCase error is never followed by a meaningless simulation.

docs.title: 5. Post-processing
docs.text:
The rest of the file runs the post-processing tools, each writing to its own subfolder of CaseDambreak_out/ (particles/, measuretool/, forces/, surface/, flow/). These commands are explained in the next section.

Adapting a batch file to your own case

The easiest way to set up a new case is to copy an example folder and change:

  1. name, to match your _Def.xml file;
  2. dirbin, if the folder has moved relative to bin/;
  3. the post-processing commands: delete those you do not need and adjust the options of the others (particle types, mk values, measurement points).

On clusters, the same commands go into the job submission script. See the notes on cluster machines in Run Your First Simulation.

docs.title: Post-processing
docs.text: The solver's output, data/Part_####.bi4, is complete but not directly usable. The post-processing tools read it and extract what you need.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool What it does Typical output PartVTK converts particles to VTK or CSV, with a choice of particles and variables particles/PartFluid_####.vtk PartVTKOut the same for particles that left the domain particles/PartFluidOut_####.vtk BoundaryVTK writes the geometry of moving and floating boundaries at each output time surface .vtk files MeasureTool interpolates velocity, pressure or free-surface elevation at chosen points (numerical gauges) .csv time series, .vtk points ComputeForces computes the force exerted by the fluid on a group of boundary particles .csv time series FloatingInfo reports the motion of floating bodies: position, velocity, rotation .csv time series IsoSurface builds the free surface as a surface mesh, and slices through it surface/Surface_####.vtk FlowTool counts particles and flow through user-defined boxes .csv, .vtk TracerParts follows the trajectories of selected particles .vtk lines

Every tool prints the full list of its options when run with -h.

docs.title: Running a post-processing tool
docs.text:
All tools share the same pattern: -dirdata says where the particle data are, and one or more -save... options say what to write. For example, the Dam Break batch file converts the fluid particles to VTK with:

WindowsLinux 
PartVTK_win64.exe -dirdata CaseDambreak_out/data -savevtk CaseDambreak_out/particles/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid

./PartVTK_linux64 -dirdata CaseDambreak_out/data -savevtk CaseDambreak_out/particles/PartFluid -onlytype:-all,+fluid
Option Meaning -dirdata CaseDambreak_out/data read the particle data from this folder -savevtk .../PartFluid write VTK files named PartFluid_0000.vtk, PartFluid_0001.vtk, … -onlytype:-all,+fluid start from no particles (-all), then add the fluid ones (+fluid)

The particle selection reads left to right: -all removes everything, then each + adds a group back. The available groups are all, bound, fixed, moving, floating and fluid. Particles can also be selected by marker (-onlymk:), by position (-onlypos:) or by velocity (-onlyvel:).

Two more options are worth knowing from the start:

  • -vars: chooses the variables written with each particle, for example -vars:+idp,+vel,+rhop,+press for particle id, velocity, density and pressure. Fewer variables make smaller files.
  • -savecsv writes a table instead of VTK files, ready to open in Python or Excel.

docs.title: Visualising the results in ParaView
docs.text:
ParaView is a free, open-source visualisation program that reads VTK files directly. The steps below show the Dam Break particles coloured by velocity.

1. Load the particles. File → Open, go to CaseDambreak_out/particles/ and select PartFluid_..vtk. ParaView groups the numbered files into a single time series. Click Apply in the Properties panel.

2. Colour by velocity. In the toolbar, change the colouring from Solid Color to Vel. Click Rescale to Data Range if the colours look washed out.

3. Show the tank. Open CaseDambreak_out/CaseDambreak_Bound.vtk (written by GenCase) and click Apply. The walls give the flow its context. In the Properties panel, lower their Opacity so they do not hide the fluid.

4. Play the simulation. Press Play in the toolbar at the top. The time shown in the toolbar is the simulated time.

5. Save an image or a video. File → Save Screenshot saves the current view; File → Save Animation saves every time step as images or as a video.

Large simulations

3-D simulations can have millions of particles per file. For a first look, write only the variables you need with -vars:, or only some output times with the -first: and -last: options of PartVTK.

docs.title: Welcome to the DualSPHysics User Guide
docs.text:
The open-source project DualSPHysics aims at promoting a user-friendly platform for numerical simulations based on the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method. As a natural evolution of the open-source SPHysics code, DualSPHysics has expanded upon the original concept and developed it into a modern software platform compatible with both CPU and GPU hardware architectures.

Video 1: 3-D dam break simulation with debris blocks.

docs.title: Official Website and Downloads
docs.text:
For more information about DualSPHysics, visit the official website.

The complete software package, including executables, examples and documentation, is available from the Downloads page.

docs.title: Background and Motivation
docs.text: The SPHysics FORTRAN code was extensively validated for different problems including wave breaking (Dalrymple and Rogers, 2006), dam-break behaviour (Crespo, 2008), interaction with coastal structures (Gómez-Gesteira and Dalrymple, 2004), and with moving breakwaters (Rogers, 2010). Although SPHysics allowed problems to be simulated using high resolution and a wide range of formulations, the main limitation for its application to real engineering problems was the excessively long computational runtimes, meaning that SPHysics was rarely applied to large domains. Hardware acceleration and parallel computing became essential requirements to make SPHysics more useful and versatile for engineering applications.

docs.title: GPU Computing
docs.text:
Originating from the computer games industry, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have established themselves as a cost-effective alternative to traditional High Performance Computing (HPC) for scientific computing and numerical modelling. GPUs are designed to manage huge amounts of data and their computing power has developed in recent years much faster than conventional Central Processing Units (CPUs).

Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) is a parallel programming framework and language for GPU computing using extensions to the C/C++ language. Researchers and engineers across different fields are achieving significant speedups by implementing their codes with the CUDA language. The parallel computing power of GPUs is particularly well-suited for SPH methods where the same operations for each particle during the simulation can be efficiently parallelized.

docs.title: The DualSPHysics Implementation
docs.text:
DualSPHysics is implemented in C++ and CUDA to carry out simulations with millions of particles on either CPU or GPU hardware. The CPU implementation presents several advantages, such as more optimized memory usage. The object-oriented programming paradigm provides code that is easy to understand, maintain, and modify, with sophisticated error control mechanisms. Furthermore, advanced optimizations are implemented—for example, particles are reordered to provide faster memory access, and the most efficient approach to create the neighbor list is utilized (Domínguez et al., 2011).

The CUDA implementation manages the parallel execution of threads on GPUs. The most effective approaches were implemented as an extension of the C++ code, incorporating the most appropriate optimizations to parallelize particle interactions on GPU hardware (Domínguez et al., 2013a; Domínguez et al., 2013b).

docs.title: Validation and Documentation
docs.text:
The first rigorous validations of DualSPHysics were presented in Crespo et al., 2011. Version 3.0 of the code is fully documented in Crespo et al., 2015, and the latest developments and capabilities are described in Domínguez et al., 2022.

Getting Started

New to DualSPHysics? Explore our User Guide to begin your first simulation or check out the Examples section for practical applications.

docs.title: Overview of Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics
docs.text: Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) is a Lagrangian meshless method that has been applied to an expanding range of applications within Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). In SPH, particles represent the fluid flow, interact with structures, and naturally handle large deformations with moving boundaries. The SPH method has matured significantly for CFD applications through continuing improvements and modifications, with accuracy, stability, and reliability now reaching acceptable levels for practical engineering use.

docs.title: Origin of DualSPHysics
docs.text: The DualSPHysics code originates from SPHysics, an open-source SPH model developed collaboratively by researchers at Johns Hopkins University (US), University of Vigo (Spain), University of Manchester (UK), and University of Rome La Sapienza (Italy). The software is freely available at www.sphysics.org, with comprehensive documentation of the FORTRAN code provided in Gómez-Gesteira et al., 2012a; 2012b.

docs.title: Validation History
docs.text: The SPHysics FORTRAN code underwent extensive validation across diverse applications including wave breaking (Dalrymple and Rogers, 2006), dam-break dynamics (Crespo et al., 2008), interaction with coastal structures (Gómez-Gesteira and Dalrymple, 2004), and moving breakwater scenarios (Rogers et al., 2010). Despite enabling high-resolution simulations with versatile formulations, SPHysics faced a critical limitation: excessively long computational runtimes that prevented application to large-scale engineering problems. This constraint highlighted the need for hardware acceleration and parallel computing to enhance the code's practical utility.

docs.title: The GPU Computing Revolution
docs.text:
Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), initially developed for the gaming industry, have emerged as a cost-effective alternative to traditional High Performance Computing (HPC) infrastructure for scientific computing and numerical modelling. GPUs excel at managing massive datasets, with their computational capabilities advancing far more rapidly than conventional CPUs in recent years.

Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) provides a parallel programming framework that extends C/C++ for GPU computing. Researchers and engineers across numerous disciplines have achieved dramatic performance improvements by leveraging CUDA. The inherently parallel nature of SPH—where identical operations are performed for each particle—makes it particularly well-suited for GPU acceleration.

docs.title: DualSPHysics: A Modern Implementation
docs.text: DualSPHysics is implemented in C++ and CUDA, enabling simulations with millions of particles on both CPU and GPU architectures. This dual implementation strategy provides flexibility while maximizing computational efficiency.

docs.title: CPU Implementation
docs.text: The modern C++ implementation offers several key advantages over the original FORTRAN code. The object-oriented programming paradigm delivers code that is easier to understand, maintain, and extend, with sophisticated error handling mechanisms. Memory management has been significantly optimized, with particles reordered to improve cache efficiency and memory access patterns. The neighbor list construction—a computationally intensive operation—employs the most efficient algorithms developed through systematic research (Domínguez et al., 2011).

docs.title: GPU Implementation
docs.text: The CUDA implementation manages parallel thread execution across GPU cores, with careful optimization of particle interaction calculations. Rather than a complete rewrite, the GPU code extends the C++ implementation with targeted parallelization strategies specifically designed for SPH algorithms (Domínguez et al., 2013a; Domínguez et al., 2013b). This approach ensures consistency between CPU and GPU results while maximizing performance on each platform.

docs.title: Validation and Maturity
docs.text: Rigorous validation of DualSPHysics was first presented in Crespo et al., 2011, demonstrating the code's accuracy and reliability for complex free-surface flows. Version 3.0 received comprehensive documentation in Crespo et al., 2015, establishing it as a mature tool for engineering applications. The latest capabilities and developments are described in Domínguez et al., 2022, showcasing the evolution from pure hydrodynamics to multiphysics simulations.

docs.title: About This Documentation
docs.text:
This user guide is organized to support both new users and experienced practitioners:

Theoretical Foundation: Detailed description of the SPH formulation implemented in DualSPHysics, including governing equations, boundary conditions, and numerical schemes.

Technical Implementation: Comprehensive coverage of optimization strategies for CPU and GPU, compilation procedures, and code architecture.

Practical Application: Step-by-step instructions for setting up, running, and post-processing simulations with the DualSPHysics package.

Advanced Topics: Coupling with external solvers, multi-physics capabilities, and extending the code for custom applications.

Next Steps

The SPH formulation behind the solver will be described in the Theory section, which is in preparation.
