docs.title: Full ChronoFEA XML format reference
docs.text:
The complete dedicated format below preserves its illustrative alternatives, comments and placeholders. It is a format collection, not a single executable simulation. Its repeated bodies and alternative definitions must not be combined indiscriminately. Use the shared Chrono reference linked above for ordinary rigid-body configuration.

doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_ChronoFEA.xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<!-- *** DualSPHysics [ChronoFea] v6.0 (16-06-2026) *** -->
<!-- *** class: JChronoObjectsFea *** -->
<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Example to define the Finite Elements using Chrono *** -->
<casedef>
    ...
    <mainlist>
        <!-- Cylinder -->                               
        <setmkbound mk="51" />
        <drawcylinder radius="0.03">
            <point x="1.5" y="0.0" z="0.01" /> 
            <point x="1.5" y="0.0" z="0.45" />
        </drawcylinder>
        <shapeout file="cylinder1" />
        <!-- Rectangle -->                                  
        <setmkbound mk="52" />
        <drawbox>
            <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
            <point x="0" y="-0.02" z="-0.02" />
            <size x="0.35" y="0.04" z="0.04" />
        </drawbox>
        <shapeout file="rectangle1" />
    </mainlist>
    ...
    <!-- Define the FEA bodies as floatings -->
    <floatings>
        <floating mkbound="51-53" rhopbody="0.01" />
    </floatings>
    <!-- Define the properties of materials -->
    <properties>
        <propertyfile file="Floating_Materials.xml" path="materials" />
        <links>
            <link mkbound="51" property="steel" comment="Property for the cylinder" />
            <link mkbound="52" property="steel" comment="Property for the rectangle" />
        </links>
    </properties>
    ...
</casedef>
<execution>
    <special>
        <chrono>
            <!-- Define a list of FEA bodies -->
            <configfea>
                <savedata value="0.01" comment="Saves CSV with node positions, forces, velocities, accelerations and rotations (0=all steps)">
                    <start value="0" comment="Start time to save data. (default=0)" />
                    <finish value="10" comment="End time to save data. (default=#TimeMax)" />
                    <precision value="6" comment="CSV precision (default=6)" />
                </savedata>

                <savevtk value="true" comment="Saves VTK nodes and geometry (default=false)" />
                <savevtk_nodes value="true" comment="Saves VTK nodes (default=savevtk)" />
                <savevtk_geo value="true" comment="Saves VTK beam geometry (default=savevtk)" />
                <!-- Define each FEA body -->
                <!-- userot=true enable the node rotations to compute the deformation/bendinf of the structure -->
                <floating mkbound="51" userot="true" />
                <!-- userot=false disable the node rotations; it uses the node positions to compute the deformation/bendinf of the structure -->
                <floating mkbound="52-53" userot="false" />
                <!-- Load external forces from csv file-->
                <!--*** onlyfile indicates which forces will be applied to the FEA object.              ***-->
                <!--*** To apply only forces loaded from file (using onlyfile="true" or onlyfile="1")   ***--> 
                <!--*** To calculate forces by the summation of the particle interaction and the forces ***-->
                <!--*** loaded from a the file (using onlyfile="false" or onlyfile="0").                ***--> 
                <!--*** It is an optional. Default=false                                                ***-->
                <floating mkbound="53">
                    <loadforces onlyfile="false" file="CaseExternalForces.csv" units_comment="N"/>
                </floating>
                <!-- Load external loads from csv file-->
                <!--*** onlyfile indicates which forces will be applied to the FEA object.              ***-->
                <!--*** To apply only loads loaded from file (using onlyfile="true" or onlyfile="1")    ***--> 
                <!--*** To calculate forces/loads by the summation of the particle interaction and the  ***-->
                <!--*** forces loaded from a the file (using onlyfile="false" or onlyfile="0").         ***--> 
                <!--*** It is an optional. Default=false                                                ***-->
                <floating mkbound="53">
                    <loadloads onlyfile="false" file="CaseExternalLoads.csv" units_comment="N/m"/>
                </floating>
                <!-- Apply linear loads along the beams-->
                <!--*** Uses the ChLoadBeamWrenchDistributed object to apply them        .              ***-->
                <!--*** It is an optional. Default=false                                                ***-->
                <floating mkbound="54">
                    <linearloads value="true" comment="Apply linear loads along the beams. (default=false)"/>
                </floating>
                <!-- Apply initial conditions -->
                <!--*** linearvelini.  Linear velocities                                                ***-->
                <!--*** angularvelini. Angular velocities                                               ***-->
                <floating mkbound="55">
                    <linearvelini x="1" y="3" z="2" units_comment="m/s" />
                    <angularvelini x="0.2" y="0.4" z="0.6" units_comment="rad/s" />
                </floating>
            </configfea>

            <!-- Disable collisions for chrono -->
            <collision activate="false" />

            <!-- Enable/Disable the gravity in Chrono for FEA. It is applied as linear loads along the segments -->
            <gravity value="true" comment="Use of gravity acceleration. (default=true)"/>
            <!-- Node section -->
            <nodes>
                <node ref="0" fixed="false" x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
                <node ref="1" fixed="false" x="0.35" y="0" z="0"/>
                <node ref="2" fixed="true" x="0.35" y="0" z="-0.35"/>
                <node ref="3" fixed="false" x="0.35" y="0" z="0" mass="0.5"/> 
                <node ref="4" fixed="true" x="0.0" y="0" z="-0.35" mass="1.5"/>
            </nodes>
            <!-- Define a FEA body floating (FEA Body)-->
            <feafloating id="cylinder1" mkbound="51" modelfile="AutoActual">
                <!-- Define type of FEA Body -->
                <beamEuler segments="10" comment="Number of nodes=Segments+1. Euler beams only use linear order.">
                    <pointA noderef="0" comment="Start of beam"/>
                    <pointB noderef="1" comment="End of beam"/>
                    <!-- Define the section properties -->
                    <!-- Circular beam -->
                    <section shape="0" comment="Shape 0:Circular, 1:Rectangular. (default=0)">
                        <radius value="0.03" comment="Radius of cylinder." units_comment="m"/>
                        <density value="7850" comment="Density of the beam." units_comment="kg/m^3"/>
                        <poisson value="0.3" comment="Poisson ratio."/>
                        <youngmodulus value="210e6" comment=" Young elastic modulus." units_comment="N/m^2"/> 
                        <rgdamping value="0.0" comment="Rayleigh damping ratio."/>
                    </section>
                </beamEuler>
            </feafloating>

            <!-- Connect a FEA node to a 3D hinge fixed in space.  If rotpoint is omitted, the initial position of noderef is used as hinge point. -->
            <link_feahinge idbody1="cylinder1" noderef="0">
                <rotpoint x="0" y="0" z="0" comment="Point for rotation in global coordinates (optional)" />
                <rotvector x="0" y="0" z="1" comment="Hinge axis in global coordinates" />
                <rotstiffness value="500" comment="Rotational stiffness around hinge axis [Nm/rad]" />
                <rotdamping value="10" comment="Rotational damping around hinge axis [Nms/rad]" />
            </link_feahinge>

            <!-- Define a FEA body floating (FEA Body)-->
            <feafloating id="rectangle1" mkbound="52" modelfile="AutoActual">
                <!-- Define type of FEA Body -->
                <beamEuler segments="10" comment="Number of nodes=Segments+1. Euler beams only use linear order.">
                    <pointA noderef="2" comment="Start of beam"/>
                    <pointB noderef="1" comment="End of beam"/>
                    <!-- Define the section properties -->
                    <!-- Rectangular beam -->
                    <section shape="1" comment="Shape 0:Circular, 1:Rectangular. (default=0)">
                        <width value="0.04" comment="Width of the beam (Y-direction)" units_comment="m"/>
                        <thickness value="0.04" comment="Thickness of the beam (Z-direction)" units_comment="m"/>
                        <density value="7850" comment="Density of the beam." units_comment="kg/m^3"/>
                        <poisson value="0.3" comment="Poisson ratio."/>
                        <youngmodulus value="210e6" comment=" Young elastic modulus." units_comment="N/m^2"/> 
                        <rgdamping value="0.0" comment="Rayleigh damping ratio."/>
                        <axrigmul value="1000" comment="Axial rigidity multiplier to avoid compressibility.(default=1)"/>
                    </section>
                </beamEuler>
            </feafloating>

            <!-- Define a FEA body floating (FEA Body)-->
            <feafloating id="rectangle1" mkbound="53" modelfile="AutoActual">
                <!-- Define type of FEA Body -->
                <beamEuler segments="10" comment="Number of nodes=Segments+1. Euler beams only use linear order.">
                    <pointA noderef="3" comment="Start of beam"/>
                    <pointB fixed="true" x="0.0" y="0" z="-0.35" comment="Unique node. This is not shared." />
                    <!-- Define the section properties -->
                    <!-- Rectangular beam -->
                    <section shape="1" comment="Shape 0:Circular, 1:Rectangular. (default=0)">
                        <width value="0.04" comment="Width of the beam (Y-direction)" units_comment="m"/>
                        <thickness value="0.04" comment="Thickness of the beam (Z-direction)" units_comment="m"/>
                        <density value="7850" comment="Density of the beam." units_comment="kg/m^3"/>
                        <poisson value="0.3" comment="Poisson ratio."/>
                        <youngmodulus value="210e6" comment=" Young elastic modulus." units_comment="N/m^2"/> 
                        <rgdamping value="0.0" comment="Rayleigh damping ratio."/>
                        <axrigmul value="1000" comment="Axial rigidity multiplier to avoid compressibility.(default=1)"/>
                    </section>
                </beamEuler>
            </feafloating>
            ...
        </chrono>
    </special>
    ...
</execution>

<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Alternative Chrono FEA collision definitions ***                -->
<!-- *** FEA bodies require SMC contacts when collisions are enabled.*** -->
<chrono>
    <collision activate="true">
        <distancedp value="0.5" comment="Allowed collision overlap according Dp (default=0.5)" />
        <contactmethod value="1" comment="Contact method type. 0:NSC, 1:SMC. SMC is required for FEA collisions.">
            <kn value="1.0e6" comment="SMC normal stiffness." />
            <gn value="100" comment="SMC normal damping." />
            <adhesion value="0" comment="SMC adhesion." />
        </contactmethod>
        <feacollision mode="mesh-rigidbody" overlap="0"
            comment="mode=mesh-rigidbody|mesh-mesh. overlap=0 uses beam radius/half-size as node-cloud contact radius." />
    </collision>
</chrono>

<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!--*** Beam shapes ***-->
<section shape="0" comment="Shape 0:Circular, 1:Rectangular. (default=0)">
    <radius value="0.03" comment="Radius of cylinder." units_comment="m"/>
    ...
</section>

<!-- Rectangular -->
<section shape="1" comment="Shape 0:Circular, 1:Rectangular. (default=0)">
    <width value="0.04" comment="Width of the beam section (Y-direction)." units_comment="m"/>
    <thickness value="0.04" comment="Thickness of the beam section (Z-direction)." units_comment="m"/>
    ...
</section>

<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!----------------------------------------------------------------------------------->

    <pointA fixed="true" x="0" y="0" z="0" comment="Start of beam"/>
    <pointB fixed="false" x="0.35" y="0" z="0" comment="End of beam"/>

docs.title: Flexible structures
docs.text:
Under review by Joseph O'Connor

Total Lagrangian SPH structural dynamics, material models, clamps and fluid–structure interaction in DualSPHysics v6.

docs.title: Scope and structural formulation
docs.text:
The Flexible Structures functionality represents deformable solids using a Total Lagrangian SPH (TL-SPH) formulation integrated into DualSPHysics. Structural particles carry the displacement, velocity and deformation of the solid. When fluid is present, the fluid treats the structure as a moving boundary and the structural dynamics responds to the fluid loading. This supports structural-only configurations as well as flexible fluid–structure interaction (FSI).

This page documents the flexstrucs functionality. Its structural model is an internal particle formulation, distinct from the partitioned SPH–FEA coupling through ChronoFEA. It does not require a beam mesh, beam-node declarations or a Chrono mechanical link to compute the deformation described here. A constitutive model number under flexstrucbody must not be interpreted as a ChronoFEA element type. The two approaches are complementary modelling choices, rather than interchangeable XML interfaces.

The formulation is described by J. O'Connor and B. D. Rogers, Journal of Fluids and Structures (2021). Three parts of the documented method are particularly relevant to configuration:

  • A material reference frame describes the solid relative to its initial configuration. Structural neighbour pairs and reference gradients use that configuration; the formulation addresses the tensile-instability problems associated with conventional solid SPH treatments.
  • Kernel correction restores linear consistency near geometric boundaries, where a truncated particle neighbourhood would otherwise affect the structural approximation.
  • Hourglass suppression controls zero-energy modes associated with rank deficiency in the collocated particle discretisation. Its coefficient can change the effective stiffness and is therefore a numerical modelling choice.

These are the roles of the formulation's components, not guarantees of stability or accuracy for every geometry and material. The structural model must still be resolved adequately and checked for the intended deformation and loading.

docs.title: Particle representation and deformation
docs.text:
The structure is generated as boundary particles with its own mkbound. A motion declaration classifies that marker as moving, while flexstrucbody assigns the structural material and links it to its clamp. Structural connectivity comes from particle neighbours in the material reference configuration; no user-specified finite-element connectivity or nodal rotational degrees of freedom are defined by this XML.

Let \(\mathbf X\) denote the initial material position and \(\mathbf x\) the current position. The current structural implementation evaluates a deformation gradient and Green–Lagrange strain:

\[ \mathbf F=\frac{\partial\mathbf x}{\partial\mathbf X}, \qquad \mathbf E=\frac12(\mathbf F^{\mathsf T}\mathbf F-\mathbf I). \]

The selected constitutive matrix maps the strain to second Piola–Kirchhoff stress; the internal force calculation uses first Piola–Kirchhoff stress:

\[ \mathbf S=\mathsf C:\mathbf E, \qquad \mathbf P=\mathbf F\mathbf S. \]

Here \(\mathsf C\) is constructed from the material properties and the chosen two- or three-dimensional model. These material stress measures differ from the fluid pressure used at the FSI boundary. The plane-stress and plane-strain choices below determine the appropriate reduced constitutive coefficients. They are not options to change the fluid equation of state.

docs.title: XML organisation and setup sequence
docs.text:
The setup has three linked parts: generate the clamp and structure, declare the structure as moving, and assign its structural properties. All three must use consistent marker values.

XML location Responsibility case/casedef/geometry Particle spacing, geometry and marker assignment case/casedef/motion Moving classification for the flexible body; prescribed motion for other moving objects case/casedef/normals Initial boundary normals when mDBC is used case/execution/special/flexstrucs List of structural-body definitions flexstrucs/flexstrucbody Body marker, clamp marker and material/numerical properties case/execution/parameters Boundary treatment, slip mode, integration and other solver settings

The snippets on this page are independent excerpts from the stated source cases. They do not form a new combined simulation. Preserve the complete selected case's constants, particle-generation order, marker assignments, data files, boundary normals and numerical settings.

docs.title: Structural-only Turek–Hron configuration
docs.text:
The CSM3 example defines the clamp first using mkbound=0, then draws the flexible strip with mkbound=1 embedded in it. Drawing order and embedding establish the intended attachment; mkclamp alone does not create missing clamp particles or repair a geometric gap.

The clamp is a sphere of radius 0.05 m centred at (0.2, 0, 0.2) m. In the two-dimensional x–z case, it appears as a circular support. The strip starts at (0.2, −0.01, 0.19) m and has size (0.4, 0.02, 0.02) m. Retain the out-of-plane generation coordinates even though the computational case is two-dimensional.

XML excerpt — csm3-geometry. XML location: case/casedef/geometry/commands. Source: examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronCSM3_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<mainlist>
    <setdrawmode mode="full" />
    <setmkbound mk="0" />
    <drawsphere radius="0.05">
        <point x="0.2" y="0.0" z="0.2" />
    </drawsphere>
    <setmkbound mk="1" />
    <drawbox>
        <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
        <point x="0.2" y="-0.01" z="0.19" />
        <size x="0.4" y="0.02" z="0.02" />
    </drawbox>
</mainlist>

Figure 1: Particle geometry of the Turek–Hron structural example. The circular clamp is mkbound 0 and the embedded flexible strip is mkbound 1.

docs.title: Moving classification with mvnull
docs.text:
The flexible marker must belong to the moving-boundary category. The current reader rejects a body marker that is not a moving boundary. In the CSM3 case, objreal ref="1" refers to that marker and mvnull supplies the required motion classification without prescribing a rigid trajectory to replace the structural solution:

XML excerpt — csm3-runtime-motion. XML location: case/casedef. Source: examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronCSM3_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<motion>
    <objreal ref="1">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvnull id="1" />
    </objreal>
</motion>

mvnull does not clamp the body or specify that it remains undeformed. Its deformation is computed by the structural solver during execution. The motion identifier inside begin/mvnull is separate from the boundary marker selected by objreal ref.

mkbound on flexstrucbody identifies the deformable population. mkclamp identifies the associated clamp population. The current reader accepts fixed or moving boundary markers as clamps and rejects a clamp marker that is itself a flexible structure. A prescribed moving support can therefore be represented separately from the deformable material. These clamp declarations do not define arbitrary hinge, contact or multibody joints.

docs.title: Material properties and hourglass control
docs.text:
The CSM3 structural definition uses density 1000 kg/m³, Young's modulus \(1.4\times10^6\) Pa, Poisson's ratio 0.4, plane strain and zero hourglass correction. Its mkbound=1 and mkclamp=0 match the preceding geometry and motion:

XML excerpt — csm3-material. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronCSM3_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="1" mkclamp="0">
        <density value="1000.0" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="1.4e6" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.4" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="1" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.0" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>
Element/attribute Physical or numerical meaning Requirement or documented default mkbound Flexible body's boundary marker Required; must identify a moving population mkclamp Marker or marker list for its associated clamp populations Retain the selected case's attachment definition density value Structural mass density, kg/m³ Required; independent of the fluid reference density youngmod value Young's modulus, Pa Required poissratio value Poisson's ratio Required; dimensionless constitmodel value Plane strain, plane stress or 3D St. Venant–Kirchhoff model Required; must agree with dimensionality hgfactor value Hourglass suppression coefficient Optional; default 0

Structural mass follows the structural density and the reference particle volume. Do not replace density with the fluid's rhop0 merely because both are densities. Similarly, youngmod is a continuum elastic modulus, rather than a spring stiffness in N/m or an FEA sectional rigidity. The documented material definition does not introduce a generic physical damping coefficient; hourglass suppression is not a substitute for a calibrated material damping law.

docs.title: Selecting the hourglass factor
docs.text:
Non-zero hgfactor suppresses zero-energy deformation modes but can increase effective structural stiffness. The documented setup guidance is to start at zero and increase it only if hourglass instabilities appear. A value of 0.1 is reported as useful in the source examples, not a universal optimum or an innocuous default.

The source cases intentionally differ: CSM3 uses 0, while the FSI2 and dam-break examples use 0.1. These values are retained below. Reducing a copied 0.1 to zero, or increasing a copied zero to 0.1, changes the numerical model even though the material density, modulus and Poisson's ratio remain the same. Review the deformation response when selecting the coefficient for a new configuration.

docs.title: Constitutive models and dimensional assumptions
docs.text:
constitmodel Available dimensionality Meaning 1 Two-dimensional Plane strain: zero out-of-plane strain 2 Two-dimensional Plane stress: zero out-of-plane stress 3 Three-dimensional Hyperelastic St. Venant–Kirchhoff model

The current reader rejects model 3 in a two-dimensional simulation and models 1/2 in a three-dimensional simulation. A small geometric thickness used to generate a two-dimensional particle section is not, by itself, a request for a three-dimensional structural calculation.

docs.title: Plane strain
docs.text:
Plane strain represents a body whose out-of-plane deformation is constrained. It is the documented approximation for problems that are very thick in that direction. Its defining assumption is

\[ \varepsilon_{\perp}=0. \]

The out-of-plane stress need not vanish. In the source two-dimensional x–z configurations, the out-of-plane direction is y. The CSM3 and dam-break examples select model 1.

Figure 2: A body extended in the out-of-plane direction and its plane-strain representation. The approximation suppresses out-of-plane strain.

docs.title: Plane stress
docs.text:
Plane stress represents a thin body with negligible out-of-plane stress:

\[ \sigma_{\perp}=0. \]

Its reduced stiffness differs from the plane-strain stiffness. Choosing model 2 therefore changes the structural response rather than simply changing an output label. The rolling-tank and flexible wave-loaded strip examples use this model.

Figure 3: A thin plate and its plane-stress representation. The out-of-plane stress is taken as zero while the in-plane structural response is retained.

docs.title: Three-dimensional St. Venant–Kirchhoff model
docs.text:
Model 3 is the documented three-dimensional option. It extends an elastic stress–strain relation to geometrically nonlinear deformation through the material strain and stress measures introduced above. It does not add plasticity, fracture or a general viscoelastic material law. The three-dimensional dam-break case retains the following structural properties and attachment markers:

XML excerpt — three-dimensional-material. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak3D_FSI_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="2" mkclamp="1">
        <density value="1161.54" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="8.75e5" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.49" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="3" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.1" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

The generic full reference at the end uses a different illustrative modulus, \(3.5\times10^6\) Pa. The case excerpt above uses its own \(8.75\times10^5\) Pa; the generic value must not replace the case value.

docs.title: Fluid loading, deformation and boundary treatment
docs.text:
In an FSI case, the fluid sees the deformable particles as a moving boundary through the selected DualSPHysics boundary treatment. Pressure and viscous interaction contribute to structural acceleration, while the evolving structural positions and velocities alter the boundary encountered by the fluid. This is a two-way interaction within the integrated SPH framework, rather than a prescribed deformation imposed independently of the fluid.

The structural internal forces use the reference-configuration neighbours, constitutive stresses, kernel correction and any selected hourglass term. Fluid boundary pressure is not the structural constitutive stress. In a structural-only case such as CSM3, the structural material and loading still determine deformation even without a surrounding fluid population; that example retains its source gravity of (0, 0, −2) m/s².

docs.title: Normals for mDBC
docs.text:
Initial surface normals are required when mDBC is selected, as for other fixed or moving boundaries. The deforming surface must have a suitable geometric description and initial normal assignment; a flexstrucs section does not generate that information by itself. See Modified Dynamic Boundary Conditions for normal generation and boundary-layer geometry.

The current structural implementation updates a non-zero initial boundary-normal vector using the inverse transpose of the deformation gradient and retains its original magnitude:

\[ \mathbf n=\lVert\mathbf n_0\rVert\, \frac{\mathbf F^{-\mathsf T}\mathbf n_0} {\lVert\mathbf F^{-\mathsf T}\mathbf n_0\rVert}. \]

Here the stored normal is the geometric boundary-normal vector; it is not an arbitrary unit vector supplied in place of the original surface geometry. Correct initial normals remain necessary even though the direction evolves during deformation.

The two-dimensional mDBC dam-break variant uses the generated actual-surface file in its existing geometry-normal workflow:

XML excerpt — dam-break-initial-normals. XML location: case/casedef. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<normals active="true">
    <norgeometry comment="Define initial configuration of normals before applying other configurations">
        <geometryfile file="[CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk" comment="File with boundary geometry (VTK format)" />
        <distanceh v="2" comment="Maximum orthogonal distance (H*value) to compute normals data (default=2)" />
        <maxsizeh v="0" comment="Maximum allowed normal size (H*value) (disabled=0, default=0)" />
        <svshapes v="true" comment="Saves VTK with geometry in triangles and quads with its normals for debug (default=false)" />
    </norgeometry>
</normals>

The source geometry creates [CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk; retain its GeometryForNormals list and generation commands when using this normal configuration. The normal block alone does not create the referenced surface file.

docs.title: Integration, slip and penetration controls
docs.text:
For flexible structures with mDBC, the documented and current-reader requirements are Symplectic integration and no-slip or free-slip. Use the named v6 values StepAlgorithm=SYM and SlipMode=NS or FS. Original mDBC (M22) and the zero-tangential-velocity option (V0) do not satisfy this flexible-structure check. The current reader also rejects mDBC with Verlet.

These requirements concern the mDBC combination; they are not a universal rejection of every DBC structural case using Verlet. The distributed three-dimensional dam-break and rolling-tank DBC examples retain their own VER choice.

For violent flows, fluid penetration through an mDBC boundary can disrupt the coupling. NoPenetration=Y selects the documented no-penetration treatment where required. This is a separate numerical choice and does not replace the normal definition, compatible slip mode or time integration. The current mDBC dam-break case uses the following values:

XML excerpt — dam-break-boundary-method. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<parameter key="Boundary" value="mDBC" comment="Boundary method: DBC, mDBC, MIX:MixBC (default=DBC)" />
XML excerpt — dam-break-slip-mode. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<parameter key="SlipMode" value="NS" comment="Slip mode for mDBC: NS:No-slip, FS:Free slip, V0:TanVel=0, M22:mDBC 2022 (default=NS)" />
XML excerpt — dam-break-integration. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<parameter key="StepAlgorithm" value="SYM" comment="Step Algorithm: SYM:Symplectic, VER:Verlet (default=SYM)" />
XML excerpt — dam-break-no-penetration. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<parameter key="NoPenetration" value="Y" comment="Activate No-Penetration option for mDBC: Y/N (default=N)" />

The older presentation expresses these choices using numeric values. The names above are the current v6 syntax. Do not transfer old numeric enumerations to new XML without checking the corresponding option. NoPenetration=Y is retained in this example; it is not asserted as a universal requirement for every flexible FSI case.

docs.title: Dam-break gate and flexible barrier
docs.text:
The dam-break setup separates the prescribed release-gate motion from the computed deformation of the downstream barrier. The source teaching diagram identifies the fluid, gate, flexible structure, base clamp and tank walls:

Figure 4: Dam-break teaching geometry: mkfluid 0 is the initial water column, mkbound 0 the release gate, mkbound 1 the base clamp, mkbound 2 the flexible barrier and mkbound 3 the lateral walls.

Marker numbers in this diagram describe that teaching geometry. The current package cases shown below use a revised grouping: mkbound=0 is the tank/base clamp, mkbound=1 the gate and mkbound=2 the flexible barrier. Preserve the current case's matching geometry, motion and mkclamp; do not copy the diagram's numbers into one section of that case.

The original teaching geometry uses the following box coordinates and sizes, in metres. These retain its original particle-generation dimensions and marker grouping, separately from the current case's variable-based geometry:

Teaching population Marker Initial point (x, y, z), m Box size (x, y, z), m Water column mkfluid 0 (0.0, −0.01, 0.0) (0.2, 0.02, 0.4) Release gate mkbound 0 (0.2, −0.01, 0.0) (0.008, 0.02, 0.5) Base clamp mkbound 1 (−0.008, −0.01, −0.016) (0.816, 0.02, 0.016) Flexible barrier mkbound 2 (0.596, −0.01, −0.008) (0.008, 0.02, 0.098) Left wall mkbound 3 (−0.008, −0.01, −0.016) (0.008, 0.02, 0.616) Right wall mkbound 3 (0.8, −0.01, −0.016) (0.008, 0.02, 0.616)

These literal boxes are not the same generation commands as the current package case. In particular, the current flexible-barrier x extent is 0.010 m and its gate thickness is expressed as 8*Dp; do not merge those definitions with the teaching boxes while assuming the discretisation is unchanged.

The current case defines its physical extents through these original variables. The water column is 0.2 m long and 0.4 m high; the tank is 0.8 m long and 0.6 m high. The flexible barrier occupies x=0.596–0.606 m up to z=0.09 m. Particle-generation offsets and the embedded lower part are specified in the complete geometry:

XML excerpt — dam-break-dimensions. XML location: case/casedef/geometry. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_DBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<predefinition>
    <newvarcte mdbc="false" />
    <newvarcte dom_padding="0.1" />
    <newvarcte tank_min_x="0.0" tank_max_x="0.8" tank_min_z="0.0" tank_max_z="0.6" />
    <newvarcte fluid_min_x="#tank_min_x" fluid_max_x="0.2" fluid_min_z="#tank_min_z" fluid_max_z="0.4" />
    <newvarcte gate_min_x="0.2" gate_min_z="#tank_min_z" gate_max_z="0.5" />
    <newvarcte struc_min_x="0.596" struc_max_x="0.606" struc_min_z="tank_min_z" struc_max_z="0.09" />
</predefinition>

The gate reads its vertical trajectory from DambreakGateTimeSeries.csv during the first 0.12 s. The flexible barrier instead uses mvnull. Both objects are moving populations, but their motion is supplied by different mechanisms:

XML excerpt — gate-and-barrier-motion. XML location: case/casedef. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_DBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<motion>
    <objreal ref="1">
        <begin mov="1" start="0.0" finish="0.12" />
        <mvfile id="1" duration="0.12">
            <file name="DambreakGateTimeSeries.csv" fields="2" fieldtime="0" fieldz="1" />
        </mvfile>
    </objreal>
    <objreal ref="2">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvnull id="1" />
    </objreal>
</motion>
XML excerpt — dam-break-structural-properties. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_DBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="2" mkclamp="0">
        <density value="1161.54" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="8.75e5" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.49" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="1" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.1" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

The current DBC and mDBC two-dimensional variants use the same structural density 1161.54 kg/m³, modulus \(8.75\times10^5\) Pa, Poisson's ratio 0.49, plane-strain model and hourglass factor 0.1. Their boundary-method selection remains a separate part of the numerical configuration. The structural properties and material density must not be replaced with CSM3 values when changing the boundary treatment.

docs.title: Turek–Hron FSI2
docs.text:
FSI2 is a fluid-loaded flexible member with its own density and marker assignments. The mDBC case uses flexible marker 2, clamp marker 1, density 10000 kg/m³, modulus \(1.4\times10^6\) Pa, Poisson's ratio 0.4, plane strain and hourglass factor 0.1:

XML excerpt — fsi2-material. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronFSI2_mDBC_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="2" mkclamp="1">
        <density value="10000.0" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="1.4e6" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.4" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="1" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.1" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

Its moving classification selects marker 2. The complete case also contains the inlet/outlet and fluid-initialisation configuration; retain those inputs when reviewing the FSI problem. See the Inlet/Outlet guide for that separate open-boundary functionality. CSM3 and FSI2 are different load cases; the density change from 1000 to 10000 kg/m³ and the hourglass change from 0 to 0.1 must not be hidden by treating the examples as identical.

docs.title: Prescribed moving clamp in a rolling tank
docs.text:
The hanging-strip case uses a rotating tank/support marker 0 and a flexible marker 1. Its support follows the original rotation file and axis, while the flexible marker uses mvnull:

XML excerpt — rolling-support-motion. XML location: case/casedef. Source: examples/flexstruc/03_RollingTank/CaseRollingTankHanging_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<motion>
    <objreal ref="0">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvrotfile id="1" duration="100" anglesunits="degrees">
            <file name="RollingTankHangingTimeSeries.csv" />
            <axisp1 x="0.3045" y="-0.01" z="0" />
            <axisp2 x="0.3045" y="0.02" z="0" />
        </mvrotfile>
    </objreal>
    <objreal ref="1">
        <begin mov="1" start="0" />
        <mvnull id="1" />
    </objreal>
</motion>
XML excerpt — rolling-strip-material. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/03_RollingTank/CaseRollingTankHanging_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="1" mkclamp="0">
        <density value="1900.0" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="4.0e6" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.49" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="2" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0.0" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

The source material is plane stress, with density 1900 kg/m³, modulus \(4.0\times10^6\) Pa, Poisson's ratio 0.49 and zero hourglass correction. The deep-strip variant instead uses density 1100 kg/m³ and modulus \(6.0\times10^6\) Pa. Do not interchange these material settings or the two rotation time-series files. A prescribed moving clamp is not a free rotational joint computed from a hinge model.

docs.title: Flexible strip under waves
docs.text:
The flexible wave-loaded strip case retains its original material and attachment definition:

XML excerpt — wave-loaded-strip-material. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/flexstruc/04_FloatingStructure/CaseFlexFloating_Def.xml. This is a selection from that case, not a complete executable configuration. Retain its surrounding geometry, variables and inputs.

<flexstrucs>
    <flexstrucbody mkbound="2" mkclamp="3">
        <density value="412" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
        <youngmod value="5.65e5" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
        <poissratio value="0.49" comment="Poisson ratio" />
        <constitmodel value="2" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
        <hgfactor value="0" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
        <dtstaggered value="0" comment="Enable staggered dt FSI: 0=No, 1=Yes (default=0)" />
    </flexstrucbody>
</flexstrucs>

The case name contains “Floating”, but the XML here is still a flexstrucbody with marker 2 and clamp marker 3. It does not declare a free six-degree-of-freedom rigid body by replacing the structural material with floatings. Its wave paddle, attachment geometry and moving classification belong to the complete case. This distinction prevents the physical appearance or filename of a buoyant strip from being mistaken for another solver interface.

docs.title: Additional current controls and limits
docs.text:
The current structural reader recognises two options beyond the older dedicated format illustration:

Element under flexstrucbody Current reader meaning Source default and use here dtstaggered value Enable staggered fluid/structural timesteps False; the wave-loaded strip explicitly retains 0 rsterm value Enable a Riemann stabilisation term for the structure False; no tuning recommendation is inferred from the older presentation

The staggered path computes structural substeps within the fluid timestep. Its availability depends on compilation; a GPU build with that path disabled rejects its activation. Merely seeing the element in a reader does not establish availability in every binary. Neither option changes the material law into a viscous damping model. The examples above preserve their original choice and do not activate an undocumented combination.

The current implementation rejects simulation restart from a saved PART when flexible structures are active, and rejects their combination with periodic conditions. The build must include Flexible Structures support. These are current configuration checks; they are separate from a particular historical test result. No general claim is made here about all multibody collisions, floating-body combinations, mixed-boundary configurations, alternative kernels or multi-GPU execution.

For mDBC, review the structure's initial surface geometry, normals, NS/FS slip choice, Symplectic integration and any penetration control together. For the solid, review attachment geometry, particle spacing, dimensional model, density, modulus, Poisson's ratio and hourglass choice. Stiff elastic properties also affect the structural timestep estimate; copying a fluid timestep without reviewing the structural response is not a substitute for the complete case's time-integration settings.

docs.title: Representative public cases
docs.text:
Public package path Configuration examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronCSM3_Def.xml Structural-only plane-strain strip; fixed clamp, hgfactor 0 examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronFSI2_DBC_Def.xml Fluid-loaded plane-strain member with DBC examples/flexstruc/02_TurekHron/CaseTurekHronFSI2_mDBC_Def.xml Corresponding mDBC configuration and initial normals examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_DBC_Def.xml Gate release and plane-strain barrier with DBC examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak2D_FSI_mDBC_Def.xml Gate release and mDBC barrier, including no-penetration choice examples/flexstruc/01_DamBreak/CaseDambreak3D_FSI_Def.xml Three-dimensional St. Venant–Kirchhoff material examples/flexstruc/03_RollingTank/CaseRollingTankDeep_Def.xml Plane-stress strip in a prescribed rolling tank examples/flexstruc/03_RollingTank/CaseRollingTankHanging_Def.xml Hanging plane-stress strip and moving support examples/flexstruc/04_FloatingStructure/CaseFlexFloating_Def.xml Wave-loaded flexible strip with an attachment marker

These paths identify complete source configurations. The excerpts explain their syntax and numerical choices; they do not establish physical validation, convergence or equivalence between DBC/mDBC, constitutive models or stabilisation settings. Assess particle motion, clamp attachment, deformation and boundary interaction using the complete selected case and its available output tools. This guide does not define a new structural-output XML API or imply that every internal stress measure is automatically exported.

docs.title: Full Flexible Structures XML format reference
docs.text:
Source: doc/xml_format/_FmtXML__FlexibleStructure.xml. The complete supplied format below retains its original 12 March 2024 header, comments, values, order and indentation. It illustrates the structural body declaration; it is not a complete executable simulation. Its ... denotes additional definitions, while the decorative separators are part of the original reference collection.

The example modulus and constitutive model are reference values, not defaults for every material. The current-reader additions dtstaggered and rsterm described above are absent from this older file; the verbatim reference is not rewritten to insert them.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<!-- *** DualSPHysics (12-03-2024) *** -->
<!-- *** class: JSphFlexibleStructure (JSphFlexibleStructure)  *** -->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Example of available execution parameters. *** -->
<!-- An option can be overridden by commenting on the XML line, using          --> 
<!-- <_parameter... or changing the key value.                                 --> 
<execution>
    <special>
        <flexstrucs>
            <flexstrucbody mkbound="1" mkclamp="0">
                <density value="1161.54" comment="Mass density" units_comment="kg/m^3" />
                <youngmod value="3.5e6" comment="Young Modulus" units_comment="Pa" />
                <poissratio value="0.49" comment="Poisson ratio" />
                <constitmodel value="3" comment="Constitutive model 1:Plane Strain (2D), 2:Plane Stress (2D), 3:St. Venant Kirchhoff (3D)" />
                <hgfactor value="0.1" comment="Hourglass correction factor: keep as low as possible (default=0)" />
            </flexstrucbody>
            ...
        </flexstrucs>
    </special>
</execution>

docs.title: Main Configuration
docs.text:
Under review by José Domínguez and Alex Crespo

Case definition, particle generation, numerical parameters and simulation output in DualSPHysics v6.

docs.title: From a case definition to a simulation
docs.text:
An XML file records the geometry, material identifiers, initial conditions and numerical configuration of a case in an editable text format. GenCase uses the case definition to create the initial particles and their associated metadata. DualSPHysics then loads that particle data together with the execution configuration. Keeping the XML and its referenced geometry and data files together makes a configuration reproducible; the XML alone does not contain external CAD surfaces, motion histories or binary initialisation fields.

This guide brings together the general XML configuration topics. Code blocks are fragments, with their required parent explained nearby; they are not complete runnable cases unless explicitly stated. Numerical values in examples illustrate the named configuration and must not be treated as universal defaults. The format references distributed with the software define the available elements and attributes. Module-specific guides provide additional prerequisites and compatibility limits.

For executable selection and the preparation, solver and post-processing sequence, see The DualSPHysics Workflow and CPU, GPU and Multi-GPU Execution. Selecting an execution backend does not establish support for every XML feature.

Figure 1: GenCase converts the editable case definition and external geometry into particle data and execution XML. The solver writes PART data and diagnostics for the post-processing tools.

docs.title: Input and output files
docs.text:
File or family Role Case_Def.xml Editable input to GenCase: case definition and user execution settings. Case.xml Execution XML written by GenCase, including generated particle information and calculated constants. Case.bi4 Initial particle data. Geometry .vtk, .stl, .ply External geometric inputs when referenced by drawing commands. Motion data and acceleration CSV files Time histories explicitly referenced by the configuration. Case_All.vtk, Case_Bound.vtk, Case_Fluid.vtk Particle geometry for visual inspection after generation. Case__Actual.vtk, Case__Dp.vtk and named shape files Geometric representations produced by the selected shape-output settings. Check the actual generated filenames. Part_Head.ibi4 Basic particle-output information used by post-processing tools. Part_XXXX.bi4 Particle state at saved times. PartOut.obi4 Particles excluded during the simulation. PartFloat.fbi4 Floating-body information. Run.out Text execution log. Post-processing VTK and measurement files Visualisation and extracted results, including particle, surface, slice, velocity, height and pressure data.

XML is organised by element names and attributes and can be edited with a text editor. Binary particle files reduce storage and input/output overhead compared with textual particle arrays; their size advantage depends on the data and representation. The presentation quotes a sixfold reduction as its comparison, rather than a guaranteed ratio for every dataset. The binary format supports double-precision positions and additional arrays; software must use the corresponding binary reader, such as the distributed JPartDataBi4 implementation. These files are not editable XML.

VTK is used for geometric inspection and result visualisation in applications such as ParaView. The source workflow uses legacy binary POLYDATA output. The current geometry template also provides explicit VTP, VTU and STL shape-output alternatives; select formats supported by the intended tool.

Case.xml is normally produced by GenCase from Case_Def.xml. The source workflow also allows an execution XML to be prepared by the user; its generated constants, particle counts, marker ranges and binary particle data must remain mutually consistent. Editing the execution XML does not regenerate its particle data.

The workflow separates PARTVTK particle conversion, BOUNDARYVTK boundary geometry, ISOSURFACE surface reconstruction and MEASURETOOL sampled measurements. Measurement points may be supplied through PointsPos.csv or Points.txt. The illustrated outputs include Particles_XXXX.vtk, Surface_XXXX.vtk, Slices_XXXX.vtk, Velocity_XXXX.vtk and Height_XXXX.vtk; their content depends on the selected post-processing operation and saved particle fields.

docs.title: XML hierarchy and editing conventions
docs.text:
The root element is case. Its casedef section supplies the information required by GenCase; execution supplies solver settings and receives generated metadata. GenCase reads and augments the execution configuration rather than treating every child as user-generated data.

Parent Principal children and purpose case/casedef constantsdef, mkconfig, geometry, initials, floatings, properties, motion and, where needed, normals. casedef/geometry Optional predefinition, particle-generation definition, and commands. geometry/commands Named auxiliary list elements and the executed mainlist. case/execution User special and parameters settings; generated particles, constants, variable exports and geometry-output information where applicable. execution/special Independent feature configurations, for example waves, damping, gauges and imposed accelerations. execution/parameters Main solver parameters and simulationdomain.

XML names are case-sensitive. A value attribute is not interchangeable with an element name: parameter uses key and value, while other features use attributes such as v, x, time or distpt. Follow the reference for the particular element. comment and units_comment describe a setting; they do not replace its numerical value or convert units. XML comments use <!-- ... -->; literal comparison characters inside attributes must be XML-escaped where required.

An underscore-prefixed element, such as _hdp, denotes a disabled alternative in the format examples. Many special features additionally support active="true" or active="false"; this is feature-specific. Do not assume that adding active to an arbitrary element implements a general switch. In older parameter lists a # at the beginning of the key disables that legacy parameter. It is distinct from # at the beginning of a value, which requests expression evaluation.

docs.title: Constants, resolution and physical scales
docs.text:
<constantsdef>
  <lattice bound="2" fluid="1" comment="Type of lattice to create the initial particles (default=1)"/>
  <gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2"/>
  <rhop0 value="1000" comment="Reference density of the fluid" units_comment="kg/m^3"/>
  <rhopgradient value="2" comment="Initial density gradient 1:Rhop0, 2:Water column, 3:Max. water height (default=2)"/>
  <hswl value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum height of still water to calculate speedofsound using coefsound" units_comment="metres (m)"/>
  <gamma value="7" comment="Polytropic constant for water used in the state equation"/>
  <speedsystem value="0" auto="true" comment="Maximum system speed (by default the dam-break propagation is used)"/>
  <coefsound value="20" comment="Coefficient to multiply speedsystem"/>
  <speedsound value="0" auto="true" comment="Speed of sound to use in the simulation (by default speedofsound=coefsound*speedsystem)"/>
  <coefh value="0.866025" comment="Coefficient to calculate the smoothing length (h=coefh*sqrt(3*dp^2) in 3D)"/>
  <_hdp value="2" comment="Alternative option to calculate the smoothing length (h=hdp*dp)"/>
  <cflnumber value="0.2" comment="Coefficient to multiply dt"/>
  <h value="0" auto="true" units_comment="metres (m)"/>
  <b value="0" auto="true" units_comment="Pascal (Pa)"/>
  <massbound value="0" auto="true" units_comment="kg"/>
  <massfluid value="0" auto="true" units_comment="kg"/>
</constantsdef>

This fragment belongs to case/casedef. The current template's example uses reference density 1000 kg/m³, gravity (0, 0, −9.81) m/s², polytropic exponent 7, coefsound=20, coefh=0.866025 and cflnumber=0.2. They illustrate a water configuration; they are not a complete specification of an arbitrary fluid. A value accompanied by auto="true" requests the associated automatic calculation. A displayed zero in such an entry does not mean that the final physical quantity is zero.

Element Meaning and interaction lattice Particle-generation setting for boundary and fluid populations; retain the configuration required by the case. gravity Gravitational acceleration vector. rhop0 Fluid reference density. rhopgradient Initial density arrangement: 1 reference density, 2 water column, 3 maximum water height. hswl Maximum still-water height used when estimating the speed of sound. speedsystem Characteristic maximum system speed; the automatic estimate uses dam-break propagation. coefsound Factor applied to the characteristic system speed. speedsound Numerical speed of sound, automatic or explicitly specified. gamma Exponent in the equation of state. coefh or hdp Alternative definitions of smoothing length. Enable the intended definition, rather than both alternatives indiscriminately. cflnumber Multiplier used in the adaptive time-step criterion. h, b, massbound, massfluid Calculated quantities, with explicit alternatives available in the template. Their values and units must remain consistent with the configuration.

docs.title: Equation of state and speed of sound
docs.text:
\[ P=B\left[\left(\frac{\rho}{\rho_0}\right)^\gamma-1\right],\qquad B=\frac{c_s^2\rho_0}{\gamma} \]

The source estimates the characteristic system speed from the still-water height when that automatic option is used. With the magnitude of gravity denoted by g:

\[ u_{\mathrm{system}}=\sqrt{g h_{\mathrm{swl}}},\qquad c_s=\mathrm{coefsound}\,u_{\mathrm{system}} \] \[ B=\frac{\mathrm{coefsound}^{2}\,g h_{\mathrm{swl}}\rho_0}{\gamma} \]

Do not apply the dam-break estimate as an identity for a case with an explicitly different characteristic speed. The numerical speed of sound affects compressibility and the time step; changing it is a numerical choice.

docs.title: Smoothing length and particle mass
docs.text:
\[ h=\mathrm{coefh}\sqrt{d_x^2+d_y^2+d_z^2}=\mathrm{coefh}\sqrt{3}\,dp\quad\text{(uniform 3D spacing)},\qquad h=\mathrm{hdp}\,dp \]

The presentation lists coefh=1 as typical and 1.2 or 1.5 as wave-propagation examples. These are choices to assess for the intended method, rather than replacement defaults. Its alternative hdp=1.5 directly specifies h/dp. Increasing h changes neighbour support and computational work as well as the numerical approximation.

\[ m=\rho_0 dp^3\quad\text{(3D)},\qquad m=\rho_0 dp^2\quad\text{(2D representation)} \]

docs.title: Markers and particle ordering
docs.text:
mkfluid and mkbound identify fluid and boundary populations. They associate geometry with initialisation, motion, floating-body definitions and other features. They are not particle IDs. mkorientfluid and mkorientbound set the ordering of particles created for a population, which can be inspected with the particle idp field.

The current template below reserves 241 boundary and 9 fluid labels; the presentation's earlier illustration uses 240 and 10. Keep the counts appropriate to the case. The source describes a standard 250-label configuration, a 65,530-label GenCase_MkWord configuration and a separate solver-compilation limit above 2,048 distinct markers. These are build-dependent capabilities; the larger generator capacity does not establish that every solver binary accepts the same number of markers.

<mkconfig boundcount="241" fluidcount="9">
  <mkorientbound mk="0" orient="YxZ"/>
  <mkorientfluid mk="0" orient="Xyz"/>
  <mkorientfluid mk="1" orient="zyx"/>
</mkconfig>
Figure 2: Changing the coordinate ordering for a marker changes particle ordering within the generated objects; it does not change the physical marker assignment.

docs.title: Geometry generation and computational bounds
docs.text:
geometry/definition establishes the lattice spacing dp and the region in which GenCase may create particles. Reducing dp increases particle count. Equal minimum and maximum Y coordinates define the two-dimensional X–Z configuration illustrated in the source; equality applies to the Y coordinates, not to all components of the two points.

After particle generation, the solver's default simulation bounds are calculated from the generated particle positions. They may be adjusted independently with execution/parameters/simulationdomain. A drawing region and a solver simulation domain are therefore different settings.

<definition dp="0.05" comment="Initial inter-particle distance" units_comment="metres (m)">
  <pointref x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <pointmin x="-0.25" y="-0.05" z="-0.05"/>
  <pointmax x="2" y="1" z="1"/>
</definition>

Particles are created only inside the generation domain. Afterwards the simulation domain is recalculated from the minimum and maximum positions of the generated particles; it can also be configured in parameters.

Figure 3: The pointmin and pointmax limits bound particle generation. The solver subsequently derives its domain from the actual particles unless simulationdomain specifies another extent.

docs.title: Command lists and drawing state
docs.text:
GenCase executes drawing commands in mainlist. Reusable lists are declared as list name="..." and called with runlist name="..."; times repeats a call. The source combines BoxList and CylinderList inside StructureList, then calls the assembled structure at different translations. List order matters because commands change the current marker, transformation and drawing state.

Command or setting Effect resetdraw Restore drawing defaults and delete previously drawn points. setdrawmode mode="wire" Draw edges. setdrawmode mode="face" Draw faces. setdrawmode mode="solid" Draw interiors. setdrawmode mode="full" Combine faces and interior. setactive drawpoints="false" Generate shapes without drawing particle points. setactive drawshapes="false" Disable shape generation; equivalent in purpose to setshapemode set to null. setactive vtkout="false" Do not register generated shape-output files in the XML output list. setshapemode Select actual coordinates or dp-aligned geometry and the population types represented in shape output. shapeout file="..." Write the accumulated geometric shapes. reset="true" starts a separate accumulation for subsequent shapes.

setshapemode contains text options separated by |, for example dp | bound; its options are not a numerical parameter enumeration. Shape output helps inspect a geometry, but does not prove that a closed volume was filled correctly with particles.

<setactive drawpoints="true" drawshapes="true" vtkout="true"/>
<setdrawmode mode="wire"/>
<setdrawmode mode="face"/>
<setdrawmode mode="solid"/>
<setdrawmode mode="full"/>
<setshapemode>bound</setshapemode>
Figure 4: Wire, face, solid and full drawing modes produce different point arrangements on the same box.

In the source tank example, fluid marker 0 is drawn with boxfill set to solid, while boundary marker 0 uses bottom | left | right | front | back, leaving the top open. The illustrated fluid box has size (0.4, 0.67, 0.3) m and the tank (1.6, 0.67, 0.4) m. The current distributed dam-break example retains these geometry values; they are case dimensions, not defaults.

setshapemode accepts coordinate choices actual and dp, and population choices fluid, bound and void; null disables shape generation. setactive enables drawpoints, drawshapes and vtkout by default in the source reference. A shape-only pass can therefore produce inspection geometry without creating SPH particles. Named outputs such as Case_Box_Dp.vtk and Case_Building_Dp.vtk distinguish selected objects; combined shape outputs such as Case__Actual.vtk and Case__Dp.vtk collect the enabled objects. The exact file prefix is supplied by the case.

The source's runlist name="StructureList" times="5" repeats a reusable structure five times. Each call executes in the current drawing state. Save and restore the transformation matrix inside a reusable list when subsequent calls should not inherit its local transformations. The following current-reference list fragments show the declaration and call syntax; their Hola names are independent of the source's named BoxList/CylinderList illustration. 

<list name="Hola">
  <debugout/>
</list>

<runlist name="Hola"/>

docs.title: Selecting populations and transforming geometry
docs.text:
setmkvoid selects empty points; setmkfluid and setmkbound select fluid or boundary points with the given local marker. setmknextfluid and setmknextbound increment or decrement the current marker according to next; setmknextauto controls automatic increments after drawing commands. A void drawing operation can remove a previously filled region before another population is drawn there.

For setmknextfluid and setmknextbound, next="true" increments the marker and next="false" decrements it. Automatic increments after each drawing command are enabled with setmknextauto auto="true" and disabled with auto="false". These commands belong in the geometry drawing list.

Transformations apply through the current drawing matrix: move translates, scale scales, rotate rotates about a direction, and rotateline defines the axis with two points. matrixsave pushes a matrix onto the stack and matrixload restores the saved matrix. matrixreset returns to the identity. Transformation order changes the result.

<move x="1" y="2" z="3"/>
<scale x="0.1" y="0.2" z="0.3"/>
<rotate ang="35" x="1.1" y="1.2" z="1.3"/>
<rotateline ang="45">
  <point x="1.11" y="1.21" z="1.31"/>
  <point x="1.12" y="1.22" z="1.32"/>
</rotateline>

The four panels show, in reading order, the original box, translation by (0.5, 0, 0), scaling by (2, 1.5, 0.5), and rotation by 45 degrees about (0, 0, 1). Each operation precedes the box drawing in its illustrated configuration. The source writes the illustrative command rows as move x="0.5" y="0" z="0", scale x="2" y="1.5" z="0.5" and rotate x="0" y="0" z="1" ang="45"; the drawing command is abbreviated there as drawbox …, rather than a complete XML fragment.

Figure 5: The source compares the original box with translation by 0.5 in X, scaling by (2, 1.5, 0.5), and a 45-degree rotation about Z.

docs.title: Geometric primitives
docs.text:
The following commands belong to a geometry command list. Drawing mode and current marker apply to them. Counterclockwise point order is required by the triangle illustration. Surface orientation also matters when assembling closed external geometry.

Family Commands and defining data Points and lines drawpoint, drawpoints, setlinebegin with drawlineto, two-point drawline, and multi-point drawlines. Triangles and quadrilaterals drawtriangle uses three points; drawquadri uses four and the source allows non-coplanar points. Connected triangles drawtrianglesstrip builds a strip; drawtrianglesfan builds triangles around the common first point. Indexed triangles drawtriangles separates a point list from triangles expressed as point indices. Box drawbox uses a corner and size or endpoint; boxfill selects interior or named faces. Pyramid drawpyramid starts with the top point followed by at least three base points. Prism drawprism requires an even number of at least six points; the first half describes the base and the second half the top. Beach profile drawbeach uses the lateral profile points. Extrusion drawextrude extrudes a point-defined line using an extrude vector; closed controls closure. Solid defined by triangles drawfigure fills the interior defined by its points and triangular planes; face-only output instead illustrates the surface. Sphere drawsphere uses centre point and radius. Ellipsoid drawellipsoid uses the two source-defined centre points and radius. Cylinder drawcylinder uses two axis points, radius and an optional face mask. 
<drawline>
  <point x="1" y="2" z="3"/>
  <point x="11" y="21" z="31"/>
</drawline>
<drawtriangle>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="3"/>
  <point x="0" y="3" z="0"/>
  <point x="3" y="0" z="0"/>
</drawtriangle>
<drawbox>
  <boxfill>bottom | left | right | front | back</boxfill>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <size x="1" y="2" z="3"/>
</drawbox>
Figure 6: Triangle-strip construction and point ordering in the source example. Figure 7: Indexed triangles connect the numbered vertices. Point indices and triangle orientation are part of the geometry definition.

In the two lower panels, all ^ top means all faces excluding the top; bottom | left | right means only the bottom, left and right faces.

Figure 8: Box interior and face selections, including all faces except top and a selection of bottom, left and right faces.

docs.title: Connected lines and quadrilaterals
docs.text:
setlinebegin establishes the current point and drawlineto joins it to a new point. drawlines joins successive points; drawquadri uses four vertices, including the non-coplanar arrangement allowed by the source. The following are current-reference command fragments, inserted in a drawing list after selecting the marker and drawing mode.

<setlinebegin x="0" y="1" z="0.5"/>
<drawlineto x="10" y="11" z="10.5"/>
<drawlines>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="1"/>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="2"/>
  <point x="0" y="2" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="0" z="0"/>
</drawlines>
<drawquadri>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="4"/>
  <point x="0" y="4" z="0"/>
  <point x="4" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="4" y="4" z="4"/>
</drawquadri>

docs.title: Triangle strips, fans and indexed faces
docs.text:
A strip reuses the last edge as each further point adds a triangle. A fan keeps the first point as its common vertex; repeating the closing outer point closes the source's circular example. Indexed faces instead refer to a shared points list. Their triangle attributes x, y and z are vertex indices, not Cartesian coordinates. Preserve ordering consistently with the intended face orientation. These current-reference fragments illustrate all three forms.

<drawtrianglesstrip>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="3" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="3" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="4" y="1" z="0"/>
</drawtrianglesstrip>
<drawtrianglesfan>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.9" y="0.5" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.5" y="0.9" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="-0.5" y="0.9" z="0"/>
</drawtrianglesfan>
<drawtriangles>
  <points>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
    <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
    <point x="1" y="1" z="0"/>
    <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="1" y="0" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="1" y="1" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="0" y="1" z="0.8"/>
  </points>
  <triangles>
    <triangle x="0" y="1" z="5"/>
    <triangle x="1" y="2" z="6"/>
    <triangle x="2" y="3" z="7"/>
    <triangle x="3" y="0" z="4"/>
    <triangle x="0" y="2" z="1"/>
    <triangle x="4" y="5" z="6"/>
  </triangles>
</drawtriangles>

The open fan uses the six-point drawtrianglesfan example above and is saved as TrianglesFan with reset="true". The closed source fan uses the following ordered points; the last repeats the first outer point, labelled 1/10 in the figure. Both source fans select boundary marker 0 and shape mode dp | bound. 

<setmkbound mk="0"/>
<drawtrianglesfan>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="1"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.8" y="0.6" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.2" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="-0.5" y="0.9" z="0"/>
  <point x="-0.9" y="0.3" z="0"/>
  <point x="-0.9" y="-0.3" z="0"/>
  <point x="-0.5" y="-0.9" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.2" y="-1" z="0"/>
  <point x="0.8" y="-0.6" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
</drawtrianglesfan>
<shapeout file="TrianglesFan2" reset="true"/>

Figure 9: Open and closed triangle fans retain the common vertex, outer-vertex order and closing-point labels.

docs.title: Polyhedra, extrusion and filled figures
docs.text:
For drawpyramid, the first point is the apex and the remaining points define the base. drawprism pairs the first half of its points with the second half: the source includes non-rectangular star profiles and a twisted prism, so this is not restricted to a rectangular box. Face masks follow that point order. A beach is described by lateral-profile points; an extrusion adds its displacement vector to each profile vertex. In the source drawfigure example, indexed point triples specify planes whose interior sides define the solid; they do not form a closed mesh of finite triangular faces. drawtriangles or face drawing represents the surface. The pyramid fragment retains the source's unmasked example (mask=0) and matching vertex coordinates; the other fragments use the current reference's own illustrative inputs. A different mask is a different face selection, not a syntax-only replacement for source masks 2 or 128.

<drawfigure>
  <points>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
    <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
    <point x="1" y="1" z="0"/>
    <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="1" y="0" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="1" y="1" z="0.8"/>
    <point x="0" y="1" z="0.8"/>
  </points>
  <triangles>
    <triangle x="0" y="1" z="5"/>
    <triangle x="1" y="2" z="6"/>
    <triangle x="2" y="3" z="7"/>
  </triangles>
</drawfigure>
<drawpyramid mask="0">
  <point x="0.25" y="0.25" z="0.7"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
</drawpyramid>
<drawprism>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="0" y="1" z="0.5"/>
</drawprism>
<drawbeach mask="1">
  <point x="0" y="3" z="1.2"/>
  <point x="0" y="3" z="0"/>
  <point x="1.7" y="3" z="0"/>
  <point x="3.5" y="3" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="5.5" y="3" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="5.5" y="3" z="1.2"/>
</drawbeach>

The twisted prism pairs the first four base points with the following four top points. The source selects boundary marker 0, mask="0", shape mode dp | bound, and output Prism4 with reset enabled. Its surrounding setdrawmode row says mode="fill"; the current template lists full, not fill. That source spelling is recorded here without silently translating its execution meaning. 

<drawprism mask="0">
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="4" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="4" y="4" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="4" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="1" z="5"/>
  <point x="3" y="2" z="5"/>
  <point x="2" y="3" z="5"/>
  <point x="1" y="2" z="5"/>
</drawprism>
<shapeout file="Prism4" reset="true"/>

Figure 10: Three views of the twisted prism defined by the paired base and top points in the editable source example.

The left panel is the source solid drawfigure; the right is its face representation (drawtriangles or face-mode drawfigure). The source uses the complete eight-point and six-triangle lists already given in the drawtriangles block above: (0,1,5), (1,2,6), (2,3,7), (3,0,4), (0,2,1) and (4,5,6). Its wrapper selects boundary marker 0 and shape mode dp | bound. The separate current-reference drawfigure fragment above contains three planes; it is a different illustrative input, whose equivalence to the source volume has not been established.

Figure 11: Solid and face views of the source triangulated polyhedron; the point and triangle definitions are documented in editable text.

A prism needs at least six points and an even point count. Its first half defines the base and its second half the corresponding top. In the star-profile illustration, both halves have the same X/Y coordinates at Z=0 and Z=6. The source selects boundary marker 0, shape mode dp | bound, and saves Prism3 with reset enabled. As in the twisted-prism source, its wrapper says setdrawmode mode="fill"; this historical spelling is not silently changed to the current template’s full. 

<drawprism mask="0">
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="-3" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="5" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="2" y="2" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="5" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="2" z="0"/>
  <point x="-3" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="6"/>
  <point x="1" y="-3" z="6"/>
  <point x="2" y="0" z="6"/>
  <point x="5" y="1" z="6"/>
  <point x="2" y="2" z="6"/>
  <point x="1" y="5" z="6"/>
  <point x="0" y="2" z="6"/>
  <point x="-3" y="1" z="6"/>
</drawprism>
<shapeout file="Prism3" reset="true"/>

Figure 12: The source demonstrates a non-rectangular prism using paired base and top points.

The labelled extrusion uses profile points P0–P5 in order and displacement (0, 3, 0). This is the source profile; the separate layered current-reference example below uses different Y coordinates and adds layers. 

<mainlist>
  <setmkbound mk="0"/>
  <drawextrude closed="false">
  <point x="0" y="0" z="1.2"/>
  <point x="0" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1.7" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="3.5" y="0" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="5.5" y="0" z="0.5"/>
  <point x="5.5" y="0" z="1.2"/>
    <extrude x="0" y="3" z="0"/>
  </drawextrude>
</mainlist>

Figure 13: Extrusion maps each profile point to its translated counterpart; source point labels and displacement arrows are retained.

docs.title: Rounded primitives and surface-width settings
docs.text:
A sphere uses a centre and radius, an ellipsoid uses the two centre points and radius specified by the command, and a cylinder uses two axial points and radius. In face drawing, ctesphere, cteellipsoid, ctecylindertube and ctecylindercover control the corresponding drawn widths. The source illustrates 0.4, 0.5, 0.6 and 0.7 respectively, whereas the current reference provides different illustrative values. These are geometry-dependent choices. ctespherenumsides and ctecylindernumsides affect the polygonal shape representation, not the particle spacing dp. The current-reference examples below preserve their values.

<setdpctes cteline="1.5" ctetriangleweight="1.5" ctetrianglelimits="1.5" ctesphere="1.5" ctespherenumsides="24" cteellipsoid="1.5" ctecylindertube="1.5" ctecylindercover="1.5" ctecylindernumsides="24" cterevolutionnumsides="24"/>
<drawellipsoid radius="1.5">
  <point x="1" y="0" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="1" z="1"/>
</drawellipsoid>
<drawcylinder radius="0.85" mask="1">
  <point x="1" y="1" z="0"/>
  <point x="1" y="1" z="1"/>
</drawcylinder>

The left cylinder is solid and the right cylinder uses face drawing. Their original input coordinates and face-width settings are reproduced here. The source’s explanatory last line names ctespherenumsides while its cylinder code uses ctecylindernumsides; that mismatch is retained as a source-text discrepancy rather than changing either setting. 

<mainlist>
  <setmkbound mk="0"/>
  <setdrawmode mode="solid"/>
  <drawcylinder radius="1" mask="0">
    <point x="1.5" y="1.5" z="0.5"/>
