</special>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Velocity definitions *** -->
<!-- Fixed Uniform velocity -->
    <imposevelocity mode="0" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocity v="2" comment="Uniform velocity" units_comment="m/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Fixed Linear velocity -->
    <imposevelocity mode="0" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocity2 v="1" v2="3" z="2" z2="3" comment="Linear inlet velocity" units_comment="m/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Fixed Parabolic velocity -->
    <imposevelocity mode="0" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocity3 v="0" v2="0.608" v3="3" z="4" z2="4.5" z3="5" comment="Parabolic inlet velocity" units_comment="m/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Fixed velocity for jet circle (only for <zone3d><circle>) -->
    <imposevelocity mode="0" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <jetcircle v="2" distance="0.010" radius="0.02" comment="Velocity for circular jet (velocity, distance and opening radius)" units_comment="m/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Uniform velocity using values in XML file-->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocitytimes comment="Uniform inlet velocity in time">
            <timevalue time="0.0" v="2" />
            <timevalue time="2.0" v="0" />
            <timevalue time="2.5" v="0" />
            <timevalue time="4.5" v="2" />
        </velocitytimes>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Linear velocity using values in XML file -->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocitytimes2 comment="Linear inlet velocity in time">
            <timevalue time="0.0" v="1" v2="3" z="2" z2="3" />
            <timevalue time="2.0" v="0" v2="0" z="2" z2="3" />
            <timevalue time="2.5" v="0" v2="0" z="2" z2="3" />
            <timevalue time="4.5" v="1" v2="3" z="2" z2="3" />
        </velocitytimes2>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Parabolic velocity using values in XML file -->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocitytimes3 comment="Parabolic inlet velocity in time">
            <timevalue time="0.0" v="0" v2="0.608" v3="3" z="4" z2="4.5" z3="5" />
            <timevalue time="2.0" v="0" v2="0" v3="0" z="4" z2="4.5" z3="5" />
            <timevalue time="2.5" v="0" v2="0" v3="0" z="4" z2="4.5" z3="5" />
            <timevalue time="4.5" v="0" v2="0.608" v3="3" z="4" z2="4.5" z3="5" />
        </velocitytimes3>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Uniform velocity using values in a external file-->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocityfile file="WavesREG_InOut_vx.csv" comment="Uniform inlet velocity data (time;v)"/>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Linear velocity using values in a external file -->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocityfile2 file="WavesREG_InOut_vx2.csv" comment="Linear inlet velocity data (time;v;v2;z;z2)"/>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Variable Parabolic velocity using values in a external file -->
    <imposevelocity mode="1" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <velocityfile3 file="WavesREG_InOut_vx3.csv" comment="Parabolic inlet velocity data (time;v;v2;v3;z;z2;z3)"/>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Extrapolated velocity -->
    <imposevelocity mode="2" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)"/>
<!-- Interpolated velocity from a CSV file -->
    <imposevelocity mode="3" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <gridveldata file="wave_h02t2d1r1o2Velxz.csv" comment="CSV file with velocity data in different times and positions" />
        <gridresetvelz value="true" comment="Reset Z velocity after interaction (default=false)" />
        <_gridposzero x="0" z="0" comment="Defines position of grid (default=0)" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- Flow velocity [l/s, gal/s or gal/min] definition instead of velocity [m/s] -->
<!-- Flow velocity [l/s, gal/s or gal/min] is suported by uniform fixed or uniform variable velocity when zsurf is fixed or undefined. -->
    <imposevelocity mode="0" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <flowvelocity active="true" units="l/s" ratio="1.0" comment="Velocity values are read as flow (units=l/s, gal/s or gal/min) and ratio is used to compute particle volume (ratio*dp^3)." />
        <velocity v="2" comment="Uniform velocity" units_comment="l/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Rhop definitions *** -->
<!-- Fixed Constant rhop -->
    <imposerhop mode="0" comment="Outlet rhop 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Hydrostatic, 2:Extrapolated from ghost nodes (default=0)"/>
<!-- Fixed Hydrostatic rhop -->
    <imposerhop mode="1" comment="Outlet rhop 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Hydrostatic, 2:Extrapolated from ghost nodes (default=0)"/>
<!-- Extrapolated rhop -->
    <imposerhop mode="2" comment="Outlet rhop 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Hydrostatic, 2:Extrapolated from ghost nodes (default=0)"/>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Zsurf definitions *** -->
<!-- Imposed fixed zsurf -->
    <imposezsurf mode="0" comment="Inlet Z-surface 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Imposed variable value, 2:Calculated from fluid domain (default=0)">
        <zsurf value="1" comment="Characteristic inlet Z-surface (used for Hydrostatic option)" units_comment="m" />
        <remove value="false" comment="Removes particles above the Zsurf limit (default=false)" />
    </imposezsurf>
<!-- Imposed variable zsurf -->
    <imposezsurf mode="1" comment="Inlet Z-surface 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Imposed variable value, 2:Calculated from fluid domain (default=0)">
        <savevtk value="true" comment="Creates VTK files with Zsurf for each PART (default=false)" />
        <remove value="true" comment="Removes particles above the Zsurf limit (default=false)" />
        <zsurftimes comment="Characteristic inlet Z-Surf changes in time" units_comment="m">
            <timevalue time="0.0" zsurf="1" />
            <timevalue time="1.0" zsurf="1" />
            <timevalue time="2.2" zsurf="0.4" />
            <timevalue time="3.0" zsurf="0.4" />
            <timevalue time="5.5" zsurf="2" />
            <timevalue time="7.0" zsurf="0.4" />
        </zsurftimes>
    </imposezsurf>
<!-- Imposed variable zsurf using values in a external file-->
    <imposezsurf mode="1" comment="Inlet Z-surface 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Imposed variable value, 2:Calculated from fluid domain (default=0)">
        <savevtk value="true" comment="Creates VTK files with Zsurf for each PART (default=false)" />
        <remove value="false" comment="Removes particles above the Zsurf limit (default=false)" />
        <zsurffile file="FileZsurf.csv" comment="Zsurf data (time;zsurf)"/>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- Zsurf calculated from fluid -->
    <imposezsurf mode="2" comment="Inlet Z-surface 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Imposed variable value, 2:Calculated from fluid domain (default=0)">
        <savevtk value="true" comment="Creates VTK files with Zsurf for each PART (default=false)" />
        <remove value="false" comment="Removes particles above the Zsurf limit (default=false)" />
        <zsurf0 value="1.0" comment="Initial Z-surface value" units_comment="m" />
        <zsurfmin value="0.8" comment="Minimum Z-surface to reduce the calculation area (default=minimun Z inlet)" units_comment="m" />
        <zsurffit valuedp="0.5" comment="Reduction of calculated zsurf with explicit value (value) or according to dp (valuedp) (default vdp=0.5)" units_comment="m" />
    </imposezsurf>
<!---------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!---------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Attribute "active" in elements <inout> and <inoutzone> to enable     *** --> 
<!-- *** (using active="true" or active="1") or disable (using active="false" *** -->
<!-- *** or active="0"). It is an optional attribute and true by default.     *** -->
<inout active="true">
    <inoutzone active="true"/>
</inout>

docs.title: Mesh-data velocity and surface alternatives
docs.text:
Source: doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_InOutMesh.xml. This separate reference covers supplied mesh fields, including the explicitly marked deprecated attribute alternatives. Multiple meshdata elements illustrate choices; they are not instructions to combine those datasets in one active definition.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<!-- *** DualSPHysics v5.3.303 (29-11-2023) *** -->
<!-- *** class: JSphInOut using MESH-IN (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oceaneng.2022.113400) *** -->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Velocity definitions *** -->
<!-- Imposed variable velocity using values in a external mesh-data file (CSV or binary format)-->
    <imposevelocity mode="3" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <meshdata file="Case_Vel.mbi4" comment="Velocity data from mesh-data file (CSV or binary)" units_comment="m/s">
            <magnitude v="false" comment="Selects velocity magnitude (using inlet direction) when available in the input data (default=true)" />
            <reverse v="false" comment="Reverse velocity values (v=-v) (default=false)" />
            <initialtime v="0" comment="Defines the initial time of mesh data (default=0)" />
            <timeloop tbegin="10" tend="12" comment="Defines the loop by start and end time (default=0,0)" />
            <setpos x="0" y="0" z="0" comment="Applies a position offset to the mesh data (default=0,0,0)" />
            <setvelmul x="1" y="1" z="1" comment="Multiply fixed value to velocity data (default=1,1,1)" units_comment="m/s" />
            <setveladd x="0" y="0" z="0" comment="Add fixed value to velocity data (default=0,0,0)" units_comment="m/s" />
        </meshdata>
        <meshdata file="Case_VelDir.csv" comment="Velocity data from mesh-data file (CSV or binary)" units_comment="m/s">
            <magnitude v="true" comment="Velocity data using magnitude or 3 components (default=true)" />
        </meshdata>
    </imposevelocity>
<!-- **DEPRECATED** Imposed variable velocity using values in a external mesh-data file (CSV or binary format)-->
    <imposevelocity mode="3" comment="Imposed velocity 0:fixed value, 1:variable value, 2:Extrapolated velocity, 3:Interpolated velocity (default=0)">
        <meshdata file="Case_VelDir.csv" magnitude="true" reverse="false" setx="0" sety="0" setz="0" initialtime="0" comment="Velocity data (magnitude or 3 components) from mesh-data file (CSV or binary)." units_comment="m/s" />
        <meshdata file="Case_Vel.mbi4" magnitude="false" reverse="false" setx="0" sety="0" setz="0" initialtime="0" comment="Velocity data (magnitude or 3 components) mesh-data file (CSV or binary)." units_comment="m/s" />
        <meshdata file="Case_Vel.mbi4" magnitude="false" setmulx="0" setmuly="0" setmulz="0" comment="Multiply fixed value to velocity data." units_comment="m/s" />
        <meshdata file="Case_Vel.mbi4" magnitude="false" setaddx="0" setaddy="0" setaddz="0" comment="Add fixed value to velocity data." units_comment="m/s" />
    </imposevelocity>
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!------------------------------------------------------------------------------->
<!-- *** Zsurf definitions *** -->
<!-- Imposed variable zsurf using values in a external mesh-data file (CSV or binary format)-->
    <imposezsurf mode="1" comment="Inlet Z-surface 0:Imposed fixed value, 1:Imposed variable value, 2:Calculated from fluid domain (default=0)">
        <savevtk value="true" comment="Creates VTK files with Zsurf for each PART (default=false)" />

docs.title: Modified Dynamic Boundary Conditions
docs.text:
Under review by Aaron English

Boundary geometry, normal vectors, slip modes and no-penetration configuration in DualSPHysics v6.

docs.title: Boundary treatment and XML organisation
docs.text:
The modified Dynamic Boundary Condition (mDBC) uses information reconstructed inside the fluid to prescribe the state of boundary particles. A normal vector connects each boundary particle to the physical boundary surface; reflection across that surface defines a ghost node inside the fluid. Fluid neighbours around the ghost node provide the data used in the reconstruction. This differs from DBC, in which the boundary-particle density evolves through the continuity equation and the associated pressure supplies the repulsive interaction. The mDBC formulation addresses the non-physical boundary density and pressure, and the fluid–wall separation associated with DBC. These are motivations for the method, rather than an accuracy guarantee for an arbitrary case.

DualSPHysics v6 supports uniform DBC, uniform mDBC and boundary conditions selected separately by boundary identifier. The geometric description, normal generation and solver selection occupy different XML sections:

XML location Responsibility case/casedef/geometry Physical surface representation, boundary layers and fluid particles case/casedef/normals Generation or assignment of boundary normal vectors case/casedef/initials Initial fields, including interpolation from previous particle data case/execution/parameters Boundary, SlipMode, NoPenetration and numerical settings case/execution/special/mixboundary Boundary treatment for individual mkbound values when Boundary=MIX

The excerpts below are independent selections from the stated case or format reference. Retain their enclosing case, geometry, input files and numerical settings. Combining excerpts from different cases does not produce a complete simulation.

Figure 1: Ghost-node reflection at a flat wall and a corner. Crosses locate ghost nodes; circles show kernel support, and pink particles identify fluid neighbours used in the reconstruction.

docs.title: Surface offset, orientation and ghost nodes
docs.text:
The stored geometric normal is a displacement from a boundary particle to the actual boundary surface. Its length therefore carries geometric information; it is not merely a unit direction. Normals point towards the fluid. For a solid obstacle this means outwards from the solid; for a container it means into the container. At corners the vector connects the boundary particle to the represented surface intersection, so replacing all vectors by unit vectors destroys the required distances.

Let \(\mathbf{x}_b\) be a boundary-particle position and \(\mathbf{N}_s\) its displacement to the surface. Reflection gives

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathbf{x}_s=\mathbf{x}_b+\mathbf{N}_s,\\ \mathbf{x}_g=\mathbf{x}_b+2\mathbf{N}_s. \end{gathered} \]

The nearest boundary-particle layer is placed half an initial particle spacing, \(d_p/2\), behind the physical surface. Additional layers lie farther inside the solid. The required number of layers depends on the kernel support and smoothing length \(h\): the teaching configuration uses three or more layers, with three sufficient when \(2h\leq3d_p\). This condition must be checked for the chosen \(h/d_p\); three layers are not a universal prescription. The sloshing example below uses \(h=2d_p\) and four layers.

Figure 2: Boundary particles lie behind the physical surface, with the nearest layer offset by half the particle spacing. Displacement vectors terminate on the surface and point towards the fluid.

docs.title: Choosing a normal-generation method
docs.text:
Two complementary approaches are available. Geometry-based generation computes the vectors from a VTK representation of the actual boundary surface. Analytical definitions instead use planes, cylinders or spheres and select particles by mkbound. They can be combined: an initial geometry reconstruction may be followed by local analytical definitions. Review the clear setting before applying a later definition over existing normal data.

Use a separate mkbound for surfaces that require different analytical definitions or different boundary conditions. The boundary identifier is not the complete particle mk: the latter also depends on the case's marker configuration. The cylinder diagram retains its own marker assignment and must not be used to infer marker numbers in another case.

docs.title: Constructing the physical surface
docs.text:
The actual surface used for normals must be distinguished from the boundary-particle drawing. In the tank-and-obstacle construction, the container surface is drawn half a spacing inside the first container-particle layer, whereas the solid-obstacle surface extends half a spacing beyond its outermost particles. Container surface normals are inverted to face the fluid; normal inversion is disabled again before drawing solid obstacles. These operations change the geometry used for normals, rather than adding fluid particles.

The illustrative tank has width \(0.5\,\mathrm{m}\), height \(0.3\,\mathrm{m}\), obstacle width \(0.2\,\mathrm{m}\), obstacle height \(0.06\,\mathrm{m}\), and a water-level setting of 40%. Variables keep repeated dimensions consistent between the surface and particle drawings. These dimensions describe the illustration; they are not the dimensions of the separate sloshing XML excerpt below.

Figure 3: Tank and internal obstacle with their actual surface outlines, boundary layers and fluid particles. The annotated dimensions describe this illustrative geometry.

The following named drawing list is copied from the sloshing case. drawpoints="0" and drawshapes="1" generate the surface representation; setshapemode selects actual boundary shapes, and shapeout file="hdp" writes the geometry used by the later normal definition. resetdraw restores the drawing configuration afterwards. The list must be called from the case’s mainlist; defining it alone does not execute it.

XML excerpt — surface-geometry. XML location: case/casedef/geometry/commands. Source: examples/mdbc/03_Sloshing/CaseSloshingLR_NSNP_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<list name="GeometryForNormals">
    <setactive drawpoints="0" drawshapes="1" />
    <setshapemode>actual | bound</setshapemode>
    <setnormalinvert invert="true" />
    <setmkbound mk="0" />
    <drawbox>
        <boxfill>all</boxfill>
        <point x="-0.45" y="-0.1" z="0" />
        <size x="0.90" y="0.2" z="0.512" />
        <layers vdp="-0.5" />
    </drawbox>
    <shapeout file="hdp" />
    <resetdraw />
</list>

XML excerpt — surface-list-call. XML location: case/casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist. Source: examples/mdbc/03_Sloshing/CaseSloshingLR_NSNP_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<runlist name="GeometryForNormals" />

The particle drawing is a separate step. Here the tank has four layers at 0,1,2,3 times the initial spacing. The negative half-spacing used by the surface drawing is deliberately absent from this particle drawing. In the tank-and-obstacle illustration, a solid obstacle can instead be filled throughout; the layer specification is then unnecessary for that obstacle.

XML excerpt — boundary-particles. XML location: case/casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist. Source: examples/mdbc/03_Sloshing/CaseSloshingLR_NSNP_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<drawbox>
    <boxfill>all</boxfill>
    <point x="-0.45" y="-0.1" z="0" />
    <size x="0.90" y="0.2" z="0.512" />
    <layers vdp="0,1,2,3" />
</drawbox>

docs.title: Reading the surface and controlling the search
docs.text:
Place norgeometry inside casedef/normals. The following complete normals element comes from the mixed dam-break case and includes the optional diagnostic controls. The geometry file must already exist when its normals are generated. [CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk follows the surface-export naming convention.

XML excerpt — geometry-normals. XML location: case/casedef. Source: examples/mdbc/11_MixBC/CaseDamBreak3D_Mix_NS_FR_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<normals active="true">
    <norgeometry comment="Define initial configuration of normals before applying other configurations">
        <geometryfile file="[CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk" comment="File with boundary geometry (VTK format)" />
        <distanceh v="2" comment="Maximum orthogonal distance (H*value) to compute normals data (default=2)" />
        <maxsizeh v="2.1" comment="Maximum allowed normal size (H*value) (disabled=0, default=0)" />
        <svshapes v="true" comment="Saves VTK with geometry in triangles and quads with its normals for debug (default=false)" />
    </norgeometry>
</normals>
Child of norgeometry Meaning Reference convention geometryfile/@file VTK boundary geometry NONE selects no external geometry file distanceh/@v Maximum orthogonal search distance Distance is the value multiplied by \(h\); documented default 2 maxsizeh/@v Maximum allowed normal length Value multiplied by \(h\); 0 disables this limit svshapes/@v Save triangles/quads with surface normals for inspection Boolean; reference default false

The orthogonal search distance and the maximum resulting vector length are separate controls, especially near corners. Their numerical values are not interchangeable. The example's maxsizeh=2.1 is an explicit choice, not the default. Geometry triangles and quadrilaterals must have consistent fluid-facing orientation.

Figure 4: Surface triangles and quadrilaterals of the tank and obstacle, with orthogonal vectors showing the orientation used for normal generation.

Figure 5: Boundary-particle normal vectors around the tank and internal obstacle. Corner vectors and vectors from deeper layers have different lengths.

docs.title: Defining normals analytically
docs.text: Analytical definitions belong under case/casedef/normals. mkbound accepts a single boundary identifier, a comma-separated list or ranges. Select only the intended particle sets: reusing one identifier for unrelated surfaces makes a single plane or cylinder definition ambiguous.

docs.title: Planar walls
docs.text:
For a plane, specify a surface point and a normal direction. The direction is common to the wall, but each particle's displacement length depends on its distance to that plane. The reference also supports point auto="true", which locates the plane from the selected particles and the direction. limitdist/@vdp controls the minimum particle-to-plane distance in multiples of \(d_p\); its reference default is 0.5.

The Poiseuille case uses two automatically located walls. Its opposing directions point from the upper and lower boundaries into the channel. These definitions preserve the case's maxdisth=2.0 search limit.

XML excerpt — channel-planes. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: examples/mdbc/02_Poiseuille/CasePoiseuille_NS_LR_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norplane mkbound="0">
    <point auto="true" comment="Point is calculated automatically accoding to normal configuration" />
    <normal x="0" y="0" z="-1" />
    <maxdisth v="2.0" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
</norplane>
<norplane mkbound="1">
    <point auto="true" comment="Point is calculated automatically accoding to normal configuration" />
    <normal x="0" y="0" z="1" />
    <maxdisth v="2.0" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
</norplane>

The following reference alternatives illustrate an explicit plane, a positional filter, and an automatically located plane with an explicit half-spacing limit. Their marker numbers and coordinates are illustrative reference values; they are not additions to the channel case.

XML excerpt — plane-reference. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norplane mkbound="5">
    <onlypos>
        <posmin x="0" />
        <posmax z="1" />
    </onlypos>
    <point x="0.1" y="0" z="0.1" />
    <normal x="0" y="0" z="1" />
    <maxdisth v="2" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
    <clear v="true" comment="Clears previous normal data (default=true)" />
</norplane>
<norplane mkbound="6">
    <point auto="true" comment="Point is calculated automatically accoding to normal configuration" />
    <limitdist vdp="0.5" comment="Minimun distance (Dp*vdp) between particles and boundary limit to calculate the point (default=0.5)" />
    <normal x="0" y="0" z="1" />
    <maxdisth v="2.5" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
    <clear v="false" comment="Clears previous normal data (default=true)" />
</norplane>

docs.title: Cylindrical and spherical surfaces
docs.text:
A cylinder is defined by two points on its axis and its radius. inside=true selects boundary particles inside a solid cylinder, producing fluid-facing vectors towards its exterior. inside=false is the container-cylinder alternative. The reference's limit1 and limit2 control the end limits for inside mode. A sphere uses its centre and radius, with the same solid/container distinction.

The following are reference options with their original coordinates, marker numbers and limits. In both definitions maxdisth is measured in multiples of \(h\); it is not a dimensional distance in metres.

XML excerpt — cylinder-reference. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norcylinder mkbound="8-9">
    <center1 x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <center2 x="0" y="0" z="0.5" />
    <radius v="0.2" />
    <inside v="true" comment="Boundary particles inside the cylinder" />
    <limit1 v="false" comment="Active normals to limit 1 for inside mode (default=true)" />
    <limit2 v="true" comment="Active normals to limit 2 for inside mode (default=true)" />
    <maxdisth v="2" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
    <clear v="true" comment="Clears previous normal data (default=true)" />
</norcylinder>

XML excerpt — sphere-reference. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norsphere mkbound="7">
    <center x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <radius v="0.2" />
    <inside v="true" comment="Boundary particles inside the sphere" />
    <maxdisth v="2" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
    <clear v="true" comment="Clears previous normal data (default=true)" />
</norsphere>

Figure 6: Fluid and boundary-particle sets for a circular cylinder between two walls. Separate boundary markers allow each surface to receive its own analytical normal definition.

Figure 7: Radial normal vectors on the solid cylinder and opposing normal directions on the two channel walls.

docs.title: Fixed vectors and local selections
docs.text:
norset assigns the same displacement vector, including its length, to every selected particle. It does not calculate a different distance for each layer. Use it only where that common displacement is geometrically appropriate. onlypos restricts the selection by coordinate limits; omitted coordinate bounds remain unspecified by the excerpt.

XML excerpt — fixed-normal-reference. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norset mkbound="0,2-4">
    <onlypos>
        <posmin x="1" y="2" z="3" />
        <posmax x="11" y="22" z="33" />
    </onlypos>
    <normal x="0" y="1" z="0" />
</norset>

The reference additionally provides norparts for selected boundary particles. It exposes a maxdisth search limit; the short option definition does not establish that particle-based reconstruction is a replacement for an accurately represented surface at a complex corner.

XML excerpt — particle-normal-reference. XML location: case/casedef/normals. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<norparts mkbound="5,7-9">
    <maxdisth v="2.1" comment="Maximum distance to boundary limit. It uses H*maxdisth (default=2)" />
</norparts>
Normal definition Geometric information supplied Important distinction norgeometry Actual boundary surface in VTK Surface orientation and offset must be correct norplane Point and direction, or automatic plane location Displacement length varies with particle position norcylinder Axis points, radius and inside/outside selection End-limit settings are separate controls norsphere Centre, radius and inside/outside selection Select the intended spherical particle set norset One complete displacement vector Same direction and length for all selected particles norparts Selected particles and search limit Inspect the resulting vectors before use

docs.title: Ghost-node density and pressure
docs.text:
The original mDBC formulation, selected by M22, reconstructs the ghost-node density and its gradient using the Liu and Liu correction matrix, with a normalised Shepard fallback when the matrix cannot be inverted. Fluid particles interact with the boundary particles in their kernel support. In three dimensions, its local system can be written as

\[ \mathbf A_g\begin{bmatrix}\rho_g&\partial_x\rho_g&\partial_y\rho_g&\partial_z\rho_g\end{bmatrix}^{T}=\mathbf b_g. \]

For an explicit definition of that matrix, let \(q_{j0}=1\), \(q_{j1}=x_j-x_g\), \(q_{j2}=y_j-y_g\), \(q_{j3}=z_j-z_g\), and let \(D_0 W=W\), \(D_1 W=\partial_xW\), \(D_2 W=\partial_yW\), \(D_3 W=\partial_zW\). With fluid-particle volume \(V_j=m_j/\rho_j\), the entries are

\[ \begin{gathered} (A_g)_{kl}=\sum_j V_j q_{jl}D_kW_{gj},\\ (b_g)_k=\sum_j\rho_j V_jD_kW_{gj},\\ k,l=0,1,2,3. \end{gathered} \]

The boundary density in this formulation is then extrapolated from the ghost node:

\[ \rho_b=\rho_g+(\mathbf x_b-\mathbf x_g)\cdot\nabla\rho_g. \]

The newer density treatment used by NS, FS and V0 first reconstructs ghost-node density, using matrix inversion when sufficiently well conditioned and a normalised Shepard sum otherwise. A pressure-cloning step accounts for gravity and boundary acceleration:

\[ \begin{gathered} p_g=c_0^2(\rho_g-\rho_0),\\ p_b=p_g+\rho_0\big[(\mathbf g-\mathbf a_b)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_b\big] \big[(\mathbf x_g-\mathbf x_b)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_b\big],\\ \rho_b=\rho_0+\frac{p_b}{c_0^2}. \end{gathered} \]

Here \(c_0\) is the reference speed of sound, \(\rho_0\) the reference density, \(\mathbf a_b\) the boundary acceleration and \(\widehat{\mathbf n}_b\) the unit normal. The unit direction in these equations is distinct from the geometric displacement supplied to normal generation. These relations describe the boundary reconstruction; they do not replace the fluid equation-of-state configuration.

The newer method also checks the divergence of position at the ghost node to distinguish submerged and unsubmerged boundary particles. Submerged particles have their density, pressure and velocity updated. Unsubmerged particles are switched off for fluid interaction and assigned reference density. This interaction state is not removal of boundary geometry.

Figure 8: Boundary particles below and above the fluid surface illustrate the distinction between submerged particles participating in reconstruction and unsubmerged particles switched off for fluid interaction.

docs.title: Velocity conditions
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf u_w\) denote wall velocity and \(\mathbf u_g\) the interpolated ghost-node velocity. The normalised interpolation is

\[ \mathbf u_g= rac{\sum_j\mathbf u_j V_jW_{gj}}{\sum_jV_jW_{gj}}. \]

The no-slip reconstruction uses the reflected velocity \(\mathbf u_b=2\mathbf u_w-\mathbf u_g\). For a stationary wall this becomes \(\mathbf u_b=-\mathbf u_g\). Its normal and tangential projections are

\[ egin{gathered} \mathbf u_b^{\perp}=(\mathbf u_b\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}_b)\widehat{\mathbf n}_b,\ \mathbf u_b^{\parallel}=\mathbf u_b-\mathbf u_b^{\perp}. \end{gathered} \]

The tangential component enters the viscous treatment, whereas the wall velocity is used for the boundary contribution to the density-gradient continuity calculation. This distinction matters: the reflected ghost velocity is not simply substituted into every boundary interaction.

In the laminar interaction equations used to illustrate this distinction, the viscous term depends on the relative velocity, while the continuity equation uses its own relative-velocity contribution:

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d\mathbf u_i}{dt}={}&-\sum_j m_j rac{p_i+p_j}{ ho_i ho_j} abla W_{ij}\ &+\sum_j rac{4 u m_j\,\mathbf r_{ij}\cdot abla W_{ij}} {( ho_i+ ho_j)(r_{ij}^2+0.01h^2)}\mathbf u_{ij}+\mathbf g_i. \end{aligned} \] \[ rac{d ho_i}{dt}= ho_i\sum_j rac{m_j}{ ho_j}\mathbf u_{ij}\cdot abla W_{ij}+\mathrm{DDT}. \]

Here \( u\) is kinematic viscosity, \(\mathbf r_{ij}\) is particle separation and \(\mathbf u_{ij}\) denotes the relative velocity appropriate to the term. For a boundary neighbour, the viscous contribution uses the tangential boundary velocity, while continuity uses wall velocity. These equations explain the laminar treatment; artificial-viscosity cases retain their own selected formulation.

For free slip, the teaching relation is \(\mathbf u_b=\mathbf u_g\), with the tangential component obtained by the same projection. This relation describes the reconstructed boundary state and should not be read as cancelling the separate normal-wall treatment of a moving boundary. The V0 option instead imposes the wall velocity, giving zero boundary velocity for a stationary wall, while retaining the newer density reconstruction. M22 also imposes wall velocity but retains the original density extrapolation.

SlipMode value Boundary treatment Density reconstruction Additional NoPenetration NS No slip; reflected ghost velocity New pressure-cloning treatment Available FS Free slip; ghost velocity used for the tangential treatment New pressure-cloning treatment Available V0 TanVel=0; boundary velocity follows wall velocity New pressure-cloning treatment Available M22 Original mDBC 2022 velocity treatment Original density extrapolation Not applied

Use ViscoBoundFactor=1 for the documented viscous wall treatment. The teaching material specifies this for NS and V0; the current reader also warns when the factor differs from 1 for NS or FS. This factor multiplies boundary viscosity and is not the switch selecting a slip mode. Retain the chosen viscosity formulation and magnitude of the complete example.

docs.title: Activating uniform mDBC in v6
docs.text:
The sloshing case below explicitly selects no slip and enables the additional no-penetration correction. Its density diffusion is Fourtakas (FO) with coefficient 0.1. Density diffusion is recommended in the mDBC teaching workflow to control fluid instabilities; this excerpt states the case's explicit configuration rather than relying on an implicit default.

XML excerpt — uniform-mdbc. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/mdbc/03_Sloshing/CaseSloshingLR_NSNP_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<parameter key="Boundary" value="mDBC" comment="Boundary method: DBC, mDBC, MIX:MixBC (default=DBC)" />
<parameter key="SlipMode" value="NS" comment="Slip mode for mDBC: NS:No-slip, FS:Free slip, V0:TanVel=0, M22:mDBC 2022 (default=NS)" />
<parameter key="NoPenetration" value="Y" comment="Activate No-Penetration option for mDBC: Y/N (default=N)" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="FO" comment="Density Diffusion Term: NO:None, FO:Fourtakas (default=FO)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value (default=0.1)" />

Boundary=mDBC activates the uniform method, and SlipMode chooses its velocity/density treatment. The documented default slip mode is NS. NoPenetration is a separate Boolean parameter, with N as its default. Set it explicitly when comparing options. Use the named v6 values shown here; older numeric boundary and slip selections are deprecated.

docs.title: Additional no-penetration correction
docs.text:
NoPenetration=Y activates an additional near-wall velocity correction for NS, FS and V0. It does not select free slip or no slip, and it does not make inaccurate normals acceptable. N disables this extra correction; the selected boundary condition still remains active.

The correction acts on nearby fluid particles approaching an enabled boundary. The current implementation first restricts boundary neighbours by particle separation, projected distance and normal length, then treats each Cartesian component separately. Consequently, proximity alone does not imply that a correction will be applied.

For the following description, \(\mathbf N=\mathbf x_g-\mathbf x_b=2\mathbf N_s\) is the internal displacement to the ghost node, \(N=|\mathbf N|\), \(\widehat{\mathbf n}=\mathbf N/N\), and \(\mathbf r=\mathbf x_f-\mathbf x_b\). The initial geometric gates are

\[ \begin{gathered} |\mathbf r|<1.25d_p,\\ |\mathbf r\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}|<0.75N,\\ N<1.75d_p. \end{gathered} \]

For a non-negligible normal component \(N_k\), the component is considered only when \(|r_k\widehat n_k|<0.75|N_k|\) and \(|N_k|>0.001d_p\). Its relative velocity must point towards the wall: \((u_{f,k}-u_{w,k})\widehat n_k<0\). The clipped distance ratio and the current cubic factor are

\[ \begin{gathered} q_k=\max\!\left(0.25,\min\!\left(\left|\frac{r_k}{N_k}\right|,0.75\right)\right),\\ f(q_k)=32q_k^3-48q_k^2+18q_k. \end{gathered} \]

Each accepted neighbour contributes

\[ \delta u_k=-f(q_k)(u_{f,k}-u_{w,k})\widehat n_k^{\,2}. \]

The accepted contributions are averaged separately for each direction before application. Particles moving away from the boundary receive no contribution from that component. The ratio is limited to 0.25–0.75; the cubic factor decreases from 2 to 0 over that interval. These are algorithm constants, not additional XML parameters to add to the case.

Figure 17: Near-wall distances and velocity directions in the no-penetration mechanism. The schematic illustrates the geometry; the component-wise conditions above define when the correction applies.

docs.title: Sloshing with moving walls
docs.text: examples/mdbc/03_Sloshing/CaseSloshingLR_NSNP_Def.xml demonstrates a moving container with geometry-generated normals, SlipMode=NS and NoPenetration=Y. The particle spacing is 0.004 m and \(h/d_p=2\). The named drawing list exports the half-spacing surface, while four boundary layers support the selected smoothing length. The wall motion remains defined by the complete case and its SloshingMotionData.dat input. The normal-generation excerpt does not replace that motion definition.

docs.title: Channel flow and wall behaviour
docs.text:
The Poiseuille examples provide planar normals and contrasting wall treatments. Read the parameter value inside each file: a filename suffix is not a reliable substitute for SlipMode.

Package path under examples/mdbc/02_Poiseuille/ Actual SlipMode NoPenetration Laminar viscosity CasePoiseuille_LR_Def.xml M22 N 0.1 m²/s CasePoiseuille_NS_LR_Def.xml V0 N 0.1 m²/s CasePoiseuille_FS_LR_Def.xml FS N 0.1 m²/s CaseRunDown_NS_Def.xml NS N 0.1 m²/s CaseRunDown_FS_Def.xml FS N 0.1 m²/s

The last two files concern run-down and are not interchangeable initial conditions for the steady channel comparison. The following selection retains the actual settings in CasePoiseuille_NS_LR_Def.xml, including its V0 value and laminar viscosity.

XML excerpt — poiseuille-settings. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/mdbc/02_Poiseuille/CasePoiseuille_NS_LR_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<parameter key="SlipMode" value="V0" comment="Slip mode for mDBC: NS:No-slip, FS:Free slip, V0:TanVel=0, M22:mDBC 2022 (default=NS)" />
<parameter key="NoPenetration" value="N" comment="Activate No-Penetration option for mDBC: Y/N (default=N)" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="LAM" comment="Viscosity formulation: LAM:Laminar, ART:Artificial (default=LAM)" />
<parameter key="Visco" value="0.1" comment="Viscosity value. Typically 0.01 for Artificial and 1e-6 m^2/s (water kinematic viscosity) for Laminar" />
<parameter key="ViscoBoundFactor" value="1" comment="Multiply viscosity value with boundary (default=1)" />
<parameter key="DensityDT" value="FO" comment="Density Diffusion Term: NO:None, FO:Fourtakas (default=FO)" />
<parameter key="DensityDTvalue" value="0.1" comment="DDT value (default=0.1)" />

docs.title: Mixed boundary conditions by boundary identifier
docs.text:
Select Boundary=MIX in execution/parameters, then specify the per-boundary conditions in execution/special/mixboundary. The global SlipMode and NoPenetration parameters are not the selectors for mixed boundaries; boundtype and nopenetration on each mixed-boundary entry determine the treatment.

boundtype Equivalent uniform treatment Per-entry nopenetration DBC DBC No additional mDBC correction MDBC_V0 M22 No additional mDBC correction MDBC_T0 V0 0 or 1 MDBC_NS NS 0 or 1 MDBC_FR FS 0 or 1

The mixed-boundary names are deliberately different from the uniform SlipMode names: MDBC_V0 means the old mDBC, whereas MDBC_T0 means the newer TanVel=0 treatment. Preserve MDBC_FR exactly for free slip. The local Boolean attribute uses 0/1 in the reference and examples; the global v6 parameter uses N/Y.

XML excerpt — mixed-activation. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/mdbc/11_MixBC/CaseDamBreak3D_Mix_NS_FR_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<parameter key="Boundary" value="MIX" comment="Boundary method: DBC, mDBC, MIX:MixBC (default=DBC)" />

XML excerpt — mixed-assignment. XML location: case/execution/special. Source: examples/mdbc/11_MixBC/CaseDamBreak3D_Mix_NS_FR_Def.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<mixboundary>
    <!-- boundtype: DBC, MDBC_V0 (Old mDBC), MDBC_T0 (mDBC2 tanvel=0), MDBC_NS (mDBC2 No-slip), MDBC_FR (mDBC2 Free slip) -->
    <!-- nopenetration: 1/0 Activate No-Penetration option for TanVel=0, No-slip or Free-slip mDBC -->
    <!-- mkbound: mkbound value or list of values (2,5,7-8) -->
    <default boundtype="MDBC_NS" nopenetration="0" />
    <bcmk mkbound="0-1" boundtype="MDBC_NS" nopenetration="1" />
    <bcmk mkbound="2,3" boundtype="MDBC_FR" nopenetration="1" />
</mixboundary>

The default entry supplies the treatment for markers without a specific assignment. The two bcmk entries above assign no slip with no penetration to 0-1, and free slip with no penetration to 2,3. Both boundtype and nopenetration must be supplied on these entries. If no default is supplied, every relevant boundary marker needs a specific assignment. Avoid overlapping marker selections: the reader applies later matching entries after earlier ones.

Prepare and inspect normals across the boundary geometry used by the mixed case, including transitions between boundary types. The workshop workflow defines normals for all boundaries, including DBC portions; the mixed dam-break case follows a geometry-wide normal-generation step. The presence of a DBC assignment does not remove the geometric requirements of neighbouring mDBC portions.

Mixed conditions can also distinguish side walls from the beach and cylinder in a wave tank. Mixed conditions should follow the intended wall physics.

docs.title: Initialising from a previous particle field
docs.text:
A previous particle dataset can supply initial velocity, density or pressure and a free-surface shape. This is useful when a new discretisation should begin from an established flow rather than from rest. It is an interpolation workflow, with its own consistency checks; it is not an exact restart of every solver state.

For a field \(F\), the documented normalised interpolation has the form

\[ F_i=\frac{\sum_j F_j(m_j/\rho_j)W_{ij}}{\sum_j(m_j/\rho_j)W_{ij}}. \]

The current GenCase template names the velocity element velpart and the density element densitypart. Both belong in casedef/initials. The following two reference options retain the template's Part_0028.bi4 input and minimum fluid-volume ratio of 0.5. They require a compatible, available PART dataset; the filename is not an instruction to generate that file automatically.

XML excerpt — previous-velocity. XML location: case/casedef/initials. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<velpart mkfluid="0">
    <minratio v="0.5" comment="Minimum fluid ratio (volume) to apply interpolated values" />
    <partfile v="Part_0028.bi4" comment="PART file with input particle data" />
</velpart>

XML excerpt — previous-density. XML location: case/casedef/initials. Source: doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml. This is a fragment, not a complete case.

<densitypart mkfluid="0">
    <minratio v="0.5" comment="Minimum fluid ratio (volume) to apply interpolated values" />
    <partfile v="Part_0028.bi4" comment="PART file with input particle data" />
    <fitpress v="true" comment="Fits the pressure instead of density" />
</densitypart>
Element or attribute Role velpart/@mkfluid Fluid set receiving interpolated velocity densitypart/@mkfluid Fluid set receiving interpolated density/pressure minratio/@v Minimum supporting fluid volume ratio for applying interpolated values partfile/@v Source PART data file fitpress/@v With true, fit pressure rather than density

A free-surface reconstruction is a separate geometry operation. The workshop workflow first fills the target domain with fluid particles and then filters that set against the previous BI4 fluid field, removing particles outside the reconstructed surface. This permits a finer target spacing while retaining the previous surface profile. Check the target mkfluid, coordinate alignment, source time and available fluid support. Interpolating properties alone does not trim the free surface.

Figure 14: A finer initial fluid distribution reconstructed from the free surface of a previous, coarser particle field.

Transfer to a new spacing still requires examination of the initial transient and the target flow state.

docs.title: Inspecting normal vectors
docs.text:
Normal checks should compare vectors with both the boundary particles and the actual surface. In ParaView, open the boundary and fluid VTK files together, add the actual-surface VTK where available, and display the normal vector field with glyphs. Choose the normal field explicitly and check its magnitude as well as its direction. Glyph scaling used for visualisation must not be mistaken for a change to the stored vectors.

Inspect flat surfaces first, then corners, oblique faces and transitions between marker sets. Vectors should point from boundary particles towards the fluid-facing surface, with lengths consistent with particle depth and the half-spacing offset. A particle-based estimate that appears reasonable on a flat wall can be misleading at a wedge or a complex intersection; overlay the actual geometry when checking such regions.

Output Interpretation [CaseName]_hdp_Actual.vtk Actual surface used by the geometry-based workflow Geometry-shape VTK produced with svshapes Triangles/quads and their surface-normal orientation CfgInit_Normals.vtk Initial vectors from boundary particles to the surface CfgInit_NormalsGhost.vtk Vectors from boundary particles to ghost nodes; twice the surface displacement for a fresh initialisation

The last two files are solver initialisation outputs; generating a geometry VTK alone does not produce them. Restart variants append _Restart to the names. Zero vectors indicate particles without assigned normal data; inspect their location rather than hiding them through glyph sampling. A complete absence of valid vectors prevents the intended mDBC reconstruction.

The source wedge view displays CaseStillWedgeHR_Bound.vtk, its Glyph1 normals and CaseStillWedgeHR_hdp_Actual.vtk. These are the original inspection filenames, rather than fixed names required by other cases. The figure retains the normal-length colour scales and both corner views.

Figure 15: Surface-normal glyphs on a wedge and adjoining flat boundary, including an enlarged view of the oblique faces and corner. The colour scale identifies vector length.

The source 3D inspection uses CaseDamBreak3D_Mix_NS_FR_Bound.vtk and CaseDamBreak3D_Mix_NS_FR_hdp_Actual.vtk; its ParaView controls are omitted from the scientific figure. The complete normal-size colour scale and wall/corner normal distributions are retained.

Figure 16: Section through a three-dimensional boundary showing normal vectors near the container and an obstacle. The section exposes vectors that would otherwise be hidden by the outer geometry.

docs.title: Requirements and diagnostic checks
docs.text:
Retain sufficient boundary layers for the smoothing length, the correct physical surface offset and fluid-facing vector orientation. Increasing a search distance cannot correct an incorrectly oriented or misplaced surface. Check that the normal-generation selection covers the particle sets used by mDBC, and that diagnostic output is interpreted with the appropriate surface/ghost length convention.

For moving or floating boundaries, use the actual wall motion in the case and preserve its collision model. The solver recommends Chrono collisions when applying mDBC to floating bodies; the Chrono XML Guide explains that separate configuration. Flexible-structure coupling imposes further integration and slip-mode restrictions, so a general mDBC excerpt must not be treated as a complete flexible-structure setup.

Observation Configuration to inspect Missing or zero normal vectors Marker selection, search limits and availability of the geometry file Vectors pointing away from the fluid Surface orientation and container normal inversion Incorrect corner vectors Actual geometry, layer placement and the maximum normal length Unexpected channel profile Actual SlipMode, wall motion, viscosity formulation and ViscoBoundFactor No additional near-wall correction NoPenetration, eligible slip mode, local mixed assignment and geometric/approach gates Different conditions not applied by marker Boundary=MIX, marker coverage and overlapping bcmk entries Poor transferred initial field PART availability, source/target coordinates, support ratio and free-surface reconstruction

For the available case families and variants, see the mDBC Examples Catalogue.

docs.title: XML reference coverage
docs.text:
The relevant definitions are distributed across doc/xml_format/GenCase_CaseTemplate.xml (geometry, initials and normals), doc/xml_format/_FmtXML__Parameters.xml (solver parameters) and doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MixBoundary.xml (per-marker boundary assignments). There is no single dedicated complete mDBC format file in this reference set. The verified excerpts above document these specific configurations without reproducing the unrelated sections of the generic case template.

doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_Initialize.xml is a limited developer-oriented initialisation example. It is not the full normal-generation reference and does not replace casedef/normals in the GenCase template.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text: The original reconstruction is described by English et al., Modified dynamic boundary conditions (mDBC) for general-purpose smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH): application to tank sloshing, dam break and fish pass problems, Computational Particle Mechanics 9, 1–15 (2022), DOI 10.1007/s40571-021-00403-3. The pressure-cloning approach is discussed by Antuono et al., Clone particles: A simplified technique to enforce solid boundary conditions in SPH, Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 409, 115973 (2023). These formulations provide context for the boundary treatment; case-specific numerical and physical validation remains necessary.

docs.title: MoorDynPlus coupling
docs.text:
Under review by Iván Martínez Estévez

XML configuration of mooring systems, line properties, floating-body connections and output data in DualSPHysics v6.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
MoorDynPlus models dynamic mooring lines coupled to floating bodies in DualSPHysics. A lumped-mass representation divides each line into nodes connected by spring-damper segments. The segments provide axial elasticity and internal damping; the model also accounts for hydrodynamic loading and seabed interaction. Anchors remain fixed, while fairleads follow their associated floating bodies and transmit mooring forces to them.

The March 2025 XML Guide presents MoorDynPlus as a new implementation of MoorDynG. This page documents the DualSPHysics v6 MoorDynPlus interface. XML and API conventions from other MoorDyn versions must not be substituted without checking their compatibility. For the general formulation, see Coupling DualSPHysics with MoorDynPlus.

The XML excerpts below require the surrounding case definitions, geometry, bodies and parameters indicated by their XML locations. Reference-format options are identified separately.

docs.title: XML configuration overview
docs.text:
The coupling configuration belongs under case/execution/special/moorings. It selects the moored floating bodies, controls the coupling's VTK/point output and contains or references the MoorDynPlus model. That model in turn defines solver/environment settings, bodies, line properties, connections and library CSV output.

The following siblings come from the two-dimensional breaking-line example. The nested model is documented in the following sections; these controls alone are not a complete case.

XML excerpt — coupling-controls. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<savevtk_moorings value="true" comment="Saves vtk with moorings (default=true)"/>
<savevtk_lines value="true" comment="Saves vtk with mooring lines (default=true)"/>
<savecsv_points value="true" comment="Saves csv with link points (default=true)"/>
<savevtk_points value="false" comment="Saves vtk with link points (default=false)"/>
<mooredfloatings>
    <floating mkbound="50" comment="Mkbound of the Floating body the mooring is linked to"/>
</mooredfloatings>

docs.title: Embedded and external configurations
docs.text:
In the embedded approach used by the package examples, moordynplus is a child of moorings. Its solverOptions, bodies, lines and savedata children are illustrated below. The reader also recognises solver as an alternative to solverOptions, and an optional connects section for shared dynamic connections. Do not add an empty connection section when the example does not use one.

The current format and coupling reader also support a separate XML file:

Reference XML excerpt — external-model. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings. Source: doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MoorDynPlus.xml. This is a reference option, not a complete case.

<moordynplus active="true" file="moordynplus.xml" comment="MoorDynPlus configuration file"/>

In this alternative, the referenced file has a moordynplus root containing the model configuration. Without file, the reader instead loads case.execution.special.moorings.moordynplus from the main case XML. Use one approach for the model; do not combine a file reference with a second, unrelated embedded configuration.

Supply a resolvable filename and a complete external moordynplus configuration. The reference excerpt supplies the file-selection element only.

docs.title: Force application and coupling outputs
docs.text:
The presentation's optional delayed application of mooring forces is retained in the current reference:

Reference XML excerpt — force-start. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings. Source: doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MoorDynPlus.xml. This is a reference option, not a complete case.

<start value="4" ramptime="0" comment="Start time of the application of mooring forces with configurable ramp time. (default ramptime=0)" units_comment="s"/>

start/@value is the simulation time when mooring forces begin to be applied; ramptime controls the force ramp. Both are in seconds. The reader defaults both to zero when absent. This is distinct from the initial relaxation time, the internal mooring step and the output start time. The primary two-dimensional case has no explicit start; do not silently add the reference's 4 s delay to it.

Coupling element Purpose Confirmed default when absent savevtk_lines Line representation in VTK true savevtk_moorings Full mooring representation in VTK true savecsv_points CSV for coupling force/link points true savevtk_points VTK for coupling force/link points false savevtk_nodes VTK with mooring node data true

These coupling switches are separate from moordynplus/savedata and line outputFlags. The current reference also documents reset_moorings and optional sphfluidvel interpolation. They are additional configuration choices, not settings to inject into the source case.

docs.title: Environmental and seabed configuration
docs.text:
The primary two-dimensional example uses a free surface at z=0 and a depth of 0.45 m. For the flat-bottom model, the reader defines the bottom elevation as the free-surface elevation minus the depth; here it is z=-0.45 m. Retain this coordinate convention when interpreting the anchor positions.

These environmental settings are selected from the case's solverOptions. Its relaxation settings are shown separately below.

XML excerpt — environment. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus/solverOptions. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<waterDepth value="0.45" comment="Water depth" units_comment="m"/>
<freesurface value="0" comment="Z position of the water free surface.(default=0)"/>
<kBot value="3.0e6" comment="Bottom stiffness constant. (default=3.0e6)" units_comment="Pa/m"/>
<cBot value="3.0e5" comment="Bottom damping constant. (default=3.0e5)" units_comment="Pa*s/m"/>
<dtM value="0.001" comment="Desired mooring model time step. (default=0.0001)"/>
<waveKin value="0" comment="Wave kinematics flag ( 0: neglect [the only option currently supported] ). (default=0)"/>
<writeUnits value="yes" comment="Write units line. value=[yes|no]. (default=yes)"/>
<frictionCoefficient value="0" comment="General bottom friction coefficient, as a start. (default=0.0)"/>
<fricDamp value="200" comment="Damping coefficient used to model the friction with speeds near zero. (default=200.0)"/>
<statDynFricScale value="1.0" comment="Ratio between static and dynamic friction (mu_static/mu_dynamic). (default=1.0)"/>
Parameter in this case Physical meaning Units waterDepth Water depth; current reader also accepts depth m freesurface Global z elevation of the still free surface m kBot Bottom contact stiffness constant Pa/m cBot Bottom contact damping constant Pa·s/m dtM Maximum internal mooring-model time step when automatic control is enabled s frictionCoefficient Bottom friction coefficient; friction is an accepted alternative Dimensionless fricDamp Friction regularisation coefficient near zero speed N·s/m in the current format reference statDynFricScale Ratio of static to dynamic friction Dimensionless

Bottom stiffness and damping govern contact response, rather than axial line stiffness. Their numerical suitability depends on discretisation and time stepping. The current reference permits per-line contact activation and optional floorgeo bathymetry; this basic example uses its flat-depth configuration.

The case's dtM value is 0.001 s. In the current reader, omitted auto means true: the value is an upper limit and the library can reduce the internal step. It must not be described as a guaranteed fixed step. The reference supports auto="false", but no change to the case's time step or automatic mode is proposed here.

writeUnits="yes" controls output unit lines. The retained waveKin="0" setting requests no legacy wave kinematics; the current reader warns for non-zero legacy waveKin and directs users to waves instead. The old comment that it is the only supported option does not describe all current wave capabilities. Regular waves in the SPH case and library wave/fluid-velocity options require their own consistent configuration.

docs.title: Initial conditions and dynamic relaxation
docs.text:
Initial line geometry is constructed before the dynamic relaxation stage. During relaxation, the library temporarily scales drag to help settle the line system, advances the model and monitors fairlead-force magnitudes. It subsequently restores drag scaling and resets the line time to the simulation origin.

XML excerpt — initial-relaxation. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus/solverOptions. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<dtIC value="1.0" comment="Period to analyse convergence of dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=1.0)" units_comment="s"/>
<cdScaleIC value="2" comment="Factor to scale drag coefficients during dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=5)"/>
<threshIC value="0.001" comment="Convergence threshold for for initial conditions. (default=0.001)"/>
<tmaxIC value="1" comment="Maximum time for initial conditions without convergence.(default=0)" units_comment="s"/>
Parameter Meaning Units dtIC Period between convergence analyses s cdScaleIC Temporary multiplier for drag during relaxation Dimensionless threshIC Threshold for relative change in fairlead-force magnitude Dimensionless tmaxIC Relaxation time budget without convergence s

Convergence is assessed from relative changes in each fairlead's force magnitude over successive samples. Relaxation stops when all fairleads meet the threshold; otherwise it can reach its time budget with a nonconvergence warning.

When tmaxIC is zero, the timed relaxation loop has no iterations. A non-zero time budget requires a positive analysis period dtIC.

docs.title: Defining moored floating bodies
docs.text:
Three references must agree in the coupled example: the floating boundary in the case, the selected mooredfloatings/floating/@mkbound, and the library body/@ref used by each line's bodyref. They refer to the same physical body but belong to different XML structures.

Figure 1: Moored floating body (mkbound=50), showing the free-surface elevation z=0 m and water depth 0.45 m.

XML excerpt — floating-boundary. XML location: case/casedef/floatings. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<floating mkbound="50" relativeweight="0.5"/>

XML excerpt — library-body. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<bodies>
    <body ref="50" comment="Floating driven structure to attach mooring lines."/>
</bodies>

The earlier coupling-controls excerpt selects mkbound="50"; the body above has ref="50", and the lines below use bodyref="50". These are explicit boundary references, not the line number or the body's internal creation index. The library can default an omitted ref to a creation index in other contexts, so ref and mkbound must not be treated as universally interchangeable identifiers.

Multiple bodies are supported: for example, 04_ConnectedBoxes selects bodies 45 and 50 and connects them with a line. Each fairlead must refer to a declared body, and duplicate body references are rejected. Use the matching complete source case for its geometry and associations.

docs.title: Body-specific water depth
docs.text:
The original slide also illustrates body 45 with a depth override of 0.5 m. That is separate from the illustrated body 50 and its global 0.45 m depth. The updated stepped-tank case demonstrates the mechanism with different source values: body 50 has a depth of 0.9 m, while body 45 inherits the global depth.

XML excerpt — body-depth. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus. Source: examples/moordynplus/05_SteppedTank/CaseSteppedTank_Def.xml.

<bodies>
    <body ref="50" comment="Fluid driven object to attach mooring lines.">
        <depth value="0.9" comment="Water depth for current object. This value overwrites the global water depth only for its lines." units_comment="m"/>
    </body>
    <body ref="45" comment="Floating driven structure to attach mooring lines."/>
</bodies>

This excerpt belongs to CaseSteppedTank_Def.xml; it must not be inserted into the two-dimensional example as though it described the same system. Body depth affects the associated lines' environment and is not a replacement for checking the physical seabed and anchor coordinates.

docs.title: Mooring-line mechanical and hydrodynamic properties
docs.text:
lines/linedefault supplies shared line properties. Individual line elements can override applicable properties, as the two breaking tensions do below. Shared settings simplify a multi-line system but remain case-specific values.

XML excerpt — shared-line-properties. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus/lines. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
    <ea value="2.9e3" comment="Line stiffness, product of elasticity modulus and cross-sectional area." units_comment="N"/>
    <diameter value="3.656e-3" comment="Volume-equivalent diameter of the line." units_comment="m"/>
    <massDenInAir value="0.0607" comment="Mass per unit length of the line." units_comment="kg/m"/>
    <ba value="-0.8" comment="Line internal damping (BA/-zeta). (default=-0.8)" units_comment="Ns"/>
    <can value="1.0" comment="Transverse added mass coefficient (with respect to line displacement). (default=1.0)"/>
    <cat value="0.0" comment="Tangential added mass coefficient (with respect to line displacement). (default=0.0)"/>
    <cdn value="1.6" comment="Transverse drag coefficient (with respect to frontal area, d*l). (default=1.6)"/>
    <cdt value="0.05" comment="Tangential drag coefficient (with respect to surface area, π*d*l). (default=0.05)"/>
    <outputFlags value="p" comment="Node output properties.(default=-) [-:None|p:Positions|v:Telocities|U:Wave Velocities|t:Tension|D:Hydrodynamic Drag Force|c=Internal Damping|s:Strain of each segment|d: rate of strain of each segment]"/>
</linedefault>

docs.title: Axial stiffness and internal damping
docs.text:
The slide's stiffness relationship, confirmed by the current implementation, is

\[EA = E\,A.\]

E is Young's modulus in N/m² and A is the model cross-sectional area in m²; the XML ea therefore has units N. This is axial rigidity, not a spring constant in N/m. The implementation obtains area from the volume-equivalent diameter using the circular-area convention.

Choose either ea or e for the shared definition. Slide 6 shows e=2.76246e+08 and ea=2.9e3 together, but the current reader rejects simultaneous definitions. The excerpt retains ea alone. Do not copy the slide's two entries into executable XML.

Property Meaning Units / condition ea Product of Young's modulus and model area N; alternative to e e Young's modulus N/m²; alternative to ea diameter Volume-equivalent line diameter m massDenInAir Line mass per unit length kg/m ba Internal damping BA, or negative damping-ratio selector Positive BA: N·s; negative input: dimensionless ratio convention breaktension Tension threshold for breaking N; zero disables breaking

The source's ba="-0.8" requests automatic damping with ratio 0.8; it does not mean negative dimensional damping of −0.8 N·s. This distinction is confirmed by the implementation and current reference, despite the older blanket “Ns” comment in the case.

Slide 6 additionally illustrates shared breaktension=500 N, segments=15, length=0.2 m and flags pv. Those illustrative settings differ from the primary two-line breaking case: the source uses 40 segments, 0.45 m lengths, line-specific 300/350 N limits and flags p. The guide preserves that source case rather than combining these separate settings.

docs.title: Hydrodynamic coefficients
docs.text:
Property Meaning Reference direction / area can Transverse added-mass coefficient Normal to the line; relative to displaced volume cat Tangential added-mass coefficient Along the line; relative to displaced volume cdn Transverse drag coefficient Frontal area, diameter × segment length cdt Tangential drag coefficient Surface area, π × diameter × segment length

These coefficients are dimensionless. They control hydrodynamic loading and are separate from internal axial damping and bottom friction. The shared values 1.0, 0.0, 1.6 and 0.05 are retained from the example; they are not proposed as universal material constants.

The current format also supports bending, pretension and time-dependent property tables/files. They require their own definitions and context. No bending stiffness, target pretension or time history is invented for this example.

docs.title: Node-output flags
docs.text:
outputFlags is a case-sensitive string. Combine supported characters directly, such as the pvt used by the moored-box examples. The two-dimensional case above uses only p.

Flag Quantity - No line-node output; use alone p Node positions v Node velocities U Wave velocities t Tensions D Hydrodynamic drag forces c Internal damping d Segment strain rates s Segment strains b Bottom contact forces f Applied fluid velocities m Bending forces

The slide's uppercase C is not in the current accepted character set; use lowercase c. U and D retain their uppercase spelling, and D differs from lowercase d. A leading - disables node output in the reader; do not mix it into a purported active combination. A line's savedata="false" attribute also disables its node-output branch. Selecting a quantity does not by itself enable the physical model supplying that quantity.

docs.title: Mooring-line geometry and connections
docs.text:
Each line requires two active connection elements. The current reader accepts both vesselconnection/fixconnection used by these cases and the shorter vessel/fix names in the format reference. Vessel connections are fairleads on a declared body; fixed connections are anchors. Shared dynamic connect endpoints require a corresponding definition in connects and are a separate topology.

Figure 2: Two mooring lines connecting body 50 to fixed anchors, showing the fairlead and anchor coordinates in metres.

XML excerpt — two-lines. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus/lines. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<line>
    <vesselconnection bodyref="50" x="-0.2" y="0.0" z="-0.1"/>
    <fixconnection x="-0.4" y="0.0" z="-0.45"/>
    <length value="0.45" comment="Unstretched length." units_comment="(m)"/>
    <segments value="40"/>
    <breaktension value="300" comment="Maximun value of tension for the lines. value=0 Break Tension is not used. (default=0)" units_comment="N"/>
</line>
<line>
    <vesselconnection bodyref="50" x="0.2" y="0.0" z="-0.1"/>
    <fixconnection x="0.4" y="0.0" z="-0.45"/>
    <length value="0.45" comment="Unstretched length." units_comment="(m)"/>
    <segments value="40"/>
    <breaktension value="350" comment="Maximun value of tension for the lines. value=0 Break Tension is not used. (default=0)" units_comment="N"/>
</line>

The first line is line 0 and the second is line 1 in the reader's sequential numbering. Their IDs are not invented XML attributes. Coordinates are initial global case positions in metres; the fairlead positions are subsequently driven by the coupled body. They are not offsets to add again to the body's centre.

Setting Line 0 Line 1 Body reference 50 50 Fairlead (m) (−0.2, 0, −0.1) (0.2, 0, −0.1) Fixed anchor (m) (−0.4, 0, −0.45) (0.4, 0, −0.45) Unstretched length (m) 0.45 0.45 Segments 40 40 Breaking limit (N) 300 350

length is the unstretched line length, rather than the straight-line endpoint distance. segments specifies the discretisation: N segments have N+1 nodes, so each 40-segment line has 41 nodes. The diagram shows the mechanism; it is not a prescription to fabricate intermediate node coordinates. The model constructs its internal line nodes from the endpoints, unstretched length and discretisation.

The two limits belong to the breaking variant. The corresponding non-breaking input has the same endpoint geometry without these per-line breaking thresholds.

docs.title: Output configuration
docs.text: There are three distinct output layers: coupling VTK/force-point controls under moorings, connection quantities under moordynplus/savedata, and per-line node quantities selected by outputFlags. Enable and interpret each layer independently.

docs.title: Connection quantities and timing
docs.text:
XML excerpt — connection-output. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus. Source: examples/moordynplus/02_WavesMoorings2D/CaseMoorings2D_Break_Def.xml.

<savedata comment="Saves CSV with the connection properties.">
    <tension value="true" comment="Stores tensions at the connections.(default: value=false)"/>
    <force value="true" comment="Stores forces at the connections.(default: value=false)"/>
    <velocity value="true" comment="Stores velocities at the connections.(default: value=false)"/>
    <position value="true" comment="Stores positions at the connections.(default: value=false)"/>
</savedata>

These explicit value="true" selections request tensions, forces, velocities and positions at connections. Use false to disable a selection. Some older case comments say “default false”; the reader defaults a present selection without value to true. That is distinct from omitting the selection altogether. Explicit booleans avoid the ambiguity.

The source case omits a time child. The current reference shows how to specify one within savedata:

Reference XML excerpt — output-time. XML location: case/execution/special/moorings/moordynplus/savedata. Source: doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MoorDynPlus.xml. This is a reference option, not a complete case.

<time starTime="0" endTime="4" dtOut="0.01" comment="dtOut=0 saves all steps. Defaults: starTime=0; endTime=TimeMax; dtOut=TimeOut." units_comment="s"/>
Control Meaning Units time/@starTime Beginning of the output window s time/@endTime End of the output window s time/@dtOut Requested output interval; zero saves every output opportunity s tension/@value Connection tension selection Boolean; output N force/@value Connection force selection Boolean; output N velocity/@value Connection velocity selection Boolean; output m/s position/@value Connection position selection Boolean; output m

The actual attribute is starTime, exactly as in the screenshot and current reader. The slide's explanatory prose says startTime, but that spelling is not read here. The reference defaults are zero for the start, simulation TimeMax for the end and the supplied output interval for dtOut; the example values 0, 4 and 0.01 above are not mandatory defaults. Output is sampled when a model output opportunity reaches the requested time; this is separate from the internal dtM setting. The compatibility alias output is also accepted for the savedata section.

docs.title: Files and output locations
docs.text:
For the embedded path, the coupling creates moordynplus_data/ inside the configured simulation output directory. The writer uses the connection files MoorDynPlus_tension.csv, MoorDynPlus_force.csv, MoorDynPlus_velocity.csv and MoorDynPlus_position.csv. The corresponding selections determine which quantities are written. Current code additionally supports bending output; it is not enabled in the source excerpt.

Per-line node files are separate: for example, Line_0_pos.csv corresponds to node positions selected with p; Line_0_vel.csv and Line_0_tension.csv are velocity and tension counterparts when selected. These node files must not be confused with the connection CSVs.

Coupling geometry appears under MooringsVtk/, with Moorings_<sequence>.vtk, MooringsLines_<sequence>.vtk and MooringsNodes_<sequence>.vtk according to the enabled switches. Coupling force-point CSV/VTK data is managed by the force-point component, independently of the library's connection and node selections.

The output directory need not be named Case_out.
