The format reference is doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MoorDynPlus.xml. It contains alternative illustrations and explanatory fragments, rather than a standalone executable case. Use the complete package cases cited above for their surrounding configuration.

docs.title: Full MoorDynPlus XML format reference
docs.text:
The complete MoorDynPlus XML format reference is provided below. It documents the configuration structure, available parameters and alternative options. This is a format reference, not a standalone executable simulation case.

doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MoorDynPlus.xml

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" ?>
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** XML format for DualSPHysics-MoorDynPlus coupling.                   *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<special>
    <moorings active="true">
        <start value="4" ramptime="0" comment="Start time of the application of mooring forces with configurable ramp time. (default ramptime=0)" units_comment="s"/>
        <savevtk_lines value="true" comment="Saves VTK with mooring lines. (default=true)"/>
        <savevtk_moorings value="true" comment="Saves VTK with moorings. (default=true)"/>
        <savecsv_points value="true" comment="Saves CSV with link points. (default=true)"/>
        <savevtk_points value="false" comment="Saves VTK with link points. (default=false)"/>
        <savevtk_nodes value="true" comment="Saves VTK with node data. (default=true)"/>
        <reset_moorings value="false" comment="Restores fairlead positions in MoorDynPlus after creating force points. (default=false)"/>
        <sphfluidvel value="true" minkersum="0.1" comment="Applies the SPH velocity on nodes. minkersum must be between 0 and 1. (default=false)"/>
        <mooredfloatings>
            <floating active="true" mkbound="45" comment="Mkbound of the floating body the mooring is linked to"/>
            <floating active="true" mkbound="50" comment="Mkbound of the floating body the mooring is linked to"/>
        </mooredfloatings>
        <moordynplus active="true" file="moordynplus.xml" comment="MoorDynPlus configuration file"/>
    </moorings>
</special>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Complete structure in <moordynplus>.                                *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <solver/> %Global solver options (or <solverOptions/>)
    <waves/> %Regular waves
    <bodies/> %Fluid-driven objects
    <connects/> %Virtual connections
    <lines/> %Mooring lines
    <savedata/> %CSV output data
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Solver options in <moordynplus>.<solver>.                                                   *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <!-- A complete example. -->
    <solver>
        <gravity x="0" y="0" z="-9.81" comment="Gravity vector (x,y,z). (default=0,0,-9.81). Legacy scalar syntax: <gravity value=\"9.81\"/>." units_comment="m/s^2"/>
        <depth value="0.5" comment="Water depth. Required when <floorgeo> is not defined." units_comment="m"/>
        <freesurface value="0" comment="Z position of the water free surface. (default=0)" units_comment="m"/>
        <rho value="1000" comment="Water density. (default=1000)" units_comment="kg/m^3"/>
        <dtM value="0.0001" auto="true" comment="Maximum mooring model time step. auto=true reduces it dynamically when needed. (default=0.0001, auto=true)" units_comment="s"/>
        <kBot value="3.0e6" comment="Bottom stiffness constant. Larger values require smaller dtM." units_comment="Pa/m"/>
        <cBot value="3.0e5" comment="Bottom damping constant. Large damping can dominate the automatic dtM limit." units_comment="Pa*s/m"/>
        <friction value="0" comment="General bottom friction coefficient. (default=0.0)"/>
        <fricDamp value="200" comment="Damping coefficient used to model friction with speeds near zero. (default=200.0)" units_comment="N*s/m"/>
        <statDynFricScale value="1.0" comment="Ratio between static and dynamic friction. (default=1.0)"/>
        <dtIC value="1.0" comment="Period to analyse convergence of dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=1.0)" units_comment="s"/>
        <cdScaleIC value="5" comment="Factor to scale drag coefficients during dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=5)"/>
        <threshIC value="0.001" comment="Convergence threshold for initial conditions. (default=0.001)"/>
        <tmaxIC value="1" comment="Maximum time for initial conditions without convergence. (default=0)" units_comment="s"/>
    </solver>

    <!-- dtM automatic control. -->
    <solver>
        <!-- auto=true  -> dtM value is only a maximum. MoorDynPlus can reduce the internal substep from the current line stiffness, bending stiffness and bottom-contact damping. -->
        <!-- auto=false -> dtM value is fixed. Use only after checking stability for the selected line discretisation and contact parameters. -->
        <!-- Typical robust option for contact-heavy cases: -->
        <dtM value="0.001" auto="true" comment="MoorDynPlus internal step." units_comment="s"/>
        <!-- Fixed-step option: -->
        <dtM value="3.0e-5" auto="false" comment="MoorDynPlus internal step." units_comment="s"/>
    </solver>

    <!-- Bottom contact model used when <contact activate="true"/> is enabled in a line. -->
    <solver>
        <kBot value="3.0e6" comment="Bottom stiffness constant. Larger values require smaller dtM." units_comment="Pa/m"/>
        <cBot value="3.0e5" comment="Bottom damping constant. Large damping can dominate the automatic dtM limit." units_comment="Pa*s/m"/>
        <friction value="0" comment="General bottom friction coefficient. (default=0.0)"/>
        <fricDamp value="200" comment="Damping coefficient used to model friction with speeds near zero. (default=200.0)" units_comment="N*s/m"/>
        <statDynFricScale value="1.0" comment="Ratio between static and dynamic friction. (default=1.0)"/>
    </solver>

    <!-- Initial-condition dynamic relaxation. -->
    <solver>
        <dtIC value="1.0" comment="Period to analyse convergence of dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=1.0)" units_comment="s"/>
        <cdScaleIC value="5" comment="Factor to scale drag coefficients during dynamic relaxation for initial conditions. (default=5)"/>
        <threshIC value="0.001" comment="Convergence threshold for initial conditions. (default=0.001)"/>
        <tmaxIC value="0" comment="Maximum time for initial conditions without convergence. (default=0)" units_comment="s"/>
    </solver>

    <!-- Irregular sea floor geometry. Use this when anchors use z="auto" or when line contact needs bathymetry.-->
    <solver>
        <floorgeo file="CaseChains_FloorGeo.vtk" scell="0.1" mkbound="" zmindef="-0.5" interpolate="true" savevtk="true" comment="Compact form. Legacy VTK POLYDATA; optional mkbound filters CELL_DATA Mk values." units_comment="scell:m, zmindef:m"/>
        <!-- Alternative -->
        <floorgeo file="CaseFloorGeo.vtk" comment="External sea floor geometry in legacy VTK POLYDATA.">
            <scell value="0.1" comment="XY sampling size." units_comment="m"/>
            <mkbound value="0-10" comment="Mkbound filter."/>
            <zmindef value="-0.5" comment="Z position for points outside the geometry domain." units_comment="m"/>
            <interpolate value="true" comment="Interpolate values within the geometry."/>
            <savevtk value="true" vtkfile="SeaFloorGeo_Contact" comment="VTK file name for the contact geometry."/>
        </floorgeo>
    </solver>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Regular waves in <moordynplus>.<waves>.                                                     *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <waves>
    <start value="4" comment="Start time. (default=0)" units_comment="s"/>
    <depth value="8" comment="Fluid depth for wave generation." units_comment="m"/>
    <pistonpos x="-15.5" y="0" z="0" comment="Position of the piston-type wavemaker. (default=(1,0,0))" units_comment="m"/>
    <waveheight value="2" comment="Regular wave height." units_comment="m"/>
    <waveperiod value="4" comment="Regular wave period." units_comment="s"/>
    </waves>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Fluid-driven objects in <moordynplus>.<bodies>.                                     *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <bodies>
        <body ref="45" comment="Fluid-driven object to attach mooring lines.."/>
        <body ref="50" comment="Fluid-driven object to attach mooring lines.">
            <depth value="0.5" comment="Water depth for this body. Overrides the global water depth only for its lines." units_comment="m"/>
        </body>
    </bodies>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Shared connections in <moordynplus>.<connects>.                                     *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <connects>
        <connect conref="0" x="-50.0" y="0.0" z="-20.0" M="1000" V="120" comment="Shared dynamic connection." units_comment="x/y/z:m, M:kg, V:m^3">
        <connect conref="1" x="-60.0" y="0.0" z="-20.0" M="1000" V="120" comment="Shared dynamic connection." units_comment="x/y/z:m, M:kg, V:m^3">
            <coeffini cda="0.0" ca="0.0" comment="Optional hydrodynamic coefficients for dynamic connect nodes." units_comment="cda:m^2"/>
        </connect>
    </connects>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Mooring lines structure in <moordynplus>.<lines>.                           *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <linedefault/> %Defines shared default properties for all lines.
    <line/> %Defines each line (one or more) with its own properties and connections.
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Default line properties in <moordynplus>.<lines>.<linedefault>.       *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <lines>
    <!-- Shared defaults used by every <line> unless a line overrides a property. Only one <linedefault> block is allowed. -->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <e value="2.76246e+08" comment="Young's modulus. Alternative to <ea>; EA is calculated as E*Area." units_comment="N/m^2"/>
        <diameter value="3.656e-3" comment="Volume-equivalent diameter of the line." units_comment="m"/>
        <massDenInAir value="0.0607" comment="Mass per unit length of the line." units_comment="kg/m"/>
        <ba value="-0.8" comment="Line internal damping (BA/-zeta). (default=-0.8)" units_comment="Ns"/>
        <can value="1.0" comment="Transverse added mass coefficient. (default=1.0)"/>
        <cat value="0.0" comment="Tangential added mass coefficient. (default=0.0)"/>
        <cdn value="1.6" comment="Transverse drag coefficient. (default=1.6)"/>
        <cdt value="0.05" comment="Tangential drag coefficient. (default=0.05)"/>
        <contact activate="true" comment="Enable bottom contact forces for this line. (default=true)"/>
        <segments value="15" comment="Number of line segments."/>
        <length value="0.2" comment="Unstretched length. Define only <length> or <pretension>." units_comment="m"/>
        <breaktension value="120" comment="Maximum tension before breaking. value=0 disables breaking." units_comment="N"/>
        <outputFlags value="pv" comment="Common node output flags. Use the zoom block below for all flags."/>
    </linedefault>

    <!-- Material alternatives, use EA directly and E will be calculated -->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <ea value="2.9e3" comment="Line stiffness EA. Alternative to <e>." units_comment="N"/>
    </linedefault>

    <!-- Pretensioned lines. Use <pretension> instead of <length> and the line will be generated with the initial tension (N) . -->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <pretension value="20" comment="Initial target tension used to compute unstretched length." units_comment="N"/>
    </linedefault>

    <!-- Disable line-bottom contact for lines.-->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <contact activate="false" comment="Line ignores bottom contact forces."/>
    </linedefault>

    <!-- Break tension. It can be defined fo the whole line or within a range of nodes. -->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <breaktension value="120" comment="Maximum tension before breaking. value=0 disables breaking." units_comment="N"/> % This applies to the whole line.
        <breaktension value="150" firstnode="4" lastnode="14" comment="Maximum tension before breaking. value=0 disables breaking." units_comment="N"/> %This applies only to nodes 1..14.
    </linedefault>

    <!-- Full output properties for nodes. -->
    <linedefault comment="Shared properties for each line.">
        <outputFlags value="pvUDtcbsfdm" comment="[-:None|p:Positions|v:Velocities|U:Wave Velocities|D:Hydrodynamic Drag Force|t:Tension|c:Internal Damping|b:Bottom contact force|s:Strain|f:Fluid velocity|d:Segment strain rate|m:Bending force]"/>
    </linedefault>
    </lines>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Mooring line definition in <moordynplus>.<lines>.<line>.              *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <lines>
        <!-- Body-to-anchor line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
            <fix x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.50" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>
        </line>

        <!-- Body-to-body line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
            <vessel bodyref="50" x="0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.50" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
        </line>

        <!-- Connect-to-connect line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <connect conref="0" comment="Connect connection."/>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Connect connection."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Body-to-connect line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Connect connection."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Body-to-connect line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Connect connection."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Connect-to-fix line. Exactly two active connection elements are required. -->
        <line>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Connect connection."/>
            <fix x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.5" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>
        </line>

        <!-- Calculate Z-position automatically. It will set the Z-coordinate based on the floor (WaterDepth/depth/floorgeo). -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body." units_comment="m"/>
            <fix x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="auto" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/> %Use z="auto" to set the Z-coordinate based on the floor.
        </line>

        <!-- Line with local material and drag overrides. -->
        <line>
            <vessel bodyref="50" x="-0.55" y="0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=50." units_comment="m"/>
            <fix x="-0.5" y="0.0" z="-2.5" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>
            <length value="1.2" comment="Unstretched length." units_comment="m"/>
            <segments value="24" comment="Number of line segments."/>
            <ea value="3.1e3" comment="Per-line stiffness override. Define only <ea> or <e>." units_comment="N"/>
            <diameter value="2.956e-3" comment="Per-line diameter override." units_comment="m"/>
            <cdn value="1.8" comment="Per-line transverse drag coefficient override."/>
            <cdt value="0.08" comment="Per-line tangential drag coefficient override."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Shared dynamic connection and pretension instead of length.-->
        <line>
            <vesselconnection bodyref="45" x="0.7" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=45." units_comment="m"/>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Reference to a shared dynamic connection in <connects>."/>
            <pretension value="10" comment="Alternative to <length>; computes unstretched length from target axial tension." units_comment="N"/>
            <segments value="10" comment="Number of line segments."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Disable output data for a line.-->
        <line savedata="false">
            <vesselconnection bodyref="45" x="0.7" y="0.0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=45." units_comment="m"/>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Reference to a shared dynamic connection in <connects>."/>
            <pretension value="10" comment="Alternative to <length>; computes unstretched length from target axial tension." units_comment="N"/>
            <segments value="10" comment="Number of line segments."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Disable bottom contact for one line.-->
        <line>
            <connect conref="1" comment="Reference to a shared dynamic connection in <connects>."/>
            <fixconnection x="0.7" y="0.0" z="-2.5" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>
            <length value="0.45" comment="Unstretched length." units_comment="m"/>
            <contact activate="false" comment="Disable bottom contact only for this line."/>
        </line>

        <!-- Bathymetry-aware anchor, bending and break tension. -->
        <line savedata="true">
            <vesselconnection bodyref="50" x="-0.75" y="0" z="-2.0" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=50." units_comment="m"/>
            <fixconnection x="1.25" y="0.0" z="auto" comment="z=auto uses floorgeo/bathymetry when available." units_comment="m"/>
            <length value="1.6" comment="Unstretched length." units_comment="m"/>
            <segments value="32" comment="Number of line segments."/>
            <bending value="1.0e6" comment="Per-line bending stiffness override." units_comment="N*m^2"/>
            <breaktension value="500" firstnode="1" lastnode="31" comment="Break tension and active node range." units_comment="N"/>
            <outputFlags value="tbsdm" comment="Save tension, bottom contact, strain, strain rate and bending force."/>
        </line>
    </lines>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Variable line properties definition in <moordynplus>.<lines>.<line>.*** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>
    <lines>
        <!-- Inline time-variable values. Use either <ea> or <e>, not both in the same line.-->
        <line comment="Inline variable values using EA.">
            <vessel bodyref="45" x="0.25" y="0.75" z="-1.8" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=45." units_comment="m"/>
            <fix x="-1.2" y="0.75" z="-2.5" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>

            <!-- Variable EA -->
            <ea comment="Variable line stiffness EA. Interpolated linearly in time." units_comment="N">
                <c time="0" value="2.9e3" comment="Initial EA value." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
                <c time="5" value="3.4e3" comment="EA value at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
            </ea>

            <!-- Variable E -->
            <e comment="Variable Young's modulus. Interpolated linearly in time." units_comment="N/m^2">
                <c time="0" value="2.76246e+08" comment="Initial Young's modulus." units_comment="time:s, value:N/m^2"/>
                <c time="5" value="3.00000e+08" comment="Young's modulus at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s, value:N/m^2"/>
            </e>

            <!-- Variable line internal damping -->
            <ba comment="Variable line internal damping. Negative values are interpreted as damping ratio." units_comment="Ns">
                <c time="0" value="-0.8" comment="Initial BA value or damping ratio." units_comment="time:s, value:Ns or ratio"/>
                <c time="5" value="-0.5" comment="BA value or damping ratio at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s, value:Ns or ratio"/>
            </ba>

            <!-- Variable transverse drag coefficient -->
            <cdn comment="Variable transverse drag coefficient.">
                <c time="0" value="1.6" comment="Initial transverse drag coefficient." units_comment="time:s"/>
                <c time="5" value="2.0" comment="Transverse drag coefficient at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s"/>
            </cdn>

            <!-- Variable tangential drag coefficient -->
            <cdt comment="Variable tangential drag coefficient.">
                <c time="0" value="0.05" comment="Initial tangential drag coefficient." units_comment="time:s"/>
                <c time="5" value="0.08" comment="Tangential drag coefficient at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s"/>
            </cdt>

            <!-- Variable bending stiffness -->
            <bending comment="Variable bending stiffness. value<=0 disables bending at that time." units_comment="N*m^2">
                <c time="0" value="1.0e6" comment="Initial bending stiffness." units_comment="time:s, value:N*m^2"/>
                <c time="5" value="5.0e5" comment="Bending stiffness at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s, value:N*m^2"/>
            </bending>

            <!-- Variable break tension -->
            <breaktension firstnode="1" lastnode="14" comment="Variable break tension. Omit firstnode/lastnode to apply it to the whole line. value=0 disables breaking at that time." units_comment="N">
                <c time="0" value="500" comment="Initial break tension." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
                <c time="5" value="350" comment="Break tension at t=5 s." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
            </breaktension>
        </line>

        <!-- File-based time-variable values. File paths are relative to the MoorDynPlus XML file; columns: time value.-->
        <line comment="File-based variable values using EA.">
            <vessel bodyref="50" x="0.25" y="0.75" z="-1.8" comment="Fairlead linked to body ref=50." units_comment="m"/>
            <fix x="-1.2" y="0.75" z="-2.5" comment="Fixed anchor." units_comment="m"/>
            <ea file="LineEA_Time.csv" comment="Variable line stiffness EA. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
            <e file="LineE_Time.csv" comment="Variable Young's modulus. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:N/m^2"/>
            <ba file="LineBA_Time.csv" comment="Variable line internal damping. Negative values are interpreted as damping ratio. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:Ns or ratio"/>
            <cdn file="LineCDN_Time.csv" comment="Variable transverse drag coefficient. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:-"/>
            <cdt file="LineCDT_Time.csv" comment="Variable tangential drag coefficient. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:-"/>
            <bending file="LineBending_Time.csv" comment="Variable bending stiffness. value<=0 disables bending at that time. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:N*m^2"/>
            <breaktension file="LineBreakTension_Time.csv" comment="Variable break tension. columns: time value." units_comment="time:s, value:N"/>
        </line>
    </lines>
</moordynplus>

<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<!-- *** Line output section in <moordynplus>.<savedata>.                    *** -->
<!-- --------------------------------------------------------------------------- -->
<moordynplus>

docs.title: Multiphase non-Newtonian
docs.text:
Under review by Georgios Fourtakas

Phase-dependent fluid properties, Herschel–Buckley–Papanastasiou rheology and the bi-viscosity alternative.

docs.title: Scope and software context
docs.text:
The multiphase non-Newtonian formulation described here is the specialised DualSPHysics v5.0 non-Newtonian module, documented in July 2020. It represents fluids with phase-dependent density and rheological properties. A phase identifies a material population; a non-Newtonian constitutive model describes how its response changes with deformation. Several phases can therefore have different properties without every phase necessarily exhibiting non-Newtonian behaviour.

The available module documentation describes the Herschel–Buckley–Papanastasiou (HBP) formulation and a Bingham bi-viscosity alternative. It also distinguishes two velocity-gradient approximations and alternative viscous-force operators. These choices describe different parts of the numerical formulation and must be considered together.

The XML examples below retain the conventions of that module. They are not established executable configurations for the principal DualSPHysics v6 solver. In particular, the module-specific constitutive-force selector must not be replaced by a similarly numbered v6 viscosity option: the meanings differ. A compatible module version and its corresponding configuration specification are required before using these examples with another release.

docs.title: Linking materials to particle blocks
docs.text:
Phase definitions belong to case/execution/special/nnphases. Each lowercase phase element has a mkfluid attribute that associates its material properties with the fluid block created by the corresponding setmkfluid command in case/casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist.

The following two excerpts illustrate that association in the documented v5.0 configuration. They show selected geometry commands and their corresponding phase definitions, rather than a complete case.

XML excerpt — phase-geometry. Historical module context; XML location: case/casedef/geometry/commands/mainlist. Source: July 2020 module description.

<setmkfluid mk="0" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0" />
    <size x="4" y="2" z="0.5" />
</drawbox>
<setmkfluid mk="1" />
<drawbox>
    <boxfill>solid</boxfill>
    <point x="0" y="0" z="0.50" />
    <size x="1" y="2" z="0.25" />
</drawbox>

XML excerpt — two-phase-definition. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution. Source: July 2020 module description.

<special>
    <nnphases>
        <phase mkfluid="0">
            <rhop value="1000" />
            <visco value="0.2" />
            <tau_yield value="0.0001" />
            <HBP_m value="100" />
            <HBP_n value="2" />
            <phasetype value="0" />
        </phase>
        <phase mkfluid="1">
            <rhop value="1000" />
            <visco value="0.1" />
            <tau_yield value="0.001" />
            <HBP_m value="10" />
            <HBP_n value="1" />
            <phasetype value="0" />
        </phase>
    </nnphases>
</special>

mkfluid="0" and mkfluid="1" refer to the two fluid blocks; they are not a count of all supported phases. Geometry, boundary particles, constants and execution controls still have to be supplied by the surrounding case. The reference uses phasetype=0 and describes it as the only non-Newtonian phase type available in the documented historical module; this does not define an enumeration for other releases.

docs.title: Density and equation-of-state properties
Material parameters
docs.text:
The HBP description uses four principal material parameters: viscosity or consistency, specific yield stress, the flow index and the exponential stress-growth parameter.

Element Meaning in the module documentation Interpretation visco Kinematic viscosity or consistency index A phase property, distinct from the global execution parameter Visco tau_yield Specific yield stress Yield stress divided by density HBP_m Papanastasiou exponential stress-growth parameter Controls the regularisation of the yield contribution; the reference gives seconds HBP_n Herschel–Buckley flow index 1 gives a linear contribution; values below or above 1 describe shear thinning or shear thickening

The specific-yield-stress convention is

\[ \tau_{\mathrm{specific}}=\frac{\tau_{\mathrm{yield,dimensional}}}{\rho}. \]

The reference expresses its units as Pa m³/kg. A dimensional yield stress must therefore not be inserted directly in a field defined as a specific stress. The reference labels visco as m²/s while also using the term consistency index. It does not establish the general dimensional convention for non-unit flow index; that label alone is insufficient to define a conversion for a material with \(n\ne1\).

This historical material-property excerpt retains the values in the documented HBP example.

XML excerpt — hbp-material. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution/special/nnphases/phase[@mkfluid="0"]. Source: July 2020 module description.

<visco value="0.2" />
<tau_yield value="0.0001" />
<HBP_m value="100" />
<HBP_n value="2" />
<phasetype value="0" />

docs.title: Stress-growth parameter
docs.text:
The documented comparison varies \(m\) between 0, 10 and 100. Increasing this parameter changes the regularised response near yielding. The chart labels describe the illustrated curves; they do not make HBP_m a universal switch between complete constitutive models independently of the other parameters.

Figure 1: Illustrated HBP shear-stress response for the stress-growth comparison. The documented curves correspond to m = 0, 10 and 100. Illustrated value Curve Label in the documented comparison Interpretation of the comparison \(m=0\) Blue Newtonian The yield regularisation contribution is suppressed; a Newtonian reduction also requires the linear flow-index setting \(m=10\) Gold Power law Finite stress-growth example; the accompanying description also refers to pseudo-Bingham behaviour \(m=100\) Green Bingham A sharper regularised yield response in the illustrated configuration

A statement that setting \(m=0\) alone makes every possible HBP parameter combination Newtonian would be too broad. Yield stress, flow index and consistency remain part of the material definition.

docs.title: Flow index
docs.text:
HBP_n controls the flow-index dependence. The documented comparison uses \(n=0.8\), \(n=1\) and \(n=2\).

Figure 2: Illustrated HBP shear-stress response for flow indices n = 0.8, 1 and 2. Illustrated value Curve Documented response \(n=0.8\) Blue Shear thinning \(n=1\) Gold Newtonian comparison / linear contribution \(n=2\) Green Shear thickening

These plots are schematic comparisons, not tabulated calibration data or validation results for a particular material. Their interpretation depends on the remaining HBP settings. The distinction between HBP_m and HBP_n follows the actual XML elements: the former controls exponential stress growth and the latter is the flow index.

docs.title: Bingham bi-viscosity alternative
docs.text:
The module documents a bi-viscosity alternative intended to avoid the singularity and large viscosity values of the ideal Bingham model. It uses the following pair of phase properties.

Element Documented role Dependency tau_max Specific Bingham yield-stress quantity Used together with Bi_multi Bi_multi Bi-viscosity multiplier Both elements must be supplied when this alternative is required

XML excerpt — bi-viscosity-pair. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution/special/nnphases/phase[@mkfluid="1"]. Source: July 2020 module description.

<tau_yield value="0.001" />
<tau_max value="0.001" />
<Bi_multi value="10.0" />

The historical module description presents tau_max and Bi_multi as overriding the Papanastasiou stress-growth setting. This does not establish that a non-zero HBP_m is inactive in every implementation of the bi-viscosity alternative. Its effective role requires confirmation for the selected module build.

The reference comment expresses the multiplier relationship as

\[ \tau_{\mathrm{bi}}=\tau_{\mathrm{max}}\,\mathrm{Bi}_{\mathrm{multi}}. \]

The symbols correspond to the reference names tau_bi, tau_max and Bi_multi. This reproduces the relationship named in the reference; it does not define an additional XML element or a complete piecewise viscosity law. The source description refers to multiplication in the yielded region, but does not provide enough mathematical detail to reconstruct all regions or threshold conventions from that statement alone.

docs.title: Stress and viscosity near the origin
docs.text:
The documented comparison contrasts the ideal Bingham response with the regularised HBP response. The ideal Bingham apparent viscosity becomes singular as shear rate approaches zero, whereas the illustrated HBP curve remains finite at the origin.

Figure 3: Comparison of ideal Bingham and regularised HBP shear-stress responses near yielding.

Figure 4: Comparison of the apparent-viscosity responses as shear rate approaches zero; the regularised HBP curve remains finite in this illustration.

In both comparisons, the gold curve represents the ideal Bingham response and the blue curve represents the regularised HBP response.

The finite value shown is a property of the illustrated regularised comparison. It is not evidence of a finite zero-shear viscosity for every possible flow index or every parameter combination. The available description supplies these response curves and parameter meanings, rather than a complete analytical HBP equation or a detailed SPH constitutive-stress discretisation.

docs.title: Velocity gradients and viscous forces
docs.text:
The v5.0 module separates the rheology treatment, velocity-gradient calculation and viscous-force evaluation.

Execution parameter Documented module options Qualification RheologyTreatment 1: single-phase classic; 2: single and multiphase The historical presentation restricts the implementation to option 2, despite the reference listing both VelocityGradientType 1: pairwise finite-difference approach; 2: symmetric SPH gradient A gradient choice, distinct from the viscous-force operator ViscoTreatment 1: artificial viscosity; 2: laminar/Morris operator, labelled Laminar+SPS in the XML; 3: full constitutive equation Artificial viscosity is described for Newtonian fluids only RelaxationDt Relaxation parameter for the viscous time-step restriction The module reference gives 0.2 as its default; examples may use other values

The method description associates the laminar viscous force with the Morris (1997) operator and distinguishes it from evaluation through the full constitutive equation using SPH. Selecting the same velocity-gradient approximation does not make these force formulations equivalent. The source does not provide a complete governing-equation or boundary-discretisation specification, so no additional stress law, integration guarantee or boundary combination is implied here.

The following controls are an exact selection from the non-Newtonian Poiseuille case for the specialised module.

XML excerpt — module-solver-controls. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/mphase_nnewtonian/05_Poiseuille/CasePoiseuilleNN_Def.xml.

<parameter key="RheologyTreatment" value="2" comment="Reology formulation 1:Single-phase classic, 2: Single and multi-phase" />
<parameter key="VelocityGradientType" value="1" comment="Velocity gradient formulation 1:FDA, 2:SPH" />
<parameter key="ViscoTreatment" value="2" comment="Viscosity formulation 1:Artificial, 2:Laminar+SPS, 3:Constitutive  eq." />
<parameter key="RelaxationDt" value="0.2" comment="Relaxation parameter for the viscous time step restricition(default=0.2)" />

The principal v6 parameter reference instead documents ViscoTreatment using LAM and ART, with turbulence configured separately. Its treatment of old numerical options does not establish an equivalent non-Newtonian constitutive formulation. In particular, the module's option 3 must retain its original meaning when interpreting historical cases.

docs.title: Viscous time-step relaxation
docs.text:
The documented relaxation relationship is

\[ \lambda=\frac{1}{\texttt{RelaxationDt}}. \]

For the illustrated RelaxationDt=0.2, this gives \(\lambda=5\). The presentation identifies this as part of the viscous-force time-step restriction, but does not specify a complete restriction formula. It must not be treated as a fixed time step or as a complete CFL condition.

The Newtonian Poiseuille comparison uses a different value:

XML excerpt — newtonian-relaxation. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/mphase_nnewtonian/05_Poiseuille/CasePoiseuille_Def.xml.

<parameter key="RelaxationDt" value="1.0" comment="Relaxation parameter for the viscous time step restricition(default=0.2)" />

That case-specific value is preserved here. It is not a recommendation to replace the non-Newtonian case's 0.2 by 1.0.

docs.title: Historical example configurations
docs.text: The examples in this section are supplied for the specialised v5.0 module. They illustrate material definitions and operator choices; they do not establish execution compatibility with the principal v6 solver. Each excerpt requires its original surrounding geometry, constants, boundary configuration and execution settings.

docs.title: Two-layer Poiseuille flow
docs.text:
The package directory examples/mphase_nnewtonian/05_Poiseuille/ contains CasePoiseuille_Def.xml and CasePoiseuilleNN_Def.xml. Both define two fluid blocks with density 1000 and visco=0.1, driven by an x-directed acceleration of 0.1 m/s². Their initial particle spacing is 0.025 m.

XML excerpt — poiseuille-driving. Historical module context; XML location: case/casedef/constantsdef. Source: examples/mphase_nnewtonian/05_Poiseuille/CasePoiseuilleNN_Def.xml.

<gravity x="0.1" y="0" z="0" comment="Gravitational acceleration" units_comment="m/s^2" />
Input mkfluid tau_yield HBP_m HBP_n RelaxationDt CasePoiseuille_Def.xml 0 0.000 1 1 1.0 CasePoiseuille_Def.xml 1 0.000 1 1 1.0 CasePoiseuilleNN_Def.xml 0 0.000 1 1 0.2 CasePoiseuilleNN_Def.xml 1 0.04 10 1 0.2

The non-Newtonian input changes the second phase's yield and stress-growth properties, and its time-step relaxation also differs. It is therefore not a comparison in which only the material yield stress changes. All four phase entries retain phasetype=0.

docs.title: Three-phase wet dam break
docs.text:
examples/mphase_nnewtonian/01_WetDambreak/CaseWetDambreak2DNN_Def.xml defines three materials with the following properties.

mkfluid rhop visco tau_yield HBP_m HBP_n 0 2000 0.2 0.0001 100 1.5 1 1500 0.1 0.001 10 1 2 1000 0.05 0.0005 0 1

All three entries use phasetype=0. The density ratio between the densest and least dense phases is two. The source retains a non-zero tau_yield in phase 2 alongside HBP_m=0; neither value has been replaced by an inferred default. The model interpretation must account for the stress-growth setting together with the flow index.

docs.title: Three-dimensional dam break and bi-viscosity
docs.text:
examples/mphase_nnewtonian/02_Dambreak3D/CaseDambreakNN_Def.xml uses two phases. Phase 0 has rhop=1000, visco=0.1, tau_yield=0.001, HBP_m=10 and HBP_n=1.5, together with the following bi-viscosity pair.

XML excerpt — dambreak-bi-viscosity. Historical module context; XML location: case/execution/special/nnphases/phase[@mkfluid="0"]. Source: examples/mphase_nnewtonian/02_Dambreak3D/CaseDambreakNN_Def.xml.

<tau_max value="0.0015" comment="User defined maximum specific yield stress of phase (Pa m3/kg)" />
<Bi_multi value="10.0" comment="tau_max multiplier for use with Bingham model or bi-viscosity model(tau_bi=tau_max*Bi_multi)" />

Phase 1 has rhop=1200, visco=0.01, tau_yield=0.0005, HBP_m=0 and HBP_n=1. Both phases retain phasetype=0. The phase-0 HBP_m value remains in the input; its role in the bi-viscosity alternative requires confirmation for the selected module build.

docs.title: Other supplied configurations
docs.text:
The same specialised-module family also supplies the following inputs. These are examples of different material and operator selections, rather than independently established v6 configurations.

Package directory and input Phase markers VelocityGradientType Module ViscoTreatment RelaxationDt 03_LockGate/CaseLockGateNN_Def.xml 0, 1 2 3 0.2 04_SloshingMotion/CaseSloshingMotionNN_Def.xml 0–4 1 3 0.2 06_Impellers3D/CaseImpellersNN_Def.xml 0–2 1 2 0.5

These paths are relative to examples/mphase_nnewtonian/. The lock-gate and sloshing inputs illustrate the historical constitutive-force option 3. The impeller input supplies tau_max and Bi_multi for all three phases. Their different relaxation and rheological values should be retained when examining the original configurations.

docs.title: Full Multiphase Non-Newtonian XML format reference
docs.text:
The directly relevant package reference is doc/xml_format/_FmtXML_MphaseNNewtonian.xml. Its header dates it to 5 April 2020, for DualSPHysics-NNewtonian. The complete text below preserves that historical module reference, including its alternative examples and comments. It is a syntax-and-options source for that module, not a complete executable simulation or a certified v6 configuration.

The reference also contains malformed separator comments, literal less-than signs in attribute text, a missing attribute name in its RelaxationDt line and several alternative top-level blocks. These features are retained verbatim for reference fidelity. Consequently, the complete block is not a well-formed standalone XML document and should not be copied wholesale as a simulation input. The focused excerpts above distinguish selected well-formed elements from this unaltered reference.

docs.title: Advanced shifting
docs.text:
Under review by Francesco Ricci and Renato Vacondio

Particle regularisation, free-surface treatment, ALE transport corrections and non-conservative pressure in DualSPHysics v6.

docs.title: Purpose and choice of method
docs.text:
Particle shifting introduces a numerical displacement to regularise the SPH particle distribution. In a fully Lagrangian calculation, particles follow the fluid motion and can develop irregular spacing, which affects the approximation of spatial operators. Shifting changes their computational positions to address this distribution error. The shift is distinct from the physical fluid velocity and from a change to prescribed wall motion.

DualSPHysics distinguishes standard shifting from Advanced Shifting. The advanced method uses a concentration-gradient displacement with a different diffusion scaling, geometric identification of the free surface and treatment of particles near that surface. Optional Arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian (ALE) corrections account for the difference between material and particle transport velocities. The non-conservative pressure option changes the pressure-gradient operator and its conservation properties.

These functions are distinct from density diffusion, divergence cleaning, boundary reconstruction and structural hourglass suppression. Their parameters cannot be substituted for one another simply because each addresses a numerical error.

Shifting Current XML meaning Configuration family 0 No shifting Default when no shifting model is selected 1 Ignore boundary Standard shifting; suppresses shifts near boundary particles 2 Ignore fixed boundary Standard shifting; suppresses shifts near fixed boundaries 3 Full standard shifting Standard coefficient and free-surface threshold 4 Full advanced shifting Advanced coefficient, ALE and non-conservative-pressure options

The selector remains numeric in v6. Advanced parameters do not activate the method unless the selected mode is 4, and they are not used by the standard modes. The word full does not remove the advanced method's free-surface, boundary and displacement restrictions.

docs.title: Concentration-gradient displacement
docs.text:
The formulation presented by Lind et al. expresses the basic shift as

\[ abla C_a=\sum_b abla W_{ab}V_b,\qquad\delta\mathbf{x}_a=-D abla C_a,\qquad D=A h^2. \]

Here \(C_a\) is particle concentration, \(W_{ab}\) is the smoothing kernel, \(V_b\) is neighbour volume and \(h\) is smoothing length. The displacement follows the negative concentration gradient. \(A\) is a positive dimensionless magnitude in this theoretical expression. \(D\) has units of length squared in this per-update displacement formula; it is not the physical viscosity.

The standard Skillen scaling shown for comparison is

\[ D_{\mathrm{standard}}=A\lVert\mathbf{u}_a Vert h\,\Delta t. \]

The dependence on fluid speed and time step differs from \(A h^2\). Consequently, the standard value ShiftCoef=-2 and the advanced value ShiftAdvCoef=-0.01 are not interchangeable coefficients.

docs.title: Strength, sign and implementation limits
docs.text:
The documented advanced coefficient is negative: the default is ShiftAdvCoef=-0.01. The original XML Guide discusses values from −0.1 for flows with strong velocity gradients to −0.01. These are source recommendations, rather than a tested admissible range or an instruction to choose the larger magnitude for every flow. In the theoretical expression, the minus sign is written separately and \(A\) is positive. Preserve the negative XML convention instead of copying positive \(A\) directly into a case.

The current CPU and GPU calculation forms a negative magnitude using the absolute coefficient. It also limits the shift using a density-variation measure and distance to the free surface, then caps the computed displacement magnitude at 0.1 times the initial particle spacing, dp, before converting it to a shifting velocity. Thus \(D=A h^2\) describes the base scaling rather than every limiter in the implementation. Reversing the sign of the XML coefficient must not be assumed to reverse the displacement.

The calculation uses the time increment when forming its velocity correction. The absence of an explicit time step in \(A h^2\) does not make the complete algorithm independent of time integration. A 2D calculation suppresses the out-of-plane y component. The current implementation rejects Advanced Shifting with Verlet; retain the complete source case's Symplectic selection.

docs.title: Candidate screening and the umbrella region
docs.text:
A truncated neighbourhood near a free surface can produce a concentration gradient even when the particle distribution is physically appropriate. Unrestricted shifting in the surface-normal direction would then move the interface artificially. Advanced Shifting first identifies surface candidates and scans an umbrella region oriented along an estimated outward normal. The presence of neighbours in that region distinguishes an interior particle from one adjacent to an empty region. The search includes the surrounding particle neighbourhood and its boundary context.

The current advanced screening uses position-divergence thresholds of 1.7 in 2D and 2.75 in 3D, with further screening and the umbrella test. These are internal criteria, not a new XML parameter range. ShiftTFS belongs to the standard configuration and does not control these Advanced Shifting thresholds, even when retained in a complete case's parameter list.

Figure 1: Umbrella region oriented along the estimated surface normal. Regions S₁ and S₂, point T and smoothing-length dimensions define the neighbourhood geometry for surface identification.

docs.title: Corrected and smoothed normals
docs.text:
A corrected concentration gradient supplies the initial normal:

\[ \mathbf{n}_a=-\frac{\mathbf{L}_a\cdot\nabla C_a}{\lVert\mathbf{L}_a\cdot\nabla C_a\rVert}. \]

\(\mathbf{L}_a\) is the Bonet–Lok correction matrix. For particles interacting with the free surface, the formulation averages surface-particle normals using kernel and volume weights:

\[ \overline{\mathbf{n}}_a=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{b\in\Omega_F}\mathbf{n}_b W_{ab}V_b}{\displaystyle\sum_{b\in\Omega_F}W_{ab}V_b}. \]

\(\Omega_F\) denotes the free-surface particles. The current reconstruction normalises the weighted direction for projection. This surface normal is a fluid-neighbourhood quantity. It is not the displacement vector from a solid boundary particle to the wall surface used by mDBC.

Figure 2: Surface-normal directions within the kernel neighbourhood of particle a. Radius 2h identifies the support shown in the formulation diagram.

docs.title: Tangential shifting and exclusions
docs.text:
For the surface treatment described by the formulation, the tangential projection is

\[ \delta\mathbf{x}_{\tau a}=\delta\mathbf{x}_a\cdot\left(\mathbf{I}-\overline{\mathbf{n}}_a\otimes\overline{\mathbf{n}}_a\right). \]

The near-surface treatment reduces the normal component according to distance from the free surface. The current implementation makes an important distinction: surface and near-surface particles receive this projected shift when ALE is active; without ALE their shift is set to zero. Interior particles retain the applicable limited shift. Enabling Advanced Shifting alone must therefore not be described as applying the same tangential treatment in both configurations.

Particles classified for exclusion receive no shift. Boundary proximity can exclude near-surface particles, and surface particles interacting with a boundary or showing a large change in normal direction can have their shift suppressed. Geometry, resolution and available neighbours therefore affect the applied displacement. The projection is not an unconditional instruction to move every particle next to a wall.

docs.title: Material and transport velocities
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{u}\) denote physical fluid velocity and \(\widehat{\mathbf{u}}\) the numerical shifting velocity. The workshop defines

\[ egin{gathered}\mathbf{u}_0=\mathbf{u}+ rac{\delta\mathbf{x}}{\Delta t},\\widehat{\mathbf{u}}= rac{\delta\mathbf{x}}{\Delta t}=\mathbf{u}_0-\mathbf{u},\qquad rac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt}=\mathbf{u}_0.\end{gathered} \]

\(\mathbf{u}_0\) is the transport velocity of computational particles. For a scalar \(\phi\), the material and ALE derivatives satisfy

\[ rac{d\phi}{dt}=\left. rac{\partial\phi}{\partial t} ight|_{\mathrm{ALE}}+\left(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{u}_0 ight)\cdot abla\phi. \]

This distinction generates additional advection terms in continuity and momentum. In the workshop's continuum notation,

\[ egin{aligned}\left. rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} ight|_{\mathrm{ALE}}-\widehat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot abla ho&=- ho abla\cdot\mathbf{u},\\left. rac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} ight|_{\mathrm{ALE}}-\widehat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot abla\mathbf{u}&=- rac{1}{ ho} abla P+ oldsymbol{\Gamma}+\mathbf{f}.\end{aligned} \]

Here \( ho\) is density, \(P\) pressure, \( oldsymbol{\Gamma}\) the viscous contribution and \(\mathbf{f}\) body-force acceleration. The ALE terms account for computational transport; they do not represent an additional physical fluid velocity imposed by an inlet or moving wall.

docs.title: Continuity and momentum corrections
docs.text:
The continuity equation separates a transport-divergence term and a density flux:

\[ \left. rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} ight|_{\mathrm{ALE}}=- ho abla\cdot\left(\mathbf{u}+\widehat{\mathbf{u}} ight)+ abla\cdot\left( ho\widehat{\mathbf{u}} ight). \]

The documented SPH operators for these terms are

\[ egin{aligned} ho_a abla\cdot\left(\mathbf{u}+\widehat{\mathbf{u}} ight)_a&= ho_a\sum_b(\mathbf{u}_b-\mathbf{u}_a)\cdot abla W_{ab}V_b\&\quad+ ho_a\sum_b(\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_b-\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_a)\cdot abla W_{ab}V_b,\ abla\cdot\left( ho\widehat{\mathbf{u}} ight)_a&=\sum_b( ho_b\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_b+ ho_a\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_a)\cdot abla W_{ab}V_b.\end{aligned} \]

The corresponding momentum correction separates a tensor flux and the divergence of shifting velocity:

\[ egin{aligned}\left. rac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} ight|_{\mathrm{ALE}}&= abla\cdot(\mathbf{u}\otimes\widehat{\mathbf{u}})-\mathbf{u} abla\cdot\widehat{\mathbf{u}}+\cdots,\ abla\cdot(\mathbf{u}\otimes\widehat{\mathbf{u}})_a&=\sum_b(\mathbf{u}_a\otimes\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_a+\mathbf{u}_b\otimes\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_b)\cdot abla W_{ab}V_b,\ abla\cdot\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_a&=\sum_b(\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_b-\widehat{\mathbf{u}}_a)\cdot abla W_{ab}V_b.\end{aligned} \]

The dots retain the pressure, viscous and body-force contributions outside the displayed ALE correction. The tensor product is denoted by \(\otimes\). The workshop associates the symmetric density-flux term with mass conservation and the symmetric momentum-flux term with linear-momentum conservation, while explicitly distinguishing angular momentum. These properties concern the stated operators; they do not establish exact volume conservation or conservation of every quantity for arbitrary boundaries, finite resolution or a separately selected non-conservative pressure operator.

The wave study below reports improved volume conservation with Advanced Shifting plus ALE relative to standard shifting under its test conditions. It does not provide a universal stability or accuracy guarantee.

docs.title: Non-conservative pressure formulation
docs.text:
The optional pressure treatment uses a corrected pressure-difference gradient for interior fluid particles and retains a symmetric pressure sum near the free surface. In the XML Guide's notation,

\[ \begin{aligned}\frac{D\mathbf{v}_a}{Dt}&=-\frac{1}{\rho_a}\sum_b f(p_a,p_b)\nabla_a W_{ab}V_b+\mathbf{f}_a+\boldsymbol{\Pi}_a,\\f(p_a,p_b)&=\begin{cases}p_a+p_b,&a\in\Omega_F\cup\Omega_{NF},\\(p_b-p_a)\mathbf{L}_a,&a\in\Omega_I.\end{cases}\end{aligned} \]

Here \(\mathbf{v}\) denotes the same material velocity as \(\mathbf{u}\) above, and lower-case \(p\) denotes pressure. \(\Omega_F\), \(\Omega_{NF}\) and \(\Omega_I\) identify free-surface, near-free-surface and interior particles. In the interior branch, the matrix acts on the kernel gradient; the near-surface branch is the scalar symmetric pressure sum. \(\boldsymbol{\Pi}_a\) collects the viscous contribution in this source notation, and \(\mathbf{f}_a\) denotes body-force acceleration. The pressure expression does not replace separate ALE transport corrections.

The corrected interior operator improves first-order consistency in the documented formulation, but it is non-conservative. The implementation also checks particle classification and neighbourhood support before using its interior correction; selecting the option does not force that operator at an under-supported free surface.

The workshop's documented configuration combines non-conservative pressure with Advanced Shifting and ALE. Use Shifting=4, ShiftAdvALE=Y and ShiftAdvNCPress=Y for that combined configuration. The current reader stores the ALE and pressure flags independently and does not reject every ALE=N, NCPress=Y combination. Reader acceptance alone therefore does not establish the documented combination or its numerical suitability.

docs.title: XML hierarchy and parameter reference
docs.text:
The controls belong in case/execution/parameters as parameter elements. There is no dedicated ShiftingAdv XML wrapper. The standard/local configuration under case/execution/special/shifting belongs to another implementation: the current reader rejects its combination with Advanced Shifting, so its shiftingzone, coefficient and fsthreshold elements must not be copied into an advanced example.

Parameter v6 values / documented default Interpretation Shifting Numeric 0–4; default 0 Select 4 for Advanced Shifting ShiftAdvCoef Default −0.01 Dimensionless advanced coefficient; assess the source case's choice ShiftAdvALE Y / N; default N ALE corrective terms for Advanced Shifting ShiftAdvNCPress Y / N; default N Non-conservative pressure for Advanced Shifting StepAlgorithm SYM / VER; default SYM Advanced Shifting requires Symplectic; Verlet is rejected

Use the exact names ShiftAdvALE and ShiftAdvNCPress. Older documentation uses numeric 1/0 switches; the current v6 format uses Y/N. This four-parameter configuration retains the original XML Guide's selection of ALE and non-conservative pressure with coefficient −0.01, using the current format and the same settings in the non-conservative wave example.

XML excerpt — combined activation. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Current supporting case: examples/shiftingadv/04_WavesDampingNC/CasePistonDampingAdvALENC_Def.xml. Retain its complete case configuration.

<parameter key="ShiftAdvCoef" value="-0.01" comment="Coefficient for advanced shifting computation (default=-0.01)" />
<parameter key="ShiftAdvALE" value="Y" comment="ALE formulation for advanced shifting: Y/N (default=N)" />
<parameter key="ShiftAdvNCPress" value="Y" comment="Non conservative pressure formulation for advanced shifting: Y/N (default=N)" />

docs.title: Standard controls retained in complete cases
docs.text:
ShiftCoef and ShiftTFS configure standard shifting, not the advanced coefficient or advanced surface detection. A migrated case may retain both standard and advanced parameters. Their presence is not evidence that both algorithms operate simultaneously. The standard wave configuration uses this independent selection:

XML excerpt — standard-wave-shifting. XML location: case/execution/parameters. Source: examples/shiftingadv/01_WavesDamping/CasePistonDampingSkillen_Def.xml. This selection requires the surrounding source case and its other settings.

<parameter key="Shifting" value="3" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full, 4:Full advanced (default=0)" />
<parameter key="ShiftCoef" value="-2" comment="Coefficient for standard shifting computation (default=-2)" />
<parameter key="ShiftTFS" value="1.5" comment="Threshold to detect free surface. Typically 1.5 for 2D and 2.75 for 3D (default=0)" />

Its threshold 1.5 is a 2D source-case setting. The 3D standard dam-break case uses 2.75. Neither threshold becomes an Advanced Shifting surface-detection control.

docs.title: Practical configurations
docs.text: Each excerpt is a selection from one actual case. Keep its geometry, boundary normals, motion/input files, wave generation, damping and solver settings together. None of the selections constitutes a standalone executable case or a newly combined configuration.

                    <waveorder value="2" comment="Order wave generation 1:1st order, 2:2nd order (def=1)" />
                    <start value="0" comment="Start time (def=0)" />

<parameter key="Shifting" value="0" comment="Shifting mode 0:None, 1:Ignore bound, 2:Ignore fixed, 3:Full, 4:Full advanced (default=0)" />
Current family / input dp (m) h/dp Shifting ALE NC pressure 01_WavesDamping/CasePistonDampingSkillen_Def.xml 0.015 2 3 N N 01_WavesDamping/CasePistonDampingAdvALE_Def.xml 0.015 2 4 Y N 02_Sloshing/CaseSloshingSkillen_Def.xml 0.002 2 3 N N 02_Sloshing/CaseSloshingAdvALE_Def.xml 0.002 2 4 Y N 03_Dambreak/CaseDamBreak3D_Def.xml 0.02 1.5 3 N N 03_Dambreak/CaseDamBreak3DAdvALE_Def.xml 0.02 1.5 4 Y N 04_WavesDampingNC/CasePistonDamping_Def.xml 0.03 1.3 0 N N 04_WavesDampingNC/CasePistonDampingAdvALENC_Def.xml 0.03 1.3 4 Y Y

These are the source inputs' choices. They do not establish equivalence between configurations or that changing only a shifting selector would reproduce a published result.

The third absolute particle spacing printed in the workshop setup, 0.075 m, is inconsistent with its ordered resolution series and the stated 20 particles per wave height. That spacing should not be adopted as a verified recipe or silently replaced by a guessed value.

A smaller h/dp changes neighbour support and must be assessed with the selected kernel, resolution and pressure treatment.

docs.title: Solid boundaries and mDBC
docs.text: Free-surface normals are reconstructed from the fluid neighbourhood. mDBC normals instead encode the geometry between solid boundary particles and the physical wall. Advanced Shifting neither generates those wall normals nor changes a selected slip condition. The wave and sloshing inputs use SlipMode=NS; the dam-break pair uses M22. Preserve each configuration. See the mDBC XML Guide for its geometry and boundary settings.

docs.title: Inlet/Outlet
docs.text: Open-boundary buffer particles have their own imposed or reconstructed kinematics. The current corrector restores their zone-prescribed motion after the ordinary shift contribution is formed. The interior-fluid displacement rule must not be read as an instruction to shift buffer particles independently of their inlet/outlet treatment. See Inlet/Outlet. These implementation relationships do not certify every possible combination of shifting and open-boundary options.

docs.title: Variable resolution
docs.text: The variable-resolution workshop specifically recommends Advanced Shifting for its wave examples. The non-conservative pressure discussion emphasises corrected interior consistency when resolution varies. Advanced Shifting, ALE, pressure discretisation and refinement geometry remain separate modelling choices; none replaces a valid refinement/buffer arrangement. See Variable resolution for its domain hierarchy and case-specific settings. A successful XML read alone cannot establish numerical suitability across an interface.

docs.title: Review of a selected configuration
docs.text: Assess particle distribution, free-surface position, conservation behaviour and resolution under the intended loading. Keep shifting strength, integration, kernel support and boundary treatment consistent with the selected case. The source comparisons do not establish physical validation, long-time stability or a universal error reduction for all simulations. Structural dynamics and other regularisation methods retain their independent numerical settings.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The formulation and implementation discussion draws on the DualSPHysics Advanced Shifting XML Guide (March 2025) and the 8th DualSPHysics Workshop presentation on ALE-SPH and non-conservative pressure (2026).

  • Skillen et al. (2013), the standard-shifting formulation cited in the DualSPHysics implementation, Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering. DOI.
  • Marrone et al. (2010), Fast free-surface detection and level-set function definition in SPH solvers, Journal of Computational Physics 229, 3652–3663.
  • Oger et al. (2016), SPH accuracy improvement through the combination of a quasi-Lagrangian shifting transport velocity and consistent ALE formalisms, Journal of Computational Physics 313, 76–98.
